verseByVerse.quote: And he rose and immediately picked up his bed and went out before them all, so that they were all amazed and glorified God, saying, "We never saw anything like this!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man got up, immediately picked up his mat and walked out in front of them all. Everyone was amazed and glorified God, saying: we never saw anything like this!

And he rose and immediately picked up his bed and went out before them all. The crowd that had blocked his way in now parted to let him walk out, carrying the mat that had carried him.

So that they were all amazed and glorified God. Praise to God, the right response.

Saying, “We never saw anything like this!” Something new had come: God’s forgiveness and God’s healing power, present in a man.

In a sentence. The healed man walked out carrying his mat, and the crowd praised God, saying they had never seen anything like it.

For worship. Glorify God, who forgives sins and heals in Jesus.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–22 — Levi, Sinners, and New Wine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Out again (vv. 13–14). Jesus leaves the house, teaches by the lake, and walks past a customs post. Sitting in it is Levi son of Alphaeus, a Jew collecting money for the occupying power, and the two words Follow me end his career in the time it takes to say them.

The dinner (vv. 15–17). Levi's first recorded act as a disciple is to throw a party for his own disreputable network and put Jesus at the centre of it. The scribes of the Pharisees do not challenge Jesus; they go at him through his followers. His answer is one sentence about a doctor, and it sorts the human race into two categories with no third.

The fasting question (vv. 18–20). Why do John's disciples fast and yours do not? Jesus answers with a wedding, quietly takes for himself a role the Old Testament gives to God alone, and in the same breath drops the first shadow of the cross into the Gospel.

Cloth and wineskins (vv. 21–22). Two pictures from ordinary domestic life make one uncomfortable point: what he has brought cannot be sewn onto what you already have.
verseByVerse.theology:
The two little parables of vv. 21–22 are the theological hinge of the chapter, and they are more radical than they look. An unshrunk patch on an old garment does not merely fail; when it is first washed it shrinks, grips, and pulls away, and the tear is worse than it was before the repair. New wine still working gives off gas; a skin that has already stretched once and gone brittle will split. In both pictures the old thing is not attacked. It is simply asked to contain something it was never built to hold, and it fails.

Jesus is not offering a reformed Judaism, and he is not offering a reformed you. Religion, as everyone naturally practises it, is patchwork — an addition to a self that stays fundamentally in charge. That, he says, does not produce a better garment; it produces a worse tear, which is exactly why adding a little Christianity to an unchanged life so often makes a person more miserable rather than less.

And then the promise at the end, which is easy to read past: new wine is for fresh wineskins. He supplies the skin as well as the wine. I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you (Ezek. 36:26); if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation (2 Cor. 5:17). He did not come to mend you. That is worse news, and far better news, than mending.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Levi cannot yet explain a doctrine, so he cooks. He gathers the only people he knows — the ones no synagogue wanted — and gets them into a room with Jesus.

Now: the newest Christian in your church, six weeks old in the faith, still knows every person from the old life; the man who has been converted thirty years often knows nobody outside the church at all. Levi's method needs no training course. Buy the food, make the call, and be in the room.

The harder half of the example is the one people skip. Jesus went to that table as the physician, not as a patient, and nobody left it unchanged — Levi, who had already left his booth to follow him, did not go back, and the meal did not end with Jesus agreeing with the guests. Both errors are live. One keeps a safe distance and calls it holiness; the other sits down at every table, says nothing about Christ for fifteen years, and calls it grace. The Pharisees would not go in. Jesus went in, and went in as himself.

verseByVerse.quote: He went out again beside the sea, and all the crowd was coming to him, and he was teaching them. And as he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, "Follow me." And he rose and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus went out again beside the lake. The whole crowd came to him, and he taught them. As he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth, and said to him: follow me. And he rose and followed him.

He went out again beside the sea, and all the crowd was coming to him, and he was teaching them. Teaching remains his priority.

And as he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth. Levi is called Matthew in the first Gospel (Matthew 9:9; 10:3). His tax booth was probably on the main road near Capernaum, collecting customs on goods passing between the territories of Herod Antipas and Philip.

Tax collectors. They were despised by fellow Jews for working for the ruling powers, for often cheating and overcharging, and for their contact with Gentiles, which made them ritually unclean. They were classed with sinners and prostitutes, and could not serve as witnesses in court.

And he said to him, “Follow me.” The same call as to the fishermen (1:17). Jesus calls a man everyone else despised.

And he rose and followed him. A fisherman could go back to fishing; a tax collector who walked away from his post could not easily get it back. Levi gave up a profitable career.

In a sentence. Jesus called Levi, a despised tax collector, from his booth, and he got up and followed him.

On a Tuesday. No one is too compromised for Jesus to call. Who have you written off?
verseByVerse.note: Tax collectors gathered tolls for the ruling authorities and were widely despised as collaborators and cheats.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he reclined at table in his house, many tax collectors and sinners were reclining with Jesus and his disciples, for there were many who followed him. And the scribes of the Pharisees, when they saw that he was eating with sinners and tax collectors, said to his disciples, "Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus reclined at table in Levi’s house, many tax collectors and sinners were eating with him and his disciples, for there were many who followed him. When the scribes of the Pharisees saw him eating with sinners and tax collectors, they asked his disciples: why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?

And as he reclined at table in his house. Levi’s house (Luke 5:29). At a formal meal guests reclined on couches around a low table, leaning on one elbow.

Many tax collectors and sinners were reclining with Jesus and his disciples. Levi invited his friends: other tax collectors and “sinners”, people known for immoral lives or for not keeping the law as the Pharisees did. His first act as a disciple was to introduce his friends to Jesus.

For there were many who followed him.

And the scribes of the Pharisees. Scribes who belonged to the party of the Pharisees (“separated ones”), a movement devoted to strict keeping of the law and its traditions, including purity rules about food and table fellowship.

Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners? In that culture, sharing a meal meant acceptance and friendship. The Pharisees avoided eating with sinners to keep themselves pure. Jesus ate with them.

In a sentence. Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners at Levi’s house, and the Pharisees’ scribes objected.

On a Tuesday. When did you last share a meal with someone others look down on?
verseByVerse.note: At a formal meal guests lay on couches around a low table, leaning on one elbow — hence “reclined.” “Sinners” here means people known for ignoring the law.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus heard it, he said to them, "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus heard it, he said: those who are well have no need of a doctor, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.

Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. A proverb. Doctors go to the sick. Jesus came as a doctor for sin-sick souls. And his holiness is not contaminated by sinners; it heals them.

I came not to call the righteous, but sinners. “The righteous” are those who think they are righteous, like the Pharisees, and so see no need of him. In truth, no one is righteous (Romans 3:10). Jesus calls those who know they are sick. Luke adds: to repentance (Luke 5:32).

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus approved of sin, or that Christians should join in it to reach people. Jesus went among sinners as a doctor, to call them to repentance. Nor were the Pharisees truly healthy; Jesus speaks with irony.

In a sentence. Jesus answered that, like a doctor going to the sick, he came to call sinners, not those who think themselves righteous.

On a Tuesday. Do you know yourself to be one of the sick whom Jesus came to heal? That is the only qualification for his call.

parallels.desc: “to seek and to save the lost”

verseByVerse.quote: Now John's disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. And people came and said to him, "Why do John's disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?" And Jesus said to them, "Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast. The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in that day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. People came and asked Jesus: why do John’s disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not? Jesus said: can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in that day.

Now John’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. Perhaps on one of the regular fast days; Pharisees fasted twice a week (Luke 18:12). The only fast required by the law was on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29).

Why do John’s disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast? Fasting was a sign of devotion and of mourning. Jesus’ disciples seemed less devout.

Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? A Jewish wedding lasted up to a week, a time of feasting and joy. Wedding guests were excused from fasting. Jesus is the bridegroom. In the Old Testament, God is the husband of his people (Isaiah 54:5; 62:5; Hosea 2:19–20). Jesus takes God’s role. His presence is a time of joy, not mourning.

The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them. “Taken away” suggests violent removal: Jesus’ first hint in Mark of his death.

And then they will fast in that day. After his departure, his disciples will fast (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23).

In a sentence. Jesus explained that his disciples did not fast because the bridegroom was with them, but they would fast when he was taken away.

On a Tuesday. Is your Christian life marked by joy in Christ’s presence? Fasting has its place, but the bridegroom has come.
verseByVerse.note: A wedding lasted days and was no time for fasting.

parallels.desc: the one yearly fast the law commanded
a Pharisee who fasted twice a week

verseByVerse.quote: No one sews a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. If he does, the patch tears away from it, the new from the old, and a worse tear is made. And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the wine will burst the skins—and the wine is destroyed, and so are the skins. But new wine is for fresh wineskins."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one sews a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, or the patch tears away from it, new from old, and a worse tear is made. And no one puts new wine into old wineskins, or the wine will burst the skins and both are lost. New wine is for fresh wineskins.

No one sews a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. New cloth shrinks when washed. Sewn onto an old garment, it pulls and tears it, making the hole worse.

And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. Wineskins were goatskins. New wine is still fermenting and expanding. An old skin has become stiff and brittle, and will burst.

But new wine is for fresh wineskins. The new life Jesus brings cannot simply be patched onto the old system of Pharisaic religion, with its traditions, fasts and purity rules. The joy and freedom of the kingdom need new forms.

What it does not mean. Not that the Old Testament is worthless. Jesus fulfils it (Matthew 5:17). The “old garments” and “old wineskins” are the human traditions of the religious system, not God’s word itself.

In a sentence. The new life Jesus brings cannot be patched onto the old religious system; it needs new forms.

On a Tuesday. Are there human traditions you cling to that hinder the new life of the gospel?
verseByVerse.note: Wineskins were goatskins. New wine is still fermenting and expanding; an old skin has lost its stretch and splits.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The field (vv. 23–24). The disciples walk through standing grain on a Sabbath, pulling heads off as they go and rubbing them in their hands. The Law explicitly allowed this; the Pharisees are not accusing them of theft. They are counting it as harvesting, threshing and winnowing — three of the thirty-nine categories of forbidden work, in one mouthful of wheat. And somebody had to be out in that field, on a Sabbath, watching.

The precedent (vv. 25–26). Jesus answers with a story rather than a ruling: David, hungry and on the run, eating the consecrated bread that only priests were permitted to eat, and Scripture recording not a word against him. The parallel is not simply that need outranks regulation. It is that a king travelling in rejection with his men has been here before.

The verdict (vv. 27–28). Two sentences that reset everything. The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath — the day is a gift, and they had turned it into a scoring system. And then: the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath. The Giver is standing in the cornfield being told off for letting hungry men eat.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath (v. 28) is a claim of breathtaking scope, and it is easy to miss how far it reaches. The Sabbath is not a national custom that a rabbi might reinterpret. It is stitched into the fabric of creation — God rested on the seventh day and made it holy before there was an Israel, a Sinai or a Jew (Gen. 2:2–3) — and it was afterwards written into the covenant by the finger of God (Exod. 20:8–11). To be lord of it is to be lord of the created order and of the covenant together.

And the day was always pointing past itself. Israel entered the land and never really entered the rest; centuries later Scripture can still say there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God (Heb. 4:9). Every seventh evening for fifteen hundred years the nation rehearsed a rest it did not yet possess.

Put Mark's two sentences side by side and see what has happened. The Sabbath was made for man — so it is a gift. And the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath — so the Giver is standing in the field. The rest the day rehearsed turns out not to be a square on a calendar but a Person, and he is the one being scolded. They were defending the gift against the Giver.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: hungry men pulling grain on a walk, and religious experts who had positioned themselves in a cornfield on a Sabbath in order to observe an infringement.

Now: the same instinct wherever the keeping of a form has become more important than the person the form was given to serve — the church where a visitor's clothes are noticed before his face is, the family where the standard is enforced and the child is not enjoyed. The institution that crushes the person it was designed to serve has inverted its own purpose, and it usually does so while feeling unusually devout.

The practical half of the day is worth taking as seriously as the doctrine of it. A modern reader does not break the Sabbath by working in a field; he breaks it by never stopping — by carrying the office in his pocket to bed. Stopping for a day feels like negligence, and it exposes precisely what a man believes about who is holding the world together. It keeps turning without you. That is the humiliation, and it is also the rest.

verseByVerse.quote: One Sabbath he was going through the grainfields, and as they made their way, his disciples began to pluck heads of grain. And the Pharisees were saying to him, "Look, why are they doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
One Sabbath Jesus was going through the grainfields, and as they made their way his disciples began to pick heads of grain. The Pharisees said to him: look, why are they doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath?

One Sabbath he was going through the grainfields. The Sabbath was the seventh day, Saturday, when God commanded rest from work, remembering creation and the exodus (Exodus 20:8–11; Deuteronomy 5:12–15). It was the sign of the covenant with Israel (Exodus 31:13).

And as they made their way, his disciples began to pluck heads of grain. The law allowed travellers to pick grain by hand from a neighbour’s field (Deuteronomy 23:25). The issue was the day.

Why are they doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath? The Pharisees’ traditions listed thirty-nine kinds of forbidden work, including reaping and threshing. Picking and rubbing grain counted as both.

In a sentence. The Pharisees accused Jesus’ disciples of breaking the Sabbath by picking grain as they walked.

On a Tuesday. Do you judge others by rules that are yours, not God’s?
verseByVerse.note: The objection was that plucking counted as harvesting, which was work.

parallels.desc: picking grain by hand was allowed

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Have you never read what David did, when he was in need and was hungry, he and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God, in the time of Abiathar the high priest, and ate the bread of the Presence, which it is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those who were with him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: have you never read what David did when he was in need and hungry, he and those with him: how he entered the house of God in the time of Abiathar the high priest and ate the bread of the Presence, which only the priests may eat, and also gave it to those with him?

Have you never read what David did. 1 Samuel 21:1–6. David, fleeing from Saul, came to the tabernacle at Nob and was given the holy bread by the priest.

When he was in need and was hungry. Human need.

In the time of Abiathar the high priest. 1 Samuel 21 names the priest as Ahimelech, Abiathar’s father. Abiathar was there (he escaped the massacre that followed, 1 Samuel 22:20), and later became the more famous high priest under David. Possible explanations: “in the time of Abiathar” means in the days of Abiathar, who was a priest then and became the better-known high priest, as we might say “in the days of King David” about events before he was king; or “at the passage about Abiathar”, referring to the section of Scripture by its best-known character (Jesus uses a similar phrase in 12:26, “in the passage about the bush”); or the names were sometimes interchanged (2 Samuel 8:17 and 1 Chronicles 18:16 have Ahimelech son of Abiathar). Verdict: no error; the phrase identifies the period or passage by its most famous priest.

And ate the bread of the Presence, which it is not lawful for any but the priests to eat. Twelve loaves placed before the LORD each Sabbath, and afterwards eaten by priests only (Leviticus 24:5–9).

And also gave it to those who were with him? David and his men ate holy bread, breaking a ceremonial law, and Scripture does not condemn them.

The argument. Human need takes priority over ceremonial rules. And David was God’s anointed; Jesus is the greater Son of David. If David’s men could eat, how much more Jesus’ disciples.

In a sentence. Jesus pointed to David eating the holy bread to show that ceremonial rules give way to need, especially for God’s anointed and his companions.

On a Tuesday. God’s laws are for our good. Rules that hurt people in need may show that we have misunderstood his purpose.
verseByVerse.note: On the name Abiathar (1 Samuel 21 names the priest Ahimelech), see the commentary.

parallels.desc: the bread of the Presence, eaten by priests

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.

The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Only Mark records this saying. God gave the Sabbath as a gift: rest for weary people, a day to delight in God (Isaiah 58:13–14; Exodus 23:12). The Pharisees had turned it into a burden, as if people existed to serve the rules. God made the day to serve people’s good.

So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath. The climax. The Sabbath was the LORD’s day (Exodus 20:10). Jesus claims authority over it: the right to say what it means and how it should be kept. Only God could make this claim.

The Sabbath and Christ. The Sabbath pointed forward to the rest Jesus gives (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10). After his resurrection on the first day of the week, Christians gathered on that day, the Lord’s Day (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10).

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath today. Some keep Saturday as the Sabbath; many Reformed Christians keep Sunday as the Christian Sabbath (Westminster Confession 21.7–8); others hold that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, so that no day is binding as a Sabbath (Colossians 2:16–17; Romans 14:5–6), while Sunday is the Lord’s Day for gathering. Verdict: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our true rest; the Lord’s Day is a privilege and gift, not a burden of rules. Believers who keep a stricter Sabbath should not be judged.

What it does not mean. Not that people may do whatever they like with God’s gifts. The Sabbath serves human good as God defines it, which includes worship and rest. Nor does “made for man” mean that our wishes override God’s commands.

In a sentence. God made the Sabbath as a gift for human good, and Jesus, the Son of Man, is Lord over it.

On a Tuesday. How do you use the Lord’s Day? As a gift for worship, rest and doing good, or as a day like any other?

2.theology:
Chapter 2 opens the conflict that ends at the cross. The scribes and Pharisees are not villains in a simple morality tale — they are serious people defending serious religious commitments, and on the doctrine of forgiveness they are exactly right. Their error is not that they take the law too seriously; it is that they have not recognised the one the law was pointing to. When the fulfilment arrives, the categories built to anticipate it can no longer contain it, which is precisely the burden of the new wine and the old skins.

Four demonstrations, then, of why Jesus could not simply be absorbed into the religious system as constituted: he forgives sins directly rather than through the temple; he receives the excluded at his own table rather than at the end of a purification process; he calls his own presence a wedding rather than a fast; and he claims lordship over the creation ordinance of the Sabbath itself. Not because he is lawless, but because he is the law's Lord.
2.examples:
The Pharisees' discomfort at Jesus eating with sinners deserves sympathetic treatment before it receives critique. Their instinct toward purity was not irrational; it was a serious attempt to guard the holiness God had commanded, in a land under pagan occupation where the pressure to blur every line was constant. Their error was a category error: they had equated association with endorsement. Jesus's presence among sinners was not approval of their sin but the physician's presence among the sick, and the cure requires proximity. The model is the incarnation itself — the holy God does not deal with human ruin from a safe distance but comes into it to heal from within, and finally takes the disease into his own body on a cross.

Then: Pharisees keeping a careful distance in order to stay clean, while the one man in Capernaum who actually was clean reclined at a tax collector's table. Now: any form of Christianity that has quietly confused holiness with non-exposure — and, on the other side, any form of it that sits down at every table and never says who it came with.

3.title: By Whose Power?
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Again he entered the synagogue, and a man was there with a withered hand. <sup>2</sup>And they watched Jesus, to see whether he would heal him on the Sabbath, so that they might accuse him. <sup>3</sup>And he said to the man with the withered hand, “Come here.” <sup>4</sup>And he said to them, “Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill?” But they were silent. <sup>5</sup>And he looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart, and said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out, and his hand was restored. <sup>6</sup>The Pharisees went out and immediately held counsel with the Herodians against him, how to destroy him. <sup>7</sup>Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the sea, and a great crowd followed, from Galilee and Judea <sup>8</sup>and Jerusalem and Idumea and from beyond the Jordan and from around Tyre and Sidon. When the great crowd heard all that he was doing, they came to him. <sup>9</sup>And he told his disciples to have a boat ready for him because of the crowd, lest they crush him, <sup>10</sup>for he had healed many, so that all who had diseases pressed around him to touch him. <sup>11</sup>And whenever the unclean spirits saw him, they fell down before him and cried out, “You are the Son of God.” <sup>12</sup>And he strictly ordered them not to make him known. <sup>13</sup>And he went up on the mountain and called to him those whom he desired, and they came to him. <sup>14</sup>And he appointed twelve (whom he also named apostles) so that they might be with him and he might send them out to preach <sup>15</sup>and have authority to cast out demons. <sup>16</sup>He appointed the twelve: Simon (to whom he gave the name Peter); <sup>17</sup>James the son of Zebedee and John the brother of James (to whom he gave the name Boanerges, that is, Sons of Thunder); <sup>18</sup>Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus, and Simon the Zealot, <sup>19</sup>and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him. <sup>20</sup>Then he went home, and the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat. <sup>21</sup>And when his family heard it, they went out to seize him, for they were saying, “He is out of his mind.” <sup>22</sup>And the scribes who came down from Jerusalem were saying, “He is possessed by Beelzebul,” and “by the prince of demons he casts out the demons.” <sup>23</sup>And he called them to him and said to them in parables, “How can Satan cast out Satan? <sup>24</sup>If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. <sup>25</sup>And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand. <sup>26</sup>And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand, but is coming to an end. <sup>27</sup>But no one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man. Then indeed he may plunder his house. <sup>28</sup>“Truly, I say to you, all sins will be forgiven the children of man, and whatever blasphemies they utter, <sup>29</sup>but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin”— <sup>30</sup>for they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit.” <sup>31</sup>And his mother and his brothers came, and standing outside they sent to him and called him. <sup>32</sup>And a crowd was sitting around him, and they said to him, “Your mother and your brothers are outside, seeking you.” <sup>33</sup>And he answered them, “Who are my mother and my brothers?” <sup>34</sup>And looking about at those who sat around him, he said, “Here are my mother and my brothers! <sup>35</sup>For whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother.”
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is where the opposition hardens into a decision and the alternative community is formed. It opens with a trap in a synagogue and closes with a redefinition of family, and between the two everything about Jesus is contested. The Pharisees and Herodians — parties who agreed on nothing — walk out of a Sabbath service together to plan his death (v. 6). His own family concludes he is out of his mind and comes to take him home (v. 21). A delegation of scribes travels ninety miles from Jerusalem and pronounces him possessed (v. 22). Three verdicts, and all of them wrong.

Against that, Jesus does two constructive things. He appoints twelve men — a number no Jew could hear innocently — so that they might be with him and be sent out (vv. 13–15); and he tells the room what the kingdom actually is: a break-in. A stronger man has entered the strong man's house, tied him up, and is carrying out his property (v. 27). Every healing and deliverance in this Gospel is loot from that raid. The chapter ends by naming who now belongs to him, and the criterion is neither blood nor pedigree but doing the will of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Withered Hand and the Widening Response
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The trap (vv. 1–2). Jesus walks into a synagogue where two things are waiting for him: a man with a ruined hand, and a row of men watching to see whether he will touch it. They are not curious. They are collecting evidence.

The question nobody would answer (vv. 3–4). He puts the man in the middle of the room and asks whether the Sabbath is for doing good or doing harm, saving life or killing. It is unanswerable, and they know it, so they say nothing.

The anger (v. 5). The one place in Mark where Jesus is said to look on people with anger — and in the same breath, grieved. Then a command to a man who cannot obey it, and a hand made new.

The verdict (v. 6). Two parties who despised each other walk out together to plan a murder, and it is still the Sabbath.

The crowds (vv. 7–12). He withdraws, and a hundred-mile radius follows him to the shore. He asks for a boat to keep from being crushed, and silences the only voices in the crowd that know exactly who he is.
verseByVerse.theology:
Verses 11–12 raise a question every attentive reader hits sooner or later: the demons keep saying true things about Jesus, and he keeps shutting them up. Why refuse free advertising from witnesses who cannot be wrong?

Two reasons converge, and the second is the one that touches the reader. The first is timing. In Galilee in that decade, to be publicly proclaimed Son of God meant one thing to a crowd — a nationalist king who would clear out the Romans. Jesus refuses to be crowned before he is crucified, because a title accepted on those terms would have to be unlearned at the cross. He will let the word be said out loud when it can be defined by his death (15:39, on the lips of the officer at the foot of it).

The second is more searching. What the unclean spirits say is doctrinally perfect. You are the Son of God is exactly right, and it saves them from nothing. James makes the point without flinching: you believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe — and shudder (Jas. 2:19). A creed can be entirely correct and entirely worthless. The spirits here fall down before him, which is more than the scribes did, and confess his identity, which is more than the disciples had managed — and they remain what they are. Right belief about Christ is not the same as belonging to him, and this chapter will end by saying who does belong.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a man with a shrivelled hand told to stand up in the middle of a watched synagogue, before anything had been healed, in front of the men who had come to build a case.

Now: every act of obedience that makes a person visible and vulnerable before the outcome is assured — the first time you say in an office that you are a Christian; the apology you make with no guarantee it will be received; the sin confessed to one other believer when it could have stayed hidden for life. He was asked to be conspicuous first and healed second, and he had no way of knowing the order in advance.

And notice what the same scene did to the watchers. They had come to see whether a rule would be broken, and they saw a crippled man made whole, and it did not move them an inch. It is possible to sit in a room where God is plainly at work and be entirely occupied with whether it is being done properly.

verseByVerse.quote: Again he entered the synagogue, and a man was there with a withered hand. And they watched Jesus, to see whether he would heal him on the Sabbath, so that they might accuse him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again Jesus went into the synagogue, and a man was there with a withered hand. They watched Jesus closely to see whether he would heal him on the Sabbath, so that they could accuse him.

Again he entered the synagogue. The fifth of five conflict stories (2:1–3:6), and the second about the Sabbath.

And a man was there with a withered hand. Shrunken or paralysed. Luke says it was his right hand (Luke 6:6), so he probably could not work. His condition was not life-threatening. The rabbis allowed healing on the Sabbath only when life was in danger.

And they watched Jesus. “Watched” (paretēroun) means watched closely, spied on. They were not there to worship but to catch him.

To see whether he would heal him on the Sabbath, so that they might accuse him. They knew Jesus would heal. Their question was not whether he could, but whether he would break their rules, so they could bring a charge. They were using a disabled man as bait.

In a sentence. In the synagogue, Jesus’ opponents watched to see if he would heal a man’s withered hand on the Sabbath, so they could accuse him.

On a Tuesday. You can sit in a place of worship looking for others’ faults instead of looking for God. Examine your own heart when you gather.
verseByVerse.note: A “withered” hand is shrunken or paralysed. Healing a condition that was not life-threatening could wait a day — which is why they watched.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to the man with the withered hand, "Come here." And he said to them, "Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill?" But they were silent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to the man with the withered hand: come here. And he said to them: is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill? But they were silent.

And he said to the man with the withered hand, “Come here.” Literally “rise into the middle”. Jesus brings him out in front of everyone. He does not heal secretly to avoid trouble.

Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill? Jesus reframes the question. Not “what work is permitted?” but “what is the Sabbath for?” To refuse to do good when you can is to do harm. And the irony is sharp: Jesus is about to restore a life, while his opponents are already planning to kill (v. 6). Which is lawful on the Sabbath?

But they were silent. They could not answer without condemning themselves.

In a sentence. Jesus brought the man forward and asked whether the Sabbath is for doing good or harm, saving life or killing, and his opponents had no answer.

On a Tuesday. Failing to do good when you can is not neutral. What good could you do today, on a day you might think of as ordinary?

verseByVerse.quote: And he looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart, and said to the man, "Stretch out your hand." He stretched it out, and his hand was restored.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart, and said to the man: stretch out your hand. He stretched it out, and his hand was restored.

And he looked around at them with anger. Only Mark records Jesus’ anger here. Jesus felt real emotions. This was righteous anger: anger at cruelty, at religion that used people instead of loving them, at hearts that cared more about rules than a suffering man. God is angry at such things (Psalm 7:11).

Grieved at their hardness of heart. His anger was mixed with grief. “Hardness” (pōrōsei) means a callus, a stony insensitivity. They were not merely mistaken; their hearts were closed. Jesus grieved over them even as he was angry with them. Righteous anger is never without sorrow for the sinner.

And said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” A command he could not obey by his own strength. Jesus’ word gave the power to obey.

He stretched it out, and his hand was restored. Healed by a word. Jesus did no physical “work” at all. There was nothing to accuse him of except the healing itself.

What it does not mean. Not that all anger is righteous. Ours is usually mixed with pride (James 1:20). Jesus’ anger was pure: aimed at sin, mixed with grief, and followed by an act of mercy (see Ephesians 4:26).

In a sentence. Angry and grieved at their hard hearts, Jesus told the man to stretch out his hand, and it was restored.

On a Tuesday. When you are angry at sin, is your anger mixed with grief and followed by good, as Jesus’ was?
verseByVerse.note: Mark alone records Jesus’ anger and grief here; Matthew and Luke do not mention them.

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees went out and immediately held counsel with the Herodians against him, how to destroy him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees went out and immediately plotted with the Herodians against Jesus, how to destroy him.

The Pharisees went out. After the healing, not before.

And immediately held counsel with the Herodians against him. The Herodians were supporters of the family of Herod and of Herod Antipas’ rule, cooperating with Rome. The Pharisees disliked Herod and Rome. Normally they were enemies; now they unite against Jesus (12:13). Shared hatred makes strange allies.

How to destroy him. The first plot to kill Jesus in Mark, early in his ministry. On the Sabbath, the day for saving life, they plot death (v. 4). From here, the shadow of the cross falls across the Gospel.

In a sentence. The Pharisees immediately joined their political enemies, the Herodians, in plotting to kill Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Religion that loses love can become murderous. Guard your heart against religious pride.
verseByVerse.note: The Herodians were supporters of the Herod family’s rule — unlikely allies for the Pharisees.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the sea, and a great crowd followed, from Galilee and Judea and Jerusalem and Idumea and from beyond the Jordan and from around Tyre and Sidon. When the great crowd heard all that he was doing, they came to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the lake, and a great crowd followed, from Galilee, Judea, Jerusalem, Idumea, beyond the Jordan, and from around Tyre and Sidon. When they heard everything he was doing, they came to him.

Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the sea. Away from the synagogue and the plot.

And a great crowd followed, from Galilee and Judea and Jerusalem and Idumea and from beyond the Jordan and from around Tyre and Sidon. From every direction. Galilee in the north, Judea and Jerusalem in the south, Idumea (the ancient Edom) further south, the land east of the Jordan, and the Gentile coastal cities of Tyre and Sidon in the northwest. Almost the whole territory of ancient Israel, and beyond. Jews and Gentiles.

When the great crowd heard all that he was doing, they came to him. Many came for healing.

In a sentence. Jesus withdrew to the lake, and great crowds came from every region, Jewish and Gentile, having heard of his works.

On a Tuesday. As the leaders plotted against Jesus, the crowds came to him. Opposition does not stop people coming to Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Idumea (old Edom) lay south of Judea; Tyre and Sidon were Gentile port cities on the coast to the north. The crowd came from every direction.

verseByVerse.quote: And he told his disciples to have a boat ready for him because of the crowd, lest they crush him, for he had healed many, so that all who had diseases pressed around him to touch him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus told his disciples to have a small boat ready for him because of the crowd, so that they would not crush him. For he had healed many, so that all who had diseases pressed around him to touch him.

And he told his disciples to have a boat ready for him because of the crowd. A small boat, so he could step off the shore if the crowd pressed too hard, and teach from it (4:1).

Lest they crush him. The crowd was dangerous.

For he had healed many, so that all who had diseases pressed around him to touch him. “Diseases” (mastigas) literally means “whips” or “scourges”: afflictions. They believed touching him would heal them (5:27–29; 6:56).

In a sentence. The crowd seeking healing pressed so hard that Jesus had a boat ready in case they crushed him.

On a Tuesday. Many came to Jesus for what he could give them. Do you come for his gifts, or for him?

verseByVerse.quote: And whenever the unclean spirits saw him, they fell down before him and cried out, "You are the Son of God." And he strictly ordered them not to make him known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whenever the unclean spirits saw him, they fell down before him and cried out: you are the Son of God. And he strictly ordered them not to make him known.

And whenever the unclean spirits saw him, they fell down before him. Not in worship but in terror, acknowledging his authority.

And cried out, “You are the Son of God.” The demons know who he is (1:24, 34). It is the truth Mark announced in his first verse. But the people and even the disciples do not yet see it clearly.

And he strictly ordered them not to make him known. Jesus would not accept testimony from demons. And he would not have his identity broadcast before people understood that the Son of God must suffer (8:29–31). The “messianic secret” runs through Mark: his full identity will be revealed at the cross (15:39).

In a sentence. The demons fell before Jesus and called him the Son of God, but he ordered them to be silent.

On a Tuesday. The demons knew the truth about Jesus and remained his enemies. Knowing is not enough; trust him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–35 — The Twelve, the Accusation, and the True Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The mountain (vv. 13–19). Jesus goes up, calls whom he wants, and constitutes twelve men — a number nobody in Israel could hear innocently. The stated purpose comes in two halves in a deliberate order: that they might be with him, and that he might send them out. The list ends on a name that ruins it.

The two accusations (vv. 20–22). Back at the house the pressure is such that they cannot even eat, and two verdicts arrive from opposite directions. His family says he is out of his mind and comes to take him home. A delegation from Jerusalem says he is possessed and works by the prince of demons. Both agree something is badly wrong with him; they differ only on whether he is mad or evil.

The answer (vv. 23–27). Jesus takes the charge apart with cold logic and then turns it round: the reason demons are leaving is that a stronger man has broken into the house, tied up the owner, and is carrying out his property.

The warning and the family (vv. 28–35). The widest promise of forgiveness in the Gospel, with one terrible exception attached — and then his mother and brothers arrive outside, and he looks round at the people sitting on the floor and calls them his family.
verseByVerse.theology:
The strong man of v. 27 is the hinge of the chapter and of the Gospel. Jesus concedes the scribes' premise that there is a real kingdom of darkness with a real ruler and a securely held house. What he denies is which side of the door he is on. He is not an agent of the owner. He is the burglar.

And the order in the picture is exact: the binding comes first, the plundering after. You cannot carry off a strong man's goods while he is loose. Every exorcism in Mark, every healing, every sinner set free, is loot being carried out of a house whose owner has already been tied up. This is why the New Testament can speak of Christians as people delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son (Col. 1:13) — transferred is a word for moving property.

Then ask when the binding happened, and the answer is the surprise at the centre of the faith. He bound the strong man by being bound himself. He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, triumphing over them in him — in the cross (Col. 2:15). The strong man was tied up by a stronger man who let himself be tied up first, so that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death (Heb. 2:14).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twelve men appointed so that they might be with him — and only then be sent out. A long season of watching him pray, eat, weep, touch lepers, sleep in boats, before they were first sent out to preach (6:7-13).

Now: the order is still not negotiable, and it is still the thing we reverse. It is entirely possible to be extremely busy for God and scarcely ever with him — to run a rota, lead a group, defend the faith online, and go months without an unhurried hour in his company. The activity is not the problem; the sequence is. Ministry that does not flow out of being with Jesus becomes performance, and performance eventually becomes exhaustion or pride, and often both.

The plainest way to test it is the calendar. Look at last week honestly. How much of it was doing things for him, and how much was being with him? If the first number is large and the second is near zero, you have inverted verse 14, and no amount of usefulness will make up for it — because the sending was never meant to be the source of the strength.

And there is comfort in the same verse for the person who cannot do much at all: the first calling on every disciple is one that illness, age and obscurity cannot take away.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went up on the mountain and called to him those whom he desired, and they came to him. And he appointed twelve (whom he also named apostles) so that they might be with him and he might send them out to preach and have authority to cast out demons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus went up on the mountain and called to him those he wanted, and they came to him. He appointed twelve, whom he also named apostles, to be with him, and to send them out to preach and to have authority to cast out demons.

And he went up on the mountain. Mountains are places of revelation and covenant in Scripture: Sinai, where God formed Israel.

And called to him those whom he desired. Jesus’ choice, by his will. They did not volunteer; he chose them (John 15:16).

And he appointed twelve. Literally “he made twelve”. Twelve matches the twelve tribes of Israel. Jesus is forming a new Israel, the restored people of God, around himself.

Whom he also named apostles. “Apostle” means one who is sent, an envoy with the sender’s authority. (Some manuscripts omit this phrase here; it is certainly in Luke 6:13.)

So that they might be with him. The first purpose of the Twelve: to be with Jesus. Before they could be sent, they had to spend time with him, learning from him. Ministry flows from relationship.

And he might send them out to preach. The second purpose: mission, proclaiming the kingdom.

And have authority to cast out demons. Sharing his power over evil (6:7, 13).

In a sentence. On a mountain, Jesus chose twelve, to be with him and to be sent out to preach with authority over demons.

On a Tuesday. Before you serve Jesus, spend time with him. Service that does not flow from being with him runs dry.
verseByVerse.note: “Apostle” means one who is sent.

parallels.desc: the Twelve and the twelve tribes

verseByVerse.quote: He appointed the twelve: Simon (to whom he gave the name Peter); James the son of Zebedee and John the brother of James (to whom he gave the name Boanerges, that is, Sons of Thunder); Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus, and Simon the Zealot,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He appointed the twelve: Simon, whom he named Peter; James son of Zebedee and his brother John, whom he named Boanerges, that is, sons of thunder; Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot.

Simon (to whom he gave the name Peter). “Peter” (Petros) means “rock”. A new name meant a new identity and calling. Peter was impulsive and unstable at first; Jesus named him for what he would become.

James the son of Zebedee and John the brother of James (to whom he gave the name Boanerges, that is, Sons of Thunder). Only Mark records this nickname, from Aramaic. It probably described their fiery temperament: they once wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village (Luke 9:54). John, the “son of thunder”, became the apostle of love (1 John 4:7–21). Jesus transforms temperaments.

Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus. Bartholomew is probably Nathanael (John 1:45). Matthew is Levi, the tax collector (2:14). Thaddaeus is probably the “Judas son of James” of Luke 6:16.

And Simon the Zealot. Literally “the Cananaean”, from the Aramaic for “zealous”. He may have belonged to the Zealots, who wanted to overthrow Rome by force. Jesus placed a former Roman collaborator (Matthew) and a former anti-Roman revolutionary (Simon) in the same group. In his kingdom, enemies become brothers.

In a sentence. Jesus appointed twelve very different men, giving Peter and the sons of Zebedee new names that described what he would make of them.

On a Tuesday. Jesus puts very different people together in his church, and transforms their temperaments. Who in your church is very different from you? Love them as family.
verseByVerse.note: Peter means “rock.” Thaddaeus is probably the “Judas the son of James” of Luke’s lists.

verseByVerse.quote: and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him.

And Judas Iscariot. Always last in the lists. “Iscariot” is often taken to mean “man of Kerioth”, a town in southern Judea, which would make him the only one of the Twelve not from Galilee; but that is uncertain. Other suggestions link it to an Aramaic word for “false one”, or to a word for an assassin’s dagger.

Who betrayed him. Mark tells the reader from the start how the story will go. Jesus chose Judas knowingly (John 6:70). Judas shared everything: the teaching, the miracles, the mission. And still he betrayed him. Being close to Jesus, and even serving in his name, is not the same as belonging to him.

What it does not mean. Not that Judas was forced to betray Jesus. God’s plan included the betrayal (Acts 2:23), and Judas acted freely and was responsible (14:21).

In a sentence. The last of the Twelve was Judas Iscariot, the one who would betray Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Judas warns us that outward closeness to Jesus is not enough. Examine your heart.
verseByVerse.note: “Iscariot” is often taken to mean “man of Kerioth,” a town in Judea, but that is uncertain.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he went home, and the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat. And when his family heard it, they went out to seize him, for they were saying, "He is out of his mind."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jesus went home, and the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat. When his family heard it, they went out to seize him, for they were saying: he is out of his mind.

Then he went home. Probably to the house in Capernaum (2:1).

And the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat. The demands were relentless.

And when his family heard it, they went out to seize him. “His family” (literally “those beside him”) means his relatives. They came from Nazareth to take him home by force. Verse 31 shows that his mother and brothers were among them.

For they were saying, “He is out of his mind.” “Out of his mind” (exestē) means beside himself, mad. His family thought he had lost his senses: neglecting food, provoking the authorities, claiming divine authority. They probably meant well, trying to protect him and the family’s reputation. But they did not understand him. His brothers did not believe in him until after the resurrection (John 7:5; Acts 1:14).

The structure. Mark tells this story in two parts, with the accusation of the scribes sandwiched in between (vv. 22–30). His family thinks he is mad; the scribes say he is demon-possessed. Both are wrong. The sandwich invites comparison: his family’s misunderstanding, though less hostile, is uncomfortably close to the scribes’ rejection.

What it does not mean. Not that Mary had lost all faith. But she, too, struggled to understand her son’s mission (Luke 2:50). Mark shows honestly that even Jesus’ family did not grasp who he was.

In a sentence. When crowds kept Jesus from even eating, his family came to take him home, thinking he was out of his mind.

On a Tuesday. If your family thinks your devotion to Christ is excessive, remember that Jesus’ family thought the same about him. Keep loving them.
verseByVerse.note: “His family” means his relatives.

parallels.desc: even his brothers did not believe

verseByVerse.quote: And the scribes who came down from Jerusalem were saying, "He is possessed by Beelzebul," and "by the prince of demons he casts out the demons."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scribes who came down from Jerusalem said: he is possessed by Beelzebul, and he casts out the demons by the prince of demons.

And the scribes who came down from Jerusalem. An official delegation from the religious capital, sent to investigate. Jerusalem is high in the hills; people went “up” to it and “down” from it.

He is possessed by Beelzebul. “Beelzebul” is a name for Satan (v. 23), probably related to Baal-zebub, the god of the Philistine city of Ekron (2 Kings 1:2), meaning “lord of the flies”, or Baal-zebul, “lord of the dwelling”. They accuse Jesus of being in league with the devil.

And by the prince of demons he casts out the demons. They could not deny his exorcisms, so they explained them: he has Satan’s power, so he can command Satan’s underlings. It was the most serious charge possible, and a deliberate rejection of the evidence.

In a sentence. Scribes from Jerusalem claimed that Jesus was possessed by Satan and cast out demons by his power.

On a Tuesday. People who refuse to accept Jesus will find explanations for the evidence. Do you look for reasons to believe, or reasons to dismiss?
verseByVerse.note: Beelzebul is a name for Satan (v. 23).

verseByVerse.quote: And he called them to him and said to them in parables, "How can Satan cast out Satan? If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand. And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand, but is coming to an end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus called them and spoke to them in parables: how can Satan cast out Satan? If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. If a house is divided against itself, it will not be able to stand. And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand, but is coming to an end.

And he called them to him and said to them in parables. “Parables” here means picture-sayings, comparisons. Jesus answers his accusers directly.

How can Satan cast out Satan? The accusation is absurd. Why would Satan destroy his own work, freeing the people he has enslaved?

If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. Civil war destroys nations.

And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand. Division destroys families.

And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand, but is coming to an end. If Jesus were Satan’s agent, Satan would be destroying himself. But in fact Satan is coming to an end, not because he is divided, but because someone stronger has come (v. 27).

In a sentence. Jesus showed the accusation was absurd: if Satan cast out Satan, his kingdom would be destroying itself.

On a Tuesday. Division destroys. Guard the unity of your family and church.

verseByVerse.quote: But no one can enter a strong man's house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man. Then indeed he may plunder his house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But no one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man. Then indeed he may plunder his house.

But no one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods. The strong man is Satan. His house is the world, or the people he holds captive. His goods are the people under his power.

Unless he first binds the strong man. To rob a strong man, you must first overpower him and tie him up. Jesus is the one stronger than Satan. John the Baptist had called him the mightier one (1:7). Isaiah 49:24–25 asks whether the captives can be taken from the mighty, and promises that God will do it.

Then indeed he may plunder his house. Every exorcism, every healing, every sinner forgiven is Jesus plundering Satan’s house, freeing his captives. The binding began in the wilderness (1:12–13) and was completed at the cross (Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14–15).

What it does not mean. Not that Satan is now inactive. He still prowls (1 Peter 5:8). But he cannot stop the gospel or hold those whom Christ frees. Revelation 20:1–3 pictures Satan bound so he cannot deceive the nations; Reformed amillennialists see this binding as the present gospel age, begun at Christ’s first coming.

In a sentence. Jesus is the stronger one who has bound Satan and is now freeing his captives.

On a Tuesday. Whatever has bound you, Christ is stronger. Ask him to set you free.

For worship. Praise Christ, who bound the strong man and set you free.

parallels.desc: the prey taken from the mighty

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, I say to you, all sins will be forgiven the children of man, and whatever blasphemies they utter, but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin"— for they were saying, "He has an unclean spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, all sins will be forgiven the children of man, and whatever blasphemies they utter, but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin. For they were saying: he has an unclean spirit.

Truly, I say to you. A solemn statement of Jesus’ own authority.

All sins will be forgiven the children of man, and whatever blasphemies they utter. A great promise. No sin is too great to be forgiven if it is repented of. Paul was a blasphemer and was forgiven (1 Timothy 1:13).

But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin. What is this? Mark tells us in the next sentence.

For they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit.” The scribes saw the Holy Spirit’s work in Jesus clearly, and deliberately called it the work of Satan. This is blasphemy against the Spirit: not a careless word, but a settled, wilful rejection of the Spirit’s clear testimony to Christ, calling good evil. It is unforgivable not because God’s grace is too small, but because it rejects the only source of forgiveness. The Spirit is the one who convicts of sin and leads to Christ (John 16:8–11). A person who calls his work satanic has shut the door on the only way back.

What it does not mean. Many anxious Christians fear they have committed this sin. If you are worried that you have, you have not. Those who commit it do not care; they are hardened. Anxiety about offending God is itself a sign of the Spirit at work in you. Nor is it a single doubt, or a terrible sin committed in weakness, even a sin of the tongue. It is a settled rejection of Christ in the face of the Spirit’s clear witness.

In a sentence. Every sin can be forgiven except deliberately calling the Spirit’s clear work in Jesus satanic, as the scribes were doing.

On a Tuesday. If you fear you have committed the unforgivable sin, your fear shows you have not. Come to Christ; he will not turn you away (John 6:37).

verseByVerse.quote: And his mother and his brothers came, and standing outside they sent to him and called him. And a crowd was sitting around him, and they said to him, "Your mother and your brothers are outside, seeking you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
His mother and his brothers came, and standing outside they sent word to him and called him. A crowd was sitting around him, and they said to him: your mother and your brothers are outside, looking for you.

And his mother and his brothers came. The second half of the story begun in verse 21. They had come to take him home.

And standing outside they sent to him and called him. “Outside”: Mark emphasises it twice (vv. 31, 32). Physically and spiritually, they stood outside the circle around him.

And a crowd was sitting around him. Inside, listening to his teaching: the posture of disciples (Luke 10:39).

Your mother and your brothers are outside, seeking you. Jesus’ brothers were James, Joses, Judas and Simon (6:3), most naturally Mary’s later children.

In a sentence. Jesus’ mother and brothers stood outside and sent for him, while the crowd sat around him inside.

On a Tuesday. It is possible to be close to Jesus by family or background and still stand outside. Come in and sit at his feet.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered them, "Who are my mother and my brothers?" And looking about at those who sat around him, he said, "Here are my mother and my brothers! For whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered: who are my mother and my brothers? Looking at those who sat around him, he said: here are my mother and my brothers! Whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother.

Who are my mother and my brothers? A startling question in a culture where family was everything.

And looking about at those who sat around him. Only Mark mentions the look. Jesus looked around the circle, at each face.

Here are my mother and my brothers! Those who sit at his feet and listen are his true family.

For whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother. Membership in Jesus’ family is not by birth, but by doing God’s will: hearing his word, repenting, believing and obeying (1:15). Anyone may join. “Sister”: women are explicitly included. The church is a family.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus rejected his mother or family. He provided for his mother from the cross (John 19:26–27), and his brothers later came to faith. But blood ties are not the deepest ties. And this passage gives no support to devotion to Mary as an intercessor. Jesus pointed away from family to faith.

In a sentence. Jesus declared that those who do God’s will are his true family: his brothers, sisters and mother.

On a Tuesday. If you do God’s will, you are Jesus’ brother or sister. Who in your church family needs your care this week?

For worship. Thank Jesus that he is not ashamed to call you his brother or sister (Hebrews 2:11).

3.theology:
Two of the most-asked questions in Mark sit in this chapter, and both deserve a straight answer.

Was Jesus's anger sinful? No — and v. 5 shows how to tell, because it gives the anger and the grief in one breath. He looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart. Sinful anger wants the other person diminished and would be quietly disappointed by their repentance; righteous anger grieves, wants the wrong put right and the wrongdoer restored, and would be glad to be made unnecessary. Be angry and do not sin (Eph. 4:26) is a command with a boundary, not a contradiction.

What is the unforgivable sin? Mark answers it himself in v. 30 and the answer is anchored, not abstract: for they were saying, He has an unclean spirit. It is the settled, informed, deliberate attribution of the Holy Spirit's unmistakable work to Satan by men who have seen it with their own eyes and chosen their verdict. It is not a slip, a doubt, or a season of confusion. And the pastoral corollary is firm: the person terrified of having committed it has not, because the fear itself requires a conscience still responsive to the Spirit, and that is precisely what this sin destroys. The hardness that commits it does not tremble; it calculates.
3.examples:
The chapter's two great alliances are worth setting side by side, because they explain a great deal about churches.

Then: Pharisees and Herodians — strict separatists and worldly courtiers, men who despised each other on religion, politics and money — in a room together within minutes, agreeing perfectly on one thing: how to destroy him. Nothing on earth unites people like a shared hatred of the light. Pilate and Herod became friends the day Jesus was sent back and forth between them (Luke 23:12).

And then: Matthew the tax collector and Simon the Zealot on the same list of twelve, walking the same roads for three years. In any other year of the world, Simon's politics would have called for a knife in Matthew's ribs. Nothing reconciled them except the man in the middle.

Now: both are still in operation. A congregation can be welded together by what it is against, and it will feel like unity and it will not be. Or it can be a collection of people with nothing whatever in common except Christ — which is more than everything they had against each other. If your church contains people you would never otherwise have chosen, that is not a defect to be managed. It is the evidence.

4.title: Seed, Soil, and the Sleeping Lord
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Again he began to teach beside the sea. And a very large crowd gathered about him, so that he got into a boat and sat in it on the sea, and the whole crowd was beside the sea on the land. <sup>2</sup>And he was teaching them many things in parables, and in his teaching he said to them: <sup>3</sup>“Listen! Behold, a sower went out to sow. <sup>4</sup>And as he sowed, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured it. <sup>5</sup>Other seed fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil, and immediately it sprang up, since it had no depth of soil. <sup>6</sup>And when the sun rose, it was scorched, and since it had no root, it withered away. <sup>7</sup>Other seed fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it, and it yielded no grain. <sup>8</sup>And other seeds fell into good soil and produced grain, growing up and increasing and yielding thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold.” <sup>9</sup>And he said, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” <sup>10</sup>And when he was alone, those around him with the twelve asked him about the parables. <sup>11</sup>And he said to them, “To you has been given the secret of the kingdom of God, but for those outside everything is in parables, <sup>12</sup>so that they may indeed see but not perceive, and may indeed hear but not understand, lest they should turn and be forgiven.” <sup>13</sup>And he said to them, “Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables? <sup>14</sup>The sower sows the word. <sup>15</sup>And these are the ones along the path, where the word is sown: when they hear, Satan immediately comes and takes away the word that is sown in them. <sup>16</sup>And these are the ones sown on rocky ground: the ones who, when they hear the word, immediately receive it with joy. <sup>17</sup>And they have no root in themselves, but endure for a while; then, when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately they fall away. <sup>18</sup>And others are the ones sown among thorns. They are those who hear the word, <sup>19</sup>but the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches and the desires for other things enter in and choke the word, and it proves unfruitful. <sup>20</sup>But those that were sown on the good soil are the ones who hear the word and accept it and bear fruit, thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold.” <sup>21</sup>And he said to them, “Is a lamp brought in to be put under a basket, or under a bed, and not on a stand? <sup>22</sup>For nothing is hidden except to be made manifest; nor is anything secret except to come to light. <sup>23</sup>If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.” <sup>24</sup>And he said to them, “Pay attention to what you hear: with the measure you use, it will be measured to you, and still more will be added to you. <sup>25</sup>For to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away.” <sup>26</sup>And he said, “The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground. <sup>27</sup>He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how. <sup>28</sup>The earth produces by itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. <sup>29</sup>But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.” <sup>30</sup>And he said, “With what can we compare the kingdom of God, or what parable shall we use for it? <sup>31</sup>It is like a grain of mustard seed, which, when sown on the ground, is the smallest of all the seeds on earth, <sup>32</sup>yet when it is sown it grows up and becomes larger than all the garden plants and puts out large branches, so that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade.” <sup>33</sup>With many such parables he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear it. <sup>34</sup>He did not speak to them without a parable, but privately to his own disciples he explained everything. <sup>35</sup>On that day, when evening had come, he said to them, “Let us go across to the other side.” <sup>36</sup>And leaving the crowd, they took him with them in the boat, just as he was. And other boats were with him. <sup>37</sup>And a great windstorm arose, and the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was already filling. <sup>38</sup>But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. And they woke him and said to him, “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?” <sup>39</sup>And he awoke and rebuked the wind and said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm. <sup>40</sup>He said to them, “Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?” <sup>41</sup>And they were filled with great fear and said to one another, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is Mark's great block of teaching, and it is built to answer one question the previous chapter forced: if Jesus really is the King, why does this look so small and go so badly? The professionals have called him demonic, his family thinks he is unwell, and the kingdom of God at this point consists of a preacher in a borrowed boat and twelve unimpressive men.

The answer comes in seed. A sower broadcasts across ground he cannot see into, and three-quarters of it appears wasted — and the harvest is still thirty, sixty, a hundredfold, when a Galilean farmer expected five or ten (vv. 3–20). A man scatters seed and goes to bed, and it grows while he sleeps and he does not know how (vv. 26–29). The smallest speck in the garden becomes the largest plant in it, with room in its branches for the birds of the air — which in Ezekiel and Daniel means the nations (vv. 30–32).

Then the teaching stops and the test begins. He says let us go across, and the crossing nearly kills them. The chapter that has been about hearing the word ends with the word spoken to a hurricane, and with a question left deliberately unanswered: Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — The Sower and the Purpose of Parables
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The pulpit (vv. 1–2). The crowd is so large that Jesus pushes a boat out a few yards and preaches from the water, with the people banked up the shore. The setting is itself a picture: one voice, one seed, going out over a great many different kinds of ground.

The parable (vv. 3–9). A sower walks a field and the seed lands in four places — a trodden path, a shelf of rock under thin soil, a patch of thorn roots, and open ground. Three losses and one harvest so large it would have made a Galilean farmer laugh.

Why parables at all (vv. 10–12). The hardest paragraph in the chapter, and Jesus does not soften it. He quotes Isaiah's commission to a nation that had already shut its eyes, and says the stories both shelter the seeker and confirm the scorner.

The explanation (vv. 13–20). The only parable Jesus takes apart line by line in this Gospel. Four soils, four fates, and the third one is the one most of us are living in.

The lamp and the measure (vv. 21–25). The hiding is temporary — a lamp goes under a basket for a moment, not for a life. And what you do with what you have heard determines what you will be given next.
verseByVerse.theology:
Verses 11–12 are the hardest words in the chapter, and they should not be smoothed over. Matthew's version says Jesus speaks in parables because people do not see (Matt. 13:13); Mark's says he speaks so that they may not see, lest they should turn and be forgiven. Read flatly, that sounds as though the Lord veils truth deliberately to stop people repenting.

Three things dissolve the difficulty. First, the words are a direct quotation of Isaiah 6:9–10 — God's charge to a prophet sent to a nation that had already, for generations, shut its own eyes. This is not fresh cruelty; it is the settled judgement of God on hardened refusal. Second, the so that carries the weight of fulfilment as much as bare purpose: the parables come to a people who have chosen blindness and confirm the choice, which is how God deals with those who insist — he gives them over to the dark they preferred (cf. Rom. 1:24). Third, and decisively, the door is never bolted. Those around him with the twelve understood nothing either. The difference between them and the outsiders is one thing only: they asked.

So the same parable is judgement and mercy at once. It hardens the scornful and shelters the seeker — hiding the truth from the mouth that would only spit on it, while keeping it within arm's reach of anyone who will turn and ask.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a farmer broadcasting seed by hand across ground he has not sorted in advance, some of it landing where it has no chance at all.

Now: every faithful preacher, parent and friend who keeps sowing without being able to see the soil. The sower in the parable does not test the ground first, and he is not blamed for the path, the rock or the thorns. That is a real relief for anyone who has taught a class for years, or raised children in the faith, and cannot see a harvest. Your job was the sowing.

And a hundredfold is not a rounded-up figure. Ordinary yields in that country ran five- or tenfold, and a farmer who got thirty would have talked about it for the rest of his life. Jesus names thirty as the lowest of the three good outcomes. Three-quarters of the field appears to fail, and the harvest is still absurd. Whatever the losses look like from where you are standing, the ledger at the end is not in doubt.

verseByVerse.quote: Again he began to teach beside the sea. And a very large crowd gathered about him, so that he got into a boat and sat in it on the sea, and the whole crowd was beside the sea on the land. And he was teaching them many things in parables, and in his teaching he said to them:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again Jesus began to teach by the lake. The crowd was so large that he got into a boat on the water and sat down, while the whole crowd stood on the shore. He taught them many things in parables.

The connection. In chapter 3, the religious leaders rejected Jesus and his family misunderstood him, while a circle of disciples gathered around him. Why do some receive him and others reject him? Chapter 4 answers in parables: the word of the kingdom is like seed, received differently by different soils, small and hidden at first, but certain to produce a great harvest.

So that he got into a boat and sat in it on the sea. The boat prepared in 3:9. A teacher sat to teach. The water carried his voice to the crowd on the slope of the shore.

And he was teaching them many things in parables. A parable (parabolē) is a story or picture from ordinary life placed beside a spiritual truth to illuminate it: farming, lamps, measures, seeds. Parables usually make one main point, though Jesus explains some details. They invite hearers to think and respond.

In a sentence. Jesus taught the huge crowd from a boat on the lake, using parables.

On a Tuesday. Jesus used ordinary things to teach eternal truths. Look for God’s lessons in ordinary things today.
verseByVerse.note: Teaching from a boat let the whole crowd on the shore see and hear him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Listen! Behold, a sower went out to sow. And as he sowed, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Listen! A farmer went out to sow. As he sowed, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and ate it up.

Listen! The parable begins and ends with a call to hear (v. 9). The great issue of the chapter is how we listen.

Behold, a sower went out to sow. Seed was scattered by hand from a bag, broadly, often before ploughing, so it fell everywhere.

Some seed fell along the path. The hard-trodden footpaths between fields. The seed lay on the surface.

And the birds came and devoured it. At once.

In a sentence. A farmer scattered seed, and some fell on a hard path, where birds ate it.

On a Tuesday. How do you listen to God’s word? The parable is a mirror.
verseByVerse.note: Seed was scattered by hand, and some fell on the hard footpaths between fields.

verseByVerse.quote: Other seed fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil, and immediately it sprang up, since it had no depth of soil. And when the sun rose, it was scorched, and since it had no root, it withered away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Other seed fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil. It sprang up quickly, because the soil was shallow. But when the sun rose it was scorched, and because it had no root it withered away.

Other seed fell on rocky ground. Not soil full of stones, but a thin layer of soil over limestone bedrock, common in Galilee.
