And he went about among the villages teaching. <sup>7</sup>And he called the twelve and began to send them out two by two, and gave them authority over the unclean spirits. <sup>8</sup>He charged them to take nothing for their journey except a staff—no bread, no bag, no money in their belts— <sup>9</sup>but to wear sandals and not put on two tunics. <sup>10</sup>And he said to them, “Whenever you enter a house, stay there until you depart from there. <sup>11</sup>And if any place will not receive you and they will not listen to you, when you leave, shake off the dust that is on your feet as a testimony against them.” <sup>12</sup>So they went out and proclaimed that people should repent. <sup>13</sup>And they cast out many demons and anointed with oil many who were sick and healed them. <sup>14</sup>King Herod heard of it, for Jesus’ name had become known. Some said, “John the Baptist has been raised from the dead. That is why these miraculous powers are at work in him.” <sup>15</sup>But others said, “He is Elijah.” And others said, “He is a prophet, like one of the prophets of old.” <sup>16</sup>But when Herod heard of it, he said, “John, whom I beheaded, has been raised.” <sup>17</sup>For it was Herod who had sent and seized John and bound him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, because he had married her. <sup>18</sup>For John had been saying to Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.” <sup>19</sup>And Herodias had a grudge against him and wanted to put him to death. But she could not, <sup>20</sup>for Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man, and he kept him safe. When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly. <sup>21</sup>But an opportunity came when Herod on his birthday gave a banquet for his nobles and military commanders and the leading men of Galilee. <sup>22</sup>For when Herodias’s daughter came in and danced, she pleased Herod and his guests. And the king said to the girl, “Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you.” <sup>23</sup>And he vowed to her, “Whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom.” <sup>24</sup>And she went out and said to her mother, “For what should I ask?” And she said, “The head of John the Baptist.” <sup>25</sup>And she came in immediately with haste to the king and asked, saying, “I want you to give me at once the head of John the Baptist on a platter.” <sup>26</sup>And the king was exceedingly sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he did not want to break his word to her. <sup>27</sup>And immediately the king sent an executioner with orders to bring John’s head. He went and beheaded him in the prison <sup>28</sup>and brought his head on a platter and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother. <sup>29</sup>When his disciples heard of it, they came and took his body and laid it in a tomb. <sup>30</sup>The apostles returned to Jesus and told him all that they had done and taught. <sup>31</sup>And he said to them, “Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while.” For many were coming and going, and they had no leisure even to eat. <sup>32</sup>And they went away in the boat to a desolate place by themselves. <sup>33</sup>Now many saw them going and recognized them, and they ran there on foot from all the towns and got there ahead of them. <sup>34</sup>When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And he began to teach them many things. <sup>35</sup>And when it grew late, his disciples came to him and said, “This is a desolate place, and the hour is now late. <sup>36</sup>Send them away to go into the surrounding countryside and villages and buy themselves something to eat.” <sup>37</sup>But he answered them, “You give them something to eat.” And they said to him, “Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give it to them to eat?” <sup>38</sup>And he said to them, “How many loaves do you have? Go and see.” And when they had found out, they said, “Five, and two fish.” <sup>39</sup>Then he commanded them all to sit down in groups on the green grass. <sup>40</sup>So they sat down in groups, by hundreds and by fifties. <sup>41</sup>And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing and broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the people. And he divided the two fish among them all. <sup>42</sup>And they all ate and were satisfied. <sup>43</sup>And they took up twelve baskets full of broken pieces and of the fish. <sup>44</sup>And those who ate the loaves were five thousand men. <sup>45</sup>Immediately he made his disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side, to Bethsaida, while he dismissed the crowd. <sup>46</sup>And after he had taken leave of them, he went up on the mountain to pray. <sup>47</sup>And when evening came, the boat was out on the sea, and he was alone on the land. <sup>48</sup>And he saw that they were making headway painfully, for the wind was against them. And about the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. He meant to pass by them, <sup>49</sup>but when they saw him walking on the sea they thought it was a ghost, and cried out, <sup>50</sup>for they all saw him and were terrified. But immediately he spoke to them and said, “Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid.” <sup>51</sup>And he got into the boat with them, and the wind ceased. And they were utterly astounded, <sup>52</sup>for they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened. <sup>53</sup>When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret and moored to the shore. <sup>54</sup>And when they got out of the boat, the people immediately recognized him <sup>55</sup>and ran about the whole region and began to bring the sick people on their beds to wherever they heard he was. <sup>56</sup>And wherever he came, in villages, cities, or countryside, they laid the sick in the marketplaces and implored him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.
6.overview:
Chapter 6 is the widest swing in the Gospel: a village that will not have him, a mission that works, a prophet murdered at a birthday party, a hillside fed until it could eat no more, and a man walking on water in the last watch of the night.

It opens at Nazareth, where the questions asked about Jesus are exactly the right ones — where did this man get these things? what is the wisdom given to him? — and the conclusion drawn is the worst in the book. They knew his trade, his mother, his brothers by name, and the knowing is precisely what stopped them.

Then Mark does something structurally deliberate. He sends the Twelve out (vv. 7–13), interrupts them with thirteen verses on the death of John the Baptist — by far the longest passage in this Gospel about anyone other than Jesus — and only then lets them come back (v. 30). Anyone reading to find out what following costs has just been told, and told at length: the greatest man born of women dies alone in a cellar because a girl danced well and a weak king could not bear to look foolish in front of his officers.

The second half answers the first. The crowd that ruins the disciples' day off is met with compassion rather than irritation, because he sees sheep without a shepherd; five loaves in his hands feed a district with twelve baskets over; and the men who could only do arithmetic are the ones who carry it out to the rows.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — Rejection, Mission, and the Death of John
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Home (vv. 1–6). He goes back to Nazareth and preaches in the synagogue he grew up in, and the village is offended. They know his trade, his mother, his brothers by name and his sisters by sight, and the knowledge is exactly what stops them. Mark records that he could do no mighty work there, and that he marvelled at their unbelief.

The sending (vv. 7–13). Twelve men are sent out in pairs with authority over unclean spirits and instructions to carry almost nothing. They preach repentance, cast out demons, and anoint the sick with oil — and they are sent before they understand very much at all.

The dungeon (vv. 14–29). Then Mark stops the mission dead and tells, at length and out of sequence, how John the Baptist died: a birthday party, a dance, a rash oath, a girl sent to ask her mother, and a head brought in on a serving dish. Herod is not a monster. He is a weak man who liked listening to a preacher and would not be changed by him.

Note where Mark has put that story. He interrupts the sending of the Twelve with a martyrdom, and only then lets them come back. Anyone reading this Gospel to find out what following costs has just been told.
verseByVerse.theology:
Could he not, or would he not? Verse 5 is one of the most startling sentences in Mark — he could do no mighty work there — and it should not be softened into he chose not to. Mark wrote what he wrote.

But read the exception clause, because it settles the meaning: except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them. Whatever the limitation was, it was not a failure of power; he healed people in Nazareth that afternoon. The impossibility is moral, not mechanical. In a village that had decided in advance what he was, mighty works would have been mere spectacle — and Jesus does not do spectacle for people who have already ruled out the conclusion. He had refused exactly that to the Pharisees (8:11–12) and would refuse it to Herod himself (Luke 23:8–9).

Faith is not a mechanism that generates miracles, as though God were a machine and belief the coin. It is the setting in which he ordinarily works, because he deals with persons and not with material. Unbelief does not disable God. It makes his help unwelcome, and he does not force it.

And he marvelled. There are only two things in the Gospels said to have astonished Jesus. He marvelled at the faith of a Roman officer who had no Bible and no upbringing in it (Luke 7:9), and he marvelled at the unbelief of the village that had raised him. The people with every advantage astonished him in the wrong direction.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Herod, who feared John, knew he was a righteous man, protected him from a wife who wanted him dead, was greatly perplexed by his preaching — and heard him gladly. Gladly. He enjoyed it. He came back for more of it.

Now: the most searching portrait in the chapter, because Herod is not a scoffer and never was. He is the rocky ground of chapter 4 given a name and a palace — the word received with real interest, real feeling, even real pleasure, and no root at all. Being moved by a sermon is not being changed by one, and the platter is the proof.

Everything was there in that man except the one thing that matters. He would not repent — and a man who will not repent will eventually have to silence the voice that keeps asking him to. It took a party, a dance and an audience to get it done, but it was decided long before the executioner was sent.

So the honest test is not whether you enjoy good preaching. Herod did. It is whether there is anything the preaching has actually cost you this year.

verseByVerse.quote: He went away from there and came to his hometown, and his disciples followed him. And on the Sabbath he began to teach in the synagogue, and many who heard him were astonished, saying, "Where did this man get these things? What is the wisdom given to him? How are such mighty works done by his hands?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus left there and went to his hometown, and his disciples followed him. On the Sabbath he began to teach in the synagogue, and many who heard him were astonished: where did this man get these things? What is this wisdom given to him? How are such mighty works done by his hands?

He went away from there and came to his hometown. Nazareth, the small village in the Galilean hills where he grew up (1:9).

And his disciples followed him. They would see how his own town received him, a lesson before he sent them out (v. 7).

And on the Sabbath he began to teach in the synagogue. As a visiting teacher, invited to read and explain Scripture. Luke records a visit where he read from Isaiah 61 and declared it fulfilled (Luke 4:16–30).

And many who heard him were astonished. Struck, overwhelmed. But astonishment is not faith.

Where did this man get these things? The right question, with an answer they would not accept: from God.

What is the wisdom given to him? They recognised that his wisdom was “given”: it came from somewhere beyond himself.

How are such mighty works done by his hands? They had heard of his miracles.

In a sentence. In his hometown synagogue, Jesus’ teaching astonished the people, who wondered where he got such wisdom and power.

On a Tuesday. Astonishment at Jesus is not enough. The question “where did this come from?” must lead to faith.
verseByVerse.note: His hometown is Nazareth.

verseByVerse.quote: Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon? And are not his sisters here with us?" And they took offense at him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is this not the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James, Joses, Judas and Simon? And are not his sisters here with us? And they took offence at him.

Is not this the carpenter. “Carpenter” (tektōn) means a builder or craftsman in wood or stone, someone who made ploughs, yokes, doors and houses. Matthew says “the carpenter’s son” (Matthew 13:55). Jesus worked with his hands for years before his ministry. To the townspeople, this settled it: he was an ordinary tradesman, one of them. How could he be anything more?

The son of Mary. Unusually, they identify him by his mother, not his father. Normally a man was called “son of” his father, even if the father was dead. This may have been a slur, a hint that his birth was irregular, since everyone knew Mary had been pregnant before her marriage (John 8:41). The town had its own explanation of his origins.

And brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon? And are not his sisters here with us? Jesus had four brothers and at least two sisters. James later led the church in Jerusalem and wrote the letter of James; Judas (Jude) wrote the letter of Jude. The most natural reading is that they were Mary and Joseph’s children born after Jesus (see Matthew 1:25).

And they took offense at him. “Took offence” (eskandalizonto) means they stumbled over him. Familiarity bred contempt. They knew his family, his trade and his ordinary life, and could not accept that God was at work in him. They had no category for the incarnation: God in an ordinary man.

Where Christians differ: Jesus’ brothers. Roman Catholic teaching holds that Mary remained a virgin, and takes the brothers to be cousins. Orthodox tradition takes them to be Joseph’s children by an earlier marriage. Verdict: the natural reading of the Gospels is that they were Mary’s younger children. Nothing in Scripture requires otherwise.

In a sentence. His hometown could not accept that the carpenter they knew, with his ordinary family, could be more, and they stumbled over him.

On a Tuesday. Has familiarity with Jesus made you stop wondering at him? Ask God to make him fresh to you.
verseByVerse.note: “Carpenter” is a general word for a builder or craftsman in wood or stone.

parallels.desc: even his brothers did not believe

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, "A prophet is not without honor, except in his hometown and among his relatives and in his own household." And he could do no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them. And he marveled because of their unbelief. And he went about among the villages teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: a prophet is not without honour except in his hometown, among his relatives and in his own household. He could do no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them. And he marvelled at their unbelief. And he went around the villages teaching.

A prophet is not without honor, except in his hometown and among his relatives and in his own household. A proverb. Only Mark adds “among his relatives and in his own household”: even his family did not yet believe (3:21; John 7:5).

And he could do no mighty work there. A striking statement. Not that his power was limited, as if he were helpless. Miracles were signs meant to lead to faith; where people refused to believe, signs had no place. Jesus would not perform for unbelievers (8:11–12). And people did not bring their sick to someone they despised. Matthew says he did not do many mighty works there (Matthew 13:58).

Except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them. Even in unbelief, a few came and were healed. His compassion was not withdrawn from those who sought him.

And he marveled because of their unbelief. Only twice in the Gospels does Jesus marvel: at the great faith of a Gentile centurion (Luke 7:9), and here at the unbelief of his own town. Jesus was truly human and could be amazed.

And he went about among the villages teaching. Rejection did not stop him. He moved on.

What it does not mean. Not that faith is a power that controls whether God can act. God is sovereign. But faith receives what God gives, and unbelief closes the door.

In a sentence. Rejected in his hometown, Jesus did few miracles there, marvelled at their unbelief, and moved on to teach in the villages.

On a Tuesday. If your own family or hometown does not honour your faith, Jesus understands. Keep going, as he did.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the twelve and began to send them out two by two, and gave them authority over the unclean spirits. He charged them to take nothing for their journey except a staff—no bread, no bag, no money in their belts— but to wear sandals and not put on two tunics.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus called the Twelve and began to send them out two by two, giving them authority over the unclean spirits. He told them to take nothing for their journey except a staff: no bread, no bag, no money in their belts, but to wear sandals and not put on two tunics.

And he called the twelve and began to send them out two by two. The purpose for which he chose them (3:14). “Two by two”: for support, safety and credible witness (Deuteronomy 19:15). Jesus later sent out seventy-two in pairs (Luke 10:1), and the early church followed the pattern: Paul and Barnabas, Peter and John.

And gave them authority over the unclean spirits. His own authority, delegated.

He charged them to take nothing for their journey except a staff. A walking stick for the road. Matthew and Luke say not even a staff (Matthew 10:10; Luke 9:3). Perhaps Mark means take the staff you have, while Matthew means do not acquire another; or one Gospel speaks of a walking staff and the other of a club for defence. The point is the same: travel light.

No bread, no bag, no money in their belts. Coins were carried in folds of the belt. The bag was a traveller’s pack, or a beggar’s bag for collecting gifts. They must depend entirely on God’s provision through those who welcomed them.

But to wear sandals and not put on two tunics. No spare clothes. Simple, urgent, dependent.

What it does not mean. Not a permanent rule for all missionaries. Later, Jesus told them to take a moneybag and knapsack (Luke 22:35–36). The principles remain: urgency, simplicity and dependence on God.

In a sentence. Jesus sent out the Twelve in pairs with authority over demons, telling them to travel light and depend on God.

On a Tuesday. What could you let go of to travel lighter in following Christ?
verseByVerse.note: Coins were carried in the belt; the “bag” was a traveller’s pack for supplies.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Whenever you enter a house, stay there until you depart from there. And if any place will not receive you and they will not listen to you, when you leave, shake off the dust that is on your feet as a testimony against them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus told them: wherever you enter a house, stay there until you leave that place. And if any place will not receive you and they will not listen to you, when you leave, shake off the dust that is on your feet as a testimony against them.

Whenever you enter a house, stay there until you depart from there. Do not move from house to house looking for better hospitality.

And if any place will not receive you and they will not listen to you. Rejection was expected, as Jesus had just experienced in Nazareth.

When you leave, shake off the dust that is on your feet. Strict Jews returning from Gentile territory shook the dust off their feet, so as not to carry unclean soil into the holy land. For the apostles to do this to a Jewish town was a startling sign: by rejecting God’s message, the town had made itself like pagan territory. Paul and Barnabas did it at Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:51).

As a testimony against them. A solemn warning, leaving them to God’s judgment. Done in sorrow, not anger.

In a sentence. The apostles were to stay with those who welcomed them and solemnly shake off the dust of places that rejected them.

On a Tuesday. You are responsible for faithfully sharing the gospel, not for how people respond. Leave the results to God.
verseByVerse.note: Shaking off the dust was a sign that a town was being left to God’s judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: So they went out and proclaimed that people should repent. And they cast out many demons and anointed with oil many who were sick and healed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they went out and proclaimed that people should repent. They cast out many demons and anointed with oil many who were sick and healed them.

So they went out and proclaimed that people should repent. The same message as John and Jesus (1:4, 15): turn back to God, for the kingdom has come near.

And they cast out many demons. Sharing Jesus’ victory over Satan.

And anointed with oil many who were sick and healed them. Olive oil was used as medicine (Luke 10:34; Isaiah 1:6), and as a sign of God’s blessing and presence. James tells church elders to pray over the sick and anoint them with oil in the name of the Lord (James 5:14–15).

What it does not mean. Not the sacrament of “extreme unction” or “last rites”, as the medieval church developed it, for preparing the dying for death. The anointing here was for healing. Reformed churches do not treat anointing as a sacrament, though some practise it in prayer for the sick, following James 5. Nor does it mean that every believer today has the apostles’ authority to heal at will. God still heals in answer to prayer, as he wills.

In a sentence. The Twelve preached repentance, cast out demons, and anointed and healed many sick people.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the sick in your church this week, by name, trusting God to answer as he knows best.
verseByVerse.note: Olive oil was used as medicine and as a sign of God’s blessing.

parallels.desc: anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord

verseByVerse.quote: King Herod heard of it, for Jesus' name had become known. Some said, "John the Baptist has been raised from the dead. That is why these miraculous powers are at work in him." But others said, "He is Elijah." And others said, "He is a prophet, like one of the prophets of old." But when Herod heard of it, he said, "John, whom I beheaded, has been raised."
verseByVerse.commentary:
King Herod heard of it, for Jesus’ name had become known. Some said: John the Baptist has been raised from the dead; that is why these miraculous powers are at work in him. Others said: he is Elijah. Others said: he is a prophet, like one of the prophets of old. But when Herod heard of it, he said: John, whom I beheaded, has been raised.

King Herod heard of it. Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruler of Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39. His official title was tetrarch, a minor ruler (Matthew 14:1), but people called him king. He later asked Rome for the title of king, and was exiled instead.

For Jesus’ name had become known. The mission of the Twelve had spread his fame.

Some said, “John the Baptist has been raised from the dead.” Others had the same idea as Herod.

Others said, “He is Elijah.” The prophet expected before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5).

And others said, “He is a prophet, like one of the prophets of old.” All honourable opinions, all inadequate. The same list appears when Jesus asks his disciples who people say he is (8:28).

But when Herod heard of it, he said, “John, whom I beheaded, has been raised.” A guilty conscience. Herod could not stop thinking about the man he had killed. Mark now goes back to tell the story.

In a sentence. People offered many explanations of Jesus, but Herod, haunted by guilt, thought he was John the Baptist raised from the dead.

On a Tuesday. A guilty conscience cannot be silenced by silencing the messenger. Bring your guilt to Christ.
verseByVerse.note: “King” Herod is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee and Perea; his official title was tetrarch.

verseByVerse.quote: For it was Herod who had sent and seized John and bound him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, because he had married her. For John had been saying to Herod, "It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it was Herod who had sent and seized John and bound him in prison, because of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, whom he had married. For John had been saying to Herod: it is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.

For it was Herod who had sent and seized John and bound him in prison. According to Josephus, at Machaerus, a fortress-palace east of the Dead Sea.

For the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, because he had married her. Herodias was the granddaughter of Herod the Great, and so the niece of both her husbands. She had been married to Antipas’ half-brother (called Philip in the Gospels). Antipas fell in love with her on a visit to Rome; both divorced their spouses and married each other.

For John had been saying to Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.” “Had been saying”: repeatedly. The law forbade marrying a brother’s wife while the brother lived (Leviticus 18:16; 20:21). John confronted the ruler with God’s law, like Elijah before Ahab and Jezebel (1 Kings 21).

In a sentence. Herod had imprisoned John because John kept telling him that his marriage to his brother’s wife broke God’s law.

On a Tuesday. God’s law applies to the powerful as much as anyone. Pray for courage to speak truth when love requires it.
verseByVerse.note: Herodias had been married to Antipas’s half-brother; the law forbade marrying a brother’s wife while he lived.

verseByVerse.quote: And Herodias had a grudge against him and wanted to put him to death. But she could not, for Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man, and he kept him safe. When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herodias had a grudge against John and wanted to put him to death. But she could not, for Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man, and he kept him safe. When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly.

And Herodias had a grudge against him and wanted to put him to death. “Had a grudge” literally means “held it in”: a nursed, settled hatred. She would not let it go. Bitterness kept and fed becomes murderous (Ephesians 4:31).

But she could not, for Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man. Only Mark tells us about Herod’s inner conflict. He was in awe of John. He knew John was right.

And he kept him safe. He protected John from Herodias, at least for a while.

When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly. Herod listened to John often. He was disturbed, confused, drawn and resistant at the same time. He enjoyed hearing John, but would not obey him. He would not give up Herodias. A divided heart: attracted to the truth, unwilling to repent. This is the thorny soil (4:18–19).

In a sentence. Herodias hated John and wanted him dead, but Herod, knowing John was holy, protected him and listened to him gladly, though perplexed.

On a Tuesday. It is possible to enjoy sermons and admire preachers without ever repenting. Do you only listen, or do you obey?

verseByVerse.quote: But an opportunity came when Herod on his birthday gave a banquet for his nobles and military commanders and the leading men of Galilee. For when Herodias's daughter came in and danced, she pleased Herod and his guests. And the king said to the girl, "Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you." And he vowed to her, "Whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But an opportunity came when Herod on his birthday gave a banquet for his nobles, military commanders and the leading men of Galilee. When Herodias’ daughter came in and danced, she pleased Herod and his guests. The king said to the girl: ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you. And he vowed to her: whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom.

But an opportunity came. The opportunity Herodias had been waiting for.

When Herod on his birthday gave a banquet for his nobles and military commanders and the leading men of Galilee. A lavish feast for the powerful. Plenty of wine.

For when Herodias’s daughter came in and danced, she pleased Herod and his guests. Josephus names her Salome. She was probably a teenager. For a princess to dance before drunken men at a banquet was shameful, and suggests a sensual performance, perhaps arranged by her mother.

Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you. A drunken, extravagant promise.

And he vowed to her, “Whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom.” Echoing the Persian king’s words to Esther (Esther 5:3; 7:2). But Herod had no kingdom to give; he ruled at Rome’s pleasure. The boast was hollow. Jesus warned against rash oaths (Matthew 5:33–37).

In a sentence. At Herod’s birthday banquet, his stepdaughter danced, and the drunken king swore to give her anything, up to half his kingdom.

On a Tuesday. Rash promises made in the moment can trap us. Be slow to promise, and never let a promise bind you to sin.
verseByVerse.note: The historian Josephus names Herodias’s daughter Salome.

parallels.desc: up to half of my kingdom

verseByVerse.quote: And she went out and said to her mother, "For what should I ask?" And she said, "The head of John the Baptist." And she came in immediately with haste to the king and asked, saying, "I want you to give me at once the head of John the Baptist on a platter." And the king was exceedingly sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he did not want to break his word to her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She went out and asked her mother: what should I ask for? She said: the head of John the Baptist. She came in immediately with haste to the king and asked: I want you to give me at once the head of John the Baptist on a platter. The king was exceedingly sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he did not want to break his word to her.

And she went out and said to her mother, “For what should I ask?” The girl was the instrument of her mother’s hatred.

And she said, “The head of John the Baptist.” Herodias seized the moment.

And she came in immediately with haste to the king. Before Herod could sober up and change his mind.

I want you to give me at once the head of John the Baptist on a platter. She adds “at once” and “on a platter”: a serving dish, as if it were another course at the feast. Grotesque.

And the king was exceedingly sorry. Herod regretted his oath.

But because of his oaths and his guests he did not want to break his word to her. Fear of losing face before his powerful guests. He valued his reputation more than a righteous man’s life, and more than his own conscience. An oath to do evil should be broken, not kept (Westminster Confession 22.7).

In a sentence. Prompted by her mother, the girl asked for John’s head on a platter, and Herod, though sorry, would not break his word in front of his guests.

On a Tuesday. Fear of what others think leads people into terrible choices. Be willing to lose face rather than do wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately the king sent an executioner with orders to bring John's head. He went and beheaded him in the prison and brought his head on a platter and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother. When his disciples heard of it, they came and took his body and laid it in a tomb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately the king sent an executioner with orders to bring John’s head. He went and beheaded him in the prison, brought his head on a platter and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother. When John’s disciples heard of it, they came and took his body and laid it in a tomb.

And immediately the king sent an executioner. “Executioner” (spekoulatora, from Latin speculator) was a soldier of the guard who carried out executions. Mark uses the Latin word, perhaps because he was writing in Rome.

He went and beheaded him in the prison. John, the greatest of the prophets (Matthew 11:11), the forerunner of the Messiah, died alone in a dungeon, killed at a drunken party to satisfy a vengeful woman and a weak man’s pride.

And brought his head on a platter and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother. Told plainly, without comment.

When his disciples heard of it, they came and took his body and laid it in a tomb. A last act of love.

Why Mark tells this story. It is the only story in Mark not directly about Jesus. Placed between the sending out of the Twelve (vv. 7–13) and their return (v. 30), it shows the cost of faithful ministry. The messenger is killed by a ruler who knows he is innocent, under pressure from others, and buried by his disciples. Every detail foreshadows Jesus’ own death: Pilate will know Jesus is innocent, yield to pressure, and Jesus will be laid in a tomb (15:15, 46). The forerunner goes before him in death too.

In a sentence. John was beheaded in prison, his head was given to Herodias, and his disciples buried his body.

On a Tuesday. Faithfulness to God may cost a great deal. Pray for those today who are imprisoned or killed for speaking God’s truth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–56 — The Feeding, the Walking, and the Healings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The rest that never happened (vv. 30–34). The apostles come back full of what they have done, and Jesus's first instruction is not a debrief but a retreat: come away and rest. They get into a boat — and the crowd works out where they are going, runs round the head of the lake on foot, and is waiting when they land. His response to a wrecked afternoon off is compassion, because they were like sheep without a shepherd.

The feeding (vv. 35–44). The disciples do the arithmetic and propose dispersal. Jesus hands the problem back: you give them something to eat. Then he seats a crowd of thousands in ranks on the spring grass, takes five loaves and two fish, and there is more left at the end than there was at the start.

The lake in the fourth watch of the night (vv. 45–52). He sends them off ahead and goes up the mountain alone to pray — and from up there, in the dark, he sees them straining at the oars. He comes to them on the water, and he means to pass by, in the language the Old Testament reserves for God showing himself.

Gennesaret (vv. 53–56). And then a summary paragraph of pure mercy: whole villages carrying the sick out into the marketplaces, and everyone who touched even the edge of his clothing made well.
verseByVerse.theology:
He meant to pass by them (v. 48) is the strangest clause in the chapter, and it is not what it sounds like. He is not trying to overtake them or slip past unnoticed. Passing by is the Old Testament's own vocabulary for God making himself visible.

When Moses asked to see the glory of God, the LORD put him in a cleft of the rock and said while my glory passes by I will cover you with my hand (Ex. 33:22). When Elijah stood at the mouth of the cave, the word was behold, the LORD passed by (1 Kgs. 19:11). And Job, describing the God no man can lay hold of, says he alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea — and then, three verses later, behold, he passes by me, and I see him not (Job 9:8, 11).

Walking on the sea and passing by, in the same sentence, out of the same book. Mark's readers who knew their Scriptures were not being told about a shortcut.

And then, when they scream, he speaks: Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid. The middle phrase is egō eimi — literally I am, the words from the burning bush (Ex. 3:14). It is the ordinary way to say it's me, and in this setting, on that water, from that Person, it is very much more.

Which makes verse 52 the saddest verse in the chapter: they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened. Mark uses of the Twelve the very word he used of the men in the synagogue who watched a withered hand restored and went out to plan a murder (3:5). Hardness is not a disease of unbelievers only.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twelve exhausted men doing sums in front of a hungry crowd — two hundred denarii, most of a year's wages, and it still would not be enough — and hearing you give them something to eat.

Now: anyone facing a need that is plainly larger than their resources. The parent who has run out of wisdom. The pastor of a small church looking at a large town. The person asked to care for someone whose needs exceed anything they have.

Jesus is not asking them to solve it. He asks a different question, and it is the practical one: how many loaves do you have? Go and see. Not how many do you need — how many have you got. Go and count it.

Five loaves and two fish is an embarrassing answer to give in front of five thousand people, and it was the right answer, because the multiplication happens in his hands and not in theirs. Bring what you actually have, including how little it is. And notice who ended up carrying the twelve baskets of surplus: the men who had nothing to give, one basket each.

verseByVerse.quote: The apostles returned to Jesus and told him all that they had done and taught. And he said to them, "Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while." For many were coming and going, and they had no leisure even to eat. And they went away in the boat to a desolate place by themselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles returned to Jesus and told him everything they had done and taught. He said to them: come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while. For many were coming and going, and they had no leisure even to eat. And they went away in the boat to a desolate place by themselves.

The apostles returned to Jesus and told him all that they had done and taught. The only time Mark calls them “apostles”, those sent, as they return from being sent. They report to him.

Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while. Only Mark records this tender invitation. After ministry comes rest. Jesus cares about his workers’ exhaustion. Rest is not laziness; it is God’s design (Exodus 20:8–11). Even in urgent ministry, Jesus calls his disciples to step away.

For many were coming and going, and they had no leisure even to eat. The demands were relentless.

And they went away in the boat to a desolate place by themselves. The “desolate place” (erēmon) is the wilderness, where God fed Israel (Exodus 16). What follows will recall that.

In a sentence. When the apostles returned and reported, Jesus invited them to come away to a quiet place and rest, because they had not even had time to eat.

On a Tuesday. Are you exhausted from serving? Hear Jesus’ invitation: come away and rest a while. Take time to be with him.

verseByVerse.quote: Now many saw them going and recognized them, and they ran there on foot from all the towns and got there ahead of them. When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And he began to teach them many things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many saw them going and recognised them, and ran there on foot from all the towns and got there ahead of them. When Jesus went ashore, he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And he began to teach them many things.

Now many saw them going and recognized them, and they ran there on foot from all the towns and got there ahead of them. The crowds ran around the lake shore and arrived first. The rest was interrupted.

When he went ashore he saw a great crowd.

And he had compassion on them. Not irritation, but deep, gut-level compassion (splanchnizomai).

Because they were like sheep without a shepherd. An Old Testament picture: Moses prayed that the LORD’s people would not be like sheep without a shepherd (Numbers 27:17). In Ezekiel 34, God condemns Israel’s shepherds, who fed themselves and not the flock, and promises that he himself will shepherd his people through a new David. Herod, the supposed king who had just killed John at a feast for the powerful (vv. 21–28), was such a false shepherd. Jesus is the true Shepherd, who will now feed his flock in the wilderness.

And he began to teach them many things. His first act of shepherding was teaching. The people’s first need was God’s word (Deuteronomy 8:3).

In a sentence. When the crowd arrived ahead of them, Jesus had compassion on them as sheep without a shepherd, and taught them.

On a Tuesday. When others interrupt your rest with their needs, ask for Jesus’ compassion. And remember that people’s deepest need is the word of God.

parallels.desc: not as sheep without a shepherd

verseByVerse.quote: And when it grew late, his disciples came to him and said, "This is a desolate place, and the hour is now late. Send them away to go into the surrounding countryside and villages and buy themselves something to eat." But he answered them, "You give them something to eat." And they said to him, "Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give it to them to eat?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When it grew late, the disciples said: this is a desolate place, and the hour is late. Send them away to buy food in the surrounding countryside and villages. But Jesus answered: you give them something to eat. They said: shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give it to them to eat?

This is a desolate place, and the hour is now late. The disciples see the problem.

Send them away to go into the surrounding countryside and villages and buy themselves something to eat. A reasonable suggestion. But it shows they did not yet think of Jesus as able to provide.

But he answered them, “You give them something to eat.” “You” is emphatic. Jesus puts the responsibility on them, to show them their inadequacy and his sufficiency.

Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give it to them to eat? A denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer. Two hundred denarii was about eight months’ wages: far more than they had. Their answer is half sarcastic.

In a sentence. The disciples wanted to send the crowd away to buy food, but Jesus told them to feed it, and they objected that it would cost eight months’ wages.

On a Tuesday. When need seems overwhelming, do you calculate what you lack, or bring what you have to Jesus?
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer; two hundred denarii was most of a year’s wages.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "How many loaves do you have? Go and see." And when they had found out, they said, "Five, and two fish." Then he commanded them all to sit down in groups on the green grass. So they sat down in groups, by hundreds and by fifties.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: how many loaves do you have? Go and see. When they found out, they said: five, and two fish. Then he commanded them all to sit down in groups on the green grass. So they sat down in groups, by hundreds and by fifties.

How many loaves do you have? Go and see. Jesus starts with what they have.

Five, and two fish. John says from a boy, barley loaves, the bread of the poor (John 6:9).

Then he commanded them all to sit down in groups on the green grass. Only Mark mentions that the grass was green: spring, near Passover (John 6:4). An eyewitness detail. And an echo of Psalm 23:1–2: the LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures. The Shepherd is making his sheep lie down in green pasture, in the wilderness, and will feed them.

So they sat down in groups, by hundreds and by fifties. Literally “in garden beds”: the groups looked like rows of flowerbeds, perhaps in colourful clothes on the green grass. “Hundreds and fifties” recalls how Moses organised Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 18:21, 25). Jesus is forming a new Israel in the wilderness, and feeding it like a new Moses.

In a sentence. With only five loaves and two fish, Jesus had the crowd sit in organised groups on the green grass, like Israel in the wilderness and sheep in green pastures.

On a Tuesday. The Lord is your shepherd too. You shall not want for what you truly need.
verseByVerse.note: The groups of hundreds and fifties recall the way Moses organised Israel in the wilderness.

verseByVerse.quote: And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing and broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the people. And he divided the two fish among them all. And they all ate and were satisfied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Taking the five loaves and the two fish, Jesus looked up to heaven, said a blessing and broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the people. And he divided the two fish among them all. And they all ate and were satisfied.

And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing. Like the head of a Jewish household at a meal: blessed are you, O Lord our God, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth. Looking up to heaven: dependence on the Father.

And broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the people. The same four verbs as the Last Supper: took, blessed, broke, gave (14:22). The feeding looks forward to the Lord’s Supper and to the great banquet of the kingdom (Isaiah 25:6). Jesus works through his disciples: they distribute what he provides.

And he divided the two fish among them all.

And they all ate and were satisfied. A full meal, not a taste. In the wilderness, God gave Israel manna, and they were satisfied (Exodus 16:12; Psalm 78:24–29). Elisha fed a hundred men with twenty loaves (2 Kings 4:42–44). Jesus feeds thousands with five. He is greater than Moses and Elisha. John records his explanation: I am the bread of life (John 6:35).

What it does not mean. Not that people simply shared hidden lunches, as some have suggested. The Gospels describe a miracle of creation. All four Gospels record it: the only miracle, apart from the resurrection, in all four.

In a sentence. Jesus blessed and broke the loaves, gave them through his disciples, and everyone ate and was satisfied.

For worship. Thank Jesus, the bread of life, who satisfies.

verseByVerse.quote: And they took up twelve baskets full of broken pieces and of the fish. And those who ate the loaves were five thousand men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They picked up twelve baskets full of broken pieces and of the fish. Those who ate the loaves were five thousand men.

And they took up twelve baskets full of broken pieces and of the fish. Twelve baskets: one for each disciple, or a sign of provision for the twelve tribes of Israel. Abundant provision: more left than they started with. The baskets (kophinoi) were wicker baskets that Jews carried for food.

And those who ate the loaves were five thousand men. “Men” (andres) means adult males. Matthew adds: besides women and children (Matthew 14:21). Perhaps fifteen to twenty thousand people altogether.

In a sentence. Twelve baskets of leftovers were gathered after five thousand men had eaten.

On a Tuesday. God’s provision is never stingy. Trust him with needs that seem too large.

verseByVerse.quote: Immediately he made his disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side, to Bethsaida, while he dismissed the crowd. And after he had taken leave of them, he went up on the mountain to pray. And when evening came, the boat was out on the sea, and he was alone on the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately Jesus made his disciples get into the boat and go ahead of him to the other side, to Bethsaida, while he dismissed the crowd. After he had taken leave of them, he went up on the mountain to pray.

Immediately he made his disciples get into the boat. “Made” (ēnankasen) means compelled. Why the urgency? John tells us: the crowd wanted to take Jesus by force to make him king (John 6:14–15). Jesus sent the disciples away before they were swept up in political excitement.

And go before him to the other side, to Bethsaida. A fishing town on the northeast shore of the lake, home of Peter, Andrew and Philip (John 1:44).

While he dismissed the crowd. He refused the crown they offered. His kingdom would come by the cross.

And after he had taken leave of them, he went up on the mountain to pray. The second of three times Mark shows Jesus praying alone at night (1:35; 14:32–39), each at a moment of temptation or decision. After refusing a political crown, he went to his Father.

In a sentence. Jesus sent his disciples away by boat, dismissed the crowd who wanted to make him king, and went up the mountain to pray.

On a Tuesday. At moments of success or temptation, do what Jesus did: go and pray.

verseByVerse.quote: And he saw that they were making headway painfully, for the wind was against them. And about the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. He meant to pass by them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus saw that they were straining at the oars, for the wind was against them. About the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. He meant to pass by them.

And he saw that they were making headway painfully, for the wind was against them. From the mountain, Jesus saw them struggling. “Painfully” (basanizomenous) means tormented, tortured. He was not unaware.

And about the fourth watch of the night. Between about 3 and 6 a.m. They had been rowing for hours against the wind.

He came to them, walking on the sea. In the Old Testament, only God walks on the sea: he alone trampled the waves of the sea (Job 9:8); your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters (Psalm 77:19).

He meant to pass by them. A puzzling phrase, found only in Mark. Not that he intended to ignore them. In the Old Testament, God “passing by” is how he reveals his glory. He passed by Moses on the mountain, proclaiming his name (Exodus 33:19–22; 34:6), and passed by Elijah at Horeb (1 Kings 19:11). Jesus intended to reveal his divine glory to the disciples, as God did to Moses and Elijah.

In a sentence. Seeing the disciples struggling against the wind, Jesus came to them walking on the sea before dawn, intending to pass by them as God passed by Moses and Elijah.

On a Tuesday. If you have been straining at the oars for a long time, Jesus sees you. He will come.
verseByVerse.note: The fourth watch was about 3 to 6 a.m. “Pass by” recalls God “passing by” Moses and Elijah to show his glory.

parallels.desc: I will make my goodness pass before you

verseByVerse.quote: but when they saw him walking on the sea they thought it was a ghost, and cried out, for they all saw him and were terrified. But immediately he spoke to them and said, "Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they saw him walking on the sea, they thought it was a ghost and cried out, for they all saw him and were terrified. But immediately he spoke to them and said: take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid.

But when they saw him walking on the sea they thought it was a ghost. A spirit, perhaps an evil sea spirit, in the dark before dawn.

And cried out, for they all saw him and were terrified. All of them.

But immediately he spoke to them. He did not leave them in terror.

Take heart. Be of good courage.

It is I. In Greek egō eimi, literally “I am”. It can simply mean “It’s me”, but it is also God’s name revealed to Moses (Exodus 3:14), and God’s words in Isaiah: I am he; I, I am he who comforts you (Isaiah 43:10, 25; 51:12). Walking on the sea, passing by as God did, and saying “I am”, Jesus reveals himself as the LORD.

Do not be afraid. God’s words when he reveals himself (Genesis 15:1; Isaiah 41:10).

In a sentence. The disciples thought Jesus was a ghost, but he comforted them at once with words that echo God’s own name: take heart; I am; do not be afraid.

On a Tuesday. In the dark and the storm, listen for Jesus: take heart; it is I; do not be afraid.
verseByVerse.note: “It is I” can also be heard as the divine name, “I am.”

verseByVerse.quote: And he got into the boat with them, and the wind ceased. And they were utterly astounded, for they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He got into the boat with them, and the wind ceased. They were utterly astounded, for they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened.

And he got into the boat with them, and the wind ceased. His presence brought calm. (Mark does not record Peter walking on water; Matthew does, Matthew 14:28–31.)

And they were utterly astounded. Literally “exceedingly, beyond measure, astonished within themselves”.

For they did not understand about the loaves. Only Mark adds this. The feeding should have taught them who Jesus is: the Lord who provides, the Shepherd of Psalm 23, greater than Moses. If they had understood the loaves, they would not have been so astonished at the walking on water. Both revealed the same truth: Jesus is God with them.

But their hearts were hardened. A shocking statement about the disciples. The same word was used of the Pharisees (3:5). Not that they had rejected Jesus, but that their hearts were dull, slow and resistant to understanding. Hardness of heart is not only the sin of opponents; disciples suffer from it too (8:17). Mark is honest: Peter told this story against himself.

What it does not mean. Not that the disciples were unbelievers like the Pharisees. But it shows that even true followers need God to open their eyes again and again (8:22–26).

In a sentence. When Jesus got into the boat the wind stopped, and the disciples were utterly astonished, because they had not understood the loaves and their hearts were hardened.

On a Tuesday. What has God done in your life that you have not yet understood? Ask him to soften your heart and open your eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret and moored to the shore. And when they got out of the boat, the people immediately recognized him and ran about the whole region and began to bring the sick people on their beds to wherever they heard he was. And wherever he came, in villages, cities, or countryside, they laid the sick in the marketplaces and implored him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret and moored the boat. When they got out, the people immediately recognised him and ran around the whole region and began to bring the sick on their beds to wherever they heard he was. Wherever he went, in villages, cities or countryside, they laid the sick in the marketplaces and begged him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.

They came to land at Gennesaret. A fertile plain on the northwest shore, between Capernaum and Magdala. The wind had blown them off course from Bethsaida.

The people immediately recognized him and ran about the whole region. His fame had spread everywhere.

And began to bring the sick people on their beds to wherever they heard he was. Carried on mats, as the paralysed man had been (2:3).

They laid the sick in the marketplaces. The open public spaces.

And implored him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment. Like the woman who was healed (5:27–29). The fringe was the tassel on the corner of a Jewish man’s garment (Numbers 15:38–40).

And as many as touched it were made well. Literally “were saved”. Not one was turned away.

The contrast. The chapter began with Jesus’ hometown, which rejected him and saw few miracles (vv. 1–6). It ends with crowds who sought him eagerly and were healed. The difference is faith.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus’ clothes had magical power. The power was his own, received by faith.

In a sentence. At Gennesaret, people brought their sick from everywhere, and all who touched even the fringe of Jesus’ garment were healed.

On a Tuesday. Bring your needs, and the needs of others, to Jesus today. No one who comes to him is turned away.
verseByVerse.note: Gennesaret was a fertile plain on the north-west shore of the lake. The fringe was the tassel the law required on a garment.

6.theology:
Could he not, or would he not? Verse 5 should not be softened — Mark wrote he could do no mighty work there, where Matthew writes did not do many (Matt. 13:58). But the exception clause settles the sense: he healed a few sick people that afternoon, so it was no failure of power. The impossibility is moral. In a village that had already decided what he was, mighty works would have been spectacle, and he does not do spectacle — he refuses a sign to the Pharisees (8:11–12) and stands silent before Herod, who wanted to watch one (Luke 23:8–9). Faith is not a mechanism that generates miracles, as though God were a machine and belief the coin. It is the setting in which he ordinarily works, because he deals with persons. Unbelief does not disable God; it makes his help unwelcome, and he does not force it.

He meant to pass by them (v. 48) is not a shortcut past a struggling boat. Passing by is the Old Testament's own vocabulary for God making himself visible: while my glory passes by (Ex. 33:22), behold, the LORD passed by (1 Kgs. 19:11). Most exactly, Job says of God that he alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea, and three verses later, behold, he passes by me, and I see him not (Job 9:8, 11). Trampling the sea and passing by, in one passage, about God. And when they scream he answers with egō eimi — it is I, the ordinary words for identifying yourself in the dark, and the words from the burning bush (Ex. 3:14).

And their hearts were hardened (v. 52) is said of the apostles, in the very word used of the men in the synagogue who watched a hand restored and left to plan a murder (3:5). Hardness is not a disease of unbelievers only. It is not disbelief — the Twelve believed a great deal. It is the slow loss of the capacity to be affected, the state in which a man can carry the bread and never taste it.
6.examples:
Herod is the most searching portrait in the chapter, because he is not a scoffer. He feared John, knew he was a righteous and holy man, protected him from a wife who wanted him dead, was greatly perplexed by his preaching — and heard him gladly. He sent for him. He came back for more. He is the rocky ground of chapter 4 given a name and a palace: real interest, real feeling, real pleasure, and no root.

Everything was there except the one thing John was actually asking for. Herodias stayed. And a man who will not repent must eventually silence the voice that keeps asking him to — it took only a party, a dance and an audience to finish what had been decided long before.

Then: a king who kept his oath and killed a prophet, because of his oaths and his guests. Not conscience — he had already lost that argument. He could not bear to look foolish in front of people whose opinion he had spent his life courting.

Now: almost nobody does the worst thing they ever do because they wanted to. They do it because backing out in front of the people watching was unthinkable — the joke laughed at, the thing gone along with once the room had turned, the stand not taken because of who would have seen. Peter is eight chapters from exactly this, in a courtyard, in front of a servant girl. The fear of man lays a snare (Prov. 29:25), and it walked a king with an army into a murder he did not want to commit.

So the test is not whether you enjoy good preaching. Herod did. It is whether you can name one thing it has actually cost you this year.

7.title: What Really Defiles a Man
7.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when the Pharisees gathered to him, with some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem, <sup>2</sup>they saw that some of his disciples ate with hands that were defiled, that is, unwashed. <sup>3</sup>(For the Pharisees and all the Jews do not eat unless they wash their hands properly, holding to the tradition of the elders, <sup>4</sup>and when they come from the marketplace, they do not eat unless they wash. And there are many other traditions that they observe, such as the washing of cups and pots and copper vessels and dining couches.) <sup>5</sup>And the Pharisees and the scribes asked him, “Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat with defiled hands?” <sup>6</sup>And he said to them, “Well did Isaiah prophesy of you hypocrites, as it is written, ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; <sup>7</sup>in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.’ <sup>8</sup>You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men.” <sup>9</sup>And he said to them, “You have a fine way of rejecting the commandment of God in order to establish your tradition! <sup>10</sup>For Moses said, ‘Honor your father and your mother’; and, ‘Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.’ <sup>11</sup>But you say, ‘If a man tells his father or his mother, “Whatever you would have gained from me is Corban”’ (that is, given to God)— <sup>12</sup>then you no longer permit him to do anything for his father or mother, <sup>13</sup>thus making void the word of God by your tradition that you have handed down. And many such things you do.” <sup>14</sup>And he called the people to him again and said to them, “Hear me, all of you, and understand: <sup>15</sup>There is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him, but the things that come out of a person are what defile him.” <sup>17</sup>And when he had entered the house and left the people, his disciples asked him about the parable. <sup>18</sup>And he said to them, “Then are you also without understanding? Do you not see that whatever goes into a person from outside cannot defile him, <sup>19</sup>since it enters not his heart but his stomach, and is expelled?” (Thus he declared all foods clean.) <sup>20</sup>And he said, “What comes out of a person is what defiles him. <sup>21</sup>For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, <sup>22</sup>coveting, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, foolishness. <sup>23</sup>All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person.” <sup>24</sup>And from there he arose and went away to the region of Tyre and Sidon. And he entered a house and did not want anyone to know, yet he could not be hidden. <sup>25</sup>But immediately a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit heard of him and came and fell down at his feet. <sup>26</sup>Now the woman was a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by birth. And she begged him to cast the demon out of her daughter. <sup>27</sup>And he said to her, “Let the children be fed first, for it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” <sup>28</sup>But she answered him, “Yes, Lord; yet even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.” <sup>29</sup>And he said to her, “For this statement you may go your way; the demon has left your daughter.” <sup>30</sup>And she went home and found the child lying in bed and the demon gone. <sup>31</sup>Then he returned from the region of Tyre and went through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, in the region of the Decapolis. <sup>32</sup>And they brought to him a man who was deaf and had a speech impediment, and they begged him to lay his hand on him. <sup>33</sup>And taking him aside from the crowd privately, he put his fingers into his ears, and after spitting touched his tongue. <sup>34</sup>And looking up to heaven, he sighed and said to him, “Ephphatha,” that is, “Be opened.” <sup>35</sup>And his ears were opened, his tongue was released, and he spoke plainly. <sup>36</sup>And Jesus charged them to tell no one. But the more he charged them, the more zealously they proclaimed it. <sup>37</sup>And they were astonished beyond measure, saying, “He has done all things well. He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.”
7.overview:
Chapter 7 takes down a wall, and then walks through the gap.

It opens with a delegation from Jerusalem who have travelled ninety miles to raise the matter of unwashed hands. Jesus does not defend his disciples; he quotes Isaiah at the delegation, and then proves the charge with a single devastating example. Corban was a vow that could put a man's money beyond his parents' reach by declaring it dedicated to God — and the tradition would not merely permit it but forbid him to change his mind. A rule invented to honour God had become a device for robbing your father, with a straight face and in God's name.

Then he calls the crowd over and says the thing that changed everything: there is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him. Mark, writing down Peter's preaching years later, adds six words in a bracket — thus he declared all foods clean — and the boundary between clean and unclean peoples, kept for fifteen centuries, is gone.

And having dissolved it, he crosses it. The second half of the chapter is two healings on Gentile ground: a Phoenician mother who takes his own hard word and finds the door in it, and a deaf man in the Decapolis brought by friends, taken quietly aside, and given his hearing with one Aramaic word. The crowd's verdict is bigger than they know — he has done all things well is the sentence pronounced over the finished creation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — Tradition, the Word of God, and the Human Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The complaint (vv. 1–5). A delegation arrives from Jerusalem — the second one in this Gospel — and what they have come ninety miles to raise is that the disciples do not wash their hands before eating. Mark stops to explain the custom, which tells you he is writing for people who have never heard of it.

The answer (vv. 6–8). Jesus does not defend his men. He quotes Isaiah at the delegation and calls them hypocrites: lips near, heart far, and human rules taught as though God had given them.

The example (vv. 9–13). Then he makes it concrete with a case anyone can follow. A man could put the money owed to his aged parents beyond their reach by pronouncing one word over it — and the tradition would back him. That is not a lapse in the system. That is the system working.

The principle (vv. 14–23). He calls the crowd over and says the most subversive thing in the chapter: nothing that goes into a man can defile him. Mark, writing years later with Peter's memory in his hand, adds a parenthesis that changed the church — thus he declared all foods clean — and then Jesus tells the disciples in private where defilement actually comes from, and lists thirteen of them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why does your Bible skip verse 16? Look down the page and the numbers run 15, 17. Nothing has been lost and nothing has been hidden.

The oldest and best manuscripts of Mark do not have a verse 16. Later copies add the familiar refrain if anyone has ears to hear, let him hear — a sentence Jesus certainly said, and which Mark records elsewhere (4:9, 4:23). What almost certainly happened is that a scribe, copying by hand, felt the sentence belonged after v. 15 and wrote it in the margin, and a later copyist took the margin note for part of the text.

The verse numbering itself is not ancient — it was added in the sixteenth century, long after the manuscripts. So when translators went back to the earliest copies and found the sentence absent, they could not renumber the whole New Testament; they simply left the number empty and put the words in a footnote.

That is worth a plain word of reassurance to any reader who finds a gap like this unsettling. Nothing has been taken out of your Bible. The opposite has happened: we now have older and better copies than were available in 1611, and where those copies show that a sentence crept in later, honest translators tell you so in the margin rather than quietly leaving it in. A faith that will not look at its own manuscripts has something to hide. This one publishes the workings.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Corban — a rule invented to honour God, turned into a device for robbing your parents, with a straight face and in God's name.

Now: the shape survives perfectly, and it is almost never dishonest. It is the man so committed at church that his mother has not had a visit in four months. It is the giving that goes to the building fund while a brother in the same congregation cannot pay his heating bill. It is any arrangement in which something genuinely religious has been placed in front of a plain duty God commanded, so that the duty can be quietly dropped without anybody feeling wicked.

So here is a test you can actually run, and it is the one this passage supplies. Take any tradition you hold — a practice, a standard, a way of doing things — and ask whether keeping it is currently costing somebody else something God told you to give them. Not whether it is in the Bible; a good many decent traditions are not, and need not be. Whether it has begun to displace a commandment.

Jesus does not attack tradition as such. He attacks tradition that has been promoted — set level with Scripture, and then used against it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the Pharisees gathered to him, with some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem, they saw that some of his disciples ate with hands that were defiled, that is, unwashed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharisees and some scribes who had come down from Jerusalem gathered around Jesus, and they noticed that some of his disciples were eating with defiled hands, that is, without washing them in the ritual way.

Setting. This is the second delegation from Jerusalem. The first decided that Jesus cast out demons by Beelzebul (3:22). Jerusalem was the centre of religious authority, and these men came as inspectors. The scene follows straight on from the feeding of the five thousand and the healings at Gennesaret (6:30–56): the crowds are being fed, healed and taught, and the experts’ concern is how the disciples hold their bread.

Now when the Pharisees gathered to him, with some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem. The Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to strict keeping of the law, including the purity rules that the Old Testament gave to priests, which they applied to ordinary daily life. The scribes were the professional experts in the law, many of them Pharisees.

They saw that some of his disciples ate with hands that were defiled. “Defiled” (koinais) literally means “common”: ordinary, not set apart as holy, and therefore ritually unclean. The issue is not dirt. It is a ceremony of purity.

That is, unwashed. Mark explains the term for his Gentile readers, probably in Rome, who would not know what “common hands” meant.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was careless about hygiene, or that his disciples were slovenly. The washing in question had nothing to do with germs. It was a religious rite that the law of Moses did not command for ordinary people.

In a sentence. Religious inspectors from Jerusalem noticed that Jesus’ disciples did not perform the ritual hand-washing before meals.

On a Tuesday. It is easy to notice what others do with their hands and miss what God is doing in front of you. Watch for that in yourself.
verseByVerse.note: The washing in question was a ritual of purity, not hygiene.

parallels.desc: the Pharisee astonished that Jesus did not wash

verseByVerse.quote: (For the Pharisees and all the Jews do not eat unless they wash their hands properly, holding to the tradition of the elders, and when they come from the marketplace, they do not eat unless they wash. And there are many other traditions that they observe, such as the washing of cups and pots and copper vessels and dining couches.) And the Pharisees and the scribes asked him, "Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat with defiled hands?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mark pauses to explain. The Pharisees, and the Jews generally, do not eat without carefully washing their hands, holding to the tradition of the elders. Coming from the market, they do not eat without washing, and they keep many other traditions, such as washing cups, pots, copper vessels and dining couches. So the Pharisees and scribes asked Jesus why his disciples did not walk by the tradition of the elders but ate with defiled hands.

For the Pharisees and all the Jews. A generalisation: the Pharisees’ practice had spread widely and was respected by ordinary Jews, even if not all kept it strictly.

Wash their hands properly. Literally “with a fist” (pygmē). The exact meaning is uncertain. It may mean cupping one hand to pour water over the other, washing up to the wrist, or rubbing the fist in the palm. Whatever the gesture, it was a precise ritual.

Holding to the tradition of the elders. Key phrase. The “tradition” (paradosis, “what is handed down”) was the body of oral rules that the rabbis had built around the written law of Moses, to apply it to every situation and, as they said, to “build a fence around the law” so that no one would come near breaking it. It was later written down in the Mishnah (about AD 200). The Pharisees believed it had been given to Moses on Sinai alongside the written law and was equally binding. Jesus will deny that.

And when they come from the marketplace, they do not eat unless they wash. In the market you might brush against a Gentile, or a Jew who was unclean, or touch something unclean. So you washed, or even immersed yourself (the Greek is literally “baptise themselves”), before eating.

The washing of cups and pots and copper vessels and dining couches. Vessels could become unclean (Leviticus 11:32–35), and the tradition multiplied the rules. Some manuscripts lack “and dining couches”, which was probably added later; the meaning is unaffected.

Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders. To “walk” is the Jewish way of speaking of how you live (the rabbis called their rules halakah, from the word for walking). The question is an accusation: your disciples are disobeying the recognised authorities, and you as their teacher are responsible.

In a sentence. The tradition of the elders demanded ritual washings of hands and vessels, and the Pharisees challenged Jesus because his disciples ignored it.

On a Tuesday. Every church and family builds habits around obedience. Some are wise. But ask which of your rules come from God and which only from “the way we do things”.
verseByVerse.note: Mark explains Jewish customs for readers who did not know them — likely Gentile Christians, perhaps in Rome. The “tradition of the elders” was the body of oral rules built around the law.

parallels.desc: zealous for the traditions of my fathers

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Well did Isaiah prophesy of you hypocrites, as it is written, 'This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.' You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered that Isaiah prophesied rightly about them, hypocrites that they were: this people honours God with their lips, but their heart is far from him; they worship him in vain, teaching human commandments as doctrine. They had left God’s commandment behind to hold on to human tradition.

Well did Isaiah prophesy of you. Jesus does not answer the question about hand-washing directly. He goes to the root: the authority of their tradition. Isaiah 29:13, written about Jerusalem in the eighth century BC, applied fully to these men. A prophecy can describe a recurring pattern that is fulfilled again and again, and supremely in the generation that met the Messiah.

You hypocrites. The only time Mark uses the word. A hypokritēs was an actor on a stage, someone wearing a mask. Their religion was performance: right on the outside, empty within.

This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. The heart, in the Bible, is the centre of the person: thought, will and love. Worship that is only on the lips is not worship. God looks at the heart (1 Samuel 16:7).

In vain do they worship me. “In vain” (matēn): pointlessly, to no effect. God does not accept it.

Teaching as doctrines the commandments of men. The second fault. Not only is their heart wrong, their authority is wrong. They put human rules on the same level as God’s word, and bind consciences where God has not bound them. Mark quotes Isaiah from the Greek translation (the Septuagint), which makes this point especially clearly.

You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men. The verdict. “Leave” (aphentes): abandon, let go. “Hold” (krateite): grip tightly. They had let go of God’s word with one hand while holding human tradition firmly with the other. Note the contrast: God’s commandment, men’s tradition. That is the distinction they had blurred.

Where Christians differ: Scripture and tradition. Roman Catholic teaching holds that Scripture and sacred tradition together form one deposit of revelation, both to be received with equal reverence, interpreted by the teaching office of the church. Protestants hold sola Scriptura: Scripture alone is the final authority, and every tradition, however old and useful, must be tested by it. Protestants value tradition (the creeds, the councils, the wisdom of the church) as a servant, not as a master. Verdict: this passage is one of the clearest grounds for the Reformation principle. Jesus judges a revered, ancient tradition, believed to come from Moses, by the written word of God, and condemns it where it contradicts that word.

In a sentence. Jesus called the Pharisees hypocrites whose worship was empty, because they had abandoned God’s command and held fast to human tradition.

For worship. Before you sing on Sunday, ask whether your heart is near to God or only your lips. And measure every custom in your church by Scripture.

parallels.desc: this people draw near with their mouth
