verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "You have a fine way of rejecting the commandment of God in order to establish your tradition! For Moses said, 'Honor your father and your mother'; and, 'Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus went on, with biting irony: what a fine way they had of setting aside God’s commandment to establish their own tradition! For Moses said, Honour your father and mother, and whoever curses father or mother must be put to death.

You have a fine way of rejecting the commandment of God. “Fine” (kalōs, “well, beautifully”) is sarcastic: how skilfully you do it! “Rejecting” (atheteite) means setting aside, declaring void. The word shows that their tradition did not simply add to the law; it cancelled it.

In order to establish your tradition. Some manuscripts read “to keep your tradition”. Either way, the tradition had become the goal, and God’s law the obstacle.

For Moses said. Note that Jesus treats Moses’ words as God’s commandment (v. 8) and God’s word (v. 13). What Moses wrote, God said.

Honor your father and your mother. The fifth commandment (Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16), the first commandment with a promise (Ephesians 6:2). In Jewish thought it included supporting your parents in old age, when they could no longer work. There were no pensions; children were their parents’ security.

And, Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die. Exodus 21:17 (also Leviticus 20:9). “Reviles” means speaks evil of, curses, treats with contempt. The death penalty showed how seriously God took dishonouring parents. Jesus quotes the strongest form of the law to show what the Pharisees were evading.

In a sentence. Jesus mocked the skill with which the Pharisees set aside God’s plain command to honour father and mother, a command God took with the utmost seriousness.

On a Tuesday. Honouring your parents includes caring for them when they are old. No religious duty excuses you from it (1 Timothy 5:4, 8).

verseByVerse.quote: But you say, 'If a man tells his father or his mother, "Whatever you would have gained from me is Corban"' (that is, given to God)— then you no longer permit him to do anything for his father or mother, thus making void the word of God by your tradition that you have handed down. And many such things you do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you say: if someone tells his father or mother that whatever support they would have had from him is Corban, that is, a gift dedicated to God, then you no longer let him do anything for his father or mother. So you cancel God’s word by the tradition you hand down. And you do many things like this.

Corban. A Hebrew word (qorban) meaning an offering, something brought near to God (Leviticus 2:1). Mark translates it: “given to God”. A man could declare his property or money Corban, dedicated to the temple. The vow did not always mean he handed it over at once; he might keep using it himself. But it could no longer be used for anyone else, including his parents.

Whatever you would have gained from me. The son speaks to his parents: the help you would have had from me is now dedicated. Perhaps in a quarrel, perhaps in anger, a son could take a vow that shut his parents out of his support.

Then you no longer permit him to do anything for his father or mother. This is the heart of the charge. Even if the son regretted the vow, the scribes held him to it, because a vow to God was sacred (Numbers 30:2). They used one law, about vows, to cancel another, about parents, and chose the interpretation that cancelled the greater command. Later rabbis, to their credit, allowed such vows to be released in cases like this.

Thus making void the word of God. “Making void” (akyrountes) is a legal word: annulling, cancelling the authority of a document. Human tradition had annulled God’s word.

By your tradition that you have handed down. Theirs, not God’s. They pass it on and it grows.

And many such things you do. Corban is one example, not the only one.

What it does not mean. Not that vows and giving to God do not matter. But no religious act can be a cover for neglecting the plain duties of love that God has commanded. God does not want gifts that are taken from the mouths of your parents.

In a sentence. By the Corban rule, the scribes let a man dedicate to God the support he owed his parents, and so they annulled God’s word by their tradition.

On a Tuesday. Watch for spiritual-sounding reasons to avoid costly love: “I’m too busy with church”, “That money is for the Lord”. God is not honoured by neglect of the people he has given you.
verseByVerse.note: Property declared Corban — dedicated to God — could no longer be used to support one’s parents.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the people to him again and said to them, "Hear me, all of you, and understand: There is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him, but the things that come out of a person are what defile him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus called the crowd to him again and said: listen to me, all of you, and understand. Nothing outside a person that goes into him can defile him. What comes out of a person is what defiles him.

And he called the people to him again. Jesus turns from the experts to the crowd. This is not a private debate; it concerns everyone.

Hear me, all of you, and understand. A solemn call to attention, like “He who has ears to hear” (4:9). What follows is weighty and easy to misunderstand.

There is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him. A revolutionary statement. The whole system of food laws (Leviticus 11; Deuteronomy 14) and the Pharisees’ hand-washings rested on the idea that what you eat or touch can make you unclean before God. Jesus says: not in the deepest sense. Uncleanness that separates you from God is not a matter of what goes into your stomach.

But the things that come out of a person are what defile him. Real defilement is moral, not ceremonial. It comes from within. Jesus does not explain the riddle yet; he calls it a parable (v. 17), and explains it to the disciples in private.

Textual note. Some manuscripts add verse 16: If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear. It is missing from the earliest and best manuscripts and was probably added from 4:9 and 4:23. The ESV puts it in a footnote, which is why the verse numbers jump from 15 to 17.

What it does not mean. Not that the Old Testament food laws were wrong or foolish. God gave them, for a time, as a picture of holiness and to mark Israel off from the nations. Jesus reveals what they were pointing to, and that their time is ending.

In a sentence. Jesus told the crowd that nothing entering a person from outside can defile him; what defiles is what comes out of him.

On a Tuesday. You cannot make yourself clean before God by what you avoid eating, touching or watching, important as those choices are. The problem is deeper: it is the heart.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 16: “If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.”

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had entered the house and left the people, his disciples asked him about the parable. And he said to them, "Then are you also without understanding? Do you not see that whatever goes into a person from outside cannot defile him, since it enters not his heart but his stomach, and is expelled?" (Thus he declared all foods clean.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he had left the crowd and gone into the house, his disciples asked him about the parable. He said: are you also without understanding? Do you not see that whatever goes into a person from outside cannot defile him, because it does not enter his heart but his stomach, and passes out? (So he declared all foods clean.)

And when he had entered the house and left the people. The pattern of Mark 4: public teaching in riddles, private explanation to the disciples (4:10, 34).

His disciples asked him about the parable. “Parable” here means a riddle, a saying that needs unlocking. Matthew tells us Peter asked (Matthew 15:15).

Then are you also without understanding? “Also”: like the crowd, like the Pharisees. A rebuke that runs through Mark’s middle section, as the disciples keep failing to understand (6:52; 8:17–21).

Since it enters not his heart but his stomach. The logic is simple. Food goes to the digestive system, not to the heart, the moral and spiritual centre. It cannot reach the place where a person is clean or unclean before God.

And is expelled. Literally “goes out into the latrine”. Mark is frank: food passes through the body and out. It has no effect on your soul.

Thus he declared all foods clean. Key phrase. Mark’s comment, in brackets, drawing out the implication for his readers. Jesus’ words meant the end of the food laws. Mark wrote probably with Peter’s preaching behind him, and Peter himself learned this lesson slowly: he had to be shown a vision of unclean animals and told three times, What God has made clean, do not call common (Acts 10:15). The church settled it at the Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15), and Paul taught it plainly (Romans 14:14; Colossians 2:16–17; 1 Timothy 4:3–5).

Why the food laws ended. They had a purpose: to separate Israel from the nations and to teach that God is holy and his people must be distinct (Leviticus 20:24–26). In Christ, the wall between Jew and Gentile is broken down (Ephesians 2:14–15), and the gospel goes to all nations. Holiness is now marked not by diet but by a changed heart. The shadow gives way to the substance (Hebrews 9:10).

Textual note. In the Greek, “declaring clean” is a participle, and older translations (like the King James) attached it to the latrine: “purging all meats”. Most modern scholars, following the ancient interpreters Origen and Chrysostom, take it as Mark’s comment on Jesus’ words, as the ESV does.

In a sentence. Jesus explained that food goes into the stomach, not the heart, and cannot defile anyone, and so he declared all foods clean.

On a Tuesday. You are free to eat with thanks (1 Timothy 4:4). But use that freedom with love toward those whose consciences are weaker (Romans 14:20–21).
verseByVerse.note: The food laws of Leviticus 11 had marked Israel off from the nations; Mark draws out that Jesus set them aside.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "What comes out of a person is what defiles him. For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, coveting, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, foolishness. All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said: what comes out of a person is what defiles him. For from within, out of the human heart, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, greed, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride and foolishness. All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person.

For from within, out of the heart of man. The source of sin is not outside us, in our environment, our food, our upbringing or the company we keep, though all these can tempt and shape us. The source is the heart. “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick” (Jeremiah 17:9). This is the biblical doctrine of human sinfulness: we sin because we are sinners.

Evil thoughts. First, because they are the root of the rest. “Thoughts” (dialogismoi) means reasonings, schemes, the plans of the mind. Every evil act begins as an evil thought.

The list. Twelve vices follow. The first six are in the plural in Greek, and describe acts. The last six are singular, and describe dispositions.

  • Sexual immorality (porneiai): any sexual activity outside marriage.
  • Theft; murder; adultery: three of the Ten Commandments.
  • Coveting (pleonexiai): greed, the restless desire to have more. The tenth commandment.
  • Wickedness (ponēriai): malice, the active desire to harm.
  • Deceit (dolos): cunning, trickery, the bait on a hook.
  • Sensuality (aselgeia): unrestrained, shameless indulgence, flaunting appetite without caring who sees.
  • Envy: literally “an evil eye”, the grudging look at another’s good.
  • Slander (blasphēmia): abusive speech against God or people.
  • Pride (hyperēphania): arrogance, showing yourself above others. Used only here in the Gospels.
  • Foolishness (aphrosynē): not lack of intelligence but moral folly, the senselessness of the person who lives as if there were no God (Psalm 14:1).

All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person. Not hands, cups or food. These. The Pharisees were careful about washing hands and careless about the heart. Jesus reverses their priorities.

What it does not mean. Not that outward actions don’t matter, or that a person who sins in deed can excuse himself because his heart is “good”. The point is the reverse: the heart is not good, which is why the deeds are evil. And not that outside influences are harmless. But removing temptation will not make a sinful heart clean. Only God can do that, by giving a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26; Psalm 51:10).

In a sentence. What defiles a person is the evil that comes out of the heart: thoughts, acts and attitudes that show the heart itself is corrupt.

On a Tuesday. When you sin today, do not blame circumstances or other people. Trace it to your heart, confess it, and ask God for the clean heart only he can create.

parallels.desc: the heart is deceitful above all things

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–37 — Two Healings Beyond Israel’s Borders
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Tyre (vv. 24–30). Having just dismantled the boundary between clean and unclean, Jesus walks across it. He goes north into pagan Phoenicia, tries to stay hidden, and fails within hours — because a woman with a demonised daughter has heard he is there. What passes between them is the hardest exchange in the Gospel and one of the greatest lessons in prayer anywhere in Scripture.

The Decapolis (vv. 31–37). Then a long looping journey back down the eastern side of the lake — through Gentile country the whole way — and a man is brought to him who is deaf and can barely speak. Jesus takes him away from the crowd, uses touch instead of words because touch is the only language the man can receive, looks up, groans, and says one word.

The two halves belong together and the order is not accidental. The teaching cleared the ground: nothing outside a man defiles him. The healings show what that means in practice — a Phoenician mother and a Gentile deaf man, both of them outside every boundary Israel had, both of them served.

And the crowd's verdict at the end is bigger than they know: he has done all things well.
verseByVerse.theology:
Was Jesus being cruel to the Syrophoenician woman? It is the first question any honest reader asks, and it deserves a straight answer rather than an embarrassed one.

Three things take the sting out without softening the difficulty. The word first (v. 27) is the hinge: let the children be fed first. That is not a refusal; it is an order of service, and it implies a second course. Paul states the same order without apology — to the Jew first and also to the Greek (Rom. 1:16). The dogs are under the table (v. 28), and the picture is domestic: not the scavengers of the street but the household pets under the table while the family eats. They are inside the house. And the outcome is the loudest commentary of all — he grants what she asks, immediately, at a distance, and Matthew records him saying O woman, great is your faith! (Matt. 15:28).

He was not insulting her. He was handing her a picture with a door in it, to see whether she would find the door. She did, in one sentence, and it is the only exchange in the Gospels where someone answers Jesus back and he says they are right.

And the deaf man's healing is the new creation beginning. The crowd's he has done all things well echoes Genesis 1:31 — God saw everything he had made, and it was very good. And he even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak is Isaiah's sign of the age of the Messiah: then... the ears of the deaf unstopped... and the tongue of the mute sing for joy (Isa. 35:5–6). They meant only that this healer was impressive. They were quoting the first page of the Bible and the promise of the last days in the same breath.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a man who could not hear, brought by friends who could — because he could not hear the news, could not ask, and could not have explained what he needed.

Now: every person who is carried to Christ by somebody else. It is the four on the roof in chapter 2 all over again, and it is worth noticing how often in this Gospel the person healed did not get there under their own power.

And look at how he handles him. He takes him aside from the crowd privately. A deaf man in a jostling crowd is a man being stared at and unable to follow a word of it. Jesus removes him from the audience before he touches him — which is a rebuke to every way of helping people that requires the helped to be visible.

Then he uses touch, because touch is the only language the man has: fingers into the ears, saliva on the tongue, a look up to heaven to say where this is coming from. It is not a ritual; it is a conversation conducted in the only vocabulary available. He tells the man what is about to happen to him in signs he can read.

And he sighed. Standing in front of one ruined pair of ears, the Creator groans — as Paul says the whole creation is making, and we with it, waiting for redemption (Rom. 8:22–23). He is not indifferent to what has been done to his world. He feels it, in the body he took, over one man nobody has named.

verseByVerse.quote: And from there he arose and went away to the region of Tyre and Sidon. And he entered a house and did not want anyone to know, yet he could not be hidden. But immediately a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit heard of him and came and fell down at his feet. Now the woman was a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by birth. And she begged him to cast the demon out of her daughter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From there Jesus went to the region of Tyre and Sidon. He entered a house and wanted no one to know, but he could not be hidden. Immediately a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit heard of him, came, and fell at his feet. She was a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by birth, and she begged him to drive the demon out of her daughter.

The placing of the story. Mark puts this straight after Jesus declared all foods clean. The barrier of the food laws between Jew and Gentile has just been removed in principle, and now Jesus goes into Gentile territory and a Gentile woman receives his blessing. The teaching is followed by the picture.

And from there he arose and went away to the region of Tyre and Sidon. Tyre was a great Phoenician port about 40 miles (65 km) north-west of Capernaum, in modern Lebanon, with Sidon further north. It was Gentile, pagan, and historically an enemy of Israel; the prophets denounced it (Ezekiel 26–28). Jesus had said that if his mighty works had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented (Matthew 11:21). People from there had already come to hear him (3:8).

And did not want anyone to know. He was seeking rest and privacy with his disciples, away from Herod’s territory and the crowds, and perhaps time to teach them.

Yet he could not be hidden. His fame had gone before him.

A woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit. “Little daughter” (thygatrion) is a tender word, the same as Jairus used (5:23). A mother’s desperate love drives her.

And fell down at his feet. The posture of a suppliant, of worship. She asks as one who has no claim.

Now the woman was a Gentile. Literally “a Greek”: Greek-speaking, and so a Gentile, not a Jew.

A Syrophoenician by birth. From Phoenicia, which was part of the Roman province of Syria (as distinct from the Libyan Phoenicians of North Africa, around Carthage). Matthew calls her a Canaanite (Matthew 15:22), using the ancient name of Israel’s enemies. Everything about her is outside: a woman, a Gentile, from a pagan city, with a demon-possessed child.

In a sentence. In Gentile Tyre, where Jesus sought privacy, a Syrophoenician mother fell at his feet and begged him to free her daughter from a demon.

On a Tuesday. No one is too far outside to come to Jesus. Bring him your children’s needs as this mother did, on your knees.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre was a Gentile port city on the coast north-west of Galilee. “Syrophoenician” means a Phoenician from the Roman province of Syria; Matthew calls her a Canaanite.

parallels.desc: Elijah and the widow of Zarephath, near Sidon

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to her, "Let the children be fed first, for it is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to her: let the children be fed first, for it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.

A hard saying. This sounds harsh, and it is meant to be taken seriously, not explained away. But it must be read carefully.

Let the children be fed first. The children are Israel, God’s covenant people. The bread is the blessing of the Messiah’s ministry. Jesus’ mission in his earthly life was first to Israel (Matthew 15:24; 10:5–6). This was God’s order of salvation: “to the Jew first and also to the Greek” (Romans 1:16). Note the word first, which only Mark records. It implies that the Gentiles will be fed after. The door is not shut; there is an order.

For it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs. “Dogs” was a common Jewish insult for Gentiles, as unclean as street dogs. But Jesus uses a diminutive, kynaria, “little dogs”, house dogs, pets under the table, not the scavengers of the street. The picture is of a household at a meal: you don’t take food from the children’s plates and give it to the family pets.

Why speak like this? Several reasons come together. First, it states the truth of salvation history: Israel had a covenant priority that she did not. Second, it tests her faith, as God tested Abraham and Jacob, and draws it out into the open. Jesus already knew what he would do. Third, the saying was a parable, an opening she could enter. His tone and look we cannot see; the house-dog word and the “first” were not a closed door.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus despised Gentiles, or was racist, or that he learned from her to widen his mission, as some modern readers suggest. He had already healed Gentiles (5:1–20) and declared all foods clean (v. 19). He is in control of this conversation from beginning to end.

In a sentence. Jesus told the woman that Israel must be fed first, like children at a meal before the house dogs, testing her faith while leaving the door open.

On a Tuesday. When God seems to say no, or not yet, do not walk away. Keep coming. His delays often draw out faith.
verseByVerse.note: “Dogs” was a common Jewish insult for Gentiles; here the picture is of household dogs under the table. “First” implies the Gentiles’ turn will come.

parallels.desc: to the Jew first and also to the Greek

verseByVerse.quote: But she answered him, "Yes, Lord; yet even the dogs under the table eat the children's crumbs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
She answered: yes, Lord; yet even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.

Yes, Lord. She accepts what he has said. She does not argue that she deserves the bread, or protest the word “dogs”. She agrees with his description of her. “Lord” (kyrie) can mean simply “sir”, but here it carries more: she acknowledges his authority. She is the only person in Mark to call Jesus “Lord”.

Yet even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs. Brilliant faith. She takes his own picture and finds hope inside it. Yes, I am a dog, not a child. But dogs in a house are fed too: the crumbs that fall from the table belong to them. I am not asking for the children’s bread, only a crumb. And a crumb of your power is enough to heal my daughter.

Faith that wins. What makes her faith great (Matthew 15:28)? She is humble: she claims nothing. She is persistent: she does not give up at an apparent refusal. And she is confident: she believes there is so much grace in Jesus that even what falls from the table is enough. She takes the place of having no claim and appeals to his abundance. That is exactly what faith is.

The contrast. In this chapter, the religious experts heard Jesus’ word and resisted it, and even the disciples failed to understand (v. 18). This Gentile woman understood his parable at once and answered it with faith.

In a sentence. Agreeing that she had no claim, the woman asked only for the crumbs that fall to the house dogs, trusting that a crumb of his grace was enough.

For worship. We come to God in exactly her posture: no merit, no claim, but complete confidence in the abundance of his mercy. “Yes, Lord; yet …” is a model prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to her, "For this statement you may go your way; the demon has left your daughter." And she went home and found the child lying in bed and the demon gone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to her: because of this answer, go; the demon has left your daughter. She went home and found the child lying on the bed, and the demon gone.

For this statement you may go your way. Literally “because of this word”. Her answer expressed faith, and Jesus honoured it. Matthew records his words: O woman, great is your faith! (Matthew 15:28).

The demon has left your daughter. Healing at a distance. The girl was not present; Jesus did not go to her, touch her or speak to the demon. His word, spoken in one house, freed her in another. Only one other healing in the Gospels is like this: the centurion’s servant (Matthew 8:5–13), also for a Gentile, also commended for great faith. In both, the Gentile is blessed from a distance, perhaps a picture of how the nations would receive Christ’s blessing after his ascension, without seeing him.

And she went home. She believed his word without any sign, and went.

And found the child lying in bed and the demon gone. “Lying” (beblēmenon, “thrown down”) may suggest she had been exhausted by the final convulsion, as with the boy in 9:26. Now she is at rest. The demon is gone, permanently.

In a sentence. Because of her answer of faith, Jesus freed her daughter by a word from a distance, and she went home to find the child at peace.

On a Tuesday. Christ’s word reaches where you cannot. Pray for those far away, and trust him to act.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he returned from the region of Tyre and went through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, in the region of the Decapolis. And they brought to him a man who was deaf and had a speech impediment, and they begged him to lay his hand on him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus left the region of Tyre and went through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, into the region of the Decapolis. People brought to him a man who was deaf and could hardly speak, and begged him to lay his hand on him.

Then he returned from the region of Tyre and went through Sidon. A long detour. Sidon is about 25 miles (40 km) north of Tyre, the wrong direction for the Sea of Galilee. Then he went south-east, around, to the Decapolis on the eastern side of the lake. A journey of perhaps 120 miles (200 km) on foot, and months long. Jesus was spending time in Gentile territory, perhaps to be alone with his disciples, away from Herod and the crowds of Galilee.

In the region of the Decapolis. The “Ten Cities”, a league of Greek cities, mainly east of the Jordan. This is where the man freed from Legion had been telling what Jesus had done for him (5:20). Now people bring their sick to Jesus there. The witness had borne fruit.

A man who was deaf and had a speech impediment. “Speech impediment” (mogilalon) means speaking with difficulty, perhaps because he had become deaf and could not hear himself. The word appears only here in the New Testament and once in the Greek Old Testament, in Isaiah 35:6: then shall the tongue of the mute sing for joy. Mark has chosen a word that points to Isaiah’s prophecy of the coming of God to save. See verse 37.

And they begged him to lay his hand on him. Friends brought him, as so often (2:3). He could not hear of Jesus or ask for himself.

In a sentence. After a long journey through Gentile lands, Jesus came to the Decapolis, where people brought him a deaf man who could hardly speak.

On a Tuesday. Some people cannot come to Jesus by themselves. Be one who brings them.
verseByVerse.note: Going from Tyre through Sidon to the Decapolis is a long loop through Gentile territory.

parallels.desc: the healed man proclaims in the Decapolis

verseByVerse.quote: And taking him aside from the crowd privately, he put his fingers into his ears, and after spitting touched his tongue. And looking up to heaven, he sighed and said to him, "Ephphatha," that is, "Be opened."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Taking him aside, away from the crowd, Jesus put his fingers into his ears, spat and touched his tongue. Then, looking up to heaven, he sighed and said to him, Ephphatha, which means, Be opened.

And taking him aside from the crowd privately. A gentle consideration. The man could not hear; in a crowd he would be confused and embarrassed. Jesus deals with him alone, face to face. It was also part of his wish not to become known as a wonder-worker (v. 36).

He put his fingers into his ears, and after spitting touched his tongue. Sign language. The man could not hear words, so Jesus showed him by touch what he was going to do: I am going to open your ears and loose your tongue. Saliva was widely believed in the ancient world to have healing power, but Jesus is not using medicine. He speaks to the man in the only language he could understand, and makes clear that the healing comes from him.

And looking up to heaven. Toward the Father, the source of power, in prayer (6:41; John 11:41). The man could see this too: help comes from God.

He sighed. A deep groan (estenaxen). Grief at the ruin sin and suffering have brought on the world, and compassion for this man. Paul uses the same word for the groaning of creation and of believers longing for redemption (Romans 8:22–23). Jesus feels it.

Ephphatha, that is, Be opened. Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke, preserved by Mark as he preserved talitha cumi (5:41), probably from Peter’s vivid memory. Mark translates it for his readers. “Be opened”: not only the ears but the whole man, closed in silence, is opened.

What it does not mean. Not a magic formula. The early church later used Ephphatha in baptism rituals, touching ears and mouth, but the power was in Jesus, not in the word or the gesture.

In a sentence. Jesus took the deaf man aside, showed him by touch what he would do, looked to heaven, groaned, and commanded, Be opened.

On a Tuesday. Jesus deals with people as individuals, in a way they can understand. Be as thoughtful in how you help others.
verseByVerse.note: Saliva was widely believed to have healing power. “Ephphatha” is Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke.

parallels.desc: spitting on the blind man’s eyes

verseByVerse.quote: And his ears were opened, his tongue was released, and he spoke plainly. And Jesus charged them to tell no one. But the more he charged them, the more zealously they proclaimed it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At once his ears were opened, his tongue was released, and he spoke plainly. Jesus ordered them to tell no one, but the more he ordered them, the more eagerly they proclaimed it.

And his ears were opened. The command was obeyed at once. Literally “his hearings were opened”.

His tongue was released. Literally “the bond of his tongue was loosed”. The picture is of something tied up being set free. Ancient people sometimes spoke of a demon binding the tongue, though Mark does not say this man was possessed. Either way, he was in bondage, and Jesus set him free.

And he spoke plainly. “Plainly” (orthōs): correctly, normally. Not only could he hear, he could speak properly at once, without having to learn.

And Jesus charged them to tell no one. The “messianic secret” again (1:44; 5:43). Jesus did not want to be known chiefly as a miracle-worker. Crowds seeking signs would hinder his teaching, and popular messianic excitement could provoke the authorities before his time. His true identity could only be understood in the light of the cross.

But the more he charged them, the more zealously they proclaimed it. “Proclaimed” (ekēryssen) is the word for preaching. Their disobedience was understandable but still disobedience. The irony is that in Mark, people told to keep silent proclaim, while the disciples later told to proclaim (16:15) were slow to understand.

In a sentence. The man was healed at once and spoke clearly; Jesus told the people to tell no one, but they spread it all the more.

On a Tuesday. Zeal is good, but obedience is better. Tell Christ’s works when and how he wants them told.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were astonished beyond measure, saying, "He has done all things well. He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people were astonished beyond all measure. They said: he has done all things well. He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.

And they were astonished beyond measure. A double strengthening in the Greek, used only here in the New Testament: they were overwhelmed, beyond the beyond.

He has done all things well. An echo of Genesis 1:31: God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good. Jesus’ works are works of new creation, restoring what was broken. The crowd may not have meant this, but Mark’s readers would hear it.

He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak. Mark’s point is Isaiah 35:4–6: Behold, your God will come… He will come and save you. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute sing for joy. The rare word in verse 32 pointed here. Isaiah said these signs would mark the coming of God himself to save. In Jesus, God has come. And these Gentiles of the Decapolis, who had no part in the promises, are the ones who see it.

The wider meaning. In Mark’s structure, this healing of a deaf man stands next to the disciples’ spiritual deafness: Having ears do you not hear? (8:18). The man is a picture of what the disciples need, and of what every person needs. We cannot open our own ears to God’s word. Only Christ can say to us, Be opened.

In a sentence. Overwhelmed, the people declared that Jesus did all things well, unknowingly confirming that the God who promised to open deaf ears had come.

For worship. “He has done all things well” is a confession for every Christian, in joy and in trial. Pray for the Lord to open the ears of those you love, and your own.

parallels.desc: the ears of the deaf unstopped, the tongue of the mute sings

7.theology:
Why does your Bible skip verse 16? The numbers run 15, then 17, and nothing has been lost. The oldest and best manuscripts of Mark have no verse 16; later copies add the familiar refrain if anyone has ears to hear, let him hear — a sentence Jesus certainly said and which Mark records elsewhere (4:9, 4:23) — almost certainly written first in a margin and then mistaken for text. The verse numbers themselves date only from the sixteenth century, so translators could not renumber the New Testament; they left the number empty and put the words in a footnote. Nothing has been removed from your Bible. We simply have older copies than were available in 1611, and honest translators tell you in the margin rather than quietly leaving something in.

Was Jesus cruel to the Syrophoenician woman? Three things settle it without softening the difficulty. The word first is a door standing open — let the children be fed first implies a second course, and Paul states the same order plainly (Rom. 1:16). And the dogs in the picture are under the table (v. 28): not the scavengers of the street but the household pets, already inside the house. And the outcome is the loudest commentary of all — he grants her request at once, at a distance, and Matthew records him saying O woman, great is your faith! (Matt. 15:28). He handed her a picture with a door in it to see whether she would find the door, and she found it in one sentence.

And the crowd at the end echoes two texts without knowing it. He has done all things well sounds like the verdict over the finished creation — God saw everything he had made, and it was very good (Gen. 1:31). He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak is Isaiah 35:5–6, the sign of the day when God himself comes to save.
7.examples:
Then: Corban — the money owed to an old man, put beyond his reach by a holy word, while his son kept the use of it and his reputation.

Now: the shape survives perfectly, and it is almost never dishonest. The man so committed at church four nights a week that his mother has not had a visit since March. The giving that goes to a fund while a brother in the same congregation cannot pay his heating bill. Any arrangement in which something genuinely religious has been set in front of a plain duty God commanded, so that the duty can be dropped without anybody feeling wicked.

So take the test the passage supplies, in one sentence: is anything I do for God currently costing somebody else something God told me to give them?

Note that Jesus does not attack tradition as such — every church has customs and must. He attacks tradition that has been promoted: set level with Scripture, and then used against it. And note what he reaches for when he wants a case anybody can measure. Not prayer, not fasting, not the temple. Whether the old people in your family are being looked after — which is exactly where the New Testament keeps landing (Jas. 1:27; 1 Tim. 5:8).

And one more, from the parenthesis in v. 19. Peter was in that house and heard the explanation with his own ears — and years later needed a sheet let down from heaven three times before he would eat with a Gentile (Acts 10:9–16), and a public rebuke from Paul after that (Gal. 2:11–14). It is possible to be taught a truth plainly by Christ himself and go years before it lands. That is not proof you were never taught. It is what learning looks like in creatures like us — and Peter is the one who tells us he had been told all along.

8.title: Who Do You Say That I Am?
8.text: <sup>1</sup>In those days, when again a great crowd had gathered, and they had nothing to eat, he called his disciples to him and said to them, <sup>2</sup>“I have compassion on the crowd, because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. <sup>3</sup>And if I send them away hungry to their homes, they will faint on the way. And some of them have come from far away.” <sup>4</sup>And his disciples answered him, “How can one feed these people with bread here in this desolate place?” <sup>5</sup>And he asked them, “How many loaves do you have?” They said, “Seven.” <sup>6</sup>And he directed the crowd to sit down on the ground. And he took the seven loaves, and having given thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples to set before the people; and they set them before the crowd. <sup>7</sup>And they had a few small fish. And having blessed them, he said that these also should be set before them. <sup>8</sup>And they ate and were satisfied. And they took up the broken pieces left over, seven baskets full. <sup>9</sup>And there were about four thousand people. And he sent them away. <sup>10</sup>And immediately he got into the boat with his disciples and went to the district of Dalmanutha. <sup>11</sup>The Pharisees came and began to argue with him, seeking from him a sign from heaven to test him. <sup>12</sup>And he sighed deeply in his spirit and said, “Why does this generation seek a sign? Truly, I say to you, no sign will be given to this generation.” <sup>13</sup>And he left them, got into the boat again, and went to the other side. <sup>14</sup>Now they had forgotten to bring bread, and they had only one loaf with them in the boat. <sup>15</sup>And he cautioned them, saying, “Watch out; beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod.” <sup>16</sup>And they began discussing with one another the fact that they had no bread. <sup>17</sup>And Jesus, aware of this, said to them, “Why are you discussing the fact that you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Are your hearts hardened? <sup>18</sup>Having eyes do you not see, and having ears do you not hear? And do you not remember? <sup>19</sup>When I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?” They said to him, “Twelve.” <sup>20</sup>“And the seven for the four thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?” And they said to him, “Seven.” <sup>21</sup>And he said to them, “Do you not yet understand?” <sup>22</sup>And they came to Bethsaida. And some people brought to him a blind man and begged him to touch him. <sup>23</sup>And he took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village, and when he had spit on his eyes and laid his hands on him, he asked him, “Do you see anything?” <sup>24</sup>And he looked up and said, “I see people, but they look like trees, walking.” <sup>25</sup>Then Jesus laid his hands on his eyes again; and he opened his eyes, his sight was restored, and he saw everything clearly. <sup>26</sup>And he sent him to his home, saying, “Do not even enter the village.” <sup>27</sup>And Jesus went on with his disciples to the villages of Caesarea Philippi. And on the way he asked his disciples, “Who do people say that I am?” <sup>28</sup>And they told him, “John the Baptist; and others say, Elijah; and others, one of the prophets.” <sup>29</sup>And he asked them, “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered him, “You are the Christ.” <sup>30</sup>And he strictly charged them to tell no one about him. <sup>31</sup>And he began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes and be killed, and after three days rise again. <sup>32</sup>And he said this plainly. And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him. <sup>33</sup>But turning and seeing his disciples, he rebuked Peter and said, “Get behind me, Satan! For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man.” <sup>34</sup>And calling the crowd to him with his disciples, he said to them, “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. <sup>35</sup>For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel’s will save it. <sup>36</sup>For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul? <sup>37</sup>For what can a man give in return for his soul? <sup>38</sup>For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him will the Son of Man also be ashamed when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.”
8.overview:
Chapter 8 is the hinge of Mark, and everything in the book turns on it. The first half asks who Jesus is; the second half walks to Jerusalem to die.

It is built around sight. Four thousand Gentiles are fed on a hillside and the disciples learn nothing from it. The Pharisees, days after a district was fed from seven loaves, ask for a sign — and he groans, refuses flatly, and gets back in the boat. Then twelve men who have twice carried the surplus away in baskets sit worrying about having one loaf between them, and Jesus asks eight questions in five verses, ending with do you not yet understand?

So Mark puts a blind man next, and has him healed in two stages — the only such healing in the Gospels. I see people, but they look like trees, walking. Not blind. Genuinely seeing. Seeing wrong shapes. It is a picture of exactly what happens next.

At Caesarea Philippi — beneath a cliff of pagan shrines, in a city named for Caesar — Peter gets it right: You are the Christ. And immediately Jesus begins to teach that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and rise, and Mark notes that he said it plainly, the first plain speech in the book. Peter takes him aside to correct him and is called Satan. Then the crowd is called over and told the terms: deny yourself, take up your cross, follow me.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Four Thousand Fed, a Sign Refused, and the Leaven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The second hillside (vv. 1–10). A crowd of four thousand has been with him three days in an empty place, and some of them have a long walk home. Seven loaves, a few small fish, and seven hampers of scraps at the end. It is not a retelling of chapter 6 — Jesus himself will insist on the difference in verse 19.

The demand (vv. 11–13). The Pharisees arrive and ask for a sign from heaven, days after a hillside was fed from a basket. He groans, refuses flatly, gets back in the boat and leaves them.

The boat (vv. 14–21). A warning about leaven is heard as a comment about catering, and Jesus asks eight questions in five verses. The list of what they have seen is read back to them, with the numbers, and it changes nothing.

Everything in this half of the chapter is about seeing — a crowd fed and not understood, a sign demanded by men who have had a hundred, and twelve men in a boat with the bread-maker, worrying about bread. Which is exactly why the next thing Mark records is a man who could not see at all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Are the two feedings one story told twice? It is the standard suggestion, and Mark closes it off himself. In vv. 19–20 Jesus makes the disciples recite both, with the figures — five loaves and five thousand and twelve baskets; seven loaves and four thousand and seven baskets — as two separate events they were present at.

The settings differ too. The five thousand were Jews on the green grass of Galilee, seated in ranks of hundreds and fifties like Israel in the wilderness, with twelve baskets over. The four thousand are in the Decapolis, on Gentile ground, with seven — and some of them have come from far away, which is how the Old Testament speaks of the nations (Isa. 60:4; Josh. 9:6). Twelve is the number of the tribes. Seven is the number of fullness. He fed Israel and had a basket for every tribe; he fed the nations and there was more than enough.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twelve men in a boat, worrying about having one loaf between them, having twice watched thousands fed out of nothing.

Now: exactly the same, and the comedy of it is uncomfortable rather than funny. We have documented evidence of God's provision — the job that came, the diagnosis that was not what we feared, the money that arrived, the marriage that held — and the next shortage finds us doing arithmetic as though none of it had happened.

Note where Jesus locates the failure. Not in their circumstances and not even in their fear. Do you not remember? The problem is memory. They had the facts; they had carried the baskets themselves; and the facts had not been converted into knowledge of the Person who supplied them.

So the practical remedy is unglamorous and it works. Keep a record. Write down what God has actually done, with dates, so that the next crisis meets a list rather than a mood. The disciples could still produce the numbers when they were asked — twelve, seven — and had drawn nothing from them. Israel was commanded to build cairns of stones in the Jordan so that children would ask what they meant (Josh. 4:6–7). We are people who forget, and God has never treated that as a small problem.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days, when again a great crowd had gathered, and they had nothing to eat, he called his disciples to him and said to them, "I have compassion on the crowd, because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. And if I send them away hungry to their homes, they will faint on the way. And some of them have come from far away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In those days a great crowd had gathered again, and they had nothing to eat. Jesus called his disciples and said: I have compassion on the crowd, because they have been with me three days now and have nothing to eat. If I send them home hungry, they will collapse on the way, and some of them have come a long way.

Setting. Jesus is still in the Decapolis, on the eastern, largely Gentile side of the lake (7:31). The feeding of the five thousand (6:30–44) was on the Jewish side. Now, having declared all foods clean (7:19) and given the crumbs to a Gentile woman (7:28), he feeds a Gentile crowd. The children were fed first; now the bread is given to the others too, and not as crumbs.

In those days, when again a great crowd had gathered. The man freed from Legion and the healed deaf man had spread the news in this region (5:20; 7:36). The crowd is the fruit.

I have compassion on the crowd. “Compassion” (splanchnizomai) is a gut-deep word: moved in the inner parts. At the first feeding, Jesus had compassion because they were like sheep without a shepherd (6:34); here the compassion is for their hunger. He cares for bodies as well as souls.

Because they have been with me now three days. They had stayed listening for three days, long enough for any food they brought to run out. Their hunger for his word was greater than their concern for their stomachs.

They will faint on the way. Jesus anticipates their need before anyone asks. At the first feeding, the disciples raised the problem (6:35); here Jesus does.

And some of them have come from far away. “From far away” (apo makrothen) is the phrase the Old Testament and the apostles use for the Gentiles: those who were far off (Joshua 9:6; Isaiah 60:4; Acts 2:39; Ephesians 2:13, 17). Mark’s first readers may well have heard it that way.

Where Christians differ: one feeding or two? Some critical scholars argue that the feedings of the five thousand and the four thousand are two versions of one event. Verdict: Mark and Matthew record both, and Jesus himself refers to both separately, with different numbers and different baskets (vv. 19–20). The differences in place, crowd, numbers, loaves, baskets and timing are real. There were two feedings.

In a sentence. In Gentile territory, Jesus had compassion on a crowd that had stayed with him three days without food, some from far away.

On a Tuesday. Jesus notices needs before they are spoken. Bring him yours, and notice the needs of others before they ask.
verseByVerse.note: This crowd, in the Decapolis, was probably largely Gentile.

verseByVerse.quote: And his disciples answered him, "How can one feed these people with bread here in this desolate place?" And he asked them, "How many loaves do you have?" They said, "Seven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
His disciples answered: how can anyone feed these people with bread here in this desolate place? He asked them: how many loaves do you have? They said: seven.

How can one feed these people with bread here in this desolate place? An astonishing question, after the five thousand. They had seen him do exactly this, perhaps only weeks before, and had gathered twelve baskets of leftovers. Yet they react as if it had never happened. This is the point Jesus will press in verses 17–21: they did not understand about the loaves (6:52). Their forgetfulness is ours. Each new difficulty can make us forget all God has already done.

Desolate place. Erēmia, a wilderness. The setting recalls Israel in the wilderness, where God fed his people with manna. Moses asked the same despairing question: Shall flocks and herds be slaughtered for them, and be enough for them? (Numbers 11:22).

How many loaves do you have? The same question as before (6:38). Jesus begins with what they have. He does not create from nothing here, but multiplies what is offered.

Seven. More than the five loaves of the first feeding, for fewer people. Some see symbolism (seven as the number of completeness, or of the nations: the seven nations of Canaan, or the seventy nations of Genesis 10). Mark does not draw it out, but Jesus does make the numbers count (vv. 19–21).

In a sentence. The disciples, forgetting the five thousand, asked how anyone could feed such a crowd in the wilderness; Jesus asked what they had, and they had seven loaves.

On a Tuesday. Remember what God has done for you before. Yesterday’s faithfulness is the answer to today’s “how can …?”

parallels.desc: Moses asks how so many can be fed

verseByVerse.quote: And he directed the crowd to sit down on the ground. And he took the seven loaves, and having given thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples to set before the people; and they set them before the crowd. And they had a few small fish. And having blessed them, he said that these also should be set before them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He told the crowd to sit down on the ground. He took the seven loaves, gave thanks, broke them and gave them to his disciples to set before the people, and they served the crowd. They also had a few small fish; he blessed them and told them to serve these too.

And he directed the crowd to sit down on the ground. No green grass this time (6:39). It is a later season, or a drier place.

And having given thanks. Eucharistēsas, from which comes “Eucharist”. At the first feeding Mark used “blessed” (6:41), the Jewish form; here “gave thanks”, the word that Paul uses for the Lord’s Supper (1 Corinthians 11:24). The two words mean the same thing: a Jewish blessing before meals was thanks to God. Jesus thanks the Father for the little there is.

He broke them and gave them to his disciples to set before the people. The same sequence as before (6:41) and at the Last Supper (14:22): took, gave thanks, broke, gave. The disciples are the servers, distributing what comes from his hands, as ministers of the gospel do.

And they had a few small fish. Ichthydia, little fish, probably dried or salted.

And having blessed them. A separate blessing for the fish.

What it does not mean. The feeding is not itself the Lord’s Supper, though the words point toward it. It is a real meal, for hungry people, that also shows who Jesus is: the one who provides bread from heaven.

In a sentence. Jesus seated the crowd, gave thanks for the loaves and the few fish, broke them, and gave them to his disciples to distribute.

For worship. Give thanks before you eat, as Jesus did, even when you have little. Thanksgiving is the beginning of every gift being multiplied.

verseByVerse.quote: And they ate and were satisfied. And they took up the broken pieces left over, seven baskets full. And there were about four thousand people. And he sent them away. And immediately he got into the boat with his disciples and went to the district of Dalmanutha.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They ate and were satisfied, and they took up the leftover pieces, seven baskets full. There were about four thousand people. He sent them away, and immediately got into the boat with his disciples and went to the district of Dalmanutha.

And they ate and were satisfied. Everyone, fully. The same phrase as before (6:42). God’s provision is not a token; it fills.

Seven baskets full. The basket here (spyris) is different from the one at the feeding of the five thousand (kophinos, a small wicker basket a Jew might carry). The spyris could be large: Paul was lowered from the wall of Damascus in one (Acts 9:25). Fewer baskets this time, but perhaps more bread. Jesus himself will remind the disciples of the distinction (vv. 19–20).

And there were about four thousand people. Matthew adds: besides women and children (Matthew 15:38).

And he sent them away. Unlike the first feeding, there is no attempt to make him king (John 6:15). These are Gentiles, without the Jewish political hopes of a Messiah.

The district of Dalmanutha. An unknown place, mentioned nowhere else in ancient literature. Matthew has “Magadan” (Matthew 15:39), also unknown, though some manuscripts there read Magdala, the home of Mary Magdalene on the western shore. It must have been somewhere on the western, Jewish side of the lake, because the Pharisees meet him there (v. 11).

In a sentence. Four thousand people ate their fill from seven loaves, with seven large baskets left over, and Jesus crossed back to the Jewish side of the lake.

On a Tuesday. Christ gives more than enough. Whatever you lack, he is not short of supply.
verseByVerse.note: The word for these baskets differs from the one used at the feeding of the five thousand and could mean a large hamper. Dalmanutha’s location is unknown; Matthew says Magadan.

parallels.desc: Paul let down in such a basket

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees came and began to argue with him, seeking from him a sign from heaven to test him. And he sighed deeply in his spirit and said, "Why does this generation seek a sign? Truly, I say to you, no sign will be given to this generation." And he left them, got into the boat again, and went to the other side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees came and began to argue with him, demanding a sign from heaven, to test him. He sighed deeply in his spirit and said: why does this generation seek a sign? Truly, I tell you, no sign will be given to this generation. And he left them, got into the boat again and went to the other side.

The contrast. Gentiles have just been fed by a miracle. Now, back on the Jewish side, the religious leaders demand a sign. They had heard of the healings, the exorcisms, the feedings. It was not evidence they lacked.

Seeking from him a sign from heaven. A “sign from heaven” meant a spectacular proof directly from God, beyond any possibility of doubt: fire from the sky like Elijah, or the sun standing still like Joshua, or manna like Moses. Exorcisms could be explained away as Satan’s work (3:22). They wanted something undeniable, on their terms.

To test him. Peirazontes, the same word used of Satan testing him in the wilderness (1:13). The demand was not sincere inquiry but a trap. If he refused, they could say he had no credentials; if he tried and failed, he was discredited.

And he sighed deeply in his spirit. A stronger word than the sigh of 7:34 (anastenaxas), a groan from the depths. Grief and indignation at their hardness.

Why does this generation seek a sign? “This generation” in the Gospels is a phrase loaded with Old Testament echoes: the wilderness generation that saw God’s works for forty years and still tested him (Psalm 95:8–10; Deuteronomy 32:5, 20). The Pharisees are repeating Israel’s ancient sin.

Truly, I say to you, no sign will be given to this generation. The Greek uses a Hebrew oath form: literally “if a sign shall be given …”, with the unspoken ending, “may God punish me”. The most emphatic possible refusal. Matthew adds: except the sign of Jonah (Matthew 12:39; 16:4), meaning his resurrection. Mark records the flat refusal: no sign of the kind they demand.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus gave no evidence. His whole ministry was full of signs. But he would not perform to order for those who had already decided against him. Signs confirm faith; they do not compel the unwilling (Luke 16:31).

And he left them. A solemn act of judgement. He turned his back and went.

In a sentence. When the Pharisees demanded a sign from heaven to test him, Jesus, groaning in spirit, refused outright and left them.

On a Tuesday. Don’t demand that God prove himself on your terms. He has given enough evidence in Christ, crucified and risen.

verseByVerse.quote: Now they had forgotten to bring bread, and they had only one loaf with them in the boat. And he cautioned them, saying, "Watch out; beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod." And they began discussing with one another the fact that they had no bread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples had forgotten to bring bread and had only one loaf with them in the boat. Jesus warned them: watch out; beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod. And they began discussing with one another that they had no bread.

Now they had forgotten to bring bread. After the seven basketfuls! In the hurry to leave, the leftovers were left behind.

And they had only one loaf with them in the boat. A detail only Mark records. Some see a deeper meaning: the one loaf they did have was Jesus himself, the bread of life (John 6:35). Mark does not say so, but the conversation that follows suggests he expects readers to think it: they were worried about bread with the Lord of the loaves in the boat.

Watch out; beware. Two words of warning together, for emphasis. The tense means: keep on watching.

The leaven of the Pharisees. Leaven, a piece of old fermented dough kept back to start the next batch, works invisibly through the whole lump (1 Corinthians 5:6–8; Galatians 5:9). In Scripture it nearly always pictures a corrupting influence. Luke says the leaven of the Pharisees is hypocrisy (Luke 12:1); Matthew, their teaching (Matthew 16:12). In context, it is their unbelief that demanded signs while refusing to see the ones in front of them.

And the leaven of Herod. Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, who had killed John the Baptist (6:14–29). His leaven was worldliness, political scheming, and the same unbelief: he wanted to see Jesus do a miracle too (Luke 23:8). The Pharisees and Herod’s supporters had already plotted together to destroy Jesus (3:6). Religious hypocrisy and worldly power are different leavens, with the same effect: hardness toward Jesus.

And they began discussing with one another the fact that they had no bread. They missed the point entirely. Jesus speaks of spiritual danger; they think he is scolding them for forgetting lunch.

In a sentence. With only one loaf in the boat, Jesus warned his disciples against the corrupting influence of the Pharisees and Herod, but they thought only of their bread.

On a Tuesday. Watch for the small influences that slowly spread through a life: cynicism, hypocrisy, the worldly mind. They work like yeast, unseen.
verseByVerse.note: Leaven (yeast) works invisibly through a whole lump; it pictures a corrupting influence. Herod stands for worldly power and its politics.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus, aware of this, said to them, "Why are you discussing the fact that you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Are your hearts hardened? Having eyes do you not see, and having ears do you not hear? And do you not remember?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus knew what they were saying and said: why are you discussing having no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Are your hearts hardened? Having eyes, do you not see, and having ears, do you not hear? And do you not remember?

Five questions. Jesus presses them with a rapid series of rebukes, the sharpest he gives the disciples in Mark.

Do you not yet perceive or understand? “Yet”: after all they had seen. They have had more time with him than anyone, and still they miss it.

Are your hearts hardened? The very charge made against the Pharisees (3:5), and the one Mark made about the disciples after the walking on the water (6:52). A hardened heart is not just slow; it is resistant, insensitive to God’s work. It is a sobering thing that Jesus asks this of his own chosen followers. Hardness is not only a problem for enemies.

Having eyes do you not see, and having ears do you not hear? The language of Jeremiah 5:21 and Ezekiel 12:2, about rebellious Israel, and of Isaiah 6:9–10, which Jesus quoted about outsiders (4:12). The disciples were in danger of being like those outside. And the words point to the healings on either side: the deaf man (7:31–37) and the blind man (8:22–26). The disciples need the same miracle in their hearts.

And do you not remember? Memory is essential to faith. Israel was always told to remember what God had done (Deuteronomy 8:2–3), and failed. Forgetfulness of God’s past works leads to anxiety in the present.

What it does not mean. Not that the disciples were reprobate. Jesus rebukes them because he loves them and is teaching them. Hardness in a believer is real and dangerous, but Christ does not abandon his own. Their eyes will be opened, slowly, like the blind man’s (vv. 22–26).

In a sentence. Jesus rebuked his disciples for their spiritual blindness, deafness, forgetfulness and hardened hearts, which left them anxious about bread.

On a Tuesday. When you worry about provision, ask: do I not remember? Make a list of God’s past faithfulness and read it.

verseByVerse.quote: When I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?" They said to him, "Twelve." "And the seven for the four thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?" And they said to him, "Seven." And he said to them, "Do you not yet understand?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many baskets full of pieces did you take up? They said: twelve. And the seven for the four thousand, how many large baskets full? They said: seven. And he said to them: do you not yet understand?

A lesson in arithmetic. Jesus makes them recite the facts. They know the numbers. They had been there and carried the baskets. The problem was not their information but what they made of it.

Twelve … seven. Jesus carefully uses the two different words for basket: kophinous for the twelve, spyridōn for the seven. He remembers precisely.

What should they have understood? At the least, that bread was no problem with Jesus in the boat. He could supply from one loaf, or none. Their worry was needless. But more: the feedings revealed who he is. He is the one who feeds his people in the wilderness, as God did with manna, the shepherd of Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34, the giver of the messianic banquet (Isaiah 25:6). And with twelve baskets on the Jewish side and seven on the Gentile side, perhaps also that his bread was enough for Israel and the nations. Mark leaves the question open, so that the reader too must answer it.

Do you not yet understand? The last word of the scene, a question left hanging. It is the question of the whole first half of Mark: who is this? The answer will come at Caesarea Philippi (v. 29), after the healing of the blind man.

In a sentence. Jesus made the disciples recite the leftovers from both feedings, and left them with the question: do you not yet understand who I am?

On a Tuesday. Knowing the facts of the gospel is not the same as understanding them. Ask God to show you what the facts mean for today.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–38 — Two-Stage Sight and the Great Confession
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The blind man (vv. 22–26). The only healing in the Gospels that happens in two stages, and it is placed here on purpose. A man is led out of the village by the hand, sees people like walking trees, is touched again, and sees clearly. It is a picture of what is about to happen to the men in the boat.

The question (vv. 27–30). At Caesarea Philippi — at the foot of a mountain, beside a cave sacred to Pan, in a city named for Caesar — Jesus asks the question the whole Gospel has been building to, and Peter answers it: You are the Christ.

The correction (vv. 31–33). And immediately Jesus starts teaching them something they cannot bear: that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and rise. Mark says he said it plainly — the first plain speech in the book. Peter takes him aside to put him right, and gets the hardest sentence any disciple ever heard.

The terms (vv. 34–38). Then he calls the crowd over, so that nobody can say the terms were for professionals only, and states them: deny yourself, take up your cross, follow me.

This is the hinge of the Gospel. Everything before it asks who he is. Everything after it walks to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why two touches? Not because the first failed. Mark places this healing between the disciples who have eyes and do not see (v. 18) and Peter's half-sighted confession, and it is an enacted parable of exactly that. I see people, but they look like trees, walking is a precise description of where the Twelve now stand: no longer blind, genuinely seeing, and seeing wrong shapes. Peter will name him Christ in verse 29 and rebuke him in verse 32.

And why "after three days"? Mark writes after three days (v. 31; also 9:31; 10:34) where Matthew and Luke have on the third day, and honest readers have wondered whether that requires a fourth day and breaks the Friday-to-Sunday timeline. It does not; it is simply the Jewish way of counting, in which any part of a day counted as a whole day. Scripture proves it on the spot: the chief priests remember this very prediction as After three days I will rise, and in the same breath ask Pilate for a guard until the third day (Matt. 27:63–64) — both phrases, of one morning, without a flicker of contradiction.

And why "Get behind me, Satan"? Not because Peter was demonic. Because the content of his objection was the wilderness temptation returning through the mouth of a friend: a kingdom without a cross. Jesus had heard it before (1:13), and he will hear it again from passers-by at the foot of the cross itself — save yourself, and come down (15:30). Peter meant it lovingly, which is precisely what made it dangerous.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a crowd in Galilee hearing the words take up his cross, in a country where Varus had crucified two thousand men within living memory. Nobody in that crowd thought of a metaphor. They had seen men carrying the crossbeam through the streets, stripped, jeered at, on a walk with one destination.

Now: we have worn the phrase smooth. A cross has become a difficulty — a hard marriage, an illness, a colleague. That is not what it meant. A man carrying a cross was not a man with a burden; he was a man already condemned, publicly, walking away from everything he had.

And note who is being addressed. Mark says he called the crowd — not just the Twelve. This is not a higher path for the heroic few. It is the entry requirement, stated to the general public, by a man who knew exactly what he was asking because he was going to do it first.

So make it concrete rather than admiring it in the abstract. Deny himself is not going without sugar; it is the removal of the self from the throne — the decision, in a specific matter this week, that what you want is no longer the deciding vote. Name the matter. If you cannot name one, the denial is theoretical.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Bethsaida. And some people brought to him a blind man and begged him to touch him. And he took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village, and when he had spit on his eyes and laid his hands on him, he asked him, "Do you see anything?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They came to Bethsaida. Some people brought a blind man to Jesus and begged him to touch him. He took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village. When he had spat on his eyes and laid his hands on him, he asked: do you see anything?

The placing of the story. Mark has placed this healing, which only he records, at the hinge of his Gospel. Just before it, the disciples were told that they had eyes but did not see (v. 18). Just after it, Peter will confess Jesus as the Christ (v. 29), and yet will not understand what that means (v. 32). The blind man is a picture of the disciples. A matching healing of blind Bartimaeus closes the next section (10:46–52). Between the two blind men, Jesus teaches about the cross.

And they came to Bethsaida. A fishing town at the north end of the lake, where the Jordan flows in, home of Peter, Andrew and Philip (John 1:44). Jesus had pronounced woe on it for its unbelief despite his mighty works (Matthew 11:21).

And he took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village. Personal and gentle. A blind man needs a guide, and Jesus himself becomes his guide. As with the deaf man (7:33), he takes him away from the crowd.

And when he had spit on his eyes and laid his hands on him. Again, touch that the man could feel, telling him what Jesus was doing, since he could not see.

Do you see anything? The only time in the Gospels that Jesus asks about the progress of a healing. It prepares for what follows.

In a sentence. At Bethsaida, Jesus led a blind man by the hand out of the village, touched his eyes, and asked if he could see anything.

On a Tuesday. Let Jesus take you by the hand. He leads the blind on paths they do not know (Isaiah 42:16).
verseByVerse.note: Bethsaida was a fishing town at the north end of the lake, home of Peter, Andrew and Philip.

parallels.desc: Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter

verseByVerse.quote: And he looked up and said, "I see people, but they look like trees, walking." Then Jesus laid his hands on his eyes again; and he opened his eyes, his sight was restored, and he saw everything clearly. And he sent him to his home, saying, "Do not even enter the village."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man looked up and said: I see people, but they look like trees, walking. Then Jesus laid his hands on his eyes again; the man looked intently, his sight was restored, and he saw everything clearly. Jesus sent him home, saying: do not even go into the village.

I see people, but they look like trees, walking. A partial healing. He can see shapes moving, but blurred: upright, vague, like tree trunks. The detail is vivid, and suggests he had once had sight and knew what trees looked like.

Then Jesus laid his hands on his eyes again. The only healing in the Gospels done in two stages.

Why two stages? Not because Jesus’ power was weak, or because the man’s faith was lacking; the text says nothing of his faith. Jesus is in complete control, and chooses to do it this way. The healing is an acted parable. The disciples are at stage one: they see something, but not clearly. Peter will see that Jesus is the Christ (v. 29), but see him blurred, a Christ without a cross (v. 32). They need a second touch. Full sight will come only after the cross and resurrection, and the gift of the Spirit.

And he opened his eyes. Literally “he looked intently” or “stared”: he focused.

His sight was restored, and he saw everything clearly. Three descriptions of complete healing. “Clearly” (tēlaugōs) means “far-shining”: he could see clearly at a distance. Nothing blurred.

Do not even enter the village. Another command to avoid publicity. Go home, not back to the crowds.

In a sentence. After a first touch the man saw blurred shapes; after a second, he saw everything clearly, an acted picture of the disciples’ partial sight.

On a Tuesday. If you see Christ only dimly, keep coming to him. He finishes what he begins (Philippians 1:6).
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark records this two-stage healing; it sits just before the disciples see who Jesus is — but only in part.

parallels.desc: the eyes of the blind opened

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus went on with his disciples to the villages of Caesarea Philippi. And on the way he asked his disciples, "Who do people say that I am?" And they told him, "John the Baptist; and others say, Elijah; and others, one of the prophets."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus went on with his disciples to the villages of Caesarea Philippi. On the way he asked them: who do people say that I am? They told him: John the Baptist; others say Elijah; and others, one of the prophets.

The turning point. This is the hinge of Mark’s Gospel. The first half (1:1–8:26) asks: who is Jesus? The second half (8:31–16:8) answers: what kind of Messiah is he, and where is he going? He is going to the cross.

The villages of Caesarea Philippi. Caesarea Philippi was about 25 miles (40 km) north of the Sea of Galilee, at the foot of Mount Hermon, at a spring that is one of the sources of the Jordan. It was a Gentile city, rebuilt by Herod’s son Philip and named in honour of Caesar (and himself). There was a shrine to the god Pan in a cave there, and Herod the Great had built a temple to Augustus as a god. In this place of pagan gods and a divine emperor, Jesus asks who he is.

And on the way. “The way” (hodos) becomes a key word in this section (8:27; 9:33–34; 10:17, 32, 46, 52). Jesus is on the way to Jerusalem and the cross, and disciples are those who follow him on it.

Who do people say that I am? Jesus is not seeking information for himself. He is preparing them to state what they believe.

John the Baptist; and others say, Elijah; and others, one of the prophets. The same opinions reported to Herod (6:14–15). All of them high. People thought Jesus was a great prophet, a messenger from God, even a figure raised from the dead. Elijah was expected to return before the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5). But all of them fall short. They see him as a forerunner or a messenger, not the one to whom the prophets pointed.

In a sentence. Near the pagan shrines of Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asked who people thought he was, and heard that they saw him as a great prophet.

On a Tuesday. Many today still think well of Jesus: a great teacher, a prophet, a good man. That is not enough, and it is not true to who he is.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea Philippi was a Gentile city at the foot of Mount Hermon, north of the Sea of Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: And he asked them, "But who do you say that I am?" Peter answered him, "You are the Christ." And he strictly charged them to tell no one about him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He asked them: but who do you say that I am? Peter answered: you are the Christ. And he strictly ordered them to tell no one about him.

But who do you say that I am? “You” is emphatic and plural: but you, all of you. The question everyone must answer. Public opinion is not enough; Jesus asks for personal confession.

Peter answered him. Peter, as usual, speaks for the Twelve.

You are the Christ. Key word. “Christ” (Christos) translates the Hebrew “Messiah”: the Anointed One. In the Old Testament, kings, priests and prophets were anointed with oil to set them apart for their office. The Messiah was the promised King, the son of David, who would bring in God’s kingdom (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Psalm 2; Isaiah 9:6–7; 11:1–10). Mark’s first line called Jesus “Christ” (1:1); now, for the first time, a human being says it. Peter sees what the crowd did not: Jesus is not a forerunner but the one himself. Matthew records the fuller confession (the Son of the living God) and Jesus’ blessing on Peter (Matthew 16:16–19). Mark, writing probably from Peter’s own preaching, records the bare confession and moves straight to Peter’s failure, as if Peter himself told it that way.

And he strictly charged them to tell no one about him. “Strictly charged” (epetimēsen) is the word for rebuke, the same word used for silencing demons (1:25; 3:12). Why silence? Because the title “Messiah” was explosive. Popular hopes imagined a political and military deliverer who would drive out the Romans. Proclaimed now, the title would provoke a revolt or a premature arrest, and would be misunderstood. The disciples themselves did not yet know what kind of Messiah he was, as the next verses show. Only after the cross and the resurrection could the title be preached rightly (9:9).

In a sentence. Peter confessed that Jesus is the Christ, the promised King, and Jesus ordered them to tell no one until they understood what that meant.

On a Tuesday. Jesus asks you, personally: who do you say I am? Your answer shapes everything.
