verseByVerse.note: “Christ” means anointed one, the Messiah — the promised king. Popular hopes for a political Messiah may explain the command to silence.

verseByVerse.quote: And he began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes and be killed, and after three days rise again. And he said this plainly. And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things, be rejected by the elders, the chief priests and the scribes, be killed, and after three days rise again. He said this plainly. And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him.

And he began to teach them. A new beginning. From now on, Jesus repeatedly teaches about his death (9:31; 10:33–34), the three passion predictions that structure this section of Mark.

The Son of Man. Jesus’ favourite title for himself. It comes from Daniel 7:13–14: one like a son of man, coming with the clouds of heaven, to whom the Ancient of Days gives everlasting dominion over all peoples. It is a title of glory. But it was less politically loaded than “Messiah”, and Jesus fills it with new content: the Son of Man suffers before he reigns.

Must suffer many things. “Must” (dei): divine necessity. Not a tragic accident or a defeat, but God’s plan, written in Scripture (Isaiah 53; Psalm 22; Zechariah 13:7). Jesus goes to the cross because the Father has willed it and he has embraced it (10:45).

And be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes. The three groups that made up the Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish council in Jerusalem. The leaders of God’s people will reject God’s Messiah, the stone the builders rejected (Psalm 118:22, quoted in 12:10).

And be killed. Unthinkable for a Messiah, in Jewish expectation.

And after three days rise again. Jewish idiom for “on the third day” (compare Matthew 16:21). The resurrection is part of the prediction from the start. The disciples seem not to have heard it at all.

And he said this plainly. “Plainly” (parrēsia): openly, no longer in riddles. Only Mark records this. Up to now Jesus had taught in parables; now he speaks of the cross directly.

And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him. Astonishing. The same word as in verse 30: Jesus rebuked them to silence, and now Peter rebukes Jesus. Peter, who has just confessed him as Messiah, cannot accept a suffering Messiah. To him the idea was a contradiction. The Messiah was supposed to conquer, not die. Matthew records his words: Far be it from you, Lord! (Matthew 16:22).

In a sentence. Jesus began to teach plainly that he must suffer, be rejected, be killed and rise again, and Peter, appalled, took him aside to rebuke him.

On a Tuesday. We, like Peter, want a Christ who fits our expectations. Let the cross reshape what you think Christ is for.

verseByVerse.quote: But turning and seeing his disciples, he rebuked Peter and said, "Get behind me, Satan! For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus turned, looked at his disciples, and rebuked Peter: get behind me, Satan! For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man.

But turning and seeing his disciples. Only Mark records this. Jesus looks at the others: Peter’s thought was theirs too, and they needed to hear the answer. The rebuke is public, because the error is dangerous.

He rebuked Peter. The third use of the word in the scene. Peter rebuked Jesus; Jesus rebukes Peter.

Get behind me. Literally “Go behind me”. Back to your place, as a follower. The same words, “behind me”, appear in Jesus’ call: Follow me (literally “come behind me”, 1:17). Peter had stepped in front of Jesus, trying to lead; he must go back behind and follow.

Satan! A shocking word to use of his chief disciple. But Peter was doing what Satan did in the wilderness: tempting Jesus to reach the kingdom without the cross (Matthew 4:8–10). Satan was using Peter’s love and ignorance. The temptation was real for Jesus, which is why the answer is so sharp. Peter was not possessed; he was being Satan’s mouthpiece.

For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man. “Setting your mind” (phroneis) means thinking, having an outlook, a mindset (Philippians 2:5; Romans 8:5). Peter thought as people naturally think: power, success, avoiding suffering. God’s way is the way of the cross. This is the great clash of the Gospel: human thinking against divine thinking about what the Messiah is and does (1 Corinthians 1:18–25).

What it does not mean. Not that Peter was rejected. Jesus still loved him, kept him, and later restored him (John 21:15–19). But even a sincere believer can speak for Satan when he puts human comfort above God’s purposes.

In a sentence. Jesus rebuked Peter as Satan for trying to turn him from the cross, because Peter was thinking in human terms, not God’s.

On a Tuesday. When you advise a fellow Christian to avoid costly obedience, check whose thoughts you are thinking.

verseByVerse.quote: And calling the crowd to him with his disciples, he said to them, "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He called the crowd to him with his disciples and said: if anyone would come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.

And calling the crowd to him with his disciples. What follows is not only for the Twelve, or for a spiritual elite. It is for everyone who would follow Jesus. Mark’s readers in Rome, who may already have been facing persecution under Nero, would hear it as addressed to them.

The logic. The way of the Messiah is the way of the cross; therefore the way of his followers is the way of the cross. As the master, so the disciple.

If anyone would come after me. “Would” (thelei): wants to, wills to. Discipleship is a choice, and Jesus sets out its terms honestly before anyone makes it.

Let him deny himself. To deny yourself (aparnēsasthō heauton) is not to deny yourself things, like giving up chocolate for Lent. It is to say no to self as the centre and master of your life. The same word is used of Peter denying Jesus (14:30, 72): to disown, to say “I do not know him”. The disciple says that of his own self-will: I no longer belong to myself.

And take up his cross. Everyone in the Roman world knew what this meant. A condemned man carried the crossbeam of his own cross to the place of execution, through jeering crowds. It was the walk of a man who had already lost everything and was going to die. To take up the cross is to accept rejection, shame and death, if need be, for Jesus’ sake. Not a metaphor for ordinary troubles (an illness, a difficult relative), but the costly path of loyalty to Jesus in a world that rejects him. Luke adds “daily” (Luke 9:23).

And follow me. Where? To Jerusalem, where he will be crucified. The present tense means keep on following.

What it does not mean. Not that we save ourselves by self-denial, or earn salvation by suffering. Jesus alone bears the cross that atones for sin (10:45). The disciple’s cross is not redemptive; it is the shape of a life that belongs to the one who was crucified. Nor is it a call to seek suffering for its own sake.

In a sentence. Whoever would follow Jesus must say no to self, accept the shame and cost of loyalty to him even to death, and keep on following.

On a Tuesday. Where today does following Jesus mean saying no to yourself? Name it, and take it up.
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution.

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel's will save it. For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul? For what can a man give in return for his soul?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel’s will save it. For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and lose his soul? What can a man give in exchange for his soul?

For whoever would save his life will lose it. “Life” (psychē) means the self, the whole person, both life now and life eternal. The same word is translated “soul” in the next verse. A paradox: hold on to your life, protecting it from the cost of following Jesus, and you lose it, eternally.

But whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel’s will save it. Give your life up, even to death, for Jesus, and you gain it, eternally. “And the gospel’s”: only Mark adds this. To be loyal to Jesus is to be loyal to the message about him. Mark’s readers might lose their lives for preaching it.

For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul? The language of a business deal. Imagine the greatest possible gain: the whole world, all its wealth, pleasure and power. Now weigh it against your soul. You would be bankrupt. “Forfeit” (zēmiōthēnai) means suffer the loss of, be fined.

For what can a man give in return for his soul? Nothing can buy it back once lost. The question echoes Psalm 49:7–8: no man can ransom another… for the ransom of their life is costly. No human price can redeem a soul. Only one ransom can, and Jesus will give it (10:45).

What it does not mean. Not that every Christian will be martyred, or that only martyrs are saved. But every Christian must be willing, and in a thousand smaller ways each day, the principle holds: what you hold back for yourself you lose; what you give to Christ you keep.

In a sentence. To cling to your life is to lose it, and to lose it for Christ and the gospel is to save it, since nothing in the world is worth a soul.

On a Tuesday. Weigh today’s choices on Jesus’ scales. What gain would you trade your soul for? Nothing is worth it.

parallels.desc: the ransom of a life is costly

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him will the Son of Man also be ashamed when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him the Son of Man will also be ashamed when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.

For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words. The pressure to deny Christ was not usually a sword but a sneer. To follow a crucified man was shameful in the Roman world, foolishness and scandal (1 Corinthians 1:23). Being ashamed of Jesus means hiding your allegiance to avoid contempt. “And of my words”: his teaching, including the teaching about the cross just given.

In this adulterous and sinful generation. “Adulterous” is the prophets’ word for Israel’s unfaithfulness to God, like a wife who leaves her husband (Hosea 1–3; Jeremiah 3; Ezekiel 16). The generation that rejects Jesus is unfaithful to God. It is in front of this kind of audience that the disciple is tempted to be ashamed.

Of him will the Son of Man also be ashamed. Measure for measure. Jesus will not acknowledge, at the judgement, those who would not acknowledge him now (Matthew 10:32–33). To be disowned by him then is the ultimate loss.

When he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels. The Son of Man of Daniel 7 again, now in full glory. The one who is about to be rejected and killed will return as judge of all. Notice the claims: the glory is his Father’s, so he is the Son of God; the angels accompany him, so they are his servants. The suffering Messiah and the glorious Judge are the same person.

The structure. Note how the whole passage moves: the cross for Jesus (v. 31), the cross for the disciple (v. 34), and the glory for both (v. 38; 9:1). Suffering now, glory later. That is the pattern of the Christian life (Romans 8:17–18).

In a sentence. Whoever is ashamed of Jesus and his words before an unfaithful world will be disowned by him when he returns in his Father’s glory.

On a Tuesday. Where are you tempted to hide that you belong to Jesus: at work, with friends, online? Remember the day when he will either own you or not.
verseByVerse.note: “Adulterous” is the prophets’ word for Israel’s unfaithfulness to God.

8.theology:
Two feedings, not one story told twice. Jesus makes the disciples recite both with the figures (vv. 19–20): five loaves, five thousand, twelve baskets; seven loaves, four thousand, seven baskets. Twelve baskets for Israel, one for each tribe; seven for the nations, the number of fullness. And some of them have come from far away is how Scripture speaks of the Gentiles coming in (Isa. 60:4; Eph. 2:13).

Why no sign? Not because evidence is illegitimate — he had given a great deal and would give more. What he refuses is a miracle produced on demand as the price of belief, from men who have already shown what they do with the evidence they have. If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31) — which proved exactly right, since somebody did, and the men who got the report first paid soldiers to say the body was stolen (Matt. 28:12–13).

After three days. Mark's phrase (v. 31; 9:31; 10:34) against Matthew's and Luke's on the third day is not a discrepancy but the Jewish reckoning, in which any part of a day counts as a day. Scripture settles it: the chief priests recall this prediction as After three days I will rise and in the same breath ask Pilate for a guard until the third day (Matt. 27:63–64).

Get behind me, Satan. Not a verdict on Peter — Jesus takes him up the mountain in the next chapter and restores him on a beach at the end. It names the source of the objection. This shall never happen to you (Matt. 16:22) is a kingdom without a cross, which is the wilderness offer (1:13) returning through the mouth of a friend, and it will come a third time from passers-by at the foot of the cross — save yourself, and come down (15:30).
8.examples:
Then: a crowd in Galilee hearing take up his cross in a country where the governor Varus had crucified two thousand men within living memory. Nobody heard a metaphor. They had watched condemned men carry the crossbeam out through the streets, stripped and jeered at, walking in one direction only.

Now: we have worn the phrase smooth and made a cross into a difficulty — a hard marriage, an illness, a colleague. That is not what it meant. A man carrying a cross was not a man with a burden; he was a man already condemned, publicly, on his way out of his own life.

And deny himself is the verb used of Peter in the courtyard: I do not know the man, he is nothing to do with me. That is what you are asked to say about yourself — not self-hatred, and not going without sugar, but the removal of the self from the throne, so that what do I want? stops being the question that decides. Name the specific matter this week where that is in play. If you cannot name one, the denial is theoretical.

And the third word is what keeps this from being grim heroism: follow me. You are not asked to carry a cross into the dark alone. You are asked to walk behind somebody whose back you can see, who is going first, and who within months will carry an actual beam up an actual road.

One more, from v. 38. He does not say whoever denies me — he says ashamed, which is not a decision or a moment but a temperature. Very few Christians in a comfortable country face a moment of denial. What we face is a thousand small pressures toward silence, each with a respectable name: the sentence not said when the conversation turned, the qualifying phrase offered up to buy distance (I'm not one of those Christians), the belief not mentioned to a colleague in four years. None of it feels like betrayal. All of it is what the verse is about.

9.title: Glory on the Mountain, Failure in the Valley
9.text: <sup>1</sup>And he said to them, “Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God after it has come with power.” <sup>2</sup>And after six days Jesus took with him Peter and James and John, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. And he was transfigured before them, <sup>3</sup>and his clothes became radiant, intensely white, as no one on earth could bleach them. <sup>4</sup>And there appeared to them Elijah with Moses, and they were talking with Jesus. <sup>5</sup>And Peter said to Jesus, “Rabbi, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah.” <sup>6</sup>For he did not know what to say, for they were terrified. <sup>7</sup>And a cloud overshadowed them, and a voice came out of the cloud, “This is my beloved Son; listen to him.” <sup>8</sup>And suddenly, looking around, they no longer saw anyone with them but Jesus only. <sup>9</sup>And as they were coming down the mountain, he charged them to tell no one what they had seen, until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. <sup>10</sup>So they kept the matter to themselves, questioning what this rising from the dead might mean. <sup>11</sup>And they asked him, “Why do the scribes say that first Elijah must come?” <sup>12</sup>And he said to them, “Elijah does come first to restore all things. And how is it written of the Son of Man that he should suffer many things and be treated with contempt? <sup>13</sup>But I tell you that Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased, as it is written of him.” <sup>14</sup>And when they came to the disciples, they saw a great crowd around them, and scribes arguing with them. <sup>15</sup>And immediately all the crowd, when they saw him, were greatly amazed and ran up to him and greeted him. <sup>16</sup>And he asked them, “What are you arguing about with them?” <sup>17</sup>And someone from the crowd answered him, “Teacher, I brought my son to you, for he has a spirit that makes him mute. <sup>18</sup>And whenever it seizes him, it throws him down, and he foams and grinds his teeth and becomes rigid. So I asked your disciples to cast it out, and they were not able.” <sup>19</sup>And he answered them, “O faithless generation, how long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you? Bring him to me.” <sup>20</sup>And they brought the boy to him. And when the spirit saw him, immediately it convulsed the boy, and he fell on the ground and rolled about, foaming at the mouth. <sup>21</sup>And Jesus asked his father, “How long has this been happening to him?” And he said, “From childhood. <sup>22</sup>And it has often cast him into fire and into water, to destroy him. But if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.” <sup>23</sup>And Jesus said to him, “‘If you can’! All things are possible for one who believes.” <sup>24</sup>Immediately the father of the child cried out and said, “I believe; help my unbelief!” <sup>25</sup>And when Jesus saw that a crowd came running together, he rebuked the unclean spirit, saying to it, “You mute and deaf spirit, I command you, come out of him and never enter him again.” <sup>26</sup>And after crying out and convulsing him terribly, it came out, and the boy was like a corpse, so that most of them said, “He is dead.” <sup>27</sup>But Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up, and he arose. <sup>28</sup>And when he had entered the house, his disciples asked him privately, “Why could we not cast it out?” <sup>29</sup>And he said to them, “This kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer.” <sup>30</sup>They went on from there and passed through Galilee. And he did not want anyone to know, <sup>31</sup>for he was teaching his disciples, saying to them, “The Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him. And when he is killed, after three days he will rise.” <sup>32</sup>But they did not understand the saying, and were afraid to ask him. <sup>33</sup>And they came to Capernaum. And when he was in the house he asked them, “What were you discussing on the way?” <sup>34</sup>But they kept silent, for on the way they had argued with one another about who was the greatest. <sup>35</sup>And he sat down and called the twelve. And he said to them, “If anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all.” <sup>36</sup>And he took a child and put him in the midst of them, and taking him in his arms, he said to them, <sup>37</sup>“Whoever receives one such child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me, receives not me but him who sent me.” <sup>38</sup>John said to him, “Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he was not following us.” <sup>39</sup>But Jesus said, “Do not stop him, for no one who does a mighty work in my name will be able soon afterward to speak evil of me. <sup>40</sup>For the one who is not against us is for us. <sup>41</sup>For truly, I say to you, whoever gives you a cup of water to drink because you belong to Christ will by no means lose his reward. <sup>42</sup>“Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to sin, it would be better for him if a great millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea. <sup>43</sup>And if your hand causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life crippled than with two hands to go to hell, to the unquenchable fire. <sup>45</sup>And if your foot causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life lame than with two feet to be thrown into hell. <sup>47</sup>And if your eye causes you to sin, tear it out. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than with two eyes to be thrown into hell, <sup>48</sup>‘where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.’ <sup>49</sup>For everyone will be salted with fire. <sup>50</sup>Salt is good, but if the salt has lost its saltiness, how will you make it salty again? Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another.”
9.overview:
Mark puts the brightest and the bleakest scenes in his Gospel back to back, and the join is the point.

Six days after telling his disciples he must be killed, Jesus takes three of them up a mountain and stops holding the veil in place. Moses and Elijah stand with him and — Luke tells us — discuss his exodus, which he is about to accomplish at Jerusalem. Peter, terrified, offers to build shelters. A cloud comes down and the Father says the only thing he commands in this Gospel: listen to him. Then the light goes, and they see Jesus only.

And they walk down into a shouting crowd, an argument with the scribes, nine defeated colleagues, and a boy convulsing on the ground. The father has been watching this since the child was small, has pulled him out of fires and out of water, and has just been let down by the disciples — which is where the if you can in his prayer came from. Out of him comes the most honest sentence anybody says to Jesus in the Gospels.

The rest of the chapter is a road and a house. Jesus tells them a second time that he will be handed over and killed; they do not understand and are afraid to ask; and they fill the silence by arguing about which of them is the greatest. So he sits down, picks up a child, and redefines greatness — then warns them, in the most violent language he ever uses, about tripping up the little ones and about keeping anything that is taking them to Gehenna. The chapter ends: be at peace with one another.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — The Transfiguration and the Failure in the Valley
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The mountain (vv. 2–8). Six days after telling them he must be killed, Jesus takes three men up a high mountain and, for a few minutes, stops holding the veil in place. Moses and Elijah stand with him. Peter, terrified, starts talking. A cloud comes down, and a voice says the one thing heaven has ever commanded about him: listen to him.

The descent (vv. 9–13). Coming down, he tells them to keep it quiet until the resurrection — and they go on down the hill privately trying to work out what rising from the dead could possibly mean.

The valley (vv. 14–29). And at the bottom: a crowd, an argument, scribes pressing their advantage, nine defeated disciples, and a father whose son has been convulsing since childhood and who has just watched the professionals fail. Out of his mouth comes the most honest sentence anybody says to Jesus in the Gospels.

Mark has put the brightest and the bleakest scenes in his book back to back on purpose. The glory on the mountain is real. The failure in the valley is real. And the same Christ is in both.
verseByVerse.theology:
What actually happened on the mountain? The word is metamorphōthē — he was transformed, changed in form. And the point is not that something was added to Jesus but that something was, for a moment, no longer withheld.

Set it beside Moses. When Moses came down Sinai his face shone (Ex. 34:29–35), and he had to veil it — but that light was borrowed, reflected off a glory he had stood near, and it faded, which Paul says is exactly why he veiled it (2 Cor. 3:13). Here the light comes out from inside. His clothes go white because of what is underneath them.

So this is not a miracle done to Jesus. It is a brief withdrawal of the ordinariness he had been wearing since Bethlehem — three men allowed to see, for a few minutes, what was true of him every day they had walked beside him without noticing.

And why these two men? Moses is the Law and Elijah the Prophets; between them they are the whole Old Testament, standing on that mountain not to be admired alongside Jesus but to attend on him. Luke tells us what they were discussing: his departure — the word is exodus — which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). Moses, who led the first one out of Egypt, is talking about the greater one with the man who will lead it, and the road out runs through a cross.

Then they are gone, and Mark writes the sentence the whole scene exists for: they no longer saw anyone with them but Jesus only.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: three men who had seen the glory of God on a mountaintop, walking down into a shouting crowd, a public argument, and nine colleagues who had just failed in front of everybody.

Now: the come-down is the most ordinary experience in the Christian life, and Mark has built the chapter to prepare you for it. The conference ends. The retreat finishes. The Sunday that lifted you is followed by a Monday. And what is waiting at the bottom of the hill is usually not glory but a mess — the same marriage, the same diagnosis, the same argument, the same failure.

Two things to take from how Mark has arranged this. First, the mountain is not the point. Peter wanted to build shelters and stay, and he was told to come down and listen. The vision was given so that three men could go into the valley knowing who was walking beside them.

Second, Jesus goes down. He does not stay in the light. He walks into the shouting, asks what the argument is about, and takes charge of it — and the boy he lifts up off the ground is lifted by the same hands that had shone on the mountain.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God after it has come with power."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them: truly, I tell you, some of those standing here will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God having come with power.

Context. This verse belongs with the end of chapter 8. Jesus has just spoken of his coming in glory as judge (8:38). Now he promises that some of them will see the kingdom come in power before they die. The chapter division here is unfortunate.

Truly, I say to you. “Truly” (amēn) at the start of a sentence was Jesus’ own way of speaking, with no parallel among the rabbis. He speaks with his own authority, not quoting others.

There are some standing here. Not all. Some, a few.

Who will not taste death. A Hebrew idiom for “die”, a vivid picture of death as a bitter cup.

Until they see the kingdom of God after it has come with power. The tense (a perfect participle, elēlythuian) means they will see it as already having come: established, a present reality. “With power”: not in weakness, as now, hidden like a seed (4:30–32), but in open demonstration.

Where Christians differ: what did they see? Some take it as a promise of the second coming, and conclude Jesus was mistaken about its timing. Others see the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, or Pentecost. Verdict: Mark places the transfiguration immediately after, six days later (v. 2), where three of those standing there, Peter, James and John, saw the kingdom in power, Jesus in his glory. That is the first and clearest fulfilment, and Peter himself understood it so (2 Peter 1:16–18). But the transfiguration was a preview of something larger. The kingdom came with power in the resurrection, by which Jesus was declared Son of God in power (Romans 1:4), at the ascension, and at Pentecost, all within the lifetime of those standing there. The transfiguration was the foretaste of all of it. Jesus was not mistaken.

In a sentence. Jesus promised that some of those with him would live to see the kingdom of God come in power, as three of them did six days later on the mountain.

On a Tuesday. The cross is not the end. Glory is promised. Take up the cross (8:34) knowing the kingdom has come in power.

verseByVerse.quote: And after six days Jesus took with him Peter and James and John, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. And he was transfigured before them, and his clothes became radiant, intensely white, as no one on earth could bleach them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six days later Jesus took Peter, James and John and led them up a high mountain by themselves. He was transfigured before them, and his clothes became dazzling, intensely white, whiter than any bleacher on earth could make them.

And after six days. An unusually precise note of time in Mark, linking the transfiguration to Peter’s confession and the first prediction of the cross. Some see an echo of Exodus 24:16, where the glory of the Lord covered Sinai for six days, and on the seventh God called Moses into the cloud. The scene that follows is full of Sinai.

Peter and James and John. The inner circle, also with him at the raising of Jairus’ daughter (5:37) and in Gethsemane (14:33). They saw his glory, his power over death, and his agony. Moses also took three named companions up the mountain (Exodus 24:1, 9).

And led them up a high mountain by themselves. The mountain is unnamed. Tradition since the fourth century has said Mount Tabor in Galilee, but it is not high (about 1,900 feet, 575 m) and probably had a fortress on top in Jesus’ day. Mount Hermon, about 9,200 feet (2,800 m) and near Caesarea Philippi, where they had just been, fits better. Mountains in Scripture are places of revelation: Sinai, Carmel, Zion.

And he was transfigured before them. Key word: “transfigured” (metemorphōthē), from which comes “metamorphosis”: changed in form. Luke says the appearance of his face was altered (Luke 9:29); Matthew, that his face shone like the sun (Matthew 17:2). Moses’ face shone after he had been with God, with a reflected glory that faded (Exodus 34:29–35; 2 Corinthians 3:7–13). Jesus’ glory was not reflected. It shone from within. For a moment, the veil of his humanity was drawn back, and the disciples saw the glory he had with the Father before the world existed (John 17:5), and the glory he would have after his resurrection. “We have seen his glory” (John 1:14).

And his clothes became radiant, intensely white. “Radiant” (stilbonta): glistening, gleaming like polished metal. White is the colour of heaven, of purity and of divine glory. The Ancient of Days had clothing white as snow (Daniel 7:9).

As no one on earth could bleach them. A homely detail, perhaps Peter’s own: a fuller (a cloth-dresser) washed and whitened wool, but no earthly fuller could produce this white. It was not of this world.

In a sentence. On a high mountain, Jesus was changed before Peter, James and John, his divine glory shining out so that even his clothes became a heavenly white.

For worship. The Jesus you pray to is this glorious Lord. And one day believers will be changed into his likeness (2 Corinthians 3:18; 1 John 3:2), the same word as here.
verseByVerse.note: The mountain is unnamed; tradition says Tabor, but Hermon, near Caesarea Philippi, is also suggested. A fuller bleached and whitened cloth.

verseByVerse.quote: And there appeared to them Elijah with Moses, and they were talking with Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elijah appeared to them with Moses, and they were talking with Jesus.

Elijah with Moses. Mark names Elijah first, perhaps because Elijah is the subject of the conversation that follows (vv. 11–13). Together they represent the whole Old Testament: Moses, the giver of the Law, and Elijah, the greatest of the prophets. The Law and the Prophets bear witness to Jesus (Luke 24:27; Romans 3:21).

Why these two? Several things link them. Both met God on a mountain, Sinai, also called Horeb (Exodus 24; 1 Kings 19:8). Both had unusual ends: Moses was buried by God himself, in a grave no one knows (Deuteronomy 34:5–6), and Elijah was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11). Both were expected, in Jewish hope, to have a role at the end: the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15) and Elijah before the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:4–5, where the two are named together, at the very end of the Old Testament).

And they were talking with Jesus. Luke tells us what about: his departure (Greek exodos), which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). Moses led the first exodus from slavery in Egypt; Jesus will lead the greater exodus, through his death and resurrection, from slavery to sin.

What it does not mean. Not that the dead can be consulted (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). This was God’s act, not a séance. And not that Moses and Elijah were equal to Jesus, as the next verses make clear. But it does show that the faithful dead are alive to God (12:26–27).

In a sentence. Moses and Elijah, representing the Law and the Prophets, appeared and talked with Jesus about the death he was about to accomplish.

On a Tuesday. Read your Old Testament as Moses and Elijah spoke on the mountain: it is all about Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: Moses and Elijah stand for the Law and the Prophets.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter said to Jesus, "Rabbi, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah." For he did not know what to say, for they were terrified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter said to Jesus: Rabbi, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you, one for Moses and one for Elijah. He did not know what to say, for they were terrified.

Rabbi, it is good that we are here. Peter’s instinct is understandable: this is wonderful, let us stay. And “Rabbi”, teacher, falls far short of what he has just seen.

Let us make three tents. “Tents” (skēnas): booths, shelters of branches. The word also means “tabernacles”, like the tabernacle in the wilderness where God’s glory dwelt among Israel (Exodus 40:34). Peter may have been thinking of the Feast of Booths (Tabernacles), when Israel lived in booths to remember the wilderness, and which looked forward to the final age when God would dwell with his people (Zechariah 14:16). If the end had come, it was time to build the booths.

One for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah. Peter’s mistake was twofold. He put Jesus on the same level as Moses and Elijah, three great figures with three equal shelters. And he wanted to stay on the mountain of glory, when Jesus had just told him that the way to glory lay through the cross (8:31). The glory was a preview, not the destination yet.

For he did not know what to say, for they were terrified. Mark’s honest comment, very probably from Peter himself, who told the story against himself. “Terrified” (ekphoboi): overcome with fear, the natural response of sinners in the presence of divine glory (Isaiah 6:5). Peter spoke because he was frightened and did not know what else to do.

In a sentence. Terrified and not knowing what to say, Peter proposed making three shelters, putting Jesus alongside Moses and Elijah and wanting to keep the glory without the cross.

On a Tuesday. When God’s presence is overwhelming, it is better to be silent than to fill the silence with nonsense (Ecclesiastes 5:2).
verseByVerse.note: The tents may recall the Feast of Booths.

verseByVerse.quote: And a cloud overshadowed them, and a voice came out of the cloud, "This is my beloved Son; listen to him." And suddenly, looking around, they no longer saw anyone with them but Jesus only.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A cloud overshadowed them, and a voice came from the cloud: This is my beloved Son; listen to him. Suddenly, looking around, they no longer saw anyone with them but Jesus only.

And a cloud overshadowed them. Not an ordinary cloud. This is the cloud of God’s own presence, the Shekinah glory: the pillar of cloud that led Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 13:21), the cloud on Sinai (Exodus 24:15–18), the cloud that filled the tabernacle and the temple (Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:10–11). “Overshadowed” (episkiazousa) is the word used of the cloud settling on the tabernacle in the Greek Old Testament (Exodus 40:35), and of the Holy Spirit coming on Mary (Luke 1:35). God himself had come down.

And a voice came out of the cloud. The Father speaks, as at the baptism (1:11). The only two times in Mark that God speaks from heaven.

This is my beloved Son. At the baptism, the voice spoke to Jesus: You are my beloved Son. Now it speaks to the disciples about him. This answers Peter’s mistake: Jesus is not one of three equals; he is the Son. Moses was a faithful servant in God’s house; Christ is the Son over the house (Hebrews 3:5–6). “Beloved” may also mean “only”, as with Abraham’s only son Isaac (Genesis 22:2).

Listen to him. Key words. An echo of Deuteronomy 18:15, where Moses promised that God would raise up a prophet like himself: it is to him you shall listen. Jesus is that prophet. And in context, the command is pointed: listen to him, especially when he tells you, as he has just done, that he must suffer and die (8:31) and that you must take up your cross (8:34). Peter had rebuked him for that. The Father says: listen.

And suddenly, looking around, they no longer saw anyone with them but Jesus only. Moses and Elijah vanish. Their work was to point to him. The Law and the Prophets give way to the Son. What remains is “Jesus only”. That is the whole meaning of the scene.

In a sentence. God’s presence came in the cloud and the Father declared Jesus his beloved Son and commanded the disciples to listen to him, and then they saw Jesus alone.

For worship. Above every other voice, even the greatest teachers and the best traditions, God says of Jesus: listen to him. Open his word today and do.
verseByVerse.note: The cloud recalls the cloud of God’s presence at Sinai and over the tabernacle.

parallels.desc: it is to him you shall listen

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were coming down the mountain, he charged them to tell no one what they had seen, until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. So they kept the matter to themselves, questioning what this rising from the dead might mean.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they were coming down the mountain, he ordered them to tell no one what they had seen until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. So they kept the matter to themselves, discussing what this rising from the dead might mean.

He charged them to tell no one what they had seen. Not even the other nine. The vision of glory without the cross would only feed the wrong expectations of a conquering Messiah.

Until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. The only time Jesus sets a limit on the secret. After the resurrection, the glory can be told, because then it will be understood: the glory comes through the cross. And Peter did tell it (2 Peter 1:16–18).

So they kept the matter to themselves. They obeyed, but they were puzzled.

Questioning what this rising from the dead might mean. Jews who believed in resurrection (as the Pharisees did) expected it at the end of the age, for all the righteous together (Daniel 12:2; John 11:24). The idea of one man, the Messiah, rising from the dead in the middle of history, before the end, made no sense to them. And they could not grasp that the Messiah must die at all. The resurrection was unexpected even by those who were told it in advance.

In a sentence. Jesus ordered the three to keep the vision secret until he had risen from the dead, and they obeyed, puzzling over what rising from the dead could mean.

On a Tuesday. Some things in Scripture make sense only in the light of the cross and resurrection. Read the whole Bible from that vantage point.

verseByVerse.quote: And they asked him, "Why do the scribes say that first Elijah must come?" And he said to them, "Elijah does come first to restore all things. And how is it written of the Son of Man that he should suffer many things and be treated with contempt? But I tell you that Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased, as it is written of him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They asked him: why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first? He said: Elijah does come first to restore all things. And how is it written of the Son of Man that he must suffer many things and be treated with contempt? But I tell you that Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased, as it is written of him.

Why do the scribes say that first Elijah must come? The question follows naturally. They had just seen Elijah. The scribes taught from Malachi 4:5–6 that Elijah must come before the day of the Lord, to turn hearts and prepare the people. If Jesus is the Messiah, where was Elijah? Was the appearance on the mountain his coming?

Elijah does come first to restore all things. Jesus affirms the scribes’ teaching. Malachi was right: Elijah comes first, and his work is restoration, turning the hearts of fathers to their children and children to their fathers (Malachi 4:6).

And how is it written of the Son of Man that he should suffer many things and be treated with contempt? But there is a puzzle in Scripture. If Elijah restores everything, how can it also be written that the Son of Man must suffer and be despised (Isaiah 53:3; Psalm 22:6–7)? “Treated with contempt” (exoudenēthē) means regarded as nothing. Both are true. The forerunner’s restoration did not prevent the Messiah’s rejection.

But I tell you that Elijah has come. The answer. Elijah has already come, in John the Baptist. Matthew adds that the disciples understood he was speaking of John (Matthew 17:13). John came in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17), even dressed like him (1:6; 2 Kings 1:8). John denied that he was literally Elijah returned (John 1:21), but he fulfilled Elijah’s role.

And they did to him whatever they pleased. Herod arrested and beheaded him (6:17–29). As Jezebel had sought to kill the first Elijah (1 Kings 19:2), so Herodias destroyed the second.

As it is written of him. Not a specific prophecy about John’s death, but the pattern of Elijah’s life in Scripture: persecuted by a wicked king and queen. And the forerunner’s fate foreshadows the Messiah’s. If they did this to Elijah, they will do it to the Son of Man.

In a sentence. Jesus affirmed that Elijah must come first, explained that he had already come in John the Baptist and been killed, and said that the Son of Man must likewise suffer.

On a Tuesday. God’s plan often looks like failure: a murdered prophet, a crucified Messiah. Trust Scripture’s pattern: suffering before glory.
verseByVerse.note: Elijah, in Jesus’ words, is John the Baptist.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they came to the disciples, they saw a great crowd around them, and scribes arguing with them. And immediately all the crowd, when they saw him, were greatly amazed and ran up to him and greeted him. And he asked them, "What are you arguing about with them?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they came back to the other disciples, they saw a great crowd around them and scribes arguing with them. As soon as the crowd saw Jesus, they were greatly amazed, ran to him and greeted him. He asked: what are you arguing about with them?

From the mountain to the valley. The contrast is deliberate. Above, the glory of God, the voice of the Father, Moses and Elijah. Below, failure, argument and a suffering child. As Moses came down from Sinai to find Israel worshipping the golden calf (Exodus 32), Jesus comes down to find faithlessness (v. 19). The glory of the mountain does not take Jesus away from the misery of the world; it sends him into it.

And scribes arguing with them. The scribes were probably using the disciples’ failure to discredit Jesus.

Were greatly amazed. Exethambēthēsan, a strong word for being overwhelmed with awe, used only by Mark. Why? Perhaps simply his sudden arrival. But some think something of the glory of the mountain still lingered on him, as Moses’ face shone when he came down (Exodus 34:29–30), though here people ran toward him rather than away.

What are you arguing about with them? Jesus takes charge and steps in to defend his disciples.

In a sentence. Coming down from the mountain, Jesus found his disciples in an argument with the scribes before a crowd, and stepped in.

On a Tuesday. Mountaintop experiences are given to equip us for the valley. Expect to come down to ordinary need and difficulty.

verseByVerse.quote: And someone from the crowd answered him, "Teacher, I brought my son to you, for he has a spirit that makes him mute. And whenever it seizes him, it throws him down, and he foams and grinds his teeth and becomes rigid. So I asked your disciples to cast it out, and they were not able."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man from the crowd answered: Teacher, I brought my son to you, because he has a spirit that makes him mute. Whenever it seizes him, it throws him down, and he foams at the mouth, grinds his teeth and goes rigid. I asked your disciples to cast it out, and they could not.

Teacher, I brought my son to you. He came looking for Jesus, and found only the disciples. Luke adds that he was his only child (Luke 9:38).

For he has a spirit that makes him mute. The spirit also made him deaf (v. 25).

It throws him down, and he foams and grinds his teeth and becomes rigid. Symptoms that resemble epilepsy, and Matthew uses a word for it (literally “moonstruck”, Matthew 17:15). But Mark is clear that the cause here was a demon, which Jesus addresses and casts out (v. 25). The two are not exclusive: a demon could cause physical symptoms. Not all illness is demonic, and the Gospels distinguish them (1:32–34). But this case was.

So I asked your disciples to cast it out, and they were not able. A painful failure. Jesus had given them authority over unclean spirits (6:7), and they had cast out many demons (6:13). Now they could not. Why? Jesus will answer in verses 19 and 29: unbelief, and prayerlessness.

In a sentence. The father described his son’s violent possession by a mute spirit, and the disciples’ failure to cast it out.

On a Tuesday. Past success in ministry is no guarantee for today. Every work depends freshly on God.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered them, "O faithless generation, how long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you? Bring him to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered them: O faithless generation, how long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you? Bring him to me.

O faithless generation. “Faithless” (apistos): without faith, unbelieving. Addressed to whom? To all of them: the crowd, the scribes, the father, and especially the disciples, whose failure was the occasion. The words echo God’s complaint against Israel in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 32:5, 20; Numbers 14:11).

How long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you? A cry of weariness and grief. These are the words of one who does not belong to this world, who has come from the Father and is going back, a visitor among unbelievers. “Bear with” (anexomai) means put up with, endure. It shows the real cost to Jesus of living among sinners, even his own disciples. And his time with them is short (8:31).

Bring him to me. Yet in the same breath, compassion. Where the disciples failed, Jesus does not. Whatever his grief, he does not turn the child away.

In a sentence. Grieved by the unbelief all around him, Jesus cried out at how long he must bear with them, and then called for the boy to be brought to him.

On a Tuesday. When others have failed to help, and you have failed too, there is still one word: bring him to me.

parallels.desc: a perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought the boy to him. And when the spirit saw him, immediately it convulsed the boy, and he fell on the ground and rolled about, foaming at the mouth. And Jesus asked his father, "How long has this been happening to him?" And he said, "From childhood. And it has often cast him into fire and into water, to destroy him. But if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They brought the boy to him. When the spirit saw Jesus, it immediately convulsed the boy, and he fell on the ground and rolled around, foaming at the mouth. Jesus asked the father: how long has this been happening to him? He said: from childhood. It has often thrown him into fire and into water, to destroy him. But if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.

And when the spirit saw him. The demon recognises Jesus and reacts with violence. Demons know who he is (1:24; 3:11), and in their last moments they rage.

And Jesus asked his father, How long has this been happening to him? An unhurried question, amid the convulsions. Jesus deals with the father as a person, drawing out his story. The father needs as much attention as the son.

From childhood. Years of suffering. The boy had never known normal life. This is a hard case, long established.

It has often cast him into fire and into water, to destroy him. The aim of the demon was destruction. That is Satan’s purpose for every human being (John 10:10; 1 Peter 5:8). In a world of open fires for cooking and of wells and lakes, the boy was in constant danger.

But if you can do anything. The father’s faith had been shaken by the disciples’ failure. He is not sure any more.

Have compassion on us and help us. “Us”: the father identifies himself completely with his son’s suffering. It is the whole family’s affliction.

In a sentence. As the demon threw the boy into a fit, the father told Jesus it had tried for years to destroy him, and asked for help, if Jesus could do anything.

On a Tuesday. Satan’s aim is to destroy. Jesus’ aim is to save. Pray for those whose lives are being torn apart.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, "'If you can'! All things are possible for one who believes." Immediately the father of the child cried out and said, "I believe; help my unbelief!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to him: “If you can”! All things are possible for one who believes. Immediately the boy’s father cried out: I believe; help my unbelief!

“If you can”! Jesus throws the father’s words back to him. The question is not whether Jesus can. The question is whether the father believes. Some manuscripts read differently here, but the meaning is the same.

All things are possible for one who believes. Not that faith is a force that can make anything happen, or that we can have anything we want if we believe hard enough. Faith is trust in God, and it is God for whom all things are possible (10:27; 14:36). Faith links us to his power. The believer does not set limits on what God can do. Who is “the one who believes” here? Primarily the father. But Jesus too is the supreme believer, perfectly trusting the Father.

Immediately the father of the child cried out. Not just spoke, but cried out, from the depths.

I believe; help my unbelief! One of the most honest prayers in the Bible, and only Mark records it. The father believes, really; he has come to Jesus and asks him. But his faith is mixed with doubt, shaken by years of suffering and by the disciples’ failure. He does not pretend. He confesses both his faith and his unbelief, and asks Jesus to help even that. And Jesus accepts it.

What it does not mean. Not that only perfect faith receives an answer. Weak faith in a strong Saviour is enough. The power is in the one believed, not in the strength of the believing. A mustard seed of faith is enough (Matthew 17:20).

In a sentence. Jesus told the father that everything is possible for one who believes, and the father cried out that he believed and asked Jesus to help his unbelief.

For worship. Make this prayer your own whenever your faith is weak: Lord, I believe; help my unbelief. It is a prayer Jesus answers.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark records the father’s cry.

parallels.desc: without faith it is impossible to please him

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus saw that a crowd came running together, he rebuked the unclean spirit, saying to it, "You mute and deaf spirit, I command you, come out of him and never enter him again." And after crying out and convulsing him terribly, it came out, and the boy was like a corpse, so that most of them said, "He is dead." But Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up, and he arose.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus saw a crowd running together, he rebuked the unclean spirit: you mute and deaf spirit, I command you, come out of him and never enter him again. Crying out and convulsing him terribly, it came out, and the boy was like a corpse, so that most of them said: he is dead. But Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up, and he arose.

And when Jesus saw that a crowd came running together. He acts before it becomes a spectacle.

You mute and deaf spirit, I command you. “I” is emphatic: I myself. The disciples had failed with their own attempts; now the master commands with his own authority. No incantation, no prayer to anyone else.

Come out of him and never enter him again. Not just out, but permanently. The father need not fear its return. Jesus’ deliverance is complete (Matthew 12:43–45).

And after crying out and convulsing him terribly, it came out. The demon’s last act of rage.

And the boy was like a corpse, so that most of them said, He is dead. Stillness after the violence. It looked as though the demon had achieved its purpose.

But Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up, and he arose. The language of resurrection. “Lifted him up” (ēgeiren) and “arose” (anestē) are the two words used for Jesus’ own resurrection (16:6; 8:31). As with Jairus’ daughter (5:41–42), Jesus takes the hand of the one who seems dead and raises him. Coming straight after Jesus spoke of his rising from the dead (v. 9), Mark wants us to see it: the one who raises this boy will himself rise.

In a sentence. Jesus commanded the spirit to come out and never return; after a last convulsion the boy lay as if dead, but Jesus took his hand and raised him up.

On a Tuesday. When it looks as though evil has won, Jesus has the last word. He takes the hand and raises up.

parallels.desc: he took her by the hand

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had entered the house, his disciples asked him privately, "Why could we not cast it out?" And he said to them, "This kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he had gone into the house, his disciples asked him privately: why could we not cast it out? He said to them: this kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer.

Why could we not cast it out? A good question. They had done it before (6:13). Asked in private, out of humiliation.

This kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer. “This kind”: some demons were more powerful or deeply entrenched. But the answer applies more widely. The disciples had perhaps begun to think of their authority as a power they possessed, a technique that would always work. They had tried to cast it out in their own strength, without depending on God. Prayer is the expression of dependence. Jesus himself had just come from a mountain of communion with the Father. The disciples had been arguing with scribes.

Faith and prayer. Jesus said their problem was faithlessness (v. 19); here, lack of prayer. The two are the same thing from different sides. Prayer is faith expressing its dependence on God. Matthew records that Jesus said: Because of your little faith (Matthew 17:20).

Textual note. Some manuscripts add “and fasting”. The words are missing from the two earliest and most reliable manuscripts, and were probably added later as the church came to practise fasting more. The ESV puts them in a footnote.

What it does not mean. Not that prayer is a more powerful technique, a formula you add to make an exorcism work. Jesus himself did not pray before casting out this demon. The point is a life of dependent prayer, not a ritual.

In a sentence. When the disciples asked why they had failed, Jesus told them that this kind of demon could only be driven out by prayer, that is, by dependence on God.

On a Tuesday. Is there a problem you have been trying to solve in your own strength? Have you prayed about it? Begin there.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “and fasting.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–50 — The Second Prediction and the Argument on the Road
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The second telling (vv. 30–32). Walking quietly through Galilee, avoiding notice, Jesus tells them again that he will be delivered up, killed, and rise. Mark adds a devastating detail: they did not understand, and were afraid to ask.

The argument (vv. 33–37). And what they were talking about instead comes out at Capernaum. He asks what they were discussing on the road, and they go silent — because they had been arguing about which of them was the greatest. His answer is to sit down, state the rule (last of all and servant of all), and then pick up a child and hold him.

The complaint (vv. 38–41). John, apparently thinking this a good moment, reports that they stopped a man casting out demons in Jesus's name because he was not one of them. He is told to leave him alone — and that a cup of water given to a disciple will not be forgotten.

The warnings (vv. 42–50). Then the hardest words in the Gospel: a millstone for anyone who trips up a little one, and a hand, a foot and an eye better lost than kept.

The whole section hangs together. Men who have just been told about a cross are arguing about rank, policing the boundaries of their group, and in serious danger of tripping up people smaller than themselves — and it ends with be at peace with one another.
verseByVerse.theology:
"The one who is not against us is for us" (v. 40) seems to collide head-on with whoever is not with me is against me (Matt. 12:30; Luke 11:23), and a reader who notices it deserves an answer.

They are not answering the same question, and that is the whole key. Here the subject is a fellow worker — a man casting out demons in Jesus's name, plainly on Christ's side, who simply does not belong to the disciples' circle; and the lesson is generosity: do not treat an ally as an enemy merely because he is not of your party. There the subject is Christ himself, and the men in view are Pharisees who had just called his works the devil's — open opponents; and the lesson is that toward Jesus there is no neutral ground.

So the two sayings guard two different errors. Toward other Christians serving under a different banner from ours we are far too quick to say against us, and Jesus says: not so — if he is for me, he is for you. Toward the Lord himself we would love to imagine a comfortable middle ground of the undecided, and Jesus says there is none. Read together they are not a contradiction but a pair of fences: be generous about the boundaries of the movement, and uncompromising about the claims of the King.

And a word about the verses your Bible skips. A reader with a King James Bible will find the refrain of v. 48, about the undying worm and the unquenched fire, three times over, at verses 44, 46 and 48. Modern Bibles print it once, at v. 48, and leave 44 and 46 as footnotes. Those two repetitions are a copyist's echo of v. 48 and are not in the earliest manuscripts. Nothing is lost. The sentence stands once, in full force, exactly where Jesus quoted it from Isaiah 66:24.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twelve men arguing on a road about which of them was the greatest, on the road after being told that their Master would be handed over and killed.

Now: the same argument, conducted with better manners. It runs under a great deal of church life — who was consulted, who was thanked from the front, whose name went on it, who got asked to do the thing you were not asked to do. Nobody says I am the greatest. Everybody knows exactly where they stand in the room.

And notice how Mark exposes it: they kept silent. They would not tell him. Which is the surest sign of all that they already knew it was wrong — you do not go quiet about a conversation you are comfortable with.

Then watch what Jesus does with it, because he does not abolish ambition; he reverses its direction. If anyone would be first — the wanting is allowed to stand — he must be last of all and servant of all. Not last of some. Not servant of the deserving. Of all.

And then he picks up a child, who in that world had no legal standing, no money, no influence and nothing whatever to offer in return — and says that receiving one such is receiving him. The test of greatness in the kingdom is not how you treat the people who can advance you. It is how you treat the ones who cannot do a thing for you, when nobody is watching.

verseByVerse.quote: They went on from there and passed through Galilee. And he did not want anyone to know, for he was teaching his disciples, saying to them, "The Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him. And when he is killed, after three days he will rise." But they did not understand the saying, and were afraid to ask him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They left there and passed through Galilee. Jesus did not want anyone to know, because he was teaching his disciples. He told them: the Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him; and when he has been killed, after three days he will rise. But they did not understand the saying, and were afraid to ask him.

And passed through Galilee. Quietly, heading south toward Capernaum and then Jerusalem. The public Galilean ministry is over.

And he did not want anyone to know, for he was teaching his disciples. His priority now is to prepare the Twelve for what is coming.

The second passion prediction. Shorter than the first (8:31), but with a new element.

The Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men. “Delivered” (paradidotai) means handed over, betrayed. The same word is used of Judas’ betrayal (3:19; 14:10), of the Jewish leaders handing Jesus over to Pilate (15:1), of Pilate handing him over to be crucified (15:15), and of God giving up his Son for us all (Romans 8:32). Behind every human act of handing over stands the Father’s purpose. And there is a play on words: the Son of Man, into the hands of men.

And they will kill him. And when he is killed, after three days he will rise. Death and resurrection again, together.

But they did not understand the saying. The second time he had said it plainly, and still they could not take it in.

And were afraid to ask him. Perhaps because they remembered Peter’s rebuke (8:33). Perhaps because they did not want to understand. Sometimes we do not ask because we are afraid of the answer.

In a sentence. Travelling quietly through Galilee, Jesus again told his disciples he would be betrayed, killed and raised, but they did not understand and were afraid to ask.

On a Tuesday. Don’t be afraid to ask Jesus your hard questions in prayer and in his word. He would rather you asked.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Capernaum. And when he was in the house he asked them, "What were you discussing on the way?" But they kept silent, for on the way they had argued with one another about who was the greatest. And he sat down and called the twelve. And he said to them, "If anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They came to Capernaum. When he was in the house, he asked them: what were you discussing on the way? They kept silent, because on the way they had argued with one another about who was the greatest. He sat down and called the Twelve, and said: if anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all.

And they came to Capernaum. Jesus’ base in Galilee, and probably Peter’s house (1:29). The last time Mark mentions it.

What were you discussing on the way? Jesus knew. “On the way”: the way to the cross, where Jesus was going to give his life. That was where they were arguing about greatness.

But they kept silent. Ashamed. They knew it did not fit.

For on the way they had argued with one another about who was the greatest. The tragic contrast. Jesus had just told them he would be betrayed and killed. They were arguing about rank. Perhaps the choosing of three for the mountain had stirred jealousy. The argument kept coming back (10:35–45; Luke 22:24). Pride is the most persistent of sins, even in disciples.

And he sat down. The posture of a teacher giving formal instruction. What follows is important.

And called the twelve. As if to say: listen, this is for you who will lead my church.

If anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all. The kingdom turns the world’s order upside down. Jesus does not condemn the desire to be first; he redirects it. True greatness is found in taking the lowest place and serving everyone. “Servant” (diakonos) is a table-waiter, the one who serves the meal while others eat. The word gives us “deacon”. Jesus will give himself as the supreme example: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve (10:45; John 13:1–17).

In a sentence. When the disciples were silent with shame about arguing over who was greatest, Jesus taught that whoever wants to be first must be last and servant of all.

On a Tuesday. Who can you serve today without being noticed? Do it, and kill the argument about greatness in your heart.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers sat to teach.

verseByVerse.quote: And he took a child and put him in the midst of them, and taking him in his arms, he said to them, "Whoever receives one such child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me, receives not me but him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He took a child, put him in the middle of them, and taking him in his arms said to them: whoever receives one such child in my name receives me; and whoever receives me receives not me but him who sent me.

And he took a child and put him in the midst of them. An acted parable. In the ancient world children had no status. They were loved, but not counted important; they could not contribute, had no rights, and were often exposed at birth if unwanted. A child was a nobody. Jesus puts this nobody in the centre.

And taking him in his arms. Only Mark records this tender detail (also 10:16). Jesus embraces the one with no status.

Whoever receives one such child in my name receives me. To “receive” is to welcome, to show hospitality, to care for. “In my name”: for my sake, because the child belongs to me. Jesus identifies himself with the least important people. The way you treat the least is the way you treat Christ (Matthew 25:40). The disciples argued about who was greatest; greatness lies in welcoming those who can give you nothing back.

And whoever receives me, receives not me but him who sent me. The chain goes all the way up: child, Jesus, the Father. Welcome a nobody in Jesus’ name, and you welcome God himself. This is also a claim about Jesus: he is the sent one, who represents the Father fully.

What it does not mean. Not that children are innocent, or that childhood is a model of moral purity. Children are sinners too (Psalm 51:5). The point is their status: they are small, dependent and unimportant in the world’s eyes. (When Jesus says that we must receive the kingdom like a child, in 10:15, the point is related: we come with nothing, as dependents.)

In a sentence. Embracing a child, Jesus taught that whoever welcomes the least important person in his name welcomes him, and the Father who sent him.

On a Tuesday. Welcome the people who can do nothing for you: children, the lonely, the overlooked. In them you welcome Christ. And value those who serve in the children’s ministry of your church.
verseByVerse.note: Children had little status in the ancient world.

verseByVerse.quote: John said to him, "Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he was not following us." But Jesus said, "Do not stop him, for no one who does a mighty work in my name will be able soon afterward to speak evil of me. For the one who is not against us is for us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John said to him: Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he was not following us. But Jesus said: do not stop him, for no one who does a mighty work in my name will be able soon afterwards to speak evil of me. For whoever is not against us is for us.

John said to him. The only time in Mark that John speaks alone. Perhaps the words “in my name” (v. 37) made his conscience uneasy.

We saw someone casting out demons in your name. Someone outside the Twelve, using Jesus’ name, and succeeding, when the disciples had just failed (v. 18). There may be a little jealousy here.

And we tried to stop him, because he was not following us. Notice: “us”, not “you”. The disciples were concerned for their own group, their own status. The issue was not his loyalty to Jesus but his membership of their circle. Joshua made the same mistake about Eldad and Medad prophesying outside the camp, and Moses answered: Would that all the Lord’s people were prophets (Numbers 11:26–29).

Do not stop him. Jesus corrects their narrowness.

For no one who does a mighty work in my name will be able soon afterward to speak evil of me. A man who is really doing good in Jesus’ name is on Jesus’ side. He will not quickly turn against him.

For the one who is not against us is for us. A generous principle. In the war between the kingdom of God and Satan (3:23–27), anyone casting out demons in Jesus’ name is fighting on the right side. Elsewhere Jesus says the reverse: Whoever is not with me is against me (Matthew 12:30). The two sayings do not contradict. One is a test for yourself: are you wholly with Jesus? The other is a rule for how to view others: if they are genuinely working in Jesus’ name, don’t exclude them because they are not of your group.

What it does not mean. Not that anyone who uses Jesus’ name is a true believer. Some who did mighty works in his name he will reject (Matthew 7:22–23), and some who tried to use his name like a spell came to grief (Acts 19:13–16). Nor that doctrine does not matter. The issue here is group loyalty, not truth.

In a sentence. When John reported stopping a man who cast out demons in Jesus’ name because he was not one of them, Jesus said not to stop him, for whoever is not against them is for them.

On a Tuesday. Rejoice when Christ is served well by believers in other churches or traditions. They are not your rivals.

parallels.desc: whoever is not with me is against me

verseByVerse.quote: For truly, I say to you, whoever gives you a cup of water to drink because you belong to Christ will by no means lose his reward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For truly, I tell you, whoever gives you a cup of water to drink because you belong to Christ will by no means lose his reward.

The link. The theme of verse 37 continues: what is done to the least, in Jesus’ name, counts with God.

Whoever gives you a cup of water to drink. The smallest act of kindness in a hot, dry land. Anyone can give it; it costs almost nothing.

Because you belong to Christ. Literally “in the name that you are Christ’s”. The motive matters: kindness shown to a disciple because he belongs to Christ is kindness to Christ.

Will by no means lose his reward. “By no means” is the strongest negative in Greek. God notices, remembers and rewards. Nothing done for Christ is lost (Hebrews 6:10).

What it does not mean. Not that we earn salvation by good works. The reward is God’s gracious recognition of what flows from love for Christ, not wages that put God in our debt (Luke 17:10).

In a sentence. Even a cup of water given to a disciple because he belongs to Christ will surely be rewarded.

On a Tuesday. No act of kindness to a fellow Christian is too small to count. Give the cup.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to sin, it would be better for him if a great millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to sin, it would be better for him if a great millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea.

The other side. If small kindnesses to disciples are rewarded, harm to them is judged severely.

One of these little ones who believe in me. Not only children, but any humble, insignificant believer, perhaps young in faith. “These little ones”: the child in his arms, and all whom the child represents (v. 37).

To sin. The verb is skandalizō, to cause to stumble, to trip up. A skandalon was the stick in a trap that sprang it, then any stumbling block. To make a believer stumble is to lead him into sin or cause him to fall away from faith, by false teaching, bad example, abuse, pride or contempt.

A great millstone. Literally “a donkey’s millstone”: not a small hand-mill that a woman would turn, but the huge upper stone of a mill, so heavy it needed a donkey to turn it.

And he were thrown into the sea. Drowning with a heavy weight was a Roman and Greek form of execution, especially horrifying to Jews because the body would not be buried. Jesus says: such a death would be better than what awaits the one who destroys the faith of a little one. Not that he should be drowned, but that judgement for such a sin will be worse than the worst death imaginable.

In a sentence. Anyone who causes a humble believer to stumble into sin faces a judgement worse than being drowned with a millstone round the neck.

On a Tuesday. Your example is seen by others: young Christians, your children, new believers. Never be the reason they fall.
verseByVerse.note: The millstone is the heavy upper stone of a mill turned by a donkey.

verseByVerse.quote: And if your hand causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life crippled than with two hands to go to hell, to the unquenchable fire. And if your foot causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life lame than with two feet to be thrown into hell. And if your eye causes you to sin, tear it out. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than with two eyes to be thrown into hell, 'where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
If your hand causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life maimed than with two hands to go to hell, to the unquenchable fire. If your foot causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better to enter life lame than with two feet to be thrown into hell. If your eye causes you to sin, tear it out. It is better to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than with two eyes to be thrown into hell, where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.

From others to yourself. Jesus turns from causing others to stumble to causing yourself to stumble. The same verb, skandalizō. Deal with sin in your own life as ruthlessly as God will deal with those who harm his little ones.

Hand, foot, eye. What you do, where you go, what you look at. Every faculty can become an instrument of sin.

Cut it off … tear it out. Hyperbole, not literal instruction. Removing a hand would not remove the sin, which comes from the heart (7:21). But the hyperbole is meant to shock: be radical with sin. Whatever leads you into sin, however precious, however much a part of you it seems, get rid of it. A relationship, a habit, a device, an ambition, a place you go. Spare nothing.

It is better for you to enter life crippled. “Life” here means eternal life, the same as “the kingdom of God” (v. 47). Better to lose something precious now and enter life, than keep everything and lose your soul (8:36).

To go to hell. Key word. “Hell” (geenna, Gehenna) comes from the Valley of Hinnom, south of Jerusalem, where under wicked kings children had been burned as sacrifices to the god Molech (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31). The prophets said it would become a place of judgement and corpses (Jeremiah 7:32). By Jesus’ day it was the name for the place of final punishment. It is Jesus, more than anyone else in the Bible, who speaks of hell.

To the unquenchable fire. Fire that cannot be put out.

Where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched. The last verse of Isaiah (66:24), describing the corpses of rebels against God. The worm devours and the fire burns, and neither ends. These are images, but images of a reality more terrible, not less, than what they describe.

Where Christians differ: the nature of hell. Some (conditionalists or annihilationists) hold that the wicked are finally destroyed and cease to exist, taking “unquenchable fire” to mean a fire that does its work completely. Others (universalists) hope that all will finally be saved. Verdict: the historic Christian view is that hell is conscious, eternal punishment. The undying worm and unquenched fire speak of punishment that does not end, and Jesus elsewhere sets eternal punishment alongside eternal life as equally lasting (Matthew 25:46). Jesus’ warnings are given in love, so that none would go there.

Textual note. Some manuscripts add verses 44 and 46, both repeating verse 48. They are missing from the best manuscripts and were probably added to make the three warnings match. The ESV puts them in footnotes.

In a sentence. Jesus calls his followers to deal ruthlessly with anything that leads them into sin, because it is better to lose what is precious than to be thrown into the unending fire of hell.

On a Tuesday. Name the hand, foot or eye in your life: the thing that keeps leading you into sin. Then cut it off. Today.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verses 44 and 46, repeating verse 48. “Hell” renders Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom by Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: their worm shall not die, their fire shall not be quenched

verseByVerse.quote: For everyone will be salted with fire. Salt is good, but if the salt has lost its saltiness, how will you make it salty again? Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For everyone will be salted with fire. Salt is good, but if the salt has lost its saltiness, how will you make it salty again? Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another.
