For everyone will be salted with fire. One of the most difficult sayings in the Gospels; there are dozens of interpretations. The best clue is the Old Testament: every sacrifice was to be offered with salt (Leviticus 2:13), and many were burned with fire. Jesus’ disciples are to offer themselves as living sacrifices (Romans 12:1), and they will be tested and purified by the fire of suffering and trial (1 Peter 1:7; 4:12). The fire of hell (v. 48) destroys; the fire of discipleship purifies. “Everyone” here most likely means every disciple. Some manuscripts add “and every sacrifice will be salted with salt”, probably added from Leviticus 2:13 to explain the saying.

Salt is good. Salt preserved food from decay, gave flavour, and in the Old Testament was a sign of the covenant: a covenant of salt, lasting and unbreakable (Numbers 18:19; 2 Chronicles 13:5).

But if the salt has lost its saltiness, how will you make it salty again? Pure salt cannot lose its saltiness. But the salt of Palestine was collected from the Dead Sea marshes, mixed with other minerals. Damp could leach out the actual salt, leaving a useless white powder that looked like salt but was worthless. A disciple who loses what makes him a disciple is like that: useless (Matthew 5:13).

Have salt in yourselves. Keep the distinctive quality of discipleship: devotion to Christ, willingness to suffer, purity. The salt is the self-sacrifice Jesus has been describing since 8:34.

And be at peace with one another. The chapter comes full circle. It began with the disciples arguing about who was the greatest (v. 34). The salt of self-denial is the cure for rivalry. People who have been salted with the fire of the cross have nothing left to fight over. In the ancient world, sharing salt in a meal was a sign of friendship.

In a sentence. Every disciple will be refined by fire, like a salted sacrifice; so keep your saltiness, the self-giving of discipleship, and live at peace with one another.

On a Tuesday. Is there a fellow believer you are quarrelling with? Self-denial is the salt that brings peace. Go and make peace.
verseByVerse.note: Salt was added to every sacrifice. Salt from the Dead Sea could have its salt leached out and lose its taste.

parallels.desc: with all your offerings you shall offer salt
let your speech be seasoned with salt

9.theology:
What happened on the mountain? The word is metamorphōthē — transformed. And nothing was added; something was, for a moment, no longer withheld. Set it beside Moses, whose face shone coming down Sinai and had to be veiled (Ex. 34:29–35) — but that light was borrowed and fading, which Paul says is why he covered it (2 Cor. 3:13). Here the light comes from inside; the clothes go white because of what is underneath them. Three men were allowed to see, for a few minutes, what was true of him every day they had walked beside him without noticing.

Who will not taste death? (v. 1) Mark's own arrangement answers it: the very next words are and after six days, and Mark almost never gives intervals. Some standing there would see the kingdom come with power — and six days later, three of them did. Peter confirms the reading himself, citing that mountain as evidence of the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ (2 Pet. 1:16–18). Serious readers have argued for the resurrection, Pentecost, or AD 70, and the instinct behind those is right — the kingdom comes in power by stages — but after six days is not decoration.

Why could the disciples not cast it out? (v. 29) Not a technique, and not a shortage of authority — he had given it and never withdrawn it. Prayer here is not a step they omitted on the day but the posture of a whole life. They had succeeded before; somewhere between that success and this valley the authority had become a possession rather than a gift held moment by moment. They did not stop believing. They stopped depending — and the two are almost impossible to tell apart from the inside until the day it does not work.

And the verses your Bible skips. A King James Bible has the refrain of v. 48, about the worm that does not die, three times, at vv. 44, 46 and 48. Those two repetitions are a copyist's echo of v. 48 and are absent from the earliest manuscripts, which is why modern Bibles footnote them. Nothing is lost: the sentence stands once, in full force, where Jesus quoted it from Isaiah 66:24.
9.examples:
Then: a father who had watched his son thrown to the ground since childhood, pulled him out of fires and out of water, never heard him speak — and who came looking for Jesus, found the disciples instead, and watched them fail in front of a crowd.

Now: the if you can in his prayer was not there when he set out. The disciples' failure damaged his faith in Christ. That still happens exactly the same way: the church that let someone down, the Christian who wronged them, the leader who fell, the prayer meeting that promised and produced nothing. People come to Christ afterwards with a clause in their mouth that somebody else put there — which is worth remembering by anyone whose conduct is watched by a weaker believer, and it is why v. 42 talks about millstones.

And then watch what the man does with the little he has. I believe; help my unbelief! — a shout, not a formulation, from a man on his knees beside a convulsing child. He will not deny the faith he has, and he will not pretend it is more than it is. He asks Christ to deal with the very thing that disqualifies him.

Most of us are not in one state or the other. We believe and doubt in the same hour about the same thing, and the great temptation is to sort ourselves out before we come — to work up the required confidence and then pray, as though faith were the entry fee. This man brought both halves and dumped them at Christ's feet.

And the boy was healed. That is the answer to the prayer and the vindication of it. Jesus does not say come back when you are sure. He meets the faith that is there, trembling and shot through with doubt, and does the very thing the man's doubt said he could not do. So if your faith this morning is a mess, do not wait for it to improve. Say this man's sentence. It is in the Bible to be prayed.

10.title: The Road, the Ransom, and the Beggar Who Followed
10.text: <sup>1</sup>And he left there and went to the region of Judea and beyond the Jordan, and crowds gathered to him again. And again, as was his custom, he taught them. <sup>2</sup>And Pharisees came up and in order to test him asked, “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?” <sup>3</sup>He answered them, “What did Moses command you?” <sup>4</sup>They said, “Moses allowed a man to write a certificate of divorce and to send her away.” <sup>5</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Because of your hardness of heart he wrote you this commandment. <sup>6</sup>But from the beginning of creation, ‘God made them male and female.’ <sup>7</sup>‘Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, <sup>8</sup>and the two shall become one flesh.’ So they are no longer two but one flesh. <sup>9</sup>What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.” <sup>10</sup>And in the house the disciples asked him again about this matter. <sup>11</sup>And he said to them, “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her, <sup>12</sup>and if she divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery.” <sup>13</sup>And they were bringing children to him that he might touch them, and the disciples rebuked them. <sup>14</sup>But when Jesus saw it, he was indignant and said to them, “Let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God. <sup>15</sup>Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it.” <sup>16</sup>And he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them. <sup>17</sup>And as he was setting out on his journey, a man ran up and knelt before him and asked him, “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” <sup>18</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone. <sup>19</sup>You know the commandments: ‘Do not murder, Do not commit adultery, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Do not defraud, Honor your father and mother.’” <sup>20</sup>And he said to him, “Teacher, all these I have kept from my youth.” <sup>21</sup>And Jesus, looking at him, loved him, and said to him, “You lack one thing: go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” <sup>22</sup>Disheartened by the saying, he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. <sup>23</sup>And Jesus looked around and said to his disciples, “How difficult it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!” <sup>24</sup>And the disciples were amazed at his words. But Jesus said to them again, “Children, how difficult it is to enter the kingdom of God! <sup>25</sup>It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” <sup>26</sup>And they were exceedingly astonished, and said to him, “Then who can be saved?” <sup>27</sup>Jesus looked at them and said, “With man it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God.” <sup>28</sup>Peter began to say to him, “See, we have left everything and followed you.” <sup>29</sup>Jesus said, “Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or lands, for my sake and for the gospel, <sup>30</sup>who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life. <sup>31</sup>But many who are first will be last, and the last first.” <sup>32</sup>And they were on the road, going up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was walking ahead of them. And they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid. And taking the twelve again, he began to tell them what was to happen to him, <sup>33</sup>saying, “See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and the scribes, and they will condemn him to death and deliver him over to the Gentiles. <sup>34</sup>And they will mock him and spit on him, and flog him and kill him. And after three days he will rise.” <sup>35</sup>And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came up to him and said to him, “Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you.” <sup>36</sup>And he said to them, “What do you want me to do for you?” <sup>37</sup>And they said to him, “Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory.” <sup>38</sup>Jesus said to them, “You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, or to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” <sup>39</sup>And they said to him, “We are able.” And Jesus said to them, “The cup that I drink you will drink, and with the baptism with which I am baptized, you will be baptized, <sup>40</sup>but to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared.” <sup>41</sup>And when the ten heard it, they began to be indignant at James and John. <sup>42</sup>And Jesus called them to him and said to them, “You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. <sup>43</sup>But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, <sup>44</sup>and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all. <sup>45</sup>For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” <sup>46</sup>And they came to Jericho. And as he was leaving Jericho with his disciples and a great crowd, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, the son of Timaeus, was sitting by the roadside. <sup>47</sup>And when he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out and say, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” <sup>48</sup>And many rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, “Son of David, have mercy on me!” <sup>49</sup>And Jesus stopped and said, “Call him.” And they called the blind man, saying to him, “Take heart. Get up; he is calling you.” <sup>50</sup>And throwing off his cloak, he sprang up and came to Jesus. <sup>51</sup>And Jesus said to him, “What do you want me to do for you?” And the blind man said to him, “Rabbi, let me recover my sight.” <sup>52</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Go your way; your faith has made you well.” And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him on the way.
10.overview:
Chapter 10 takes the three things people build their lives out of — marriage, children, money — and hands them, one after another, to a man walking to Jerusalem to die.

The Pharisees open with the question that cost John the Baptist his head, and Jesus refuses to argue about grounds for divorce. He goes behind Moses to Genesis: male and female, one flesh, what therefore God has joined together, let not man separate. Then parents bring children and the disciples turn them away, and Jesus is indignant — the only time in Mark that word is used of him, and it is aimed at his own men. Then a rich man runs, kneels, asks the best question in the Gospel, is looked at and loved by the Son of God — and goes home, because there was one thing he would not give.

The second half is a road. Jesus walks ahead with a set face while the twelve follow amazed and the crowd follows afraid, and he tells them for the third time exactly what is waiting: handed over, condemned, given to the Gentiles, mocked, spat on, flogged, killed, raised. James and John's response is to ask for the two best seats — and out of that squabble comes the summit of the Gospel: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.

Then Jericho, and a blind beggar who shouts a messianic title none of the disciples has used, is told to be quiet, shouts louder, throws away the only thing he owns, and follows Jesus up the road. The chapter opened with a rich man who would not follow and closes with a beggar who did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–31 — Divorce, Children, and the Danger of Riches
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The trap (vv. 1–12). He crosses into Herod's jurisdiction, and the Pharisees immediately ask him about divorce — the question that cost John the Baptist his head. Jesus refuses to argue about grounds and goes behind Moses to Genesis: male and female, one flesh, joined by God.

The children (vv. 13–16). Parents bring their children to be touched, the disciples turn them away as an interruption, and Jesus is indignant — the only time in Mark that word is used of him, and it is aimed at his own men. Then he picks the children up and blesses them.

The rich man (vv. 17–22). A man runs, kneels, and asks the best question in the Gospel. Jesus looks at him and loves him, and asks for the one thing he will not give. He goes away sorrowful, and Mark does not soften the ending.

The impossibility (vv. 23–31). A camel through a needle's eye, disciples asking then who can be saved?, and the only answer there has ever been — with man it is impossible, but not with God.

Three subjects, and one thread running under them: marriage, children, money. The three things people build their lives out of, handled one after another by a man walking to Jerusalem to die.
verseByVerse.theology:
Divorce, and what Mark leaves out. A reader with Matthew open will notice that Mark's version is starker. Matthew twice records an exception — except for sexual immorality (Matt. 5:32; 19:9) — and Mark records none, while adding, for his Roman readers, the case of a wife who divorces her husband.

That is not a contradiction but a difference of purpose. Mark gives the principle in its unguarded, creation-order form, the way a thing is stated when you want its full weight felt. Matthew, writing where the rabbis argued endlessly over grounds, records the one qualification Jesus actually allowed. Paul adds a second — the believer deserted by an unbelieving spouse is not enslaved (1 Cor. 7:15). So the Reformed churches have long recognised two grounds on which the bond may be broken and the innocent party freed: adultery and desertion, and no others.

Mark's silence is not a denial. It is a refusal to lead with the exception — because the moment the exception becomes the headline, hardness of heart starts hunting for a way in. Jesus will not begin where the Pharisees wanted to begin, with the escape clause. He begins with the joining that God himself performs.

And "Why do you call me good?" (v. 18) is not Jesus denying that he is good or that he is God — and note that he never withdraws the word or corrects the man for using it. He holds it up to the light. The young man has tossed off Good Teacher as easy flattery. Jesus stops him: do you know what you are saying? Goodness in the full sense belongs to God alone. So either you should not have called me good — or, if the word is right, you must reckon with who I am. It is not a denial of his deity but a door held open to it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a man who ran, knelt, asked the right question, had kept the commandments since boyhood, was looked at and loved by the Son of God — and went home.

Now: he is the most alarming figure in the Gospel precisely because there is nothing wrong with him. He is not a Pharisee, not a hypocrite, not hostile. He is sincere, moral, eager and respectful, and he is the one person in Mark who meets Jesus, is loved by him, and walks away.

And notice what stopped him. Not an argument. Not doubt. One thing he would not hand over.

So the question the passage actually asks is not am I a good person? — he was, by every visible measure. It is: what is the one thing? What would you be unable to say yes to, if Christ named it tonight? For this man it was money, and Jesus went straight to it, because a rival throne is always specific.

The test is not hypothetical either. Most people know the answer within a few seconds and then spend a while explaining why that particular thing is different. He went away sorrowful, which means he knew exactly what he was refusing. Mark records no second visit.

verseByVerse.quote: And he left there and went to the region of Judea and beyond the Jordan, and crowds gathered to him again. And again, as was his custom, he taught them. And Pharisees came up and in order to test him asked, "Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus left Galilee and went to the region of Judea and beyond the Jordan. Crowds gathered to him again, and, as was his custom, he taught them again. Pharisees came and, to test him, asked: is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?

Setting. Jesus has left Galilee for the last time. He is on his way to Jerusalem and the cross (v. 32). Chapter 10 gathers teaching on the life of the kingdom along the way: marriage, children, wealth, and greatness, ending with the Son of Man who came to serve and give his life (v. 45).

The region of Judea and beyond the Jordan. “Beyond the Jordan” is Perea, the land east of the river, which, like Galilee, was ruled by Herod Antipas. This is significant. Herod had divorced his wife to marry Herodias, who had divorced his brother, and John the Baptist had been beheaded for saying it was unlawful (6:17–18). The question about divorce, asked in Herod’s territory, was dangerous.

And again, as was his custom, he taught them. Teaching was his first work, ahead of miracles (1:38).

In order to test him. The Pharisees did not want instruction. They wanted a trap. If he took a strict line, he might offend the crowds, and Herod. If he took a loose line, he could be accused of undermining Moses.

Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife? All Jews agreed that divorce was permitted. The debate was over the grounds. Deuteronomy 24:1 allowed a man to divorce his wife if he found “some indecency” in her. The school of Rabbi Shammai said this meant sexual immorality only. The school of Rabbi Hillel said it meant anything that displeased him, even burning the dinner; a later rabbi, Akiba, said finding a prettier woman was enough. Matthew records the question in this form: for any cause? (Matthew 19:3). Mark gives the bare question, the more radical one: is divorce lawful at all?

In a sentence. In Herod’s territory, on the way to Jerusalem, the Pharisees tried to trap Jesus with the disputed question of divorce.

On a Tuesday. Some people ask about marriage only to find the minimum required. Ask instead what God intended.
verseByVerse.note: “Beyond the Jordan” is Perea, the land east of the river, ruled by Herod Antipas — who had imprisoned John for his marriage. Rabbis debated the grounds for divorce.

verseByVerse.quote: He answered them, "What did Moses command you?" They said, "Moses allowed a man to write a certificate of divorce and to send her away." And Jesus said to them, "Because of your hardness of heart he wrote you this commandment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He answered: what did Moses command you? They said: Moses allowed a man to write a certificate of divorce and send her away. Jesus said to them: because of your hardness of heart he wrote you this commandment.

What did Moses command you? Jesus goes to Scripture, as always. Notice the word “command”.

Moses allowed a man to write a certificate of divorce and to send her away. They correct him: “allowed”, not “commanded”. They are referring to Deuteronomy 24:1–4. Read carefully, that passage does not command divorce or even approve it. It regulates something already happening. Its actual command is that a man who has divorced his wife, and she has married another, may not take her back. The certificate of divorce protected the woman: it proved she was free and could remarry without being accused of adultery. It also required a formal process, which might give the husband time to reconsider.

Because of your hardness of heart he wrote you this commandment. Key phrase. “Hardness of heart” (sklērokardia): stubbornness, an unteachable heart. The law of divorce was a concession to human sin. Because men would divorce their wives anyway, God through Moses set limits to protect the vulnerable. It was never God’s ideal. A law can regulate sin without approving it.

What it does not mean. Not that Moses was wrong, or that the law was not from God. But laws for a sinful society are not always statements of God’s perfect will. Some laws restrain evil; they do not define good.

In a sentence. Jesus said that Moses’ provision for divorce was a concession to the hardness of human hearts, not a statement of God’s will for marriage.

On a Tuesday. Don’t confuse what God permits because of sin with what he desires. Ask what pleases him, not what you can get away with.
verseByVerse.note: A certificate of divorce freed a woman to remarry.

verseByVerse.quote: But from the beginning of creation, 'God made them male and female.' 'Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.' So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But from the beginning of creation, God made them male and female. Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh. So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.

But from the beginning of creation. Jesus goes behind Moses to creation. Before sin, before the law of Sinai, God established marriage. That original design is the standard. Deuteronomy 24 was a concession; Genesis 1–2 is the pattern.

God made them male and female. Genesis 1:27. Two sexes, created by God, made for each other. Marriage is grounded in the way God made humanity, as man and woman, not in human custom or legislation. This is the foundation of the Christian understanding of marriage as between one man and one woman.

Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife. Genesis 2:24. Jesus treats the narrator’s words in Genesis as God’s own word (Matthew 19:4–5 says: he who created them … said). “Leave”: a new primary loyalty replaces the old one. “Hold fast” (proskollēthēsetai): be glued, joined, cleave. Marriage is a permanent bond.

And the two shall become one flesh. A union of the whole person, physical, emotional and spiritual, of which sexual union is both the expression and the seal. A new unit is created.

So they are no longer two but one flesh. Jesus’ own conclusion. A married couple is a single new reality.

What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate. Key words. In marriage, God is the one who joins. A wedding is not merely a human contract; God himself creates the bond. Therefore no human being, not the husband, not the wife, not a court or a rabbi, has the right to tear it apart. “Separate” (chōrizetō) is the word used of divorce (1 Corinthians 7:10–11).

In a sentence. Going back to creation, Jesus taught that God made marriage as the lifelong union of a man and a woman as one flesh, which no human being may separate.

On a Tuesday. If you are married, God joined you. Treat your marriage as his work, and guard it.

parallels.desc: male and female he created them

verseByVerse.quote: And in the house the disciples asked him again about this matter. And he said to them, "Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her, and if she divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the house the disciples asked him again about this. He said to them: whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her; and if she divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery.

And in the house the disciples asked him again. They were startled. Matthew records their reaction: If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is better not to marry (Matthew 19:10). Jesus’ teaching was stricter than either rabbinic school.

Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her. Since God’s bond still holds in his eyes, remarriage after a divorce God does not recognise is adultery. “Against her”: this was revolutionary. In Jewish law, adultery was a sin against a husband; a man could only commit adultery against another man, by taking his wife. Jesus says a husband can commit adultery against his own wife. She has rights. Marriage creates obligations on both sides equally.

And if she divorces her husband and marries another. Jewish law did not allow a wife to divorce her husband, but Roman and Greek law did. Mark, writing probably for Roman readers, records that Jesus’ teaching applies to both. (Herodias had in fact divorced her husband, which may be in the background.)

The exceptions. Mark gives the principle without exception. Matthew records an exception: except for sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9; 5:32). Paul adds another: if an unbelieving spouse leaves, the believer is not bound (1 Corinthians 7:15). These exceptions do not contradict Mark. They show that some sins so break the marriage covenant that the innocent party may lawfully end it.

Where Christians differ: divorce and remarriage. Roman Catholic teaching holds that a valid sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved; remarriage while the spouse lives is never permitted, though an annulment may declare that no true marriage existed. Some Protestants hold that remarriage is never right while a spouse lives, even after divorce for adultery. Others allow divorce for many reasons, such as abuse, or simply breakdown. Verdict: the Westminster Confession (24.5–6) states the position best grounded in Scripture: God’s design is lifelong marriage, and divorce is always a tragedy; but adultery, and wilful desertion that cannot be remedied, are grounds on which the innocent party may divorce and be free to remarry. Abandonment through serious abuse may fall under desertion, and the church should protect the vulnerable. Those who have divorced and remarried wrongly may repent and find full forgiveness in Christ, as with any sin.

In a sentence. Jesus taught that divorce and remarriage, whether by husband or wife, is adultery in God’s eyes, because the marriage bond God made still stands.

On a Tuesday. If divorce has touched your life, don’t despair; Christ forgives and restores. If you are married, keep your vows. If you are single, honour marriage in how you speak of it.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish law did not allow a wife to divorce her husband, but Roman law did; Mark’s wording covers both.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were bringing children to him that he might touch them, and the disciples rebuked them. But when Jesus saw it, he was indignant and said to them, "Let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
People were bringing children to him so that he might touch them, and the disciples rebuked them. When Jesus saw it, he was indignant and said to them: let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God.

The placing. After marriage comes children, the fruit of marriage. Mark is giving a picture of the household in the kingdom.

And they were bringing children to him that he might touch them. Parents, probably, wanting his blessing. Luke says some were babies (brephē, Luke 18:15). Jewish parents customarily brought children to rabbis and elders for a blessing.

And the disciples rebuked them. Perhaps they thought Jesus was too busy, or too important, for children. On the way to Jerusalem there were weightier matters. They had not learned the lesson of 9:36–37.

He was indignant. A strong word (ēganaktēsen), found only here about Jesus. He was angry with his disciples. Mark, unlike Matthew and Luke, records Jesus’ emotions freely.

Let the children come to me; do not hinder them. Two commands, positive and negative. Nothing must stand between children and Jesus.

For to such belongs the kingdom of God. “To such”: to children, and to all who are like them. The kingdom belongs to those who, like children, have nothing to offer and simply receive. Not because children are innocent, but because they are dependent.

Where Christians differ: children and baptism. Paedobaptists (Presbyterians, Anglicans, Lutherans, Catholics) often appeal to this passage for infant baptism: if the kingdom belongs to children, they should receive the sign of the covenant. Credobaptists (Baptists) answer that Jesus did not baptise these children; he blessed them, and the passage is about how all must receive the kingdom, not about a sacrament. Verdict: the passage shows Christ’s welcome for children and the need to bring them to him, which both sides agree on. It does not mention baptism, and it cannot settle the question. The New Testament pattern links baptism to repentance and faith, so the credobaptist position is best. This is a disagreement among brothers, held charitably.

In a sentence. Jesus was indignant when his disciples kept children away, commanding that they be allowed to come, for the kingdom belongs to such as these.

On a Tuesday. Bring your children to Jesus: pray for them, teach them, take them to worship. Never be a hindrance to a child coming to Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Children had little status in the ancient world.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it." And he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, I tell you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it. And he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.

Whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child. How does a child receive? As a gift, with open hands, without thinking they have earned it. A small child cannot do anything to deserve its parents’ love; it simply receives. The kingdom must be received in exactly that way, as grace, not achievement. This is the gospel in a sentence. The rich man of the next scene is the opposite: what must I do? (v. 17).

Shall not enter it. A strong negative. This is the only way in. Adults must become like children; they cannot come in as adults, with their merits.

And he took them in his arms. Only Mark records it, as in 9:36. The people brought the children for a touch; he gave them an embrace.

And blessed them, laying his hands on them. “Blessed” (kateulogei) is an intensive form, used only here in the New Testament: he blessed them fervently, again and again. The laying on of hands was the sign of blessing (Genesis 48:14).

In a sentence. Jesus said that only those who receive the kingdom as a child receives a gift will enter it, and he embraced and blessed the children.

For worship. Come to God today as a child, with nothing in your hands. That is the only way anyone comes.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he was setting out on his journey, a man ran up and knelt before him and asked him, "Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?" And Jesus said to him, "Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he was setting out on his journey, a man ran up, knelt before him and asked: Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life? Jesus said to him: why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.

A man ran up and knelt before him. Eager and respectful. Matthew tells us he was young (Matthew 19:20), Luke that he was a ruler (Luke 18:18), and all three that he was rich (v. 22). So he is often called the rich young ruler. He had everything, and still lacked something.

Good Teacher. An unusual title. Jewish teachers were not normally called good, a word reserved for God.

What must I do to inherit eternal life? A sincere question, and the most important there is. But note the word “do”. He thinks eternal life is something to be achieved. And “inherit” is a strange word to pair with doing: an inheritance is received, not earned. The contrast with the children (v. 15) is deliberate.

Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone. Jesus is not denying that he is good, or denying that he is God. He is making the man think. Do you know what you are saying? If only God is good, and you call me good, then either you are speaking carelessly, or you are recognising who I am. The question also prepares for what follows. If only God is good, then the man is not good either, whatever he thinks about his keeping of the commandments.

What it does not mean. Not a confession by Jesus that he is a sinner, as some have argued. The New Testament is clear that he was without sin (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22).

In a sentence. A rich man ran to Jesus asking what he must do to inherit eternal life, and Jesus challenged his casual use of “good”, since only God is good.

On a Tuesday. If you think of God’s standard as “good” the way you are good, think again. Only God is good, which is why we need grace.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew says he was young, Luke that he was a ruler. Jesus does not deny his goodness; he asks the man to think about what he is saying.

verseByVerse.quote: You know the commandments: 'Do not murder, Do not commit adultery, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Do not defraud, Honor your father and mother.'" And he said to him, "Teacher, all these I have kept from my youth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You know the commandments: do not murder, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness, do not defraud, honour your father and mother. The man said: Teacher, all these I have kept from my youth.

You know the commandments. Jesus points him to God’s law. If the question is about doing, the law sets out what to do.

The list. Jesus lists the second table of the Ten Commandments, the commandments about our neighbour: the sixth, seventh, eighth and ninth, then the fifth. “Do not defraud” is not one of the ten; it may stand for the tenth (do not covet), since defrauding is covetousness in action, and it is especially relevant to a rich man (Deuteronomy 24:14; Malachi 3:5). Jesus leaves out the first table, about God, and the tenth, about desire. Those are where the man will be exposed.

Teacher, all these I have kept from my youth. He drops the “good”. His claim is sincere, and by outward standards perhaps true. Paul could say the same of his life before Christ: as to righteousness under the law, blameless (Philippians 3:6). But he has not understood how deep God’s law goes (Matthew 5:21–28). And if he has kept everything, why does he still feel the lack (Matthew 19:20 records him asking: What do I still lack?)?

In a sentence. Jesus pointed the man to the commandments about his neighbour, and the man sincerely claimed to have kept them all since his youth.

On a Tuesday. Outward obedience can hide an unexamined heart. Ask God to search you (Psalm 139:23–24).
verseByVerse.note: Jesus lists the commandments about one’s neighbour; “do not defraud” is not one of the Ten in so many words; it may stand for the tenth, against coveting (cf. Lev 19:13).

parallels.desc: the second table of the Ten Commandments

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus, looking at him, loved him, and said to him, "You lack one thing: go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me." Disheartened by the saying, he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, looking at him, loved him, and said to him: you lack one thing. Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me. Disheartened by the saying, he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions.

And Jesus, looking at him, loved him. Only Mark records this, and it is the key to the passage. What follows is not harsh. It is love. Jesus saw his sincerity and his need, and the demand he makes is the loving cure for what was killing him.

You lack one thing. For all his keeping of the law, there is a gap. His wealth had his heart. It was his god. He had broken the first commandment: You shall have no other gods before me (Exodus 20:3), and the tenth.

Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor. The surgery: cut out the idol. Jesus does not ask everyone to sell everything (Zacchaeus gave half, Luke 19:8; many disciples kept homes, as Peter did). He asks this man to give up the thing that stood between him and God. For him, it was money.

And you will have treasure in heaven. Not a payment for salvation, but a promise. He would not be poorer; he would exchange earthly treasure for heavenly (Matthew 6:19–21).

And come, follow me. The real point. Selling everything was the means; following Jesus was the end. Eternal life is not earned by giving away money, but found in following Christ. The man had asked what to do; Jesus answers with the call to discipleship. Love of God (the first table) is shown in following the one in whom God has come.

Disheartened by the saying. “Disheartened” (stygnasas) means his face fell, darkened like a gloomy sky (the word is used of a lowering sky in Matthew 16:3).

He went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. The only person in the Gospels who was called by Jesus to follow him and refused. He went away. He wanted eternal life, but not more than he wanted his money. His possessions possessed him.

What it does not mean. Not that salvation is by giving away your wealth, or that riches are themselves evil. But anything you love more than Christ will keep you from him, and Christ has the right to ask for it.

In a sentence. Out of love, Jesus told the man to give up the wealth that ruled him and follow him, but he went away sad, because he could not let go.

On a Tuesday. What is your “one thing”, the thing you could not give up for Christ? Look at it honestly, and give it to him.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark notes that Jesus looked at him and loved him.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus looked around and said to his disciples, "How difficult it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!" And the disciples were amazed at his words. But Jesus said to them again, "Children, how difficult it is to enter the kingdom of God! It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus looked around and said to his disciples: how difficult it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God! The disciples were amazed at his words. But Jesus said to them again: children, how difficult it is to enter the kingdom of God! It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.

And Jesus looked around. At his disciples, as the rich man walked away.

How difficult it will be for those who have wealth. Riches are dangerous. They give a sense of security and self-sufficiency, of not needing God (Deuteronomy 8:11–14). They tie the heart to this world. They make it hard to receive the kingdom like a child, with empty hands.

And the disciples were amazed at his words. Because in Jewish thought, wealth was a sign of God’s blessing (Deuteronomy 28:1–14; Job 42:10). The rich were thought to have the best chance: they could afford to give alms, offer sacrifices, and study the law. If the rich can hardly enter, what hope for anyone?

Children, how difficult it is to enter the kingdom of God! “Children”: a tender word, and it links back to the children of v. 15. Jesus now widens it: it is hard for anyone to enter.

It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle. The camel was the largest animal in the land; a needle’s eye, the smallest opening. Deliberate, comic exaggeration, to say: impossible. Some have suggested that “the eye of a needle” was a small gate in the wall of Jerusalem, which a camel could squeeze through on its knees, but there is no evidence for such a gate, and the idea softens what Jesus meant to be impossible. Others suggest a scribal confusion between kamēlos (camel) and kamilos (rope); also without support. A similar Jewish saying spoke of an elephant passing through a needle’s eye. Jesus means exactly what the disciples heard: humanly impossible (v. 27).

In a sentence. Jesus told his amazed disciples that it is so hard for the rich to enter the kingdom that a camel would more easily pass through the eye of a needle.

On a Tuesday. By the world’s standards, most readers of this are rich. Hold your wealth with an open hand.
verseByVerse.note: The camel was the largest animal in the land; the picture is deliberate exaggeration. The idea of a gate called “the Eye of the Needle” is a much later invention.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were exceedingly astonished, and said to him, "Then who can be saved?" Jesus looked at them and said, "With man it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were exceedingly astonished and said to him: then who can be saved? Jesus looked at them and said: with man it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God.

Then who can be saved? The right conclusion. If even the rich, who seemed most blessed, cannot, then no one can. They had heard correctly.

Jesus looked at them. A deliberate, steady look, Mark’s third “look” in this passage (vv. 21, 23).

With man it is impossible. Yes, they had understood. Salvation is not difficult for human beings; it is impossible. No one, rich or poor, can save himself. Not by keeping commandments, giving money, or any effort. This is the heart of the gospel’s bad news: we are unable.

But not with God. For all things are possible with God. And this is the good news. What man cannot do, God does. An echo of the angel to Sarah: Is anything too hard for the Lord? (Genesis 18:14). Salvation is God’s work from beginning to end: he gives the new heart, he grants repentance and faith, he draws us (John 6:44; Ephesians 2:8–9). If God can save a rich man, and he can (Zacchaeus, Joseph of Arimathea), he can save anyone. The camel can go through the needle if God takes it through.

What it does not mean. Not that people have no responsibility to repent and believe. But even our repentance and faith are God’s gifts, the fruit of his grace, not our contribution to it.

In a sentence. Jesus told his astonished disciples that salvation is impossible for human beings but not for God, for whom all things are possible.

For worship. Pray for the hardest cases you know with confidence. Salvation is impossible with man, which is why it is always God’s work.

parallels.desc: is anything too hard for the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: Peter began to say to him, "See, we have left everything and followed you." Jesus said, "Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or lands, for my sake and for the gospel, who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life. But many who are first will be last, and the last first."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter began to say to him: see, we have left everything and followed you. Jesus said: truly, I tell you, there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or lands for my sake and for the gospel who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life. But many who are first will be last, and the last first.

See, we have left everything and followed you. Peter contrasts the disciples with the rich man: we have done what he would not. It is true (1:18, 20). Matthew adds his question: What then will we have? (Matthew 19:27). There is a hint of self-congratulation.

There is no one who has left. Jesus does not rebuke Peter. He promises reward. Following him costs: home, family, property. In the early church, many converts were disowned by their families or lost their property (Hebrews 10:34).

For my sake and for the gospel. As in 8:35, only Mark adds “and for the gospel”. The cost is borne for Jesus and his message.

Who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time. Not only in heaven, now. How? In the family of God. The one who loses his earthly family gains brothers, sisters and mothers in the church (3:34–35), homes opened to him, and a share in all that belongs to the people of God (Acts 2:44–46). Notice that “fathers” is missing from the list of what is received: in God’s family, there is one Father (Matthew 23:9).

With persecutions. Only Mark adds this, and it is honest. The reward is not a comfortable life. Following Jesus brings persecution as well as family. Mark’s readers in Rome knew this well.

And in the age to come eternal life. The answer to the rich man’s question (v. 17). What he would not give up everything for, they will receive.

But many who are first will be last, and the last first. A warning, perhaps to Peter. The rich and powerful, first in this world, may be last in the kingdom. The disciples, last in the world’s eyes, will be first. But also: those who think of themselves as first, because of their sacrifices, may find themselves last. Reward is grace, not wages earned (Matthew 20:1–16).

In a sentence. Jesus promised that everyone who leaves family and property for him and the gospel will receive a hundred times more now, in God’s family, with persecutions, and eternal life to come.

On a Tuesday. If following Christ has cost you family or property, look around at the church. These are your brothers, sisters and mothers. And if you have a home, open it to those who have lost theirs.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–52 — The Road to Jerusalem, the Ransom, and Bartimaeus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Walking ahead (vv. 32–34). Mark gives us a picture worth stopping over: a road going up to Jerusalem, Jesus striding out in front, and behind him a group that is amazed and a crowd that is frightened. Then he tells them, for the third and most detailed time, exactly what is waiting — handed over, condemned, given to the Gentiles, mocked, spat on, flogged, killed, raised.

The request (vv. 35–45). And immediately James and John ask for the two best seats. The other ten are furious, which is not righteous indignation but competition. So Jesus lays down the law of his kingdom — the great one is the servant, the first is the slave — and grounds it in himself: he came to give his life as a ransom for many.

Jericho (vv. 46–52). The last miracle before Jerusalem. A blind beggar shouts a messianic title that none of the disciples has yet used, is told to be quiet by the crowd, shouts louder, throws away the only thing he owns, and follows Jesus up the road to the cross.

The chapter opened with a rich man who would not follow and closes with a beggar who did.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mark 10:45 is the theological centre of this Gospel, and every word repays weighing.

A ransom — lytron — was the price paid to set a captive free: the sum laid down to buy a slave out of bondage or a prisoner off the block. Jesus says his own life is that price.

And a ransom is a substitute — one thing given instead of another. He does not merely die for our benefit; he dies in our stead, the many going free because the One is handed over.

Behind it stands Isaiah 53, where the Servant poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many, and by his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous (Isa. 53:11–12). That word many rings through the prophecy, and Jesus claims it as his own errand.

And to whom is the price paid? Not, as some early teachers imagined, to the devil, as though Satan held a rightful claim. The debt is owed to the justice of God — and God, in the person of his Son, pays it himself.

Here, then, is why he came. Not first to teach, or to heal, or even to model servanthood, though he did all three. To die in the room of sinners who could never buy themselves back. Nineteen verses earlier the disciples asked then who can be saved? and were told with man it is impossible, but not with God. This is how.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the same question — What do you want me to do for you? — asked twice in fifteen verses.

It is put to James and John in verse 36 and to a blind beggar in verse 51. Mark has done that deliberately, and the two answers are the whole chapter.

James and John ask for glory. They open with a blank cheque — we want you to do for us whatever we ask — and then name the two best seats in the kingdom. They get a redirection and a warning.

Bartimaeus asks for mercy, and then for sight. He gets exactly what he asks for, immediately.

Now: the question is still being asked, and most of us answer it more like the brothers than the beggar. The blank-cheque prayer — do what I have decided — dressed up religiously. The request framed around position, comfort, and being noticed.

And notice what makes Bartimaeus's answer better. It is not humility as a technique. He asked for the thing he actually needed, from someone he had correctly identified, having first asked for mercy rather than a favour. He had no credentials, no standing, and no way of repaying anybody — which is precisely the child of verse 15, arriving at the other end of the chapter with nothing in his hands.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were on the road, going up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was walking ahead of them. And they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid. And taking the twelve again, he began to tell them what was to happen to him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were on the road, going up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was walking ahead of them. They were amazed, and those who followed were afraid. Taking the Twelve aside again, he began to tell them what was going to happen to him.

And they were on the road, going up to Jerusalem. The first time Mark names the destination. Jerusalem stands about 2,500 feet (750 m) up in the Judean hills, so one always went “up” to it, especially from the Jordan valley, which is below sea level. The road from Jericho climbs about 3,500 feet (1,000 m) in 15 miles (25 km).

And Jesus was walking ahead of them. A vivid picture, probably from Peter’s memory. Jesus leads, resolute, going to his death on purpose. Luke says: he set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51). He is not dragged to the cross; he walks ahead to it. A shepherd goes before his sheep (John 10:4).

And they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid. Something in his manner awed them. Two groups may be meant: the Twelve, who were amazed, and the wider group of followers, who were afraid. They sensed that something terrible lay ahead.

And taking the twelve again. Aside, privately, as before.

He began to tell them what was to happen to him. He knows. Nothing will take him by surprise.

In a sentence. On the road up to Jerusalem, Jesus walked ahead of his awed and frightened followers and began to tell the Twelve what would happen to him.

On a Tuesday. Jesus walks ahead of you into every hard road. Follow him there.
verseByVerse.note: Jerusalem stands high in the hills; one always went “up” to it.

verseByVerse.quote: saying, "See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and the scribes, and they will condemn him to death and deliver him over to the Gentiles. And they will mock him and spit on him, and flog him and kill him. And after three days he will rise."
verseByVerse.commentary:
See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and the scribes. They will condemn him to death and hand him over to the Gentiles. They will mock him, spit on him, flog him and kill him. And after three days he will rise.

The third prediction. The fullest and most detailed of the three (8:31; 9:31). It reads almost like a summary of chapters 14–16, and Mark’s readers would recognise each step.

See, we are going up to Jerusalem. “See” (idou): look, pay attention.

Delivered over to the chief priests and the scribes. Betrayed into the hands of the Jewish leaders (14:10, 43).

And they will condemn him to death. The Sanhedrin’s verdict (14:64).

And deliver him over to the Gentiles. New detail. The Jewish leaders did not have the right to carry out executions under Roman rule (John 18:31), and so they would hand him to Pilate (15:1). God’s Messiah would be rejected by both Jews and Gentiles; the whole world is guilty (Acts 4:27).

And they will mock him and spit on him, and flog him and kill him. Every one was fulfilled: mocking (14:65; 15:17–20, 29–32), spitting (14:65; 15:19), flogging (15:15), killing (15:24, 37). Isaiah had foretold it: I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting (Isaiah 50:6). Roman flogging, with a whip of leather straps weighted with bone or metal, was so savage that men sometimes died under it.

And after three days he will rise. Again the promise. It is always there.

In a sentence. Jesus told the Twelve in detail that in Jerusalem he would be betrayed, condemned, handed to the Gentiles, mocked, spat upon, flogged and killed, and would rise after three days.

For worship. He knew every detail of what he would suffer, and still walked ahead. That is the measure of his love.
verseByVerse.note: This third prediction is the fullest, naming the Gentiles, mocking, spitting and flogging.

parallels.desc: I gave my back to those who strike

verseByVerse.quote: And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came up to him and said to him, "Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you." And he said to them, "What do you want me to do for you?" And they said to him, "Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory."
verseByVerse.commentary:
James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came to him and said: Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask. He said to them: what do you want me to do for you? They said: grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory.

The contrast. Each time Jesus predicts his suffering, the disciples respond with something that shows they have not understood: Peter’s rebuke (8:32), the argument about greatness (9:34), and now this. Immediately after hearing that he will be spat on and killed, two of his closest friends ask for the best seats.

James and John, the sons of Zebedee. Two of the inner three, who had been with him on the mountain. Matthew says their mother asked on their behalf (Matthew 20:20). She was probably Salome, possibly the sister of Mary, which would make them Jesus’ cousins (compare 15:40 with Matthew 27:56 and John 19:25). Family closeness may have encouraged the request.

Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you. A blank cheque. They approach Jesus as one might approach a king, asking for a favour before stating it. Herod had made such a promise (6:22–23), with disastrous results.

What do you want me to do for you? Jesus will ask the very same question of blind Bartimaeus (v. 51). The two requests are a study in contrast: they ask for glory, he asks for sight.

Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory. To sit at a king’s right and left was the place of highest honour and power. They believe he is the Messiah, and that he will reign in glory. They have seen that glory on the mountain. But they want the glory without the cross, and they want it for themselves, above the others. Ironically, those who will be at his right and left when he is “enthroned” will be two criminals on crosses (15:27).

In a sentence. Straight after Jesus predicted his suffering, James and John asked him for the highest places of honour in his glory.

On a Tuesday. What are you asking Jesus for? Make sure your prayers are not a request for position but for his will.
verseByVerse.note: To sit at a king’s right and left was the place of highest honour.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, or to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?" And they said to him, "We are able." And Jesus said to them, "The cup that I drink you will drink, and with the baptism with which I am baptized, you will be baptized, but to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them: you do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, or to be baptised with the baptism with which I am baptised? They said: we are able. Jesus said: the cup that I drink you will drink, and with the baptism with which I am baptised you will be baptised; but to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to grant; it is for those for whom it has been prepared.

You do not know what you are asking. They do not know what his glory involves, or the path to it.

The cup that I drink. Key image. In the Old Testament, the “cup” is often a picture of God’s judgement and wrath, which the wicked must drink (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17, 22; Jeremiah 25:15–28). Jesus will pray in Gethsemane: Remove this cup from me (14:36). The cup he drinks is the wrath of God against sin, which he takes in our place. This is penal substitution: Christ bears the penalty that sinners deserved.

Or to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized. “Baptism” here means being overwhelmed, submerged, as by a flood of waters (Psalm 42:7; 69:1–2). Jesus speaks of his coming suffering and death as a baptism (Luke 12:50).

We are able. Brave and ignorant.

The cup that I drink you will drink. Jesus predicts that they will indeed suffer. James was the first of the apostles to be martyred, beheaded by Herod Agrippa about AD 44 (Acts 12:2). John suffered exile on Patmos (Revelation 1:9) and, by tradition, lived to an old age. But their cup will not be the same as his. Only he drinks the cup of God’s wrath for sin. Theirs is the cup of suffering for his sake (Colossians 1:24 speaks of this in a different sense).

But to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to grant. Not that Jesus lacks authority, but that he submits to the Father’s will (13:32). The places are assigned by the Father.

But it is for those for whom it has been prepared. Prepared by God, in his eternal purpose. The places of honour in the kingdom are not won by ambition or asking, but by God’s sovereign appointment. Matthew adds: by my Father (Matthew 20:23).

In a sentence. Jesus told James and John they did not understand that his glory comes through the cup of suffering and wrath; they would suffer too, but places of honour are the Father’s to give.

On a Tuesday. Following Christ will involve a cup of suffering. But he has drunk the cup of wrath, so you never will.
verseByVerse.note: The “cup” is the Old Testament picture of God’s judgment poured out; “baptism” pictures being overwhelmed by suffering. James was later killed by Herod Agrippa.

parallels.desc: the waters have come up to my neck
I have a baptism to be baptized with

verseByVerse.quote: And when the ten heard it, they began to be indignant at James and John. And Jesus called them to him and said to them, "You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the ten heard this, they began to be indignant at James and John. Jesus called them to him and said: you know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you. Whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all.

They began to be indignant at James and John. Not because the request was wrong, but because the two had got in first. The ten had the same ambitions.

And Jesus called them to him. All twelve. This is for all of them.

Those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles. “Considered”, “seem to rule”: a hint of irony. Their power is not what it looks like; the real ruler is God.

Lord it over them … exercise authority over them. Both verbs have a prefix (kata-) that means power used downward, against people, to dominate. The world’s pattern of leadership is power over others for the leader’s benefit. Rome knew this well.

But it shall not be so among you. A flat contradiction. Not “it should not”, but “it is not”: this is not how my community works.

Whoever would be great among you must be your servant. “Servant” (diakonos): one who waits at table.

And whoever would be first among you must be slave of all. “Slave” (doulos) goes further still: one who belongs to another and has no rights. Two steps down: servant, slave. The way up is down. Greatness in the kingdom is measured by service.

What it does not mean. Not that there is no authority in the church. Elders are to lead and be obeyed (Hebrews 13:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:12). But Christian authority is exercised as service, for the good of others, never for the leader’s benefit (1 Peter 5:1–3).

In a sentence. When the others resented James and John, Jesus taught that in his kingdom, unlike the world, greatness is shown by being a servant and the first must be the slave of all.

On a Tuesday. If you lead at work, home or church, ask: am I using my power for others or for myself?

verseByVerse.quote: For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.

The key verse of Mark. This one sentence sums up the whole purpose of Jesus’ coming. It explains the three passion predictions and everything that follows in chapters 11–16.

For even the Son of Man. The Son of Man of Daniel 7, to whom all nations will give service (Daniel 7:14). If anyone had the right to be served, it was he.

Came not to be served but to serve. “Came”: implying that he came from somewhere, from heaven, with a purpose. And the purpose reversed every expectation. The King came as a servant. He washed his disciples’ feet (John 13:1–17). He took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7).

And to give his life. The supreme service: his life itself. Not taken from him but given (John 10:18).

As a ransom. Key word. A “ransom” (lytron) was the price paid to free a slave, a prisoner of war, or someone condemned to death. In the Old Testament, the firstborn were redeemed with a payment (Numbers 3:46–48), and a man whose ox had killed someone could pay a ransom for his own life (Exodus 21:30). We are slaves of sin and under the sentence of death (Romans 6:23). Jesus pays the price of our freedom with his own life. The price is not paid to Satan, as some of the early fathers thought, but to the justice of God, whose law we have broken.

For many. “For” (anti) means “in place of”, “instead of”. This is substitution: he gives his life in place of theirs. The background is Isaiah 53, the suffering servant, who poured out his soul to death… yet he bore the sin of many (Isaiah 53:12; also 53:10–11). Jesus is that servant. His death is a substitutionary payment, bearing the penalty of sin in the place of sinners.

Who are the many? “Many” contrasts the one who dies with the great number of those for whom he dies. The phrase comes from Isaiah 53, where the servant bears the sin of many and makes many to be accounted righteous. Reformed theology reads this as definite: Christ gave his life as a ransom for his people, those the Father had given him (John 10:11, 15; 17:9), and his death actually secures their freedom. A ransom that is paid frees the captive. Other traditions read “many” as “all”, a universal offer. Verdict: the ransom is real and effective; it does not merely make freedom possible but actually purchases it for the many. This is definite atonement. And the gospel offer still goes freely to all, since no one who comes to Christ will be turned away (John 6:37).

In a sentence. The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as the price that frees many, in their place.

For worship. You were bought at a price (1 Corinthians 6:20). Worship the servant King who gave his life as your ransom, and serve others as he served you.
verseByVerse.note: A ransom was the price paid to free a slave or captive.

parallels.desc: he bore the sin of many

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Jericho. And as he was leaving Jericho with his disciples and a great crowd, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, the son of Timaeus, was sitting by the roadside. And when he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out and say, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!" And many rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, "Son of David, have mercy on me!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They came to Jericho. As he was leaving Jericho with his disciples and a great crowd, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, the son of Timaeus, was sitting by the roadside. When he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out: Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me! Many rebuked him, telling him to be silent, but he cried out all the more: Son of David, have mercy on me!

The placing. The second healing of a blind man, matching the one at Bethsaida (8:22–26). Between them, Jesus has taught about the cross and his disciples have been blind to it. Now, at the end of the section, a blind man sees and follows Jesus on the way. He is a model disciple, set against James and John.

And they came to Jericho. About 15 miles (25 km) north-east of Jerusalem, near the Jordan. The last stop before the climb to the city. Pilgrims for Passover passed through in crowds.

As he was leaving Jericho. Luke says as he drew near to Jericho (Luke 18:35). There were two Jerichos, the ancient ruined city and the new Herodian town a short distance away; Jesus may have been leaving one and approaching the other. Matthew mentions two blind men (Matthew 20:30); Mark names the one who was perhaps known to the early church.

Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, the son of Timaeus. The only person healed in Mark who is named. “Bar” is Aramaic for “son of”, so Mark translates. Naming him suggests he was known to Mark’s readers, a living witness in the church.

Jesus of Nazareth. The crowd’s name for him, a man from a small town.

Jesus, Son of David. Bartimaeus’ name for him, and a far greater one. “Son of David” is a messianic title: the promised king from David’s line (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 11:1). This is the first time in Mark anyone uses it. The blind man sees what the crowd does not. The Messiah was expected to give sight to the blind (Isaiah 35:5; 61:1). And Jesus does not silence him: the hour for the secret is ending. He is about to enter Jerusalem as the Son of David (11:10).

Have mercy on me! The cry of one with no claim, only need. The prayer of the tax collector (Luke 18:13). The church has prayed it for centuries (Kyrie eleison, Lord, have mercy).

And many rebuked him, telling him to be silent. Like the disciples with the children (v. 13). A beggar was a nuisance.

But he cried out all the more. Persistent, unembarrassed, desperate faith. He knows this is his one chance; Jesus is passing by and will not come this way again.

In a sentence. As Jesus left Jericho, blind Bartimaeus cried out to him as the Son of David for mercy, and would not be silenced.

For worship. Pray the beggar’s prayer: Son of David, have mercy on me. And don’t let anyone shame you out of crying to Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: Jericho lay about 15 miles north-east of Jerusalem, near the Jordan. Bartimaeus means “son of Timaeus.” “Son of David” is a title for the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stopped and said, "Call him." And they called the blind man, saying to him, "Take heart. Get up; he is calling you." And throwing off his cloak, he sprang up and came to Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus stopped and said: call him. They called the blind man, saying to him: take heart; get up; he is calling you. Throwing off his cloak, he sprang up and came to Jesus.

And Jesus stopped. On his way to the cross, with the weight of the world on him, Jesus stops for one blind beggar.

Call him. He does not go to Bartimaeus. He calls him to come, and Bartimaeus must respond. And he involves the crowd: those who had rebuked him are now told to call him.

Take heart. Get up; he is calling you. Three short commands, and the crowd changes its tune. These could be the words of every evangelist: take heart, get up, Jesus is calling you.

And throwing off his cloak. A beggar’s cloak was spread on the ground to collect coins, and was his covering at night (Exodus 22:26–27). It was all he had. He throws it aside. The rich man would not leave his possessions (v. 22); the beggar leaves his only one, without being asked.

He sprang up and came to Jesus. Eager, joyful, at once. A blind man, guided by the voice.

In a sentence. Jesus stopped and called Bartimaeus, who threw off his cloak, sprang up and came to him.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is calling you. What cloak do you need to throw aside to come to him?
verseByVerse.note: A beggar’s cloak was spread to collect coins and was also his covering at night.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, "What do you want me to do for you?" And the blind man said to him, "Rabbi, let me recover my sight." And Jesus said to him, "Go your way; your faith has made you well." And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him on the way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to him: what do you want me to do for you? The blind man said: Rabbi, let me recover my sight. Jesus said: go your way; your faith has made you well. Immediately he recovered his sight and followed him on the way.

What do you want me to do for you? The same question as to James and John (v. 36). They asked for glory; he asks for mercy and sight. It is obvious what a blind man wants, but Jesus asks him to say it: to express his need and his faith.

Rabbi. Literally Rabbouni, “my master”, a more personal and reverent form, used elsewhere only by Mary Magdalene at the empty tomb (John 20:16).

Let me recover my sight. “Recover” suggests he once could see.

Go your way; your faith has made you well. “Made you well” (sesōken) is literally “has saved you”, the same word as for the woman with the bleeding (5:34). Physical healing and spiritual salvation are both in it. His faith was the empty hand that received what Jesus gave; the power was Jesus’.

And immediately he recovered his sight. No touch, no saliva, no second stage. Just the word.

And followed him on the way. The last words of the section, and the most important. Jesus told him to go his way; his way was Jesus’ way. “On the way”: the road to Jerusalem and the cross (v. 32). He is the picture of the true disciple, which the Twelve should be: his eyes opened, he follows Jesus to the cross. This is what Mark wants for his readers.

In a sentence. Asked what he wanted, Bartimaeus asked for his sight, received it at once through faith, and followed Jesus on the way to Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. Has Jesus opened your eyes? Then follow him on the way, wherever it leads.

parallels.desc: the eyes of the blind opened

10.theology:
Divorce, and what Mark leaves out. Matthew twice records an exception — except for sexual immorality (Matt. 5:32; 19:9) — and Mark records none, while adding, for his Roman readers, the case of a wife who divorces her husband. Not a contradiction but a difference of purpose: Mark gives the principle in its unguarded, creation-order form, the way a thing is stated when you want its full weight felt; Matthew, writing where the rabbis argued endlessly over grounds, records the one qualification Jesus allowed. Paul adds a second — the believer deserted by an unbelieving spouse is not enslaved (1 Cor. 7:15). So the Reformed churches have long recognised two grounds on which the bond may be broken and the innocent party freed: adultery and desertion, and no others. Mark's silence is not denial but a refusal to lead with the exception — because the moment the exception becomes the headline, hardness of heart starts hunting for a way in.

"Why do you call me good?" is not a denial that Jesus is good or that he is God, and he never withdraws the word or corrects the man for using it. He holds it up to the light. Good Teacher was easy flattery; Jesus stops him and asks whether he knows what he is saying. Either the word should not have been used — or it is right, and the man must reckon with who is standing in front of him. A door held open, not a door shut.

And v. 45 is the theological centre of Mark. A ransom (lytron) is the price paid to buy a captive out of bondage. The word rendered for is anti — in the place of, one thing given instead of another — so he does not merely die for our benefit but in our stead. Behind it stands Isaiah 53, where the Servant poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many (Isa. 53:12), that word many tolling through the prophecy and claimed here by Jesus as his own errand. And the price is not paid to the devil, as some early teachers imagined — he is a thief with stolen goods (3:27) and God owes him nothing. The debt is owed to the justice of God, and God in the person of his Son pays it himself.
10.examples:
Then: the same question asked twice, fifteen verses apart. What do you want me to do for you? — to James and John (v. 36), and to a blind beggar (v. 51).

The brothers open with a blank cheque — we want you to do for us whatever we ask — and name the two best seats in the kingdom. Bartimaeus asks for mercy, and then for sight.

Now: most of us pray more like the brothers than the beggar. The blank cheque dressed up religiously — a decision already taken, brought to God for endorsement rather than judgement. The request framed around position, comfort, and being noticed.

And note what actually makes Bartimaeus's answer better. Not humility as a technique. He had correctly identified who was passing — Son of David, a messianic title not one of the disciples had yet used out loud — and he asked for mercy, which is what you ask for when you have no claim of any kind and the only ground of the request is the character of the one you are asking.

And then there is the cloak (v. 50). A beggar's outer cloak was his equipment: spread on the ground to catch coins, his bed at night, his shelter, and the one possession the Law protected (Ex. 22:26–27). It was everything he owned. He flung it aside, blind, with no idea where it landed, because it might slow him down by four seconds.

Set that against the man at the start of the chapter, asked to give up his possessions and going away sorrowful because he had a great many. One had much and would not let go of any of it; one had a single thing and did not think about it twice. Mark put them at opposite ends of the same chapter on purpose.

11.title: Leaves Without Fruit
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when they drew near to Jerusalem, to Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two of his disciples <sup>2</sup>and said to them, “Go into the village in front of you, and immediately as you enter it you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it. <sup>3</sup>If anyone says to you, ‘Why are you doing this?’ say, ‘The Lord has need of it and will send it back here immediately.’” <sup>4</sup>And they went away and found a colt tied at a door outside in the street, and they untied it. <sup>5</sup>And some of those standing there said to them, “What are you doing, untying the colt?” <sup>6</sup>And they told them what Jesus had said, and they let them go. <sup>7</sup>And they brought the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks on it, and he sat on it. <sup>8</sup>And many spread their cloaks on the road, and others spread leafy branches that they had cut from the fields. <sup>9</sup>And those who went before and those who followed were shouting, “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! <sup>10</sup>Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest!” <sup>11</sup>And he entered Jerusalem and went into the temple. And when he had looked around at everything, as it was already late, he went out to Bethany with the twelve. <sup>12</sup>On the following day, when they came from Bethany, he was hungry. <sup>13</sup>And seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see if he could find anything on it. When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. <sup>14</sup>And he said to it, “May no one ever eat fruit from you again.” And his disciples heard it. <sup>15</sup>And they came to Jerusalem.
