In his human knowledge he genuinely doesn’t have it, and he says so to four men who would have given anything for it.

parallels.desc: not for you to know times or seasons

verseByVerse.quote: Be on guard, keep awake. For you do not know when the time will come. It is like a man going on a journey, when he leaves home and puts his servants in charge, each with his work, and commands the doorkeeper to stay awake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Watching for Christ means faithfully doing the work he has given each of us until he returns.

Because no one knows. “Be on guard, keep awake. For you do not know when the time will come.” The reason is the ignorance he has just confessed: because no one knows, therefore watch. The uncertainty isn’t a problem to solve but the very ground of the command.

A real absence. “A man going on a journey.” The master is genuinely away — not watching from round the corner. The house runs without him for an indefinite time, which is the church’s situation between the ascension and the return. It is fair to admit that it feels like absence, because the parable says it is.

Real trust. “Puts his servants in charge.” He doesn’t lock the doors or leave a caretaker; he hands the running of the house to those who work in it — real authority, responsibility and trust.

Each with his work. This phrase defines watchfulness here, and it isn’t what the word suggests to us. Every servant has a specific, assigned job, different from the next. So the servants aren’t standing at the window scanning the road; they are working. Watching means doing what you were left to do.

The doorkeeper. One man’s post is at the door, and his job is the watching — the one occupation that produces nothing visible and looks like doing nothing. It is still work, and he was told to do it.

Two mistakes. The parable corrects both standard errors. One is anxious calculation — reading every crisis as a countdown, with charts and confident dates. No servant here is doing that. The other is practical forgetting — living as though he isn’t coming back because he hasn’t yet. The one who is ready isn’t the one who worked out the date but the one found at his post when the door opens.

A question you can answer. So the chapter becomes a question you can answer this week — not “when?” but “what did he leave me to do, and am I doing it?” The children in your house; the work you are paid for; the person you were asked to visit; the gift you haven’t used in years. A test: if he came today, would he find you at the work he gave you?

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore stay awake—for you do not know when the master of the house will come, in the evening, or at midnight, or when the rooster crows, or in the morning— lest he come suddenly and find you asleep. And what I say to you I say to all: Stay awake."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every Christian is called to live ready for Christ’s return, and his grace remains for disciples who fail.

The whole night. He lists the four Roman watches — evening, midnight, cockcrow, morning — roughly 6 p.m. to 6 a.m. The whole of the dark, divided up, and he could come in any of them.

Written into the passion. Watch what Mark does with that night in the next two chapters. Evening: “when it was evening, he came with the twelve” (14:17) to the supper. Then the night in Gethsemane, where he asks them to watch, finds them sleeping three times, and says to Peter, “Could you not watch one hour?” (14:37). Cockcrow: Peter’s third denial, “and immediately the rooster crowed a second time” (14:72). Morning: “as soon as it was morning, the chief priests held a consultation” and handed him to Pilate (15:1). Mark has written the parable into the passion.

Found asleep. “Lest he come suddenly and find you asleep.” That is exactly what happens. He came to them in the garden, in his hour of greatest need, and found them sleeping — and the verb for “stay awake” here is the one used three times in Gethsemane (14:34, 37, 38). They were told this days before and failed it on the night.

Mercy as well as warning. That is a mercy, not merely an indictment. The men who failed in the garden are the men Christ died for, restored, and sent to the ends of the earth. Failing to watch isn’t the end of a disciple. But don’t imagine, reading comfortably, that you would have stayed awake. They loved him, they were exhausted, they meant it, and they couldn’t manage an hour.

To all. “And what I say to you I say to all: Stay awake.” The last words of the discourse reach past the four men on the hillside. With his final sentence he speaks to everyone who would ever read this — including, deliberately, you. The chapter that began with a question about dates ends with a command instead: not calculate, not fear, but stay awake — at your post, doing your work, in a house whose master is coming back. A test: what would staying awake look like in your life this week?

He stayed awake. Then he rises from that hillside and goes down into the watches of his own night — evening, the garden, cockcrow and morning — awake through every one, while everyone who loved him slept.
verseByVerse.note: These are the four Roman watches of the night, roughly from 6 p.m. to 6 a.m.

13.theology:
Two questions, two answers, one discourse. The key to Mark 13 is that the disciples asked about the temple (v. 4), and the seam between the two answers is visible if you look for it. Everything down to v. 30 carries signs and a timeframe — false messiahs, wars, the abomination in the holy place, the flight from Judea — and this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Every one of them did happen, in AD 70. Then v. 32 turns the corner: But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows. From there, the opposite of everything before — no sign, no date, nobody knows. Read this way, Jesus was not mistaken by a day: the temple fell in their lifetime as he said, and his own coming remains unmarked as he said.

Not even the Son (v. 32) is the verse most often used against Christ's deity, from Arius onwards. The answer is not a dodge but the heart of the incarnation: the one person, the eternal Son, took a complete human nature without ceasing to be fully God. As God he knows the hour; as man he increased in wisdom (Luke 2:52), which a mind that already knew everything could not do. It is the same structure as sleeping in a boat from exhaustion and then silencing the storm with a word (4:38–39) — the one as a weary man, the other as Lord of creation.

And Mark set the proof one verse earlier. In v. 31 the same speaker says heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away — a claim no creature could dare make, setting his own sentences above the created order. In v. 32 the same mouth says he does not know the day. The starkest claim to deity and the starkest confession of human limitation, one breath apart, both true. This verse is not a problem for his deity; it is one of the clearest windows in the Gospel onto the two natures in the one Christ.

And the signs will work (v. 22). Jesus does not say the wonders will be faked. Pharaoh's magicians duplicated the plagues (Ex. 7:22); Deuteronomy legislates for a prophet whose sign comes to pass and who then leads you to other gods (Deut. 13:1–3). The supernatural is not self-authenticating. It works is never by itself a reason to follow anybody; the test is always the doctrine underneath (1 Jn. 4:2–3).
13.examples:
Then: in the evening, or at midnight, or when the rooster crows, or in the morning — the four watches of the Roman night, listed as the hours at which the master might come home.

And Mark writes all four into the next two chapters, in order. When it was evening, he came with the twelve (14:17). At midnight, Gethsemane — where he asks them to watch, comes back and finds them sleeping, three times, and says could you not watch one hour? (14:37). At cockcrow, the courtyard, and immediately the rooster crowed a second time (14:72). And as soon as it was morning, the chief priests delivered him to Pilate (15:1).

The parable's own words are the passion narrative's words. Lest he come suddenly and find you asleep — and he came to them in the garden at his hour of greatest need and found them asleep.

Now: do not read that as an indictment only. The men who failed it in the garden are the men he died for, restored on a beach, and sent to the ends of the earth. But do not imagine you would have stayed awake either. They loved him, they meant it, they were exhausted — and they could not manage an hour.

And note how the closing parable defines watchfulness: the servants are given jobs, each with his work. Not scanning the road; working. The man who is ready is not the one who calculated the date but the one found at his post when the door opens. So the question this chapter finally asks is answerable this week: what did he leave me to do, and am I doing it?

14.title: The Cup, the Kiss, and the Fire
14.text: <sup>1</sup>It was now two days before the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread. And the chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to arrest him by stealth and kill him, <sup>2</sup>for they said, “Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar from the people.” <sup>3</sup>And while he was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, as he was reclining at table, a woman came with an alabaster flask of ointment of pure nard, very costly, and she broke the flask and poured it over his head. <sup>4</sup>There were some who said to themselves indignantly, “Why was the ointment wasted like that? <sup>5</sup>For this ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor.” And they scolded her. <sup>6</sup>But Jesus said, “Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has done a beautiful thing to me. <sup>7</sup>For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want, you can do good for them. But you will not always have me. <sup>8</sup>She has done what she could; she has anointed my body beforehand for burial. <sup>9</sup>And truly, I say to you, wherever the gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her.” <sup>10</sup>Then Judas Iscariot, who was one of the twelve, went to the chief priests in order to betray him to them. <sup>11</sup>And when they heard it, they were glad and promised to give him money. And he sought an opportunity to betray him. <sup>12</sup>And on the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they sacrificed the Passover lamb, his disciples said to him, “Where will you have us go and prepare for you to eat the Passover?” <sup>13</sup>And he sent two of his disciples and said to them, “Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him, <sup>14</sup>and wherever he enters, say to the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says, Where is my guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’ <sup>15</sup>And he will show you a large upper room furnished and ready; there prepare for us.” <sup>16</sup>And the disciples set out and went to the city and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover. <sup>17</sup>And when it was evening, he came with the twelve. <sup>18</sup>And as they were reclining at table and eating, Jesus said, “Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me, one who is eating with me.” <sup>19</sup>They began to be sorrowful and to say to him one after another, “Is it I?” <sup>20</sup>He said to them, “It is one of the twelve, one who is dipping bread into the dish with me. <sup>21</sup>For the Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.” <sup>22</sup>And as they were eating, he took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to them, and said, “Take; this is my body.” <sup>23</sup>And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, and they all drank of it. <sup>24</sup>And he said to them, “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many. <sup>25</sup>Truly, I say to you, I will not drink again of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God.” <sup>26</sup>And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. <sup>27</sup>And Jesus said to them, “You will all fall away, for it is written, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’ <sup>28</sup>But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee.” <sup>29</sup>Peter said to him, “Even though they all fall away, I will not.” <sup>30</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.” <sup>31</sup>But he said emphatically, “If I must die with you, I will not deny you.” And they all said the same. <sup>32</sup>And they went to a place called Gethsemane. And he said to his disciples, “Sit here while I pray.” <sup>33</sup>And he took with him Peter and James and John, and began to be greatly distressed and troubled. <sup>34</sup>And he said to them, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. Remain here and watch.” <sup>35</sup>And going a little farther, he fell on the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him. <sup>36</sup>And he said, “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will.” <sup>37</sup>And he came and found them sleeping, and he said to Peter, “Simon, are you asleep? Could you not watch one hour? <sup>38</sup>Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” <sup>39</sup>And again he went away and prayed, saying the same words. <sup>40</sup>And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were very heavy, and they did not know what to answer him. <sup>41</sup>And he came the third time and said to them, “Are you still sleeping and taking your rest? It is enough; the hour has come. The Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. <sup>42</sup>Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand.” <sup>43</sup>And immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve, and with him a crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the scribes and the elders. <sup>44</sup>Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying, “The one I will kiss is the man. Seize him and lead him away under guard.” <sup>45</sup>And when he came, he went up to him at once and said, “Rabbi!” And he kissed him. <sup>46</sup>And they laid hands on him and seized him. <sup>47</sup>But one of those who stood by drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. <sup>48</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? <sup>49</sup>Day after day I was with you in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. But let the Scriptures be fulfilled.” <sup>50</sup>And they all left him and fled. <sup>51</sup>And a young man followed him, with nothing but a linen cloth about his body. And they seized him, <sup>52</sup>but he left the linen cloth and ran away naked. <sup>53</sup>And they led Jesus to the high priest. And all the chief priests and the elders and the scribes came together. <sup>54</sup>And Peter had followed him at a distance, right into the courtyard of the high priest. And he was sitting with the guards and warming himself at the fire. <sup>55</sup>Now the chief priests and the whole council were seeking testimony against Jesus to put him to death, but they found none. <sup>56</sup>For many bore false witness against him, but their testimony did not agree. <sup>57</sup>And some stood up and bore false witness against him, saying, <sup>58</sup>“We heard him say, ‘I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and in three days I will build another, not made with hands.’” <sup>59</sup>Yet even about this their testimony did not agree. <sup>60</sup>And the high priest stood up in the midst and asked Jesus, “Have you no answer to make? What is it that these men testify against you?” <sup>61</sup>But he remained silent and made no answer. Again the high priest asked him, “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?” <sup>62</sup>And Jesus said, “I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven.” <sup>63</sup>And the high priest tore his garments and said, “What further witnesses do we need? <sup>64</sup>You have heard his blasphemy. What is your decision?” And they all condemned him as deserving death. <sup>65</sup>And some began to spit on him and to cover his face and to strike him, saying to him, “Prophesy!” And the guards received him with blows. <sup>66</sup>And as Peter was below in the courtyard, one of the servant girls of the high priest came, <sup>67</sup>and seeing Peter warming himself, she looked at him and said, “You also were with the Nazarene, Jesus.” <sup>68</sup>But he denied it, saying, “I neither know nor understand what you mean.” And he went out into the gateway and the rooster crowed. <sup>69</sup>And the servant girl saw him and began again to say to the bystanders, “This man is one of them.” <sup>70</sup>But again he denied it. And after a little while the bystanders again said to Peter, “Certainly you are one of them, for you are a Galilean.” <sup>71</sup>But he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear, “I do not know this man of whom you speak.” <sup>72</sup>And immediately the rooster crowed a second time. And Peter remembered how Jesus had said to him, “Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.” And he broke down and wept.
14.overview:
The longest chapter in Mark, and the clock runs in hours. Two days before Passover the chief priests decide to take him quietly — not during the feast — and are overruled by their own accomplice, so that the Lamb dies at Passover after all.

Mark wraps that plot around a woman in Bethany who breaks a flask of nard worth a year's wages over his head. The room calls it waste; he calls it beautiful, and says she has anointed him for burial. Then Judas goes out and sells him for less than the perfume cost.

In a borrowed upper room he takes the Passover bread — the meal that had looked backwards to Egypt for fourteen centuries — and turns it round: this is my body, and this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many. Then they sing the Hallel and walk out into the dark.

What follows is the most exposed scene in the Gospels. In an olive grove, appalled and shaking, he asks his Father to take away the cup — the Old Testament's cup of wrath — and adds the words that hold the world together: yet not what I will, but what you will. Three times he comes back to friends who cannot stay awake for an hour.

Then a kiss, an armed crowd, and every one of them running. Upstairs in the high priest's house he answers the direct question at last — I am — and is condemned for it. Downstairs, at a charcoal fire, Peter says, in effect, "I am not", three times, and a bird calls.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — Anointing, Betrayal, and the Last Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The plot and the perfume (vv. 1–11). Two days before Passover the chief priests are looking for a way to take him quietly. Mark then interrupts them with a woman in a house in Bethany breaking a flask of nard over his head — and closes the sandwich with Judas going to the priests for money. The plot frames the anointing, and the anointing interprets the plot: while men calculate the price of his death, a woman prepares his body for burial.

The upper room (vv. 12–21). Two disciples are sent into the city with a sign — a man carrying a water jar — and find everything as he said. And at the table, with the twelve reclining round him, he says that one of them will hand him over, and none of them looks at Judas.

The Supper (vv. 22–26). He takes the bread of the Passover, the meal that had commemorated the exodus for fourteen centuries, and says this is my body. He takes the cup and says this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.

Then they sing, and go out into the night.
verseByVerse.theology:
He is not attending the Passover. He is the Passover.

For fourteen hundred years Israel had killed a lamb, put its blood where the destroyer would see it, and eaten a meal standing up, ready to leave — and told their children that this was the night God brought them out. Every element of that meal pointed backwards.

Jesus takes it and turns it round. The bread is his body. The cup is my blood of the covenant — which is Moses's phrase at Sinai, where he threw blood over the people and said behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you (Ex. 24:8), and it is Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant written on hearts, with sins remembered no more (Jer. 31:31–34).

So there is a new exodus, and he is the lamb of it, and the blood goes not on a doorframe but into a cup that is handed round a table and drunk.

And poured out for many is Isaiah 53 — the Servant who poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many (Isa. 53:12) — and it is his own word from 10:45, where the Son of Man gives his life as a ransom for many. Not a tragedy that overtook him. A ransom, deliberately paid, for a definite number of people whom he knew by name.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a woman breaks a flask worth a year's wages over his head, and the room objects that it could have been sold for the poor.

The objection is not stupid. Three hundred denarii would have fed a great many families, and the New Testament is fierce about the poor. But Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 15:11 at them — you always have the poor with you — and it is worth knowing that the verse he is quoting goes on: therefore I command you, You shall open wide your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor, in your land. He is not excusing anyone from generosity. He is saying that this particular week will not come again.

Now: and then the sentence for everyone who has ever felt they had nothing worth giving: she has done what she could.

Not what she should have. Not what somebody more capable would have. What she could — which was one thing, and she did it, and he called it beautiful and said it would be told wherever the gospel went. It has been, for two thousand years, and Mark does not even record her name.

That is the measure. Not the scale of the service but whether it was the whole of what you had.

verseByVerse.quote: It was now two days before the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread. And the chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to arrest him by stealth and kill him, for they said, "Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar from the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Men plan freely and wickedly, yet God’s purpose governs the timing: the true Passover Lamb will die at Passover.

The clock starts. From here to the end of the chapter, time is measured in hours. And the setting matters. Passover was the feast of deliverance, the night God brought Israel out of Egypt behind the blood of a lamb, and Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims, its population swollen several times over.

Not whether but how. “Seeking how to arrest him by stealth and kill him.” They have wanted this since chapter 3, when Pharisees and Herodians left a synagogue together to plan it (3:6). Now it is an operational question. “By stealth” — by cunning: away from the crowd, in the dark, without witnesses.

Their plan overruled. “Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar.” A policy decision by Israel’s highest religious authority, on grounds of crowd control: wait until the pilgrims have gone home. And he died at that very feast. They didn’t change their minds because they were persuaded, but because an opportunity arrived they hadn’t counted on — a man from the inside offering to do it quietly. So the timing of the crucifixion was set not by the council’s plan but against it.

The Lamb at Passover. The date wasn’t negotiable. “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7); the pattern had been fixed since Exodus 12. Watch this chapter: the most powerful men in Jerusalem make a plan and are overruled by their own accomplice. Judas thinks he is arranging a transaction, the priests a public-order problem, Pilate a provincial dispute. Each acts freely, doing what he wants, and each runs to a schedule God set beforehand: “this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23). Both halves are true, and Mark holds them together to the end.

For your life. That means the worst plans of evil people never slip from God’s hand. A test: when events seem driven by others’ schemes, do you trust that God still rules the timing?
verseByVerse.note: Passover recalled Israel’s rescue from Egypt; Unleavened Bread was the week-long feast that followed it. Jerusalem swelled with pilgrims.

parallels.desc: the council resolves to kill him

verseByVerse.quote: And while he was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, as he was reclining at table, a woman came with an alabaster flask of ointment of pure nard, very costly, and she broke the flask and poured it over his head. There were some who said to themselves indignantly, "Why was the ointment wasted like that?
verseByVerse.commentary:
She gives Christ the most precious thing she has, wholeheartedly — and devotion like that always looks like waste to the calculating.

A healed man’s house. Bethany is the village over the ridge where Jesus has been staying (11:11). The house belongs to “Simon the leper” — plainly no longer a leper, since he is hosting a dinner. A leper lived outside the town and cried “Unclean” at anyone who came near (Leviticus 13:45–46). So someone had healed him, the nickname stuck, and now the man who once warned strangers away has the Son of God at his table days before the cross. Whether or not he is the leper of chapter 1, who said, “If you will, you can make me clean” (1:40–42), it is the same kind of house — and it is where the Lord chose to spend one of his last evenings.

A costly flask. Alabaster was a soft translucent stone carved into small sealed perfume flasks; the neck was probably snapped to open it. Nard was pressed from a plant that grows in the Himalayas, carried thousands of miles, and priced accordingly; “pure” may mean genuine, undiluted. “Very costly” — verse 5 gives the figure: three hundred denarii, about a year’s wages for a labourer. Perfume was a portable way of storing wealth, and for a woman such a flask may have been her security against hard times.

All of it. “She broke the flask and poured it over his head.” Once broken, it couldn’t be resealed; there was no using half and keeping half. The breaking was a decision that all of it was going to him. And she pours it over his head — not a drop on the wrist, but the whole flask, running down his hair and beard onto his clothes, until the room smelled of nothing else. It is also, though no one says so, how a king is anointed (1 Samuel 10:1; 2 Kings 9:6).

“Wasted.” “Why was the ointment wasted like that?” The room turns on her. Waste is the only verdict available to a calculating mind: something valuable destroyed, and nothing to show for it. A test: is there anything you would hold back from Christ because giving it to him seems a waste?
verseByVerse.note: John names the woman as Mary, sister of Martha and Lazarus. Nard was a costly perfume imported from India. Alabaster was a soft stone used for perfume flasks.

verseByVerse.quote: For this ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor." And they scolded her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A sound principle can become cover for criticising someone else’s costly devotion while giving nothing ourselves.

A good objection. It must be taken seriously, because it is a good one. Three hundred denarii was a year’s wages and would have fed many families in a city where the only safety net was almsgiving, and giving to the poor was a particular duty at Passover (cf. John 13:29). The New Testament is fierce about this: “Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction” (James 1:27). Jesus himself told a rich man to sell everything and give to the poor (10:21). So it isn’t stupid or obviously wicked. It is what any sensible, socially concerned, morally serious person might say. That is why the passage is so searching.

They went at her. “And they scolded her.” She has just done the most extravagant thing of her life, in public, in a room full of men, perhaps on an impulse she couldn’t have explained — and the room rounds on her and calls her a fool who wasted the hungry’s money. Mark records not one word from her.

Who started it. John tells us who started it, and it changes everything: Judas Iscariot said, “Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?” — “not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it” (John 12:4–6). The objection about the poor came first from a man stealing from the fund for the poor, and the rest agreed because it sounded reasonable.

The mechanism hasn’t aged. A sound principle can be used as cover, and those repeating it needn’t be insincere; most in that room weren’t. It is easy to criticise someone else’s costly devotion in the name of a good cause, feel morally serious doing it, and give nothing yourself. A test: when you criticise how others spend on Christ, what are you giving?

Side by side. Soon Judas will have his silver, and this woman will have nothing left. Mark puts them side by side on purpose: one person in this chapter turns Jesus into money; another turns money into worship.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; three hundred denarii was about a year’s wages. John says the complaint came from Judas.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus said, "Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has done a beautiful thing to me. For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want, you can do good for them. But you will not always have me. She has done what she could; she has anointed my body beforehand for burial. And truly, I say to you, wherever the gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wholehearted love for Christ is beautiful to him, even when others call it waste, and he treasures what we give him with all we have.

Protection first. “Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her?” He defends her before he explains her. His first words aren’t theology but protection: they are giving her a hard time, and he has seen what the room is doing to a woman who can’t answer back.

Beautiful. “She has done a beautiful thing to me.” The word (kalos) means good, fine, lovely — not merely permissible but beautiful. That is the answer to “waste.” The objectors had only one category, usefulness: what did it achieve, what could it have bought? Jesus introduces another, which a purely practical religion has no room for. There is a place for the beautiful and “useless,” and worship is exactly that. Nobody is fed by it, nothing is produced, and God calls it lovely — which is why he commanded gold and blue and scarlet for a tent in the desert.

The poor with you. “You always have the poor with you, and whenever you want, you can do good for them.” This has been misused as a shrug — poverty is permanent, so don’t exert yourself. But it echoes Deuteronomy 15:11, and the original settles it: “For there will never cease to be poor in the land. Therefore I command you, ‘You shall open wide your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor, in your land.’” The permanence of poverty is the reason for open-handedness, not an excuse from it. And his own words — “you can do good for them” — assume they will.

Not always me. “But you will not always have me.” This isn’t a general rule about extravagance versus charity, but a statement about days that won’t come again. The chance to do anything for the body of Jesus of Nazareth is closing, and this woman seems to be the only one in Jerusalem who has noticed.

What she could. “She has done what she could” — a sentence for anyone who feels what they have to offer isn’t worth offering. Not what she should have done, or what a more capable person might have managed, but what she could: one thing, done once, with everything she had, and he called it beautiful. The question is never the scale of the service but whether it was the whole of what you had. The widow’s two coins outweighed the treasury (12:44); this flask outweighed the criticism of the apostles. A test: what could you give Christ that you have been holding back because it seems too small?

Anointed for burial. “She has anointed my body beforehand for burial.” He tells them what she has done, more than she likely knew. Bodies were anointed for burial; the women will come to the tomb to do it and find it empty (16:1). This woman is the only one who managed it, and while he was still alive. She came to honour him; he says she has prepared him for burial.

Remembered. “Wherever the gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her.” A prophecy kept for two thousand years. And Mark doesn’t give her name (John identifies her as Mary of Bethany, John 12:3). The whole world knows what she did; the Gospel that promises she will be remembered doesn’t say who she was. She isn’t famous; the deed is — noticed and valued by the one who watched a widow give two coins nobody heard.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were anointed with spices for burial.

parallels.desc: there will never cease to be poor in the land

verseByVerse.quote: Then Judas Iscariot, who was one of the twelve, went to the chief priests in order to betray him to them. And when they heard it, they were glad and promised to give him money. And he sought an opportunity to betray him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Betrayal of Christ seldom begins with a dramatic decision; it seizes a convenient moment when loyalty becomes costly.

The contrast. The sandwich closes — plot, anointing, plot — and the contrast is unavoidable: a woman pours out a year’s wages on him, and a man goes out to sell him.

One of the twelve. Mark says it here, Jesus says it at the table (v. 20), and Mark says it again when the mob arrives (v. 43). Not a follower or sympathiser, but one of the twelve — appointed on the mountain (3:14–19), sent out with authority over unclean spirits (6:7), present at every private explanation.

They were glad. Chilling in its ordinariness. The men who had decided “not during the feast” are delighted, because the problem they couldn’t solve has walked through the door offering to solve itself.

The price. Mark doesn’t give the figure; Matthew does — thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15), the compensation the law set for a slave gored by an ox (Exodus 21:32), and the wage thrown to the rejected shepherd in Zechariah, with the LORD’s dry comment, “the lordly price at which I was priced by them” (Zechariah 11:12–13). Set it against the perfume: three hundred denarii against a sum that was probably less than half that. A woman spent more on his head than the priests paid for his life.

A convenient moment. “He sought an opportunity to betray him” — a good moment, a convenient time, the same idea as the “opportunity” Herodias found at the birthday feast (6:21). So it doesn’t happen at once. Judas goes back to the group, waits, eats with them, and watches for a gap. He sat through the supper knowing.

Why did he do it? The Gospels don’t give a full account, and we should resist supplying one. John names greed and pilfering (John 12:6), so money is plainly in it. Luke and John both say Satan entered him (Luke 22:3; John 13:27).

How betrayal works. Mark gives not a motive but a mechanism, and it is more useful. Betrayal of Jesus works by an opportune time: privately, quietly, when no one is watching, the cost of loyalty has suddenly become visible, and a reasonable-looking alternative appears. Almost nobody decides to abandon Christ. A moment simply arrives when it is much easier not to be associated with him, there is a way out you can explain to yourself, and it is taken. A test: where is it becoming convenient for you to keep your distance from Christ? Judas found his moment in a garden after dark; Peter will find his by a fire within hours. The difference between them isn’t the failure; it is what each did next (v. 72).
verseByVerse.note: Matthew says the price was thirty pieces of silver.

verseByVerse.quote: And on the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they sacrificed the Passover lamb, his disciples said to him, "Where will you have us go and prepare for you to eat the Passover?" And he sent two of his disciples and said to them, "Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus isn’t caught by events; he deliberately secures the time to give his disciples the Supper before he is betrayed.

While the lambs died. “On the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they sacrificed the Passover lamb” — traditionally the Thursday. That afternoon in the temple the slaughter went on for hours: household heads brought lambs, they were killed in the court, the blood was passed along lines of priests to the altar, and the carcass taken home to be roasted whole. While that happened, the Lamb of God was arranging where he would eat.

Was the Supper a Passover meal? John seems to set the Passover a day later: on Friday morning the leaders wouldn’t enter Pilate’s headquarters “so that they would not be defiled, but could eat the Passover” (John 18:28), and Friday is “the day of Preparation of the Passover” (John 19:14). Several solutions have been offered: that different groups followed different calendars that year; that Jesus held a Passover meal a day early; or that in John “the Passover” means the whole week-long feast and its sacrifices, and “Preparation” means the day before the Sabbath of Passover week (cf. Mark 15:42). The last is the most likely. The Supper was a Passover meal, as Matthew, Mark and Luke all say, and John’s words refer to the meals of the feast that followed.

A real problem. “Where will you have us go and prepare?” The Passover had to be eaten inside Jerusalem, and the city was packed. Finding a room for thirteen men that afternoon wasn’t a small matter.

A man with a jar. No address, no name: go into a crowded city and look for a man with a jug. But the sign isn’t as vague as it sounds. Carrying water in a jar was usually women’s work; a man with a water pot would stand out. Whether arranged in advance or known beforehand, Mark doesn’t say. He told them where to find a colt the same way (11:2), and that worked too.

Buying an evening. Why the secrecy? Judas has been to the priests and is waiting for his chance. If the place of the meal were known in the morning, the arrest could happen in the middle of it. So Jesus arranges a meeting point that even his own disciples can’t disclose, because they don’t know it. He is buying an evening: he has something to give those men that must be given before the arrest, and he takes careful practical steps to make sure he gets the time. Nothing in this chapter happens to him by accident; he plans around them — very different from being caught. A test: do you believe Christ is in command of your hard days too, not merely caught up in them?
verseByVerse.note: The lambs were sacrificed at the temple on the afternoon before the Passover meal. Carrying water was usually women’s work, so a man with a jar would stand out.

verseByVerse.quote: and wherever he enters, say to the master of the house, 'The Teacher says, Where is my guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?' And he will show you a large upper room furnished and ready; there prepare for us." And the disciples set out and went to the city and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ word proves exactly true in small things as in great, and he is served by ordinary people who give what they have.

The password again. “The Teacher says, Where is my guest room…?” — as with the colt (11:3), and apparently enough. So there is a man in Jerusalem who knows who the Teacher is, has a room ready, and asks no questions — another of the unnamed people in this Gospel whose property was asked for and who didn’t say no. And note “my guest room”: not “a room,” but the confidence of an arrangement.

Large and ready. “Large” — big enough for thirteen men to recline, as Passover was eaten by this time: free people reclined at table, in contrast with the first Passover, eaten in haste with sandals on (Exodus 12:11). “Furnished and ready” — spread with couches and cushions. Someone has already prepared it.

The church’s first address. An upper room appears again in Acts: after the ascension the eleven go to “the upper room, where they were staying,” and soon about a hundred and twenty gather (Acts 1:13–15). Whether or not it was the same house, the church’s first home in Jerusalem was an upstairs room lent by someone nobody bothered to name. A test: what do you have that the Lord could use if you held it open for him?

Just as he said. “They… found it just as he had told them” — the pattern of the colt (11:4–6), and deliberate. In the last week the things Jesus predicts keep turning out exactly right, in small matters and large: a colt, a man with a jar, a room ready. And in a few hours he will say, “one of you will betray me,” “you will all fall away,” and “before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times” — and those will prove exactly right too.

Preparing a lamb. “And they prepared the Passover” — real work: taking a lamb to the temple, waiting, holding it while it was killed, carrying it back, roasting it whole, and setting out unleavened bread, bitter herbs and wine. Two disciples spent that afternoon preparing a lamb for the man about to become one.
verseByVerse.note: Larger houses had an upper room reached by an outside stair.

verseByVerse.quote: And when it was evening, he came with the twelve. And as they were reclining at table and eating, Jesus said, "Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me, one who is eating with me." They began to be sorrowful and to say to him one after another, "Is it I?" He said to them, "It is one of the twelve, one who is dipping bread into the dish with me. For the Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s plan doesn’t excuse human guilt — and the right response to warnings about betrayal is honest self-examination.

Evening. “When it was evening, he came with the twelve” — the first of the watches named in the parable (13:35). Mark’s reader is meant to feel the clock start.

One who is eating with me. He opens with the solemn “Truly, I say to you,” which in Mark introduces things that mustn’t be missed. “One who is eating with me” doesn’t narrow anything down — all twelve are eating with him. It is there for the weight. Sharing a meal bound people together; to eat a man’s bread and then harm him was the deepest treachery. It echoes the psalm: “Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me” (Psalm 41:9), which Jesus quotes that evening in John (John 13:18).

Nobody looks at Judas. “They began to be sorrowful and to say to him one after another, ‘Is it I?’” Eleven men have spent three years with him, trusted Judas with the money bag, and when the Lord says one of them is a traitor, not one turns his head. Judas wasn’t obviously a Judas; he had gone out with the others and passed for a disciple among disciples. And it tells you about them: their question isn’t “Who is it?” but “Is it I?” — framed to expect “no,” a fearful hope rather than a confession. Still, each one, hearing that a betrayer was present, looked first at himself.

Self-suspicion is sanity. That instinct is the healthiest thing in the chapter and the opposite of Peter’s mistake shortly after, when he says, “Even though they all fall away, I will not” — and then denies Christ with oaths. Self-suspicion isn’t morbid. “Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12). A test: when Scripture warns of falling away, do you look first at others or at yourself?

Every chance to stop. “One who is dipping bread into the dish with me.” He doesn’t name him. Matthew and John record a further exchange that identifies him to those close by; Mark leaves a description that fits everyone at the table. So Judas is given every chance, to the last minute, to stop. The warning is public, the identification private. Nobody drags him out. He could have got up.

Written, yet guilty. “The Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed!” Two truths Mark won’t separate. It is written — in Isaiah 53, in Psalm 41; the cross isn’t the failure of the plan but the plan. And the man who does it is fully answerable; God’s purpose doesn’t make Judas a puppet or excuse him an inch. Scripture holds both without resolving them into a formula (Acts 2:23).

Better not born. “It would have been better for that man if he had not been born” — the most terrible thing Jesus ever said about anyone, and it shouldn’t be softened: there is something worse than never having lived. And it is said in Judas’s hearing, at the table, while he could still turn — not a verdict pronounced afterward but a last warning to his face, which makes it mercy as well as judgment.
verseByVerse.note: Dipping bread in a shared dish was a mark of close fellowship.

parallels.desc: my close friend, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were eating, he took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to them, and said, "Take; this is my body." And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, and they all drank of it. And he said to them, "This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the Lord’s Supper Christ gives himself to his people: his body given and his blood poured out to establish the new covenant and secure their forgiveness.

Took, blessed, broke, gave. By now the reader knows these verbs: he did the same on a hillside with five loaves (6:41) and with seven (8:6). What he did for the hungry he now does for the twelve, and this time the bread is himself. And understand what he is reshaping. The Passover meal had a set order, and the head of the household explained each element; in the later liturgy the bread is “the bread of affliction” eaten in Egypt. Jesus takes the bread and says something new.

What does “This is my body” mean? The church has divided over it, so let it be said plainly and without heat. All Christians agree that this meal is commanded, central, more than a bare memory, and that Christ is truly given to faith in it. They differ on what “is” means. Rome teaches transubstantiation: the bread’s substance becomes Christ’s body. Lutherans hold that the body is present in, with and under the bread. The Reformed churches, with Calvin, hold that the bread remains bread and signifies the body, and that the risen Christ, bodily in heaven, is truly given to the believer by the Holy Spirit as he eats — a real communion without the bread ceasing to be bread. The text supports that last reading. He was holding the bread in his own living body as he spoke; no one in that room could have thought the loaf had become the man before them. And he speaks this way often — “I am the door,” “I am the vine” — without anyone thinking him timber or a plant.

Taken, not admired. But don’t let the argument cost you the thing itself. The point isn’t metaphysics; it is that he gave it, and told them to take it. Whatever else the Supper is, it is Christ given, to be received — not watched, admired or discussed, but taken. A test: when you come to the Lord’s Table, do you come to receive Christ by faith, or merely to observe a ritual?

They all drank. “And they all drank of it.” Mark notes it, and it is worth noting: Judas was at that table.

The blood of the covenant. Every phrase of the cup comes from the Old Testament. “My blood of the covenant” is Moses’ sentence at Sinai, when he threw the sacrificial blood over the people: “Behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you” (Exodus 24:8). A covenant is being made, and it is new (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25), as Jeremiah promised: “I will make a new covenant… I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts… and I will remember their sin no more” (Jeremiah 31:31–34). At Sinai the blood was thrown over the people from outside; here it is put into a cup to be drunk.

Poured out for many. This is Isaiah 53, where the Servant poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many (Isaiah 53:12), and his own word: the Son of Man came “to give his life as a ransom for many” (10:45). Not a death that happened to him, but one poured out deliberately, for people.

For many — or for all? Many Christians read “for many” as a Hebrew way of saying “all,” the multitude set against the one (cf. Romans 5:15–19), and so as a death for every person. The reading given here is the Reformed one: Christ’s blood was poured out for his people and actually secured their forgiveness — not made sins forgivable, but dealt with them. But both readings agree that his death is sufficient for all, offered to all, and that no one who comes is turned away. If you are trusting him tonight, you are one of the many he had in mind as he held that cup.
verseByVerse.note: At the Passover meal the head of the household explained the bread and cups; Jesus gives them a new meaning. The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert “new” before “covenant.”

parallels.desc: he bore the sin of many

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, I will not drink again of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God." And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the night before his death Jesus looks with certainty past the cross to the coming feast of God’s kingdom, and goes to his suffering praising God’s steadfast love.

The last meal. “I will not drink again of the fruit of the vine.” His last word at the table isn’t about his death but about a feast. He knows he won’t eat with them again this side of it, and there is real renunciation here — giving up the ordinary comfort of wine and company because tomorrow is what it is.

Certain of the feast. “Until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God.” Hours from Gethsemane, he looks past the arrest, the flogging, the nails and the grave, and speaks with complete confidence of a future meal at which he will be present. There is no “if” in it. And it is a real appointment, promised long before: “On this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine… He will swallow up death forever” (Isaiah 25:6–8). “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9).

Back and forward. So every time the church takes this cup it does two things at once — looks back to a death and forward to a feast: “as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26). A test: when you take the Lord’s Supper, do you look forward with longing to the feast he has promised?

The hymn. “And when they had sung a hymn, they went out.” Easily read past. The Passover meal ended, by Jewish custom, with the second part of the Hallel psalms (Psalms 115–118), and that is very likely what they sang. If so, the last thing Jesus sang before Gethsemane included lines like these: “The snares of death encompassed me… Then I called on the name of the LORD” (Psalm 116:3–4); “Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints” (Psalm 116:15); “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Psalm 118:22), the verse he had put to the chief priests (12:10); “Bind the festal sacrifice with cords, up to the horns of the altar!” (Psalm 118:27).

His love endures forever. And the psalm ends: “Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever!” (Psalm 118:29). On the way to Gethsemane, in a voice that within the hour would be praying in agony, he sang that God is good and his love never stops. That is how to walk into a dark night.
verseByVerse.note: The hymn was probably from the Hallel psalms (Pss 113–118), sung at Passover.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The warning (vv. 27–31). On the walk out he tells them they will all fall away — and in the same breath tells them where to meet him afterwards. Peter says he will not, and says it twice, and the rest say the same.

The garden (vv. 32–42). Then the most exposed scene in the Gospels. He takes three men further in, tells them his soul is sorrowful to the point of death, falls on the ground and asks his Father to take the cup away — and adds the words that hold the world together. Three times he comes back and finds them asleep.

The arrest (vv. 43–52). Judas arrives with a crowd carrying swords and clubs, and identifies him with a kiss. A sword is drawn, an ear comes off, and Jesus asks whether they think he is a robber. Then everybody runs — including a young man who gets away leaving his only garment in a soldier's hand.

And in three of the four watches of the parable he preached two nights ago (13:35), the disciples are asleep or running, and he is awake.
verseByVerse.theology:
What is the cup? Everything in Gethsemane depends on it, and the answer is not the general dread of dying.

Men far less brave than Jesus have gone to horrible deaths singing — including thousands of his own martyrs, many of them under torture, some of them within living memory of this night. If the cup were merely execution, the Christian would have the awkward position of a Lord less composed at the prospect than his servants.

The cup is an Old Testament image, and it is fixed. In the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine, well mixed, and he pours out from it, and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs (Ps. 75:8). Wake yourself, wake yourself, stand up, O Jerusalem, you who have drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of his wrath (Isa. 51:17). Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink it (Jer. 25:15).

The cup is the wrath of God against sin. That is what is set in front of him in that garden, and it is why a man who had faced hurricanes and legions without a flicker is on the ground shaking.

And he drank it. For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin (2 Cor. 5:21). Which means there is nothing left in that cup for anyone who is in him — the reason a Christian can face death more calmly than Christ did in the garden is precisely that Christ was not calm in the garden.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: You will all fall away (v. 27) — and then, before Peter has said a word, but after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee (v. 28).

Read those two verses in the order he said them, because the order is the gospel. He announces the restoration before the failure has happened. Not after they repent. Not on condition of anything. He tells eleven men who are about to abandon him where to meet him afterwards.

And the word he uses is a shepherd's word — I will go before you, the way a shepherd walks ahead of the flock. He has just quoted Zechariah about the shepherd struck and the sheep scattered (Zech. 13:7); now he says he will gather them again himself.

Now: and the angel at the empty tomb repeats it, with one addition that has comforted more failing Christians than almost any other line in Scripture: go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee (16:7).

The one who was named in the failure is named in the restoration. If you have failed him badly and are wondering whether there is a road back, notice that the road was mapped and announced before you ever took the wrong turn.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, "You will all fall away, for it is written, 'I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.' But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God appointed the striking of his Shepherd, and Christ announced his restoring grace before his disciples even failed.

All of you. “You will all fall away.” Not some; all — said walking down the hill with them in the dark. The verb means to be tripped up, to stumble — the word used of the rocky ground that falls away when the heat comes (4:17), and of Nazareth’s offence at him (6:3).

Who strikes. He quotes Zechariah 13:7, and the striking thing is who does the striking. Zechariah has God saying, “Awake, O sword, against my shepherd… Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.” Jesus puts it in God’s first person: “I will strike the shepherd.” So the hand behind tomorrow isn’t finally Judas’s, Caiaphas’s or Pilate’s. They act freely and are answerable, but over them stands the Father’s settled purpose: “it was the will of the LORD to crush him” (Isaiah 53:10).

Their failure foreseen. So the disciples’ scattering isn’t an unforeseen embarrassment. It was written centuries before, in the same sentence as the striking of the shepherd, and he tells them so before it happens.

Before the failure. “But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee.” The whole force is in where it stands: before the failure, not after. Peter hasn’t boasted yet; no one has run; the garden and the courtyard haven’t happened. Having told them every one will abandon him within hours, he tells them where he will meet them afterward. No condition: not if you repent, come back or prove yourselves — simply, I will go ahead and see you in Galilee.

The shepherd in front. “Go before” is a shepherd’s word, to lead out in front so the flock can follow. He has just quoted a prophecy of a struck shepherd and scattered sheep, and in the next breath says he will be out in front of them again — in Galilee, not Jerusalem where it all went wrong, but home, where they were called from their boats.

For those who have failed. The angel at the empty tomb repeats this, with one addition that has done more for failing Christians than almost any line in the Bible: “go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you” (16:7). So if you have failed him — not a slip, but the kind of failure that makes you wonder if there is any road back — take it in the order Mark gives it. The restoration was announced before the failure happened; the meeting place was fixed while they were still swearing they would never need it. A test: are you letting a past failure keep you from returning to the Shepherd who has gone ahead of you?

parallels.desc: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered
he is going before you to Galilee

verseByVerse.quote: Peter said to him, "Even though they all fall away, I will not." And Jesus said to him, "Truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times." But he said emphatically, "If I must die with you, I will not deny you." And they all said the same.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Confidence in our own untested strength is dangerous; real disciples must rely on Christ, not on their own resolve.

Meant well, and wrong. “Even though they all fall away, I will not.” Entirely characteristic, meant well — and wrong. He accepts the prophecy for the others and exempts himself, in front of them: not only presumption about himself but a low estimate of his brothers, said in their hearing. Someone who thinks he alone will stand has already begun to fall, because he has stopped needing anyone.

The precise warning. “Truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.” Not a rebuke but a specification, and Mark’s is the most precise of the four: this very night, twice, three times. It is the kind of detail only the man it happened to would remember so exactly, and this Gospel carries Peter’s preaching. He has preserved the sentence that broke him, numbers and all.

Twice or once? Matthew, Luke and John say “before the rooster crows”; only Mark says “twice.” The others give the general warning; Mark, from Peter’s memory, gives the precise form, with a first crowing Peter ignored and a second that broke him. There is no contradiction; one account is simply fuller.

He meant it. “If I must die with you, I will not deny you” — said emphatically. And he meant it. That is what makes the passage useful rather than merely a story about a boaster. Peter wasn’t lying; he loved him. Within hours he will draw a sword against an armed crowd, more than the others manage. He wasn’t a coward. He simply didn’t know himself.

All of them. “And they all said the same.” Mark won’t let Peter carry it alone: every one said it, and every one ran.

Untested strength. The practical lesson is aimed at anyone who feels reasonably safe. The danger isn’t that you might one day decide to abandon Christ; no one in that room decided anything. It is confidence in a strength that has never been tested — the quiet assumption that you would hold, would speak up, wouldn’t do what others did. “Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12). A test: where are you trusting your own resolve rather than praying for Christ’s keeping?

The love behind the boast. Notice what Jesus doesn’t say. He doesn’t say, “Then you were never mine,” or withdraw the promise of verse 28. He tells Peter exactly what he will do, takes him into the garden anyway, dies for him, and has him named by an angel on the third day. The boast was hollow; the love behind it wasn’t, and Christ knew the difference.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark mentions the rooster crowing twice.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went to a place called Gethsemane. And he said to his disciples, "Sit here while I pray." And he took with him Peter and James and John, and began to be greatly distressed and troubled. And he said to them, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. Remain here and watch."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son of God truly felt overwhelming anguish as he faced the cross, and he is a Saviour who understands our deepest sorrow.

The garden. Gethsemane (the name means “oil press”) was an olive grove on the lower slope of the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron. “Sit here while I pray” — the others are left behind.

The same three. He takes Peter, James and John — the three taken into Jairus’s house to see a dead girl raised (5:37) and up the mountain to see him transfigured (9:2). They have seen him at his most glorious; now they see him at his lowest. That is no accident. No one is fit to speak about the glory who hasn’t also seen the garden.

Overwhelmed. “He began to be greatly distressed and troubled.” Mark reaches for two of the strongest words he has — appalled, shuddering, distress with no bottom to it. And “began”: this isn’t a settled sorrow carried all week. It falls on him in the garden.

He told them. “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death.” The Son of God, in the worst hour of his life, turns to three friends and tells them how bad it is. A certain kind of piety thinks that weakness. It isn’t in this Gospel. He asked for company and told them the truth. And his words echo the psalmist’s, “Why are you cast down, O my soul?” (Psalm 42:5, 11; 43:5), where the Greek Old Testament uses the same word. He is praying the Psalms in his agony. “Even to death” means sorrow heavy enough to kill. Luke records what it did to his body: “his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground” (Luke 22:44).

How can the Son of God be so distressed? Because he is truly man as well as God. His human soul shrank from the cup of God’s wrath, as any holy man would, and he said so. But his will was never set against the Father’s; he asked, and then submitted: “not what I will, but what you will” (v. 36). This isn’t a crack in the Trinity. It is the obedience of the Son, offered “with loud cries and tears” (Hebrews 5:7).

Stay awake near me. “Remain here and watch” — the word of the parable, “stay awake” (13:34–37). He isn’t asking them to fix anything, only to stay awake near him. That is the plainest description of what friendship costs in someone else’s grief: you can’t fix it and aren’t asked to; you are asked not to fall asleep. A test: whose grief is Christ asking you simply to stay near this week?

He knows. Whatever you are carrying, he doesn’t look at it from a distance. There was a night when the Son of God was appalled and shaking and told his friends the sorrow was killing him — and he is the one you bring yours to.
verseByVerse.note: Gethsemane (the name means “oil press”) was an olive grove on the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron Valley.

parallels.desc: why are you cast down, O my soul?

verseByVerse.quote: And going a little farther, he fell on the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him. And he said, "Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus shrank from drinking the cup of God’s wrath against sin, yet submitted to the Father’s will, so that we might be spared it.

He fell. Not knelt — fell; Matthew says on his face. The man who slept through a storm, faced down a legion and overturned the temple tables is on the ground among the olive roots.

A real request. “That, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him.” Mark gives the substance first, then the words. And note the condition: if it were possible. He isn’t demanding; he is asking whether there is another way, and the asking is real.

Abba. Mark keeps the Aramaic, as with “Talitha cumi” and “Ephphatha” — and this time it is the very sound of Jesus praying. “Abba” was the family word for father used in the home. It is sometimes over-translated “Daddy,” which is too small — grown men used it of their fathers — but it is unmistakably intimate, not the language of formal worship, and Jewish prayer very rarely if ever addressed God that way. He prays as a son at home, and in his deepest agony that is the word he reaches for. And he handed it on: “you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6). A test: do you come to God in your trouble as a child to his Father?

The confession first. “All things are possible for you.” Before the request, the confession. He doesn’t ask whether God is able; he states that he is, and then asks — the reverse of how most of us pray in a crisis.

What is the cup? Not simply death. Reading Gethsemane as fear of dying leaves us a Lord less composed at his execution than many of his martyrs, who went to worse deaths singing. The cup is a fixed Old Testament image for God’s wrath: “in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine… and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs” (Psalm 75:8); “you who have drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of his wrath” (Isaiah 51:17); “Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath” (Jeremiah 25:15). That is what stands before him: not the nails, but God’s holy anger against the sins of all he came to save, to be drunk to the dregs. He isn’t afraid of pain. He is looking into the cup.

Not my will. “Yet not what I will, but what you will.” He doesn’t withdraw the request; he asks honestly for what he wants, then submits. Both are prayer: the asking isn’t unbelief, the submitting isn’t resignation. And it reverses Eden. In a garden a man knew the Father’s will and said, in effect, “Not your will but mine,” and the world broke. In a garden a man who could have had anything said, “Not what I will, but what you will,” and it was mended.

Your model and permission. When you pray about something God hasn’t taken away, this is your model and your permission. Ask plainly for what you want; he did. Then hand it over; he did that too. The cup didn’t pass, and he drank it — which is why nothing is left in it for those who trust him.
verseByVerse.note: “Abba” is Aramaic for “father,” the word a child used at home. The “cup” pictures God’s judgment poured out.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came and found them sleeping, and he said to Peter, "Simon, are you asleep? Could you not watch one hour? Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Prayerful watchfulness prepares us for temptation, and Christ deals tenderly with our weakness even when we fail him.

Found asleep. He rises, walks back through the trees, and they are asleep. Mark’s reader was prepared for this by the parable of the master who comes home at night: “lest he come suddenly and find you asleep” (13:36). He came; they were asleep. The parable is acted out on the men it was told to.

“Simon.” He speaks to Peter by his old name — not Peter, the rock, but Simon, the name he had pulling nets out of the lake. It is the only time in Mark that Jesus calls him Simon, and it is deliberate, gentle and devastating. The man who said, “Even though they all fall away, I will not,” can’t stay awake.

One hour. Not the night — an hour. The smallest request, from a man overwhelmed with grief a stone’s throw away, and it was too much. But before using it against them, be honest about the circumstances. It was late; they had eaten a festal meal with wine and walked; and Luke kindly records that he found them “sleeping for sorrow” (Luke 22:45). Grief exhausts people. They weren’t indifferent; they were shattered.

Prepare before the test. “Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation.” Two commands that belong together, and the reason is preventive: very soon they will be tested, and this hour is the preparation. They slept through the preparation and failed the test. That is the plainest practical lesson in the chapter: the battle is lost or won before the temptation arrives. The person who hasn’t prayed doesn’t fall in the moment; he fell in the hours before, when nothing seemed to be happening and there was no obvious reason to be on his knees. Gethsemane is where the courtyard was decided. A test: what temptation do you know is coming that you haven’t yet prayed about?

Willing spirit, weak flesh. “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” Having named their failure, he explains it with a sympathy almost unbearable, given who is speaking. He grants that their intentions were real; Peter meant every word. “Flesh” here is human nature in its frailty — weakness, not wickedness. He isn’t calling them hypocrites; he is saying they are men.

He knows our frame. And the one diagnosing it is himself on the ground, his own flesh bearing a weight none of them can imagine. He knows exactly how weak it is. So this is comfort as well as warning: “he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust” (Psalm 103:14). Your Lord isn’t surprised by your weakness and doesn’t despise it. He has been more tired, more frightened and more alone than you will ever be, and he stayed awake for you.

verseByVerse.quote: And again he went away and prayed, saying the same words. And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were very heavy, and they did not know what to answer him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Persistent, repeated prayer in anguish is right and good, and the disciples’ failure shows the honesty of the Gospel record and the need of grace.

The same words. “Again he went away and prayed, saying the same words.” Don’t hurry past this; it says something about prayer many Christians have never been told. Some treat repetition as a failure of faith, as though asking twice meant you didn’t believe the first time, or prayer needed fresh and eloquent phrasing to be genuine. Jesus prayed the same request repeatedly in one hour, in the most important prayer meeting in history. Paul did the same about his thorn: “Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this” (2 Corinthians 12:8). And when words run out, “the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words” (Romans 8:26).

Praying in Gethsemane. So if all you can do tonight is say the same desperate sentence over and over, you aren’t praying badly. You are praying as he prayed in Gethsemane. A test: have you given up asking God for something because you have asked before?

Heavy eyes. “Again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were very heavy” — a small human detail, the phrase you would use of yourself in the small hours.

Nothing to say. “And they did not know what to answer him” — the saddest clause in the paragraph, surely Peter’s own memory. They woke, he stood over them, and there was nothing to say; no excuse would work. Mark has recorded this before: at the transfiguration Peter blurted out a suggestion about tents, “for he did not know what to say, for they were terrified” (9:6). The same three men, in the two moments they saw most clearly who he was, both times with nothing to say.

Honest reporting. That is one reason this Gospel reads like testimony, not legend. No one inventing a founding story writes that its leaders slept through the crisis and had no answer when caught. Peter told it against himself for the rest of his life — and there is mercy in that too, because the church has never been able to pretend its first leaders were made of better material than the rest of us.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came the third time and said to them, "Are you still sleeping and taking your rest? It is enough; the hour has come. The Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having submitted to the Father in prayer, Jesus goes willingly and steadily to meet his betrayer and his death.

The third time. “Are you still sleeping and taking your rest?” Three times he came back, three times they were asleep — and within hours Peter will deny him three times. The words can be read as a question or as a resigned statement (“sleep on now”); the Greek allows either. Either way, the tone has changed. He is no longer asking anything of them.

Settled. Something has happened in that prayer. He went into the grove appalled and shaking; he comes out settled, and every sentence from here to the cross has the same steadiness. The struggle was real, and it is over. He asked, he submitted, the answer was no — and he takes the no and gets up. A test: have you brought your hardest thing to God and left it with him, so that you can rise and face it?

The hour has come. “It is enough; the hour has come” — the very hour he prayed might pass from him (v. 35). It hasn’t passed; it has arrived. The whole Gospel has been walking toward it, and it doesn’t sneak up on him. He announces it.

Now happening. “The Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners.” He has said this in his predictions of the passion (8:31; 9:31; 10:33). Now the tense has changed: not “will be,” but happening.

Toward them. “Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand.” For half a second it sounds like escape — get up, we are leaving. It is the opposite. Torches are coming up from the Kidron (John 18:3), and he walks toward them. The disciples are drowsy, Judas is arriving with an armed crowd, and the man who has spent an hour on the ground begging for another way stands up and says, let us go and meet him. No one takes him; he goes: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18).

My betrayer. Notice the pronoun: not “the betrayer” but “my betrayer.” So Gethsemane ends with the sleepy disciples roused by their Lord walking toward the men who have come to kill him, having settled the matter in prayer while they slept.

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve, and with him a crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the scribes and the elders. Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying, "The one I will kiss is the man. Seize him and lead him away under guard." And when he came, he went up to him at once and said, "Rabbi!" And he kissed him. And they laid hands on him and seized him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The deepest treachery uses the sign of love — and the Lord who could not be overpowered lets himself be taken.

One of the twelve. “Immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve.” Mark says it a third time in the chapter. He can’t leave it alone, and neither should we.

Armed against an unarmed man. “A crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the scribes and the elders” — an armed party sent by the council, and John adds soldiers with lanterns and torches (John 18:3). They come at night, into a garden, in force, to arrest an unarmed teacher who stood in the temple all week in broad daylight.

They needed a sign. “The one I will kiss is the man.” The arresting party couldn’t reliably pick him out at night, by torchlight, among Galileans dressed alike. That is believable realism, and it tells you Jesus didn’t look like anything in particular: no halo, nothing to distinguish the Son of God from the fishermen beside him. “Seize him and lead him away under guard” — securely. Judas knows what this man has done to crowds and storms, and takes no chances.

The kiss. “He went up to him at once and said, ‘Rabbi!’ And he kissed him.” A kiss was the ordinary greeting of a disciple to his teacher — respect, affection, belonging — and Mark’s verb here is the stronger form: he kissed him warmly. So the sign chosen to mark him for death was the sign of love. Scripture knows there is nothing worse: “Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me” (Psalm 41:9); “profuse are the kisses of an enemy” (Proverbs 27:6). And “Rabbi” — my teacher — not “Lord.” It is Judas’s last word in Mark, a title of respect emptied of its meaning.

He received it. Matthew records Jesus’ answer: “Friend, do what you came to do” (Matthew 26:50); Luke another: “Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke 22:48). He didn’t turn his face away or step back. He received the kiss. A test: is your outward affection for Christ matched by your loyalty when it costs?

Seized. “And they laid hands on him and seized him.” The Gospel turns. From here until the resurrection, Jesus is in custody, and everything is done to him: he is led, handed over, questioned, struck, flogged and crucified. The one who stilled storms, cast out a legion and raised the dead lets temple guards lay hands on him in the dark and take him away — because he chose to.
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was the normal greeting of a disciple to his teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: But one of those who stood by drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear.
