The gospel in mockery. “He saved others; he cannot save himself.” They state the gospel more accurately than anyone else in Mark, and don’t believe a syllable. “He saved others” is a concession, made in mockery by enemies with nothing to gain — about as good as hostile testimony gets. They never disputed the miracles (3:22). “He cannot save himself” is true too, and the most important sentence in the chapter. Not because the power was gone; he could have called legions of angels (Matthew 26:53). He couldn’t save himself because saving himself and saving others couldn’t both be done. That had been the choice since the wilderness: if he comes down, he is safe and we are lost; if he stays, we are saved and he is not. They thought they had found a contradiction. They had found the heart of the atonement, and said it aloud where it was happening.

“That we may see and believe.” “Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross that we may see and believe.” The demand for a sign again, from men refused one before (8:11–12). And it is false; they had already proved it. They had seen a withered hand restored in their own synagogue and gone out to plot murder (3:5–6), and they will soon pay soldiers to say the body was stolen (Matthew 28:12–13). He didn’t come down, and that is why anyone believes at all. Had he come down, the crowd would have seen a miracle and gone home impressed and unforgiven. He stayed — and before long a Roman officer who had asked for no sign was saying, “Truly this man was the Son of God!” A test: are you demanding that God prove himself on your terms before you trust him?

The robbers. “Those who were crucified with him also reviled him.” Two men in the same agony, dying the same death, and they join in. Luke tells us one of them changed before the day was out: he rebuked the other and said, “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom,” and was told, “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:39–43). So one of the men reviling him in this verse died hours later with a promise from Christ in his ears. Remember that about anyone you have given up on, including yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the sixth hour had come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour. And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, "Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?" which means, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the cross Jesus bore God’s judgment against our sin and was truly forsaken in our place, so that those who trust him will never be forsaken.

Darkness at noon. From noon until three, the brightest hours of a spring day, the light goes out. It isn’t an eclipse: Passover falls at full moon, when a solar eclipse can’t happen, and no eclipse lasts three hours. Mark offers no mechanism; he reports that the sun failed over the land while the Son of God was dying. And a reader of the prophets hears Amos: “‘And on that day,’ declares the Lord GOD, ‘I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight. I will turn your feasts into mourning… I will make it like the mourning for an only son’” (Amos 8:9–10) — darkness at noon, at a feast, mourning for an only son.

Darkness before the firstborn. There was another darkness, in Egypt, before the first Passover — three days of darkness “to be felt,” and then the night the firstborn died (Exodus 10:21–23; 11:4–5). In the Bible, darkness at midday isn’t atmosphere. It is judgment: the day of the LORD has come. For three hours no one sees anything, and Mark records no voice. Whatever passed between the Father and the Son in those hours happened where no one could watch.

The cry. “At the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice.” Out of the dark comes the loudest sound of the day. Mark keeps the Aramaic, as with “Talitha cumi,” “Ephphatha” and “Abba” — moments of extremity, and the very sound of his voice. And it is shouted, though a crucified man struggles for every breath.

Psalm 22 spoken. “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” — Psalm 22:1. The psalm that has surfaced all chapter — the garments, the lots, the wagging heads, the mockery — is now spoken aloud by the one it was about.

Was he really forsaken? Two errors must be kept off this verse. The first softens it, as though he were merely quoting a psalm that ends in triumph and wasn’t truly forsaken. He was. He was bearing sin, and God’s holy judgment fell on the sin-bearer: “he made him to be sin who knew no sin” (2 Corinthians 5:21); “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). The second breaks God in two, as though the Trinity were torn, the Father ceasing to love the Son, or the Son ceasing to be God. That didn’t and couldn’t happen. He remained the beloved Son and remained God throughout. What he bore was not the loss of his Father’s love or his own deity, but the withdrawal of the felt light of the Father’s face, under judgment, in our place.

“My God.” Notice his words. He doesn’t cry, “God, why have you abandoned me,” but “My God, my God” — twice claiming as his own the One he can no longer feel. It is faith stripped of every comfort and still holding on in the dark, and the only recorded prayer of his in which he doesn’t say “Father.”

For those in the dark. This is the word for the believer who has prayed into silence and wondered if the darkness proves God has let go. It doesn’t. Real God-forsakenness, its full weight, was entered by the Son so it would never fall on you. “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5) was bought with this cry. If you must pray in the dark, pray as he did: “my God” — to the God you can’t feel. A test: when God seems absent, will you still call him “my God”?
verseByVerse.note: The sixth hour was about noon, the ninth about 3 p.m. Jesus cries out in Aramaic the opening words of Psalm 22.

parallels.desc: my God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
I will make the sun go down at noon

verseByVerse.quote: And some of the bystanders hearing it said, "Behold, he is calling Elijah." And someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink, saying, "Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to take him down."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even at the cross people misunderstood him, waiting for a rescue that was never meant to come, because Jesus had come to die.

Misheard. “Behold, he is calling Elijah.” “Eloi” and “Elijah” sound close enough that a dying man’s shout could be taken either way, and popular belief held that Elijah came to help the righteous in distress. So the deepest sentence ever spoken on earth is misheard as superstition. It is what has happened throughout Mark: people hear his words and get the meaning wrong. They thought he was John the Baptist, Elijah, or a prophet (8:28). He quotes Scripture in agony, and they think he is calling for a folk hero. A test: do you hear what Christ is really saying to you, or what you expect?

Sour wine. “Someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink.” Cheap, vinegary wine, the ordinary drink of soldiers on duty. It isn’t the drugged wine of verse 23, which he refused; this is a mouthful for a man dying of thirst, and there is no reason to think it cruel — someone ran. It also fulfils Psalm 69:21: “for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink.” Another line fulfilled by someone who perhaps thought he was being kind.

An audience. “Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to take him down.” The reason turns kindness into something else: keep him going a little longer, to see if anything happens. The crowd has become an audience waiting for an ending.

Elijah had come. What nobody at Golgotha knew: Elijah had already come. Jesus said so on the way down from the mountain: “Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased, as it is written of him” (9:13) — meaning John the Baptist, who preached in Elijah’s spirit and lost his head in prison at a king’s order. They stand under the cross wondering if Elijah will rescue him. Elijah had come, been killed for telling a king the truth, and no one rescued him either.

No rescue. There was never going to be a rescue. That was the whole point, and it is why he is on the cross and not in the crowd: he stayed there to rescue us.
verseByVerse.note: Sour wine was the cheap wine soldiers drank.

parallels.desc: for my thirst they gave me sour wine

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus uttered a loud cry and breathed his last.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He didn’t die worn down and overcome; he gave up his life deliberately, finishing the work he came to do.

A loud cry. Mark says nothing else, and two things in this short sentence are extraordinary — the observations of people who stood there. First, the loud cry. Crucifixion usually killed slowly, by exhaustion and suffocation: the body hangs, every breath requires pushing up on the nails, and death comes when the strength runs out, often after a long time, when speech has long since failed. Dying men on crosses rarely shouted; they could barely whisper. He shouted. Twice in a few verses Mark records a loud voice, and the second is at the moment of death. John tells us what he said: “It is finished” (John 19:30). That isn’t a man dying of exhaustion; it is a man finishing something.

He breathed his last. Literally, “he breathed out.” Set it beside his words long before: “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (10:45). To give: nobody took it. “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again” (John 10:18).

The last act of his freedom. So the death of Jesus isn’t the moment Rome finally overcame him. It is the last act of his freedom — a shout, then a giving up of his life, in the afternoon of Passover week, near the temple where the lambs had been killed. He was in command of his own dying, and he chose the hour.

For your life. If he gave his life freely, then your forgiveness rests not on an accident of history but on his deliberate love. A test: do you see the cross as something that happened to Jesus, or as something he did for you?

In the temple. And in the same instant, inside the temple, something happened that no one outside could have seen.

verseByVerse.quote: And the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By his death God himself opened the way into his presence, removing the barrier that sin had placed between God and his people.

What the curtain was. The veil before the Most Holy Place, the inner room where God had said he would dwell. Josephus describes the temple curtains as huge and embroidered in blue, purple and scarlet; later Jewish sources speak of a curtain tens of feet high and a handbreadth thick.

What it said. It was a locked door made of cloth. Behind it no one went except the high priest, once a year on the Day of Atonement, and never without blood (Leviticus 16:2; Hebrews 9:7). The curtain said one thing, and said it for centuries: you can’t come in. It was the standing announcement that sin has separated a holy God from unholy people, and the separation isn’t negotiable.

And it tore. Mark puts it in the same breath as the death — the shout, the last breath, the curtain. Not three days later at the resurrection, but the moment he died. And “from top to bottom.” Had men torn it, they would have started at the bottom, where hands reach. This opened from the top, beyond human reach — Mark’s way of telling you whose hands did it. The way into God’s presence wasn’t forced open from our side; it was torn open from his.

Torn twice. It is the second tearing in Mark. At Jesus’ baptism the heavens were “torn open” (1:10) — the same verb, which Mark uses only these two times. Heaven ripped open at the start, the veil ripped at the end, and between them the whole ministry.

Through his flesh. The barrier is gone — not lowered or made easier, but destroyed by God from his side when his Son died. Hebrews spells it out: “we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh” (Hebrews 10:19–20). His body was torn so that the way could be opened.

When you pray. So when you pray tonight — an ordinary person in an ordinary room with an ordinary week’s failures behind you — understand what you are walking through. There is no queue, no annual appointment, no priest to send in for you, no blood to carry, because the blood has been shed and the way is open. The most exclusive room in the world was opened to all who come through Christ, and he opened it by dying. A test: do you come to God boldly through Christ, or still stand outside as if the curtain were there?
verseByVerse.note: The curtain separated the Most Holy Place from the rest of the temple; only the high priest entered, once a year.

parallels.desc: a new and living way through the curtain

verseByVerse.quote: And when the centurion, who stood facing him, saw that in this way he breathed his last, he said, "Truly this man was the Son of God!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole Gospel builds to this: people learn who Jesus is at the cross, and the first human confession comes from a Gentile soldier.

The goal of the Gospel. Mark opened: “The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (1:1). Since then the Father has said it twice, at the Jordan and on the mountain, and demons have shrieked it (3:11; 5:7). But no human being in this Gospel has said it. Peter got as far as “You are the Christ” and then argued against the cross; the disciples asked, “Who then is this?”; the crowds said John, or Elijah, or a prophet. The first person in Mark to look at Jesus and call him the Son of God is a Roman execution officer.

Did he mean “a son of God”? Could a pagan soldier have meant only “a son of God,” a hero or divine man? The Greek has no article, so the words could mean that, and the centurion may have understood less than he said. But Mark records them as the confession his whole book has been building toward (1:1). Whatever the man meant, he said more than he knew, and he said it at the cross.

The man. A centurion commanded a company of soldiers, a seasoned professional who had very likely supervised executions before. He was a pagan, and had spent the day watching his men gamble for the prisoner’s clothes. And he “stood facing him” — not off to the side or in the crowd, but directly before the cross, close enough to see his face, for hours.

The way he died. What moved him wasn’t a miracle but how Jesus died: “when the centurion… saw that in this way he breathed his last.” The refused drug, the silence under mockery, the absence of cursing, the cry in the dark, and finally a shout from a man who shouldn’t have had breath to whisper. He had seen men die and never seen anything like it.

Learning at the cross. That answers the question Mark keeps asking. You learn who Jesus is by watching him die. Not by the healings — the crowds saw those and stayed baffled; not by the teaching — the scribes heard it and plotted murder. At the cross, where he looks least like the Son of God, a human being finally sees it. A test: has the cross shown you who Jesus is — and what he is to you?

The gospel crosses the wall. And the confession doesn’t come from Israel but from a Gentile — a foreigner, an occupier, with no covenant, no Scriptures, no synagogue. At the hour when Israel’s chief priests stand nearby jeering, a soldier of the empire that killed him becomes the first to confess him. The gospel has already leapt the wall; the nations are coming in, and the first of them stands before a cross.
verseByVerse.note: A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers.

verseByVerse.quote: There were also women looking on from a distance, among whom were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome. When he was in Galilee, they followed him and ministered to him, and there were also many other women who came up with him to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the men had fled, these faithful women stayed, serving Christ and witnessing his death.

They were there. Mark has said little of them, and now, when everyone else has gone, he tells you they were there. “Looking on from a distance” — nearly the phrase used of Peter in the courtyard (14:54). But Peter’s distance was chosen and theirs imposed: women couldn’t stand among the soldiers at a Roman execution. As near as they were allowed, they were. Nobody made them stay, there was nothing they could do, and they stayed.

Named witnesses. Mark names three, and naming matters: these are witnesses who could be found and questioned by anyone in the early church who wanted to check. Mary Magdalene, from Magdala by the lake, from whom seven demons had gone out (Luke 8:2) — and the first person to see him risen. Mary the mother of James the younger and Joses, known by her sons, presumably because the church knew them. And Salome, probably the mother of James and John (compare Matthew 27:56) — so the woman who asked for her sons to have the best seats in the kingdom (Matthew 20:20–21) now watches what those places cost, with two robbers occupying them.

Disciples and servants. “When he was in Galilee, they followed him and ministered to him.” “Followed” is this Gospel’s word for discipleship, used of the fishermen leaving their nets (1:18), and Mark applies it to women without comment, in a world where rabbis seldom had women disciples. “Ministered” is one of Mark’s great words: what the angels did for him in the wilderness (1:13), what Peter’s mother-in-law did when healed (1:31), and the word of his mission: “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve” (10:45). Luke adds that they “provided for them out of their means” (Luke 8:3). For years a group of women funded and fed the ministry of Jesus, and no one wrote down what it cost them. A test: is your service to Christ steady when no one notices it?

Many others. “And there were also many other women who came up with him to Jerusalem” — not three, but a company.

Who stayed. Hold the chapter together. The twelve men who swore they would die with him aren’t here: one sold him, one denied him with oaths, the rest ran and are hiding. The women stayed. They watched him die (v. 40), saw where he was buried (v. 47), and will be at the tomb at dawn with spices they won’t need (16:1). The chain of eyewitnesses runs unbroken from the cross to the empty tomb, and its links are women — in a culture where a woman’s testimony carried little weight in court, which is why no one inventing a story would have built it this way.
verseByVerse.note: Salome may be the mother of James and John, named in Matthew as “the mother of the sons of Zebedee.”

parallels.desc: the women who provided for him

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The request (vv. 42–43). Evening is coming and with it the Sabbath, and a body left on a cross overnight would defile the land under the Law. And a member of the very council that condemned him goes to the governor and asks for the corpse.

Mark says he took courage, and he needed it. Joseph of Arimathea is a man of standing who has kept his hopes to himself, and he chooses the moment when Jesus is a convicted criminal and every one of his friends has run — to go public.

The verification (vv. 44–45). Pilate is surprised that he is dead already and sends for the officer in charge to confirm it. So the death of Jesus of Nazareth is certified by a professional executioner and reported to a Roman governor before the body is released.

The tomb (vv. 46–47). A linen shroud, a grave cut in rock, a stone rolled across — and two women sitting where they can see, memorising the address.
verseByVerse.theology:
The burial is not a postscript. It is evidence, and Mark reports it like a man building a case.

Four facts are established in six verses, and every one of them closes off an objection that would be raised later.

He was really dead. Pilate was surprised, because crucifixion normally took two or three days — so he summoned the centurion and asked. A professional soldier who had stood facing him for six hours confirmed it to the governor before the body was signed over. Any theory that Jesus survived the cross has to get past a Roman execution officer's report to his prefect.

He was really buried, in a known place. Not a common grave, which is where crucified bodies usually went, but a rock-cut tomb belonging to a named man of the council — a man the authorities could have produced and questioned.

The tomb was sealed. A stone rolled across the entrance.

And the location was witnessed. Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid — Mark's last sentence of the chapter, and it exists to say that the women who go to the tomb on Sunday morning went to the right one.

There is no room in this account for a mistaken address, a swoon, or a grave nobody could find.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council... took courage and went to Pilate.

John tells us he had been a disciple of Jesus, but secretly, for fear of the Jews (John 19:38), and Luke that he had not consented to the council's decision (Luke 23:51). So here is a man who had believed quietly for some time and had never said so.

And of all the moments to come out, he chooses this one.

Not the Sunday, when the tomb is empty and there is something to be glad about. Not the triumphal entry, when the crowds were shouting and it would have cost him nothing. He declares himself on the Friday afternoon, when Jesus is a convicted blasphemer executed by Rome, when the movement is finished, when every one of the twelve has vanished — and he does it by walking into the governor's residence and asking, as a member of the Sanhedrin, for the body of the man his own colleagues had just killed.

Now: he had everything to lose and nothing to gain. There was no upside. Association with a crucified criminal ended a career in that city, and he must have known it.

Which is worth putting to any Christian who has been quiet for a long time and is waiting for an easier moment to speak. The easier moment does not come, and it is not supposed to. Joseph's courage arrived on the worst possible day, and it is why he is in the Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: And when evening had come, since it was the day of Preparation, that is, the day before the Sabbath, Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council, who was also himself looking for the kingdom of God, took courage and went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
True faith eventually steps into the open, and Joseph confesses Christ on the darkest day, when it costs most and gains nothing.

The day before the Sabbath. “The day of Preparation, that is, the day before the Sabbath” — Mark explains for his readers. Friday was the day for getting ready, finishing all that couldn’t be done once the Sabbath began at sunset. And the law added urgency: an executed man’s body wasn’t to stay on the tree overnight, “but you shall bury him the same day, for a hanged man is cursed by God” (Deuteronomy 21:22–23). Paul applies the verse to this death: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree’” (Galatians 3:13). So little daylight is left, a body is on a cross, and no one has claimed it. Roman practice often left the crucified unburied.

How is Friday to Sunday “three days”? In Jewish reckoning any part of a day counted as a day, so “after three days” and “on the third day” mean the same span (cf. Esther 4:16 with 5:1). Even “three days and three nights” (Matthew 12:40) is a way of saying three days, not a count of seventy-two hours. Some have argued for a Wednesday or Thursday crucifixion, but Mark is plain that Jesus died on the day before the Sabbath. And John’s “day of Preparation of the Passover” (John 19:14) most likely means the Friday of Passover week, the preparation for that week’s Sabbath — just as Mark explains it here (cf. 14:12).

Joseph. “Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council” — the very body that had condemned Jesus in the night. Luke calls him “a good and righteous man, who had not consented to their decision and action” (Luke 23:50–51). He is a man of standing, with colleagues, a reputation and a rock-cut tomb. And he “was also himself looking for the kingdom of God” — a believer’s description, like Simeon and Anna and all the quiet people of Israel watching for God to act. John says what had kept him silent: he “was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews” (John 19:38).

Courage on the worst day. “Took courage and went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.” He had to steel himself. And consider the timing, the whole point of the man. He doesn’t come out on Sunday, when there is something to be glad of, or on the day of the entry, when it would cost nothing. He declares himself on Friday afternoon, when Jesus is a dead criminal, the movement is over, the twelve have vanished, and association means only ruin. He walks into the residence of the governor who executed the man, as a member of the court that demanded it, and asks for the corpse. Everyone will know where he stands.

For the quiet Christian. Put it to anyone who has been a quiet Christian a long time, waiting for a better moment to say so. The better moment doesn’t come, and isn’t meant to. Joseph’s courage came on the worst day of the worst week — and it is why a man from a village we can no longer locate is named in all four Gospels. A test: what would it mean for you to stop following Christ secretly?
verseByVerse.note: The day of Preparation was Friday, the day before the Sabbath. Arimathea was a town of Judea. Bodies of the crucified were often left unburied.

parallels.desc: not left on the tree overnight

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate was surprised to hear that he should have already died. And summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he was already dead. And when he learned from the centurion that he was dead, he granted the corpse to Joseph.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus really died — certified by a Roman officer to a Roman governor — so his resurrection was a true rising from death.

Surprised. “Pilate was surprised to hear that he should have already died.” Pilate’s surprise is professional. Crucifixion was meant to be slow; victims commonly lasted a day or more. So slow that soldiers sometimes broke the legs to hasten death, as they did to the two men beside him (John 19:32). Jesus had been on the cross about six hours — quick enough for the governor to check.

Confirmed. “Summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he was already dead.” Pilate doesn’t take Joseph’s word or guess. He sends for the officer commanding the execution — very likely the man who had just said, “Truly this man was the Son of God” — and asks him directly. Only when the soldier confirms it does Pilate release the body.

Not a swoon. Mark builds something without seeming to argue. He writes for a church whose central claim was that this man came out of the grave alive. The obvious objection, then and now, is that he never really died — fainted, was taken down early, revived in the cool tomb and walked out. Mark shuts that door simply by reporting the procedure. The death was doubted by the governor, checked on his order, and certified by the officer who had stood facing the cross for hours and had watched men die before. Any theory that Jesus survived has to get past that report — and then explain how a man scourged, crucified and sealed in a rock tomb without food, water or care rolled away a stone from inside and convinced terrified men that he was the risen Lord of life.

A corpse. And notice the word Mark chooses in verse 45. Pilate grants “the corpse” — the blunt word, used only once more in Mark, of John the Baptist’s body (6:29). Mark isn’t being callous but exact, because everything depends on it. What Joseph carried off that cross was a dead man — not a swoon or a coma, but a corpse, with a Roman officer’s word on it and a governor’s release.

For your faith. That is why what happens on the third morning matters. Christ’s resurrection isn’t a recovery but a victory over real death — and so it is the pledge that your death, too, isn’t the end for those who are his. A test: are you facing death, yours or another’s, in the light of a Saviour who truly died and truly rose?
verseByVerse.note: Crucified men often lingered for days; a death within hours surprised Pilate.

parallels.desc: the soldiers find him already dead

verseByVerse.quote: And Joseph bought a linen shroud, and taking him down, wrapped him in the linen shroud and laid him in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. And he rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb. Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus was truly buried in a known tomb, as Scripture foretold, and faithful love serves him even when all hope seems gone.

The linen. “Joseph bought a linen shroud” — at short notice, on the eve of the Sabbath, with his own money. A man who woke a secret disciple is buying grave clothes for an executed criminal. And the word for linen appeared a chapter ago: the young man who fled the garden “left the linen cloth and ran away naked” (14:51–52). One man abandoned his linen to get away from Christ; another bought linen to wrap him in.

Taking him down. Someone had to get the nails out, take the weight of the body, carry and wrap it — and it was a member of the council, on the eve of the Sabbath, making himself ceremonially unclean for a week by touching a corpse (Numbers 19:11) during the feast. John adds that Nicodemus came too, with about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes (John 19:39). Two members of the council that condemned him are the only men in Jerusalem tending his body. A test: what would you be willing to lose to honour Christ when others have abandoned him?

A rich man’s tomb. “Laid him in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock.” Matthew says it was Joseph’s own new tomb (Matthew 27:60). A rock-cut tomb was costly, prepared for a man and his family; Joseph gives away his own grave. And the prophecy is exact: “they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death” (Isaiah 53:9) — executed among criminals, buried in a rich man’s tomb, both on the same afternoon.

The stone. “He rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb” — a heavy disc set in a groove, needing great effort to move, which is why the women will worry about it on the third morning (16:3). That is the last thing anyone does for Jesus of Nazareth: a stone across a door, and then everyone goes home because the sun is setting.

They saw where. “Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid.” They are still there. Everyone else has gone; two women stay in the fading light and note which tomb it is. Mark records it because it matters. These women are named at the cross (v. 40), at the burial (v. 47) and at the tomb on the first day of the week (16:1). The chain of witness is unbroken and the place confirmed; no one went to the wrong grave.

The silence. So the chapter ends in the deepest silence in the Bible. The King of the Jews is dead, his body in a borrowed grave with a stone across it. The disciples are hiding; the women walk home in the dark with nothing to do until the Sabbath ends. Everyone who loved him believed that night that it was finished — and they were right, and had no idea what the word meant. He had told them repeatedly that he would rise after three days. None of them remembered. And this is Friday.
verseByVerse.note: Rock tombs were sealed with a large stone, often disc-shaped, rolled into a groove.

15.theology:
The cry of dereliction (v. 34) has two errors to be kept off it. The first would soften it, as though he were merely reciting a psalm and not truly forsaken — he was; he was bearing sin, and God's holiness turned from the sin-bearer (2 Cor. 5:21; Gal. 3:13). The second would break God in two, as though the Trinity were torn and the Father ceased to love the Son — that did not happen and could not. He remained the beloved Son and remained God through every moment; what he lost was the felt light of his Father's face, borne in our place.

And notice the word he uses. Not God, why have you abandoned me, but my God, my God — twice claiming as his own the very One he could no longer feel. That is faith stripped of every comfort and still gripping in the dark, and it is the only place in the Gospels where he addresses the Father as anything but Father.

The curtain (v. 38) may be the most important sentence in the book. Sixty feet of woven fabric, a handbreadth thick, whose entire purpose for fifteen centuries was to say you cannot come in — torn at the instant he died, and torn from the top, which is beyond human reach. The way in was not forced from our side; it was opened from his. And it is the second thing in Mark torn from above: the heavens being torn open at the baptism (1:10), the same violent word, at the beginning and the end. We have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Heb. 10:19–20).

And the burial is evidence, not postscript. Pilate was surprised he had died so soon — crucifixion normally took days — so he summoned the centurion and asked. The death was doubted by the governor, examined on his order, and certified by the officer who had stood facing him for six hours, before the body was released. Mark even switches words in v. 45 to ptōma, corpse. Any theory that he survived the cross has to get past a Roman execution officer's report to his prefect.
15.examples:
Then: He saved others; he cannot save himself (v. 31) — the chief priests, jeering at the foot of the cross, stating the gospel with complete accuracy and believing none of it.

Both halves are true. He did save others, and his enemies concede it at the moment they have nothing to gain by conceding anything. And he could not save himself — not for lack of power, since he could have called twelve legions of angels (Matt. 26:53), but because saving himself and saving others were the two things that could not both be done. They thought they had found a contradiction; they had found the mechanism of the atonement.

Now: and the demand attached to it — come down now from the cross that we may see and believe — has the order exactly backwards, and it is the standing human demand. Show me and I will trust you.

He did not come down, and that is why anyone believes at all. Had he come down, the crowd would have seen a miracle and gone home impressed and unforgiven. He stayed up; and within three hours a Roman officer who had asked for no sign whatever was saying truly this man was the Son of God.

And notice what converted that officer. Not a wonder — Mark is precise: he saw that in this way he breathed his last. He saw how he died. That is the answer to the question this Gospel keeps asking. You learn who Jesus is by watching him die. The crowds saw the healings and stayed baffled; the scribes heard the teaching and planned a murder; and at the cross, where he looks least like the Son of God, a pagan finally sees it — and he is the first human being in fifteen chapters to say the words Mark opened his book with (1:1).

16.title: He Has Risen; He Is Not Here
16.text: <sup>1</sup>When the Sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices, so that they might go and anoint him. <sup>2</sup>And very early on the first day of the week, when the sun had risen, they went to the tomb. <sup>3</sup>And they were saying to one another, “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?” <sup>4</sup>And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled back—it was very large. <sup>5</sup>And entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe, and they were alarmed. <sup>6</sup>And he said to them, “Do not be alarmed. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him. <sup>7</sup>But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you.” <sup>8</sup>And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid. <sup>9</sup>Now when he rose early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons. <sup>10</sup>She went and told those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept. <sup>11</sup>But when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they would not believe it. <sup>12</sup>After these things he appeared in another form to two of them, as they were walking into the country. <sup>13</sup>And they went back and told the rest, but they did not believe them. <sup>14</sup>Afterward he appeared to the eleven themselves as they were reclining at table, and he rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who saw him after he had risen. <sup>15</sup>And he said to them, “Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation. <sup>16</sup>Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned. <sup>17</sup>And these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; <sup>18</sup>they will pick up serpents with their hands; and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not hurt them; they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will recover.” <sup>19</sup>So then the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God. <sup>20</sup>And they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message by accompanying signs.
16.overview:
Three women buy spices when the shops reopen on Saturday evening, and set out at first light to finish a burial. Not one of them expects a resurrection — he had told them three times and it had gone in nowhere. They are carrying ointment for a corpse, and the only thing on their minds is a stone they cannot move.

They arrive and find it moved, and a young man in white sitting inside, and the most important sentence in the book: He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him. Not a symbol and not an experience — an event with an address, and an invitation to inspect the evidence.

Then a message with two extra words in it: tell his disciples and Peter. And they run away and say nothing to anybody, because they are terrified — which is where the oldest manuscripts of this Gospel stop.

The twelve verses that follow are printed in brackets in the ESV and most modern Bibles, and the question they raise is answered here in full rather than buried in a footnote. They summarise appearances recorded elsewhere, give the commission, and end with the Lord Jesus taken up and seated at the right hand of God — exactly as he had told the high priest he would be, on the night they condemned him for saying it.

And the last sentence of Mark is the reversal of verse 8: the people who said nothing went out and preached everywhere.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The errand (vv. 1–4). The Sabbath ends at sunset on Saturday, the shops open, and three women buy spices. They set out at first light on Sunday to finish a burial, and the only thing worrying them on the road is a practical problem they cannot solve: the stone. They arrive and find it solved.

The announcement (vv. 5–7). Inside the tomb a young man in white is sitting on the right, and what he says is the most important sentence in the book. He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him. And then a message with one name added to it that has comforted failing Christians for two thousand years.

The silence (v. 8). And they run, and say nothing to anybody, because they are terrified.

That is where the oldest manuscripts of this Gospel stop — mid-sentence, almost, on the word afraid. Which raises the question this chapter cannot avoid, and which is dealt with plainly below rather than left in a footnote.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why is 16:9–20 in brackets, and can I trust my Bible?

Open the ESV at this page and you will find, before verse 9, a line in square brackets: Some of the earliest manuscripts do not include 16:9–20. That deserves a straight answer, because a reader who meets it for the first time can feel the ground move.

Here are the facts, plainly. The two oldest complete manuscripts of the New Testament we possess — Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, both fourth century — end Mark at verse 8. Eusebius and Jerome, writing in the fourth and fifth centuries, both say that the accurate copies known to them ended there. Some manuscripts have a different, shorter ending; a few have both. And the Greek of verses 9–20 does not read like Mark: it uses more than a dozen words found nowhere else in the book, and verse 9 introduces Mary Magdalene as though for the first time, though she has just been named in verse 1.

The honest conclusion is that Mark very probably did not write these twelve verses, and that they were added early — early enough to be widely known and read in churches by the second century.

And here is what that does not mean. It does not mean anything has been smuggled into your Bible. Every substantial thing in the passage is taught plainly elsewhere: the appearance to Mary Magdalene (John 20), the two on the Emmaus road (Luke 24), the commission to all nations (Matt. 28), the ascension and session at God's right hand (Luke 24; Acts 1; Eph. 1:20). No doctrine of the Christian faith stands or falls here.

So take the reassurance the right way round. The reason you know about this is that the church kept the evidence and printed it in the margin instead of quietly tidying it away. A faith that could not survive its own manuscripts would hide them. This one puts the workings at the bottom of the page — which is precisely why the rest of the text can be trusted.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: tell his disciples and Peter (v. 7).

Two extra words, and they are there because somebody in heaven knew exactly which man in Jerusalem was certain he had forfeited his place.

Peter had denied him three times with oaths and a curse, in a courtyard, to a servant girl, and had gone out and wept. As far as he knew, he was finished — not merely ashamed, but out.

And the first message from the other side of the grave has his name in it, added on, as though the general term might not reach him. In effect: tell the disciples, and make sure you tell Peter.

Now: and notice that this is not new. Jesus had promised it before the failure happened: you will all fall away... but after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee (14:27–28). The angel repeats his promise, and adds the name.

So if you are a Christian who has failed badly enough to wonder whether there is a road back, the answer is in two words at the empty tomb. The road was mapped before you took the wrong turn, and when the message came, the one who had failed worst was named.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices, so that they might go and anoint him. And very early on the first day of the week, when the sun had risen, they went to the tomb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The women expected to find a corpse — so the resurrection wasn’t wishful thinking but an event that broke in on people who had given up hope.

After the Sabbath. Saturday evening after sunset, when shops could open again. They had watched him buried on Friday as the light went (15:47), and then the Sabbath shut everything down. That long, silent day Mark passes over without a word.

Named witnesses. The same names as at the cross (15:40) and, for two of them, at the burial (15:47). Mark keeps naming them because they are witnesses, and a named witness could be found and questioned. And they spend money: somebody’s savings went on those spices, the last thing they expected ever to do for him.

Nobody was hoping. “So that they might go and anoint him.” Understand the errand, because it decides how you read what follows. They are going to a grave to do the last service for a corpse. Friday’s burial had been done in haste, racing the sunset; they mean to finish it. So not one of them expected a resurrection. No one in this chapter goes to the tomb to see whether it worked. They carry grief and burial spices to a body they expect to find there. He had told them repeatedly that he would rise after three days (8:31; 9:31; 10:34), and it had gone in nowhere. So whatever else the first Easter was, it wasn’t wish-fulfilment. The people closest to him had given up, and the story of the resurrection begins with his friends buying ointment for a dead man.

The first day. “Very early on the first day of the week, when the sun had risen” — they set out in the dark and arrived as it grew light. And “the first day of the week” changed the calendar of the world. All four Gospels use it; within a generation Christians were meeting on it (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2), and John called it “the Lord’s day” (Revelation 1:10). The Sabbath was the seventh day, the rest at the end of creation; the church gathered on the first, the day the new creation began.

Is Sunday the Christian Sabbath? Many Reformed Christians, following the Westminster Confession, hold that it is. The more likely reading is that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), and that Christians meet on the first day not as a law but because it is the day of the resurrection. The apostles’ churches did so from the beginning (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2), and it remains a good and wise practice. A test: does your Lord’s Day gathering proclaim to you that Christ is risen?
verseByVerse.note: The Sabbath ended at sundown on Saturday; the first day of the week is Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were saying to one another, "Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?" And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled back—it was very large.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God had gone ahead of them, and the stone was moved not to let Jesus out but to let the world see in.

The worry on the road. “Who will roll away the stone for us?” They kept saying it, all the way. And it was reasonable: they had watched Joseph roll it across (15:46). Women carrying spices, on a path outside the city at dawn, faced a stone they couldn’t move and had no plan for. Yet they set out anyway. They had no solution and went — worth something, because a more calculating person stays home until the problem is solved.

Very large. “They saw that the stone had been rolled back—it was very large.” Mark puts the size at the end, as someone tells a story afterward: it had been moved — and it was huge. A tomb’s blocking stone was a heavy disc set in a groove; rolling it into place took effort, and moving it out again far more.

Moved so the world could see. The stone wasn’t moved so the women could get in, nor to let him out. Matthew says an angel rolled it back and sat on it (Matthew 28:2); a sealed tomb was no obstacle to a risen Christ, who that evening would stand among disciples behind locked doors (John 20:19). The stone was moved so the world could look in.

Already dealt with. But the pastoral point stands, the plainest comfort in the chapter. They spent the walk on a difficulty already settled. God had gone ahead of them in the dark, while they were still grieving and certain nothing had changed. That is often the shape of it. The thing you rehearse in the small hours — the conversation you can’t see through, the obstacle you have no plan for — may be dealt with before you reach it. It was still right to set out without a solution. A test: what are you refusing to step toward until you can see how God will solve it?

verseByVerse.quote: And entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe, and they were alarmed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s messenger sits calmly where the dead body had been, because the work of salvation is finished.

Inside a room for the dead. They go in. A rock-cut tomb had a low doorway and a chamber with a ledge where the body lay; they stoop through and stand inside a room built for the dead.

A young man. Mark says “a young man”; Matthew says plainly it was an angel (Matthew 28:2–5), and the white robe and their reaction confirm it. Mark simply describes what they saw.

One angel or two? Matthew has one angel, Luke two men and John two angels; the women and the times vary too. Each Gospel tells the story selectively, and none says there was only one. The women evidently came in more than one group and at slightly different times. The core is the same in all four: the women came first, the tomb was empty, and the message was that he had risen.

Two young men. And the bracket, easy to miss. “A young man” appears only twice in Mark. First in the garden on the night of the arrest: “a young man followed him, with nothing but a linen cloth about his body. And they seized him, but he left the linen cloth and ran away naked” (14:51–52). Then here: a young man seated in white inside an empty grave, telling women that Christ is risen. One fled from Christ stripped and ashamed in the dark; the other sits in the place of death, clothed in white, with the news. That is the gospel: what happens between Friday and the first day of the week.

Sitting, at the right. He is sitting — the posture of someone whose work is done and who is waiting. There is no urgency in that tomb; the crisis is over. And the right side is the place of honour, the place the sons of Zebedee asked for (10:37), where Jesus himself now sits (v. 19).

Alarmed. They came expecting a corpse and found a living stranger where it should have been. Every encounter with God’s power in Mark brings fear, never serenity: the disciples in the boat (4:41), the crowd after the demoniac’s healing (5:15), the three on the mountain (9:6). No one in the Bible meets the power of God and finds it comfortable — which is why the angel’s first word is the one heaven always speaks first. A test: has the reality of the risen Christ ever unsettled you, or only comforted you?

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Do not be alarmed. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus truly and bodily rose from the dead, and the empty tomb is evidence offered for inspection, not a symbol of hope.

Fear first. “Do not be alarmed.” He deals with their terror before giving the news, as heaven habitually does — “Do not be afraid” to Zechariah, to Mary, to the shepherds, to John on Patmos.

The same man. “You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified.” The personal name; the village, the ordinary origin that made people take offence (6:3); and the manner of death, stated flatly. There is no doubt who is meant or what happened to him. The risen one is the crucified one, the same man, still bearing the identity; when he appears to Thomas he will still have the wounds (John 20:27). Christianity has never offered a Jesus who got around the cross, but one who went through it and out the other side and is known by it forever: “a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain” (Revelation 5:6).

Raised. “He has risen; he is not here” — the hinge of history. The verb is passive, “he was raised,” as the New Testament usually puts it: God raised him (Acts 2:24; Romans 6:4). The resurrection is the Father’s public verdict on the Son, the answer to the cry from the dark, the reversal of the council’s sentence. The court of heaven has overturned the court of Caiaphas.

Not here. And the second half is a claim about a physical place on a spring morning. Not that his spirit lives on, or his cause continues, but that the body isn’t in the room — a room the women had watched him carried into (15:47).

Come and look. “See the place where they laid him.” The angel offers evidence and invites inspection: look at the ledge; there is nothing on it. The resurrection isn’t presented as a spiritual experience, a symbol, or a way of saying hope survives death, but as an event with an address, a date and witnesses — and the first thing anyone is told to do is examine the evidence. Paul stakes everything on it: “if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins” (1 Corinthians 15:17). The tomb was open, its location known, the authorities had soldiers; all they had to do was produce the body. No one did. The place was empty, and it still is. A test: is your hope resting on a feeling, or on the risen Christ who truly left that tomb?

verseByVerse.quote: But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Christ restores failed disciples, singling out Peter, and keeps every promise he made before they failed.

“And Peter.” The first commission after the resurrection is given to women in a graveyard, and it contains two extra words that have done more for failing Christians than almost any phrase in Scripture. Peter was one of the disciples; the word covered him. There was no need to add anything — unless someone in heaven knew which man in Jerusalem was certain it no longer did. Peter had denied him three times, with oaths and a curse on his own head, and broken down (14:71–72). He had spent the Sabbath with nothing to think about but that. As far as he knew, he wasn’t only ashamed; he was out. And the first message from the other side of the grave has his name on the end of it, as though the general word might not reach him: tell the disciples — and make sure you tell Peter. A test: is there a failure that has convinced you Christ’s invitation no longer includes you?

A promise repeated. “He is going before you to Galilee” isn’t new information but a quotation. On the walk to Gethsemane, before anyone had failed, Jesus said, “You will all fall away… But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee” (14:27–28). The angel repeats it almost word for word. The restoration was promised before the failure happened, and the meeting place fixed while they were still swearing they would never need it.

The shepherd ahead. “Go before” is a shepherd’s picture — walking out in front of the flock. He had quoted Zechariah about the struck shepherd and scattered sheep, and now the struck Shepherd is out in front again. And Galilee: not Jerusalem, where it all went wrong, but home — the lake, the boats, where they were first called. He takes them back to the beginning to start again.

Galilee or Jerusalem? Luke and John record appearances in Jerusalem, and Luke has Jesus tell them to stay in the city (Luke 24:49). The Jerusalem appearances came first, that Sunday and the week after; the meeting in Galilee followed (Matthew 28:16; John 21); and they returned to Jerusalem to wait for the Spirit. Luke’s command to stay belongs to the end of the forty days.

“Just as he told you.” The angel’s own gentle, slightly pointed comment. He had told them, repeatedly — the betrayal, the scattering, the denial, the death, the third day — and none had held on to it. So the Easter message isn’t a rebuke or a reward. It is a reminder that he said so, that he keeps his word even when no one believed it, and that he had arranged their restoration before they failed.
verseByVerse.note: Peter is named — the one who had denied him.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mark closes with human weakness before God’s overwhelming act, leaving the reader to carry on the gospel he called only “the beginning.”

Undone. “They went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them.” They run, physically shaking and out of their senses — the word behind our “ecstasy,” with none of its pleasantness.

Silent when told to speak. “And they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.” There is an irony here, Mark’s last word about human beings. All through this Gospel, people commanded to be silent couldn’t keep quiet: the cleansed leper “went out and began to talk freely about it” (1:45); in the Decapolis, “the more he charged them, the more zealously they proclaimed it” (7:36). Here, where the women are commanded to speak, they say nothing. They told someone eventually, or the account wouldn’t exist; the sense is that they spoke to no one on the way. But Mark ends on it deliberately: the last thing recorded of Jesus’ followers is that they were too frightened to deliver the best news in the world.

Does Mark really end here? The oldest and best manuscripts stop at this word, and the last word in Greek is “for” — an extraordinarily abrupt ending, like closing on “because.” Three explanations are offered, and honesty requires saying we don’t know which is right. The original ending may have been lost; the last leaf of an early book is the likeliest thing to be torn off. Mark may have been prevented from finishing; tradition places him in Rome under Nero, when Peter was executed. Or he meant to stop here — a reading that has grown stronger the longer people look at it, because it fits Mark’s abruptness, urgency and relentless honesty about the disciples.

The book in your hands. Consider what an ending at verse 8 does to the reader. The resurrection is announced, not described; the appearances promised — “there you will see him” — not narrated; and the last people in the book fail to pass the message on. That leaves the story unfinished, in the reader’s hands. Mark opened by calling his book “the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (1:1). If it ends here, then all sixteen chapters are the beginning, and the rest is carried on by whoever picks it up. A test: will you be silent about the risen Christ, or speak?

Nothing lost. And nothing is lost. The resurrection is stated as fact in verse 6 by God’s messenger. The appearances are recorded by Matthew, Luke, John and Paul — and Paul’s list of witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:3–8) was written down within about twenty-five years, while most of them were alive to be asked. Mark’s Gospel ends with frightened women running from an empty grave. It doesn’t end with any doubt that the grave was empty.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some of the earliest manuscripts end the Gospel here, and brackets verses 9–20.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
What this passage is. Before verse 9 your Bible prints a line in square brackets: Some of the earliest manuscripts do not include 16:9–20. It is the most significant textual question in the New Testament, and it is dealt with fully at verses 9–11 rather than hidden in a note, because a reader who meets it for the first time deserves a straight answer.

What it contains. A summary of resurrection appearances — to Mary Magdalene, to two men walking into the country, and to the eleven at table — with the disciples disbelieving every one of them until Jesus stands in front of them and rebukes them for it.

Then the commission: go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation. Then a promise of accompanying signs, including the two sentences about serpents and poison that a handful of churches have built a lethal practice on.

And then the ending. He is taken up into heaven and sits down at the right hand of God — which is exactly what he told the high priest would happen, on the night they condemned him for saying it (14:62).

And the last verse of Mark is the disciples doing the one thing the women in verse 8 could not.
verseByVerse.theology:
Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved (v. 16) can sound, read at speed, as though baptism were half of what saves you. Read closely it says something more careful.

Believing and being baptized are named together in the first half because in the New Testament they belong together — nobody in Acts comes to faith and then quietly declines to be baptized; the washing is the ordinary, public, commanded seal of the faith professed.

But look at the second half, which is where the sentence settles the matter. The condemnation clause is not whoever is not baptized. It is whoever does not believe. Baptism drops out of it entirely.

That asymmetry is doing deliberate work. What saves is Christ, received by faith; baptism is the sign and seal of that faith, not the ground of it. Which is why a dying thief with no water within reach could be told, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43).

So take the verse whole and let it cut both ways: do not despise baptism, because your Lord commanded it and it is no empty ceremony — and do not lean your weight on it, because it was never the thing holding you up.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: they will pick up serpents with their hands; and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not hurt them (v. 18).

On the strength of that sentence, a handful of churches — mostly in the Appalachian hills — have taken up handling rattlesnakes and drinking strychnine in their services to prove their faith. People have died doing it.

Now: two things must be said, and they are enough.

First, these are among the words whose place in Mark is most doubtful of all. To build a practice on a passage the earliest manuscripts do not contain is unwise twice over.

Second — and this holds even reading the verse at face value — it describes what may happen to Christ's servants, not what they are to seek out. When a viper fastened on Paul's hand on Malta and he shook it off unharmed (Acts 28:3–6), it was an accident of ministry he neither courted nor expected, not a stunt to test God.

Deliberately reaching for a snake or a poison cup to prove one believes is precisely what Satan urged in the wilderness — throw yourself down — and precisely what Jesus refused, with the words you shall not put the Lord your God to the test (Luke 4:12).

Faith trusts God. It does not dare him.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when he rose early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons. She went and told those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept. But when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they would not believe it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These verses were very probably added after Mark wrote, yet everything in them is taught elsewhere in Scripture: the disciples weren’t eager to believe, and Christ showed himself first to a woman he had rescued.

The brackets. Before the content, the question in the brackets, the largest textual question in the New Testament, and a reader deserves a straight answer. The ESV prints before verse 9: “Some of the earliest manuscripts do not include 16:9–20.”

The evidence. The two oldest complete manuscripts of the New Testament, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (both fourth century), end Mark at verse 8, as do the oldest manuscripts of several early translations. Eusebius, in the early fourth century, says the accurate copies he knew ended at verse 8, and Jerome says much the same. Some manuscripts have a short alternative ending instead; a few have both — what copyists do when they know two and can’t decide. And the Greek doesn’t read like Mark: a number of words here appear nowhere else in the book, and the style differs. Most tellingly, verse 9 introduces Mary Magdalene as though for the first time — “from whom he had cast out seven demons” — though she was named in verse 1. That isn’t how a writer refers to someone he has been following all morning; it is how a different writer begins.

Is the longer ending Scripture? Some Christians defend the longer ending as Mark’s own. They point out that it is found in the great majority of manuscripts, that Irenaeus quotes it in the second century, and that it seems unlikely Mark meant to end with “for they were afraid.” But the oldest manuscripts and early writers who knew the evidence point the other way. The more likely answer is that it is an early and faithful summary added to Mark, not part of what he wrote. It can be read and taught, but nothing should be built on it that is not taught elsewhere in Scripture.

Your confidence in the Bible. Should this unsettle you? No. First, nothing has been smuggled in: the appearance to Mary Magdalene is in John 20, the two on the road in Luke 24, the commission in Matthew 28 and Acts 1, the ascension and session at God’s right hand in Luke 24, Acts 1, Ephesians 1:20 and Hebrews 1:3. No doctrine stands or falls here. Second, this is what a reliable text looks like. We have thousands of New Testament manuscripts, far more and far earlier than for any other ancient document, so we can see exactly where copyists differed, and the differences are printed in the margin. A faith that couldn’t survive its own manuscripts would hide them; this one prints the workings at the foot of the page. Third, what isn’t in doubt: the empty tomb, the announcement of the resurrection and the promise of appearances are in verses 1–8, in every manuscript. A test: do you trust Scripture more, or less, for its honesty about its own copies?

First to Mary. “He appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons.” The first person to see the risen Christ was a woman from whom he had driven seven demons — not Peter, John or his mother, but a woman whose past was so wrecked that her deliverance needed a number. In a culture that gave little weight to a woman’s testimony, no one would invent that; it is in John (John 20:11–18) because it happened.

They wouldn’t believe. She told the others “as they mourned and wept” — not waiting hopefully, but grieving. “But when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they would not believe it.” That fits all Mark says of them. They didn’t believe the resurrection when told; they had to be convinced, against their will, by the man himself. They weren’t primed to believe; they were the hardest audience in the story.
verseByVerse.note: These verses are not found in some of the earliest manuscripts; the ESV prints them in brackets. They largely summarise appearances recorded in the other Gospels.

parallels.desc: Mary Magdalene meets the risen Lord
from whom seven demons had gone out

verseByVerse.quote: After these things he appeared in another form to two of them, as they were walking into the country. And they went back and told the rest, but they did not believe them. Afterward he appeared to the eleven themselves as they were reclining at table, and he rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who saw him after he had risen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles weren’t credulous but slow to believe, and Christ still sent such people with his gospel.

The road. “He appeared in another form to two of them, as they were walking into the country.” This is Luke 24 in a sentence: the road to Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem, two disciples who walked with him without recognising him and knew him when he broke the bread. “In another form” explains why they didn’t recognise him; Luke puts it differently: “their eyes were kept from recognizing him” (Luke 24:16). The risen body was both the same and changed; Mary took him for the gardener (John 20:15).

Still disbelieving. “They went back and told the rest, but they did not believe them.” Two more witnesses, and the eleven still won’t have it.

At table. “Afterward he appeared to the eleven themselves as they were reclining at table.” It takes the Lord in person to end it. And it is at a meal, where the risen Christ keeps turning up: at Emmaus, in the room where he asks for fish, on a beach in Galilee cooking breakfast.

Rebuked. “He rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart.” “Hardness of heart” is the phrase used of the synagogue leaders who watched a withered hand restored and plotted murder (3:5), and of the disciples who carried the baskets and understood nothing (6:52; 8:17). So before commissioning them, the risen Christ rebukes them — not congratulating them for surviving the weekend, but because they had been told plainly and had refused the witnesses’ reports. A test: what has Christ plainly told you that you are slow to believe?

Not credulous. Two things belong together here. First, these men weren’t credulous. The apostles are often accused of wanting a resurrection so badly they talked themselves into it. Every account says the opposite: they dismissed the women, dismissed the two from the road, had to be confronted in person, and even then “some doubted” (Matthew 28:17), and Thomas held out a week.

Sent anyway. Second, and more astonishing, he sends them anyway. In the next verse this company — who ran in the garden, denied him in the courtyard, wept through the weekend, refused the reports and were just rebuked for hardness of heart — is handed the gospel for the whole creation. He doesn’t wait for better material. There was none, and there never has been — which is good news for you.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church is sent to announce Christ to every nation, and salvation comes through faith, which baptism outwardly signs and seals.

Go. “Go into all the world.” The movement is outward. The Old Testament pattern was largely of the nations coming to Zion (Isaiah 2:2–3); now the direction reverses and God’s people are sent out — eleven men from one lakeside district of one small province, with no money, organisation or standing, one of whom had denied him days before.

Proclaim. The herald’s word: to announce publicly what a king has decreed. A herald doesn’t rework the message or improve it; he carries it. A test: are you adding to or softening the message, or simply carrying it?

The whole creation. The widest phrase: not only all people, but “the whole creation” — the scope Paul reaches for, the creation “groaning together” and waiting to be set free “from its bondage to corruption” (Romans 8:21–22), and God’s purpose “to unite all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth” (Ephesians 1:10). The rescue isn’t only of souls out of a doomed world; it is the beginning of the repair of everything.

Belief and baptism. “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.” Read quickly, this can sound as though baptism were half of what saves, and many anxious people have stumbled here. In the New Testament, believing and being baptized belong together as a matter of course. No one in Acts comes to faith and then quietly declines baptism; it is the ordinary, public, commanded sign of the faith professed. An unbaptized Christian would have puzzled the apostles — not because the water saves, but because a believer who refuses the sign refuses his Lord’s plain command.

The decisive half. The second half settles it. The condemnation isn’t “whoever is not baptized,” but “whoever does not believe.” Baptism drops out. That asymmetry is deliberate: if baptism were part of what saves, its absence would be part of what condemns, and the sentence carefully doesn’t say so. What saves is Christ, received by faith; baptism is the sign and seal of that faith, not its ground. So a dying thief, with no water within reach, could be told, “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

Does baptism save? Roman Catholic, Lutheran and some other Christians read this verse as teaching that baptism is part of the means by which God saves, and point to Peter’s “Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins” (Acts 2:38) and Ananias’ “be baptized and wash away your sins” (Acts 22:16). But in those verses, as here, baptism is joined to repentance and faith as their outward sign; forgiveness is given to faith (Acts 10:43), and the washing is the picture of it. The dying thief, who was never baptized, went with Christ to paradise.

Both ways. So take the verse whole. Don’t despise baptism: your Lord commanded it, it is no empty ceremony, and a professing believer who has never been baptized should speak to his elders about it this week. And don’t lean your weight on it: if your confidence before God rests on a rite done to you rather than on Christ received by faith, you are resting on the sign and not the thing signified.

verseByVerse.quote: And these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents with their hands; and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not hurt them; they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will recover."
verseByVerse.commentary:
These signs confirmed the apostles’ message, but God’s promises are to be trusted, never tested or treated as dares.

Signs that follow. “These signs will accompany those who believe.” Notice the verb: they accompany. They aren’t the point; they come behind. Verse 20 says the same: the Lord “confirmed the message by accompanying signs.” The message goes first; the signs attend it.

Recorded in Acts. Casting out demons and new tongues are recorded in Acts — Paul at Philippi (Acts 16:18), Pentecost and after (Acts 2:4; 10:46; 19:6). And “in my name” matters: the authority is borrowed, never owned, as the disciples learned painfully at the foot of the mountain (9:28–29). Laying hands on the sick is recorded too — Paul on Malta (Acts 28:8) — and James tells the elders to pray over the sick and anoint them (James 5:14), the ordinary provision Christ has left in every congregation.

Do these signs continue today? Pentecostal and charismatic Christians believe they do: the promise is to those who believe, with no end date given. But the verse goes on to say that the signs confirmed the message the apostles preached (v. 20), and Hebrews describes the same thing as past: God bore witness by signs and wonders to those who first heard the Lord (Hebrews 2:3–4). Paul calls them “the signs of a true apostle” (2 Corinthians 12:12). The more likely reading is that these signs belonged to the apostolic age and ceased with it. The new tongues were the real languages of Acts 2. God still heals in answer to prayer as he pleases; but a church should seek his word, not signs.

Serpents and poison. “They will pick up serpents with their hands; and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not hurt them.” This sentence has done real harm. On its strength a few churches, mostly in the Appalachian hills of the United States from the early twentieth century, have handled rattlesnakes and drunk poison in services to demonstrate their faith. People have been bitten and have died, pastors among them, some refusing medical treatment on principle. Two things must be said. First, these are among the words whose place in Mark is most doubtful; to build a dangerous practice on a text the oldest copies don’t contain is doubly unwise. Second, even taken at face value, the verse describes what may happen to Christ’s servants, not what they should go looking for. Scripture gives the example: on Malta a viper fastened on Paul’s hand as he gathered firewood, and he shook it into the fire unharmed (Acts 28:3–6). He didn’t seek it or expect it and wasn’t proving anything; he was collecting sticks to warm shipwrecked strangers. It was an accident of ministry, not a demonstration.

Trusting, not daring. And there is a deeper objection. Deliberately handling a snake or drinking poison to prove you believe is what Satan urged in the wilderness — “throw yourself down” — quoting a promise of protection (Psalm 91:11–12). Jesus refused: “You shall not put the Lord your God to the test” (Luke 4:12). That applies far beyond serpents. There is a way of treating God’s promises as dares — engineering a crisis to see if he will come through, refusing the doctor to prove one’s faith, taking a foolish risk and calling it trust. Faith trusts God; it doesn’t dare him. They look alike and are opposites: one rests on his character, the other demands he prove it on our terms — the very demand shouted at the cross. A test: are you trusting God’s promises, or testing him to prove them?

verseByVerse.quote: So then the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God. And they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message by accompanying signs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ reigns from heaven with his saving work finished, and he still works through his weak people as the gospel goes into the world.

Taken up. “The Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven.” The ascension in a sentence — the last thing the book says about Jesus. The Father receives him; Luke gives the scene — the Mount of Olives, the cloud, the two men in white asking why they stand looking up (Acts 1:9–11).

Exactly as he said. “And sat down at the right hand of God.” Set it beside the night in the high priest’s house. Bound, mocked, spat on, he had answered plainly: “I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven” (14:62). They tore their robes and condemned him for it. And here, in one flat sentence: he sat down at the right hand of God — as he said, in the words he used, within weeks of being executed for saying them.

He sat down because it was done. The sitting is itself doctrine. Priests in the temple stood at their work, because sacrifice was never finished. Hebrews makes the point: “every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God” (Hebrews 10:11–12). He sat down because it was finished. A test: are you still trying to add to a work Christ has finished?

The reversal of verse 8. “And they went out and preached everywhere.” The book ends with the disciples, in the exact reversal of verse 8. There, women ran from a tomb and said nothing, for they were afraid. Here, the same frightened company goes out and preaches everywhere. What happened in between wasn’t a change of temperament; only the risen Christ standing in the room turns that group into this. Men who wouldn’t believe the reports and had to be rebuked to their faces went out and told the world, and, as early tradition records, many of them died for it.

The Lord worked with them. “While the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message by accompanying signs.” He has just sat down in heaven, and in the same sentence he works alongside them on earth.
