That isn’t a contradiction; it is the shape of the Christian age: “behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). The going out was never the disciples carrying on a work he had finished. It was, and is, his work, done through people who had just proved themselves unreliable.

Only the beginning. Look back at the first line: “The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (1:1). Mark called all sixteen chapters — the baptism, the demons, the storms, the bread, the blind man who saw people like trees, the confession at Caesarea Philippi, the cup in the garden, the cry in the dark, the torn curtain, the empty grave — the beginning. And it hasn’t stopped. The centurion’s confession was carried along the roads of an empire and into languages that didn’t exist when Mark wrote, and it has reached you. The Lord is still working with his people and confirming his message. And the one who was appalled and shaking in a garden, and cried into the darkness that his God had forsaken him, is seated — because the work is finished, and the last of his people will be brought home.

16.theology:
Why is 16:9–20 in brackets, and can I trust my Bible? The facts, plainly. The two oldest complete manuscripts of the New Testament — Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, both fourth century — end Mark at v. 8, as do the oldest Syriac, Armenian and Georgian versions. Eusebius and Jerome both report that the accurate copies known to them ended there. Some manuscripts carry a different, shorter ending; a few carry both. And the Greek does not read like Mark: more than a dozen words appear nowhere else in the book, and v. 9 introduces Mary Magdalene as though for the first time, though she has just been named twice.

The honest conclusion is that Mark very probably did not write these verses, though they were known and read by the middle of the second century.

And here is why that need not unsettle anybody. Nothing has been smuggled in: every substantial thing in the passage is taught plainly elsewhere — Mary Magdalene (John 20), the Emmaus road (Luke 24), the commission (Matt. 28; Acts 1), the ascension and session (Luke 24; Acts 1; Eph. 1:20; Heb. 1:3). No doctrine stands or falls here. And the reason you know about it at all is that the church kept the evidence and printed it in the margin instead of tidying it away. A faith that could not survive its own manuscripts would hide them; this one prints the workings at the bottom of the page — which is precisely why the rest can be trusted. Nothing in the discussion touches vv. 1–8, which are in every manuscript there is.

Does Mark end at v. 8? The last word is gar — for — an extraordinarily abrupt way to end a book, rather like closing on because. Three explanations are offered and we do not know which is right: the last leaf of an early codex was lost; the author was interrupted (tradition places him in Rome under Nero); or he meant to stop there. The third has grown stronger the longer people look at it, because an ending at v. 8 leaves the resurrection announced and not described, the appearances promised and not narrated, and the story unfinished in the reader's hands. Mark called his book the beginning of the gospel (1:1) — and the women are sent to Galilee, where chapter 1 began.
16.examples:
Then: and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid (v. 8).

There is a superb irony in that sentence, and it is Mark's last word about human beings. All through this Gospel, people commanded to be silent could not keep quiet — the cleansed leper went out and began to talk freely about it so that Jesus could no longer enter a town openly (1:45); the Decapolis crowd was charged to tell no one, and the more he charged them, the more zealously they proclaimed it (7:36).

And here, where the women are commanded to speak, they say nothing at all.

Now: and the last verse of the chapter is the exact reversal — they went out and preached everywhere. The same frightened company. Something happened in between, and it was not a change of temperament.

These were not credulous people. They dismissed the women, dismissed the two from the road, and had to be confronted in person and rebuked to their faces for unbelief and hardness of heart (v. 14). Every account we have says the apostles were the hardest audience in the story, not the softest.

And he sent them anyway — a company of men who had run from a garden, denied him in a courtyard, spent the weekend weeping and refused three separate eyewitness reports. He did not wait for better material. There was none, and there never has been.
